groups.title: Get started
groups.summary: Install Tachyon, build your first app, learn where each file goes, and preview it.

groups.title: Pages (Tac)
groups.summary: Tac is the frontend part of Tachyon. Make pages, show values, and keep data in the browser.

groups.title: Server (Yon)
groups.summary: Yon is the backend part of Tachyon. Answer requests, return models, check values, and read settings and data.

groups.title: Real-time

groups.summary: Choose the language of each service and controller.

groups.summary: Build the same pages as a desktop or mobile app.

groups.summary: Topics for later: injection, behavior annotations, middleware, other languages, modules, security, cohesive services, utilities, helpers the design rules and simpler forms.

install.title: Install
install.summary: Tachyon is a full-stack framework: it makes both the frontend (the pages that run in the browser) and the backend (the server that answers requests). Tac is the frontend part. Yon is the backend part. You install one program, `ty`. It creates, previews, builds and tests your app.

sections.heading: Install
sections.body: Tachyon comes as one binary, `ty`. You do not need a package manager to install it. A runtime toolchain is the extra tools that a language needs to run code, and `ty init` offers to install the ones that your app needs. On macOS or Linux, run the commands below. On Windows, install `ty` in PowerShell with `irm https://github.com/d31ma/Tachyon/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex`, then run the other commands. Each installer compares the binary with the checksum in the release's SHA256SUMS file. A checksum is a short value computed from the bytes of a file. The installer stops if the checksum is missing or wrong. The last three commands create an app and start the development server. In a terminal, `ty init` first asks what the app should have. Press Enter to keep each answer that it shows. The next section explains the questions. Tachyon checks whether a project has a client/ folder, a server/ folder, or both. It serves them on one port. Tachyon creates identifiers itself.
sections.code:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/d31ma/Tachyon/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
ty init my-app --name "My App"
cd my-app
ty preview

sections.heading: Choose what ty init creates
sections.body:
`ty init` works like a project generator. In a terminal it asks five short questions, one at a time. Each question shows a numbered list. Type the numbers that you want, separated by commas, or press Enter to keep the answer in the question. The questions are: which parts the app has (a client with pages, a server, or both), which Tac languages the pages use, which Yon languages the server uses, where the app runs (the web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android), and which examples you want (storage, sockets, topics, streams, an HTTP client, error handlers). A question that does not fit your answers is skipped. For example, a server-only app has no page languages.

Every question is also an option, so a script can create the same app: `--realm`, `--tac`, `--yon`, `--target` and `--features`. When no terminal is attached and you give no options, `ty init` uses the defaults: both parts, JavaScript, and the web. `ty init` creates only the folders and files for your answers. Each language gets one small example class, a test unit that calls each public method, and a test setup, so `ty test --coverage` (on Node.js or Bun) and `ty preview` pass on the new app without any change. In a JavaScript or TypeScript app, `tsc -p client/jsconfig.json` and `tsc -p server/jsconfig.json` pass too, after `ty types` writes the composed types. The examples are written in JavaScript, or in TypeScript when TypeScript is the only JavaScript-family language that you chose. A Swift or Kotlin page service also gets a JavaScript copy, so the page works on the web without the Swift or Kotlin WebAssembly tools. A Java page service has no JavaScript copy: it reaches the page as WebAssembly through TeaVM, so it needs a JDK 21 and TeaVM 0.15.0.

Then `ty init` checks the tools that your answers need, with the same checks as `ty doctor`. For each missing tool it shows the exact commands and asks before it runs them. It installs with each vendor's official installer into your home folder, for example rustup, the Go and Dart archives, the Bun archive, the .NET install script, SDKMAN for Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Gradle, emsdk for Emscripten, the TinyGo and Binaryen archives, which make release WebAssembly smaller (see WebAssembly compilers per language), and the five TeaVM 0.15.0 jars from Maven Central for Java page services, which go into the Tachyon cache instead of your home folder. It uses versions that Tachyon is tested with, and it checks each download against the SHA-256 that the vendor publishes (Tachyon pins the emsdk, TinyGo and TeaVM hashes itself). It never runs a command with administrator rights: it prints such a command, for example `sudo apt-get install -y php-cgi`, and you run it yourself. Xcode and the Android SDK cannot be installed by a command, so `ty init` shows a link and the steps. It finds the Android SDK through `ANDROID_HOME` or `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`. Two server languages also need one library the first time they build: a Rust server builds with Cargo and the `http` crate, and a Dart server runs `dart pub get` for the `shelf` package. Both try the local cache first, so they need the network only when the library is not there yet. `--yes` answers yes for every tool, and `--skip-tools` skips the check. In a project that already exists, `ty doctor --install` runs the same check and offers the same installs.

Later, `ty add` grows the app with the same examples, tests and tool check: `ty add language server py`, `ty add target ios` and `ty add feature sockets`. It never overwrites a file; it stops with TY1402 when a file that it would write already exists.
sections.code:
# Answer the questions in a terminal:
ty init my-app

# Or give every answer as an option:
ty init my-app --realm both --tac ts --yon py,go --target web,ios --features sockets,http-client

# Install every missing tool without asking:
ty init my-app --tac rs --yes

# Grow the app later:
ty add language server java
ty add target android
ty add feature topics

first-app.title: Your first app
first-app.summary: Build a small app in five steps. First make a page. Then add a service with a field that updates the page. Then add a Yon controller that returns a model, and call the controller from the page. Last, test the service and the controller. Each step shows every file, where it goes, and what you see.

sections.heading: Step 1: Make a page
sections.body:
Start in the folder that `ty init my-app` made on the Install page. The questions of `ty init` choose the language of the pages (Tac) and the language of the server (Yon). The default is JavaScript for both, and `ty init my-app --tac dart --yon py` chooses other languages without questions. Each step below shows its code in every language: choose yours above the code. A page is a `tac.html` file in `client/pages`. Its folder is its URL, so `client/pages/hello/tac.html` is the page at /hello. A component is a part of a page that you can use again. The folder `client/components/hello/card` becomes the tag `<hello-card>`.

Run `ty preview` in the project folder, and keep it running while you follow the steps. It builds the app again each time you save a file. When `ty preview` starts, it checks that every public method has a test. The project from `ty init` already has its tests, and step 5 adds the tests for the classes that you add. Open the address that `ty preview` prints, and add /hello at the end.

Result: the page shows the heading Hello and the text This is my first page.

sections.heading: Step 2: Add a service
sections.body:
A service is a class in `client/services` that holds the data and the actions of a view. The view calls `CounterService` by the name `counter`: Tachyon removes `Service` from the class name and starts the rest with a small letter. A field is a value that belongs to the service, such as `count`. `{counter.count}` shows the field in the page. `on:click="counter.increment()"` calls the method when you click the button. When the method changes the field, the page updates.

Change the component and add the service. In the page, add `hydrate="load"`: it starts the component and its service as soon as the page opens. A component without a service must not have `hydrate`, so step 1 did not use it. Save the files, and `ty preview` builds the app again. Choose your language above the code. Go, C# and F# start public names with a capital letter, such as `Count` and `Increment`, but the view still writes `counter.count` and `counter.increment()`. A Python service runs on the pinned Python runtime, so it needs one more setting: add `"python": {"runtime": "pyodide-314.0.7", "profile": "offline"}` under `tac` in `client/manifest.json`, and put the Pyodide files in the Tachyon cache (`ty doctor` shows where). `ty init --tac py` writes that setting for you. A C++ service is one header-only class in `client/services/CounterService.hpp`; its public fields and methods are what the view uses, and `em++` from Emscripten builds it.

Result: each click on Click me adds one to the number on the page.

sections.heading: Step 3: Add a controller that returns a model
sections.body:
Yon is the server part of Tachyon. A controller is a class in `server/controllers` that answers HTTP requests. `RequestRoute("/api/greeting")` gives its path. `Public` says that anyone may call it: every route must say who may call it, or the build stops (see Who may call a route). `GetRoute` makes the method `getGreeting` answer GET requests on that path. Each language writes the name in its own style, such as `get_greeting` in Python or `GetGreeting` in C#. A Rust controller also has `fn new()`, because Tachyon makes the controller with it.

A model is a data type that describes the shape of a value. Here the model `Greeting` has one text field, `message`. The model lives in `server/models`, in a file named after it, such as `Greeting.ts` or `Greeting.py`. JavaScript reads the TypeScript model with `/** @import { Greeting } from '/models/Greeting.ts' */`. The method returns a Greeting, and Yon turns it into JSON. The same `ty preview` serves the pages and the controller on one port.

Result: open /api/greeting. It shows {"message":"Hello from Yon"}.

sections.heading: Step 4: Call the server from the page
sections.body:
This step is shown in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, C#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby and C++. Dart, C#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby and C++ use the default same-origin browser transport, which waits without blocking the page (ADR 0090). Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. F# has the browser transport, but it does not inject an HTTPClient yet: an F# service makes its own BehaviorContext and asks its REST client, as the F# section of Calling the server from a page shows. A client class sends HTTP requests for the page. Put it in `client/remotes`. `HTTPClient` marks the class. `GetRequest("/api/greeting")` makes the method `getGreeting` send a GET request to the controller of step 3. Leave the method body empty: Tachyon writes it. An empty body returns nothing to the type checker, so the method declares its answer as `Promise<Greeting | void>`. `export default` lets the type checker and the other classes find the client without an import.

In Dart, the client is an abstract interface whose method declares `Future<Greeting>`. Leave the declaration without a body: Tachyon generates the method and reads the typed model after the request completes. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the default transport handles this relative URL; a matching configured custom adapter still takes precedence. The browser remains responsive while the Future is pending. Credentials are omitted, including same-origin cookies. This default transport refuses other origins; the Dart example does not promise the separate outgoing-host support of other adapters.

In the service, `Needs` asks Tachyon to put a `GreetingClient` into the field `greetingClient`. The method `askServer` waits for the answer. The private method `messageOf` gives its message, or an empty text when there is no answer, and `askServer` saves it in the field `message`. A public method of a service holds no decision (TY1314), so the check sits in the private method. The page has its own copy of the model in `client/models/Greeting.ts`, because the browser cannot read files in `server/`. JavaScript reads its type with `/** @import { Greeting } from '/models/Greeting.ts' */`. Change the component, the service and add the client. The page file stays the same as in step 2.

Dart has its own `client/models/Greeting.dart`. Its immutable injected `GreetingClient` is created by Tachyon; the service does not construct a client or call fetch. `Future<void> askServer()` awaits the typed answer and saves its message. Step 5 uses a typed Fake field and `construct<CounterService>(CounterService)` to test this same HTTP-enabled service. The test constructs its generated `GreetingClient` with its own BehaviorContext, whose HelloTestSetup supplies a custom HTTP adapter. The awaited test checks typed decoding and the saved message without calling the server.

In C#, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient`. Its generated `getGreeting()` returns `Task<Models.Greeting>`. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the same-origin browser transport handles the request and omits cookies and authorization. The service receives a private readonly client through `Needs`; it does not construct one or use browser APIs. Its public `AskServer()` coordinates the request, and its private `_accept` method awaits the typed answer and saves the message. This example uses a registered scalar record; it does not promise arbitrary or nested Task result models. Step 5 supplies a typed Fake client with a caller-owned BehaviorContext and tests the same service without a network request.

In Rust, `GreetingClient` is a trait marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method is `async fn get_greeting(&self) -> BehaviorResult<Greeting>;` without a body: Tachyon writes it, sends the request, and reads the answer into the `Greeting` model of `client/models/Greeting.rs`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `BehaviorConfiguration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `#[Needs]` above `greeting_client: std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>` asks Tachyon for the client; the other fields start empty. The service has no `fn new` now, because Tachyon builds it. `pub async fn ask_server(&mut self) -> BehaviorResult<()>` awaits the answer with `.await`, and `?` passes an error, such as `HTTP_STATUS`, back to the page. While `ask_server` waits, the page keeps working and shows the fields as they were; a click on Click me runs after the answer.

In Go, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `// @HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `GetGreeting() (Greeting, error)` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` model of `client/models/Greeting.go`, with its `json` tags. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty configuration, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `// @Needs` above `greetingClient *GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `AskServer` calls it like any Go function and returns its error. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own goroutine: while `AskServer` waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns.

In Kotlin, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `suspend fun getGreeting(): Greeting` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` data class of `client/models/Greeting.kt`, which the client imports with `import models.Greeting`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `Behaviors.Configuration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private val greetingClient: GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `suspend fun askServer()` calls the client like any other function. While it waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `Behaviors.Failure` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Swift, `GreetingClient` is a protocol marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `func getGreeting() async throws -> Greeting` has no body: Tachyon writes it and decodes the answer into the `Codable` struct `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.swift`. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private let greetingClient: GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `func askServer() async throws` calls the client with `try await`. While it waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `BehaviorError` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Java, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `Greeting getGreeting();` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the record `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.java`, which the client imports with `import models.Greeting;`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `Behaviors.Configuration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private final GreetingClient greetingClient;` asks Tachyon for the client. `void askServer()` calls the client like any other method; Java has no async keyword. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own TeaVM fiber: when the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once, as before. When it waits for the server, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `Behaviors.Failure` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Ruby, `GreetingClient` is a class marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `get_greeting` has an empty body: Tachyon writes it. The comment `# @return [Greeting]` above it tells Tachyon to read the answer into the model `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.rb`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty Hash, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `#[Needs]` above `attr_reader :greeting_client`, with `# @return [GreetingClient]` between them, asks Tachyon for the client, and the service calls it as `greeting_client`. `ask_server` calls the client like any other method; Ruby has no async keyword. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own Ruby fiber: when the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once, as before. When it waits for the server, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request raises a `BehaviorError` whose `behavior_code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In C++, `GreetingClient` is a class marked with `[[HTTPClient("/api")]]` in `client/remotes/GreetingClient.hpp`. Its method `Task<Greeting> getGreeting();` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` struct of `client/models/Greeting.hpp`. C++ needs no Setup, because every C++ request goes through the browser transport to the same origin, without cookies. In the service, `[[Needs]] GreetingClient& greetingClient;` asks Tachyon for the client. `Task<void> askServer()` waits for the answer with `co_await`, and the page gets a promise that settles when the task ends. A failed request throws an `HttpRequestException` whose code names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

Result: click Ask the server. The text Hello from Yon appears under the buttons. A path such as `/api/greeting` stays on the same origin, so no host needs to be listed. For adapters that support requests to another host, that host must be listed in `tac.outgoing.hosts`; the current Dart default transport remains same-origin only.

sections.heading: Step 5: Test the service and the controller
sections.body:
A test unit is a class in `client/tests` or `server/tests` whose name ends with `Test`. Each method whose name starts with `test` is one test case. `Test(HelloTestSetup)` names the Setup that the test uses. The Setup file must be in the same folder as the test.

`this.construct(CounterService)` makes the service in the same way that Tachyon makes it for the page. `Fake` marks the field `greetingClient`, and `construct` gives the fake to the service in place of the real `GreetingClient`. So the test does not call the server. A controller is made in the same way: `this.construct(GreetingController)` makes the controller, and the test calls `getGreeting` directly, without HTTP. `GreetingClient` needs no test, because Tachyon writes its method. The Ruby controller test also uses `construct`. Where a tab does not use `construct`, the test makes the class itself, such as `GreetingController()` in Python, because the class needs nothing from Tachyon. The Tac languages without step 4 have no `greetingClient`, so their test checks only `increment`. Python and Lua have no step 4, so their test makes the service and checks `increment` only: Python with `CounterService()`, Lua with `self:construct(CounterService)`. A Fake field is not needed, and Lua could not have one: the build refuses Fake in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Dart uses `construct<CounterService>(CounterService)` with a typed `Fake` field. Its generated `GreetingClient` is bound to this test’s BehaviorContext, and HelloTestSetup supplies a fake HTTP adapter returning the typed greeting data. The awaited `askServer` case exercises the service and its generated client decoder without a network request. Each service keeps the fake passed at construction; changing the test field does not replace an existing service’s dependency.

C# uses `construct<CounterService>()` with a typed `Fake` field. Each test creates its own BehaviorSignal and BehaviorContext, then passes that context to the generated `GreetingClient` constructor. `HelloTestSetup` explicitly constructs the stateless `GreetingFakeHelper` adapter and returns the typed greeting data through the existing adapter boundary. The service captures its client when constructed. The three cases check increment, typed message decoding, and independent captured contexts: disposing the first context refuses its later call with `CANCELLED`, while the second service still succeeds. Changing or clearing the Fake field does not replace either existing service’s client. The helper stays in `client/helpers`, and the TestSetup stays beside the test in `client/tests`.

Rust uses a `Fake` field `greeting_client: std::cell::RefCell<Option<std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>>>` and `let mut counter: CounterService = self.construct();`. `construct` calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is empty, it gives the service a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the typed greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, put it in the field first. A test case can be an `async fn`; Tachyon runs it to the end, and `counter.ask_server().await` then saves the message.

Go uses a `// @Fake` field `greetingClient *GreetingClient` and `test.construct(counter)`, which fills the `Needs` fields of the service. While the Fake field is empty, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so `HelloTestSetup` answers through its `Exchange` method and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first.

Kotlin uses a `Fake` field `var greetingClient: GreetingClient? = null` and `construct(CounterService::class)`, which calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `null`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. A test case can be a `suspend fun`; Tachyon runs it to the end, so `counter.askServer()` has saved the message when the next line runs.

Java uses a `Fake` field `GreetingClient greetingClient = null;` and `construct(CounterService.class)`, which calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `null`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. Test units run on the JVM, which has no browser transport: a client without an adapter fails with the code `http-adapter`.

Ruby uses a `Fake` field, `#[Fake]` above `attr_accessor :greeting_client`, and `construct(CounterService)`. While the Fake field is `nil`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first, for example with `self.greeting_client = ...`. Test units run in CRuby, which has no browser transport: a client without an adapter fails with `Required behavior adapter is missing.`

Swift uses a `Fake` field `var greetingClient: GreetingClient? = nil` and `let counter: CounterService = try construct()`, which calls the initializer that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `nil`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. A test case is an `async throws` method, so `try await counter.askServer()` has saved the message when the next line runs.

C++ uses a `Fake` field `[[Fake]] GreetingClient greetingClient;` and `CounterService counter = construct<CounterService>();`. `construct` makes the service the way the page makes it, and every `Needs` field of the Fake's type gets the Fake field's object instead of the shared one. `HelloTestSetup` has a static `configure()` method that returns `BehaviorAdapters`. `adapters.http["greeting"]` answers each request of `GreetingClient` (the adapter name is the client name without `Client`), here with the typed `Greeting`, so no request leaves the test. A request with no answer fails its case with the code `HTTP_ADAPTER`. A test case can return `Task<void>`; Tachyon runs it to the end, so `co_await counter.askServer();` has saved the message when the next line runs. C++ test units compile with clang++ and run as a native binary.

Run `ty test` in the project folder. Then stop `ty preview` (press Ctrl+C) and run `ty preview` again. It starts, because a test case now calls every public method. A test must really call a method: a call on the fake `greetingClient` does not count for `GreetingClient`, and writing only the name of a method does not count at all. `ty test --coverage` shows which case first called each method.

Result: `ty test` prints one ok line for each test case and ends with 0 failed.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.body: Your app has a page, a component, a service, a controller, a model and a client. Project folders and roles explains where every kind of file goes. Test units explains test units, fakes and the test check of `ty preview`. Templates, Services, Controllers and Calling the server from a page explain each part in more detail.

project-folders.title: Project folders and roles
project-folders.summary: Tachyon finds your code by its folder and its file name, so you write no setup code. A role is the job of a class, such as service or controller. The role decides the folder. A file in the wrong folder fails with `TY1310` before the app runs. Role types for `Allow`, such as `Admin`, are empty classes in `server/roles`.

sections.heading: Where each file goes
sections.body:
Pages are in client/pages. Components are in client/components. Services are in client/services. Backend controllers are in server/controllers. A controller is a class that answers HTTP requests. A page contains components. A component is a tac.html view and an optional tac.css file. Behaviour is in a service class. The view refers to that class by name. Shared browser assets, data and scripts are in client/shared, and Tac utility classes are in client/shared/utils.

Every other class goes in the folder of its role, in client/ for the page and in server/ for the server: models, remotes (HTTP clients), stores, setups, entities, helpers, converters and tests. A role folder may hold nested folders. The server also has roles for the role types of `@Allow`, errors for application error types, utils for utility classes, shared for plain code, workers, and packages for the vendored Go module. The tree below shows one file of each kind. Project folders and roles explains each rule.

  pages/tac.html                  a page: its folder is its URL
  components/hero/card/tac.html   a component: the <hero-card> tag
  services/HeroService.js         @Service: data and actions of a view
  models/Hero.ts                  data types, no role
  remotes/HeroClient.js           @HTTPClient: calls the server
  stores/HeroStore.js             @Store: saved records
  setups/HeroSetup.js             @Setup: adapters and settings
  entities/HeroEntity.js          @Entity: the shape of a saved record
  helpers/HeroHelper.js           @Helper: shared work for services
  converters/HeroConverter.js     @Converter: turns one type into another
  tests/HeroServiceTest.js        @Test units and their test setups
  shared/utils/TextUtils.js       utility classes: static methods only
  shared/assets/  shared/data/  shared/scripts/
server/
  application.json

  services/PostsService.js        @Service

sections.heading: Generated folders and saved data
sections.body:
Tachyon writes two generated folders. `.tachyon` in the project holds types for your editor, prepared copies of your Yon files, route contracts and the record of the methods that `ty test` called. `dist/.tachyon` in the build holds the page runtime, the component styles and the compiled services that the browser loads. Tachyon writes both again when it needs them, so you can delete them at any time, and `ty init` puts `.tachyon/` and `dist` in `.gitignore`. Neither folder holds saved data.

Saved data lives in `data`. The topic logs are in `data/topics` unless `topics.directory` in `server/application.json` names another folder (see Topics). Back up this folder. `ty init` does not ignore it, so decide yourself whether to commit it: commit sample events that everyone needs, and ignore real user events.
sections.code:
.tachyon/          generated by ty; safe to delete; in .gitignore
  types/           types for your editor, per realm
  handlers/        prepared copies of your Yon files
  contracts/       the route contracts that ty checks
  coverage/        the methods that ty test called
dist/              the built app; safe to delete; in .gitignore
  .tachyon/        the page runtime, component styles and services
data/
  topics/          saved topic logs; back them up (topics.directory)

sections.heading: Roles decide the folder, modifiers do not
sections.body:
A MoneyService with Service belongs in services/MoneyService.<ext>. RequestRoute (a controller), Service, Store, HTTPClient (a client), Helper, Converter, Setup and Entity each require their standard suffix. They also require their lowercase plural role folder: controllers, services, stores, remotes (the old name clients still works), helpers, converters, setups and entities. The file may sit in a nested folder inside it, such as services/billing/InvoiceService.ts. A nested folder adds no new injection name, so two variants of the same service in one language are still an error. `ty migrate fix --write` moves the files of an old clients/ folder to remotes/ and changes the imports that it recognizes; it refuses to overwrite a file that already exists in remotes/ (ADR 0088). Abstract classes, interfaces, protocols, traits, type aliases and files that only re-export are not roles, so they need no marker. A folder does not register a class: a class in a role folder without its marker fails with TY1363 (ADR 0091). An IdentityProvider class also lives in controllers and ends with IdentityProvider. A role type for Allow is an empty class in server/roles, named after the role, such as server/roles/Admin.ts. The type name needs a domain prefix (a word for its subject, such as Money). The filename stem (the name without the extension) must match the type name with exact case. An annotated source file contains exactly one class and its imports. A worker and the project-root middleware follow the same rule, even without a framework marker. For a Rust impl, the compiler checks its target type. For a Go method, it checks the receiver type. Conflicting primary roles fail, so split the types into separate files. No second top-level class, function, interface, type alias, enum, constant, variable or statement is allowed. Pure data types belong in models/. Plain helper code becomes a static method of a utility class in client/shared/utils or server/utils (a class whose name ends with Utils, with no annotation), or a method on the class that owns it. Annotated helper types need their own file. When the helper is a managed provider, use a role file such as helpers/PriceHelper.ts with Helper. Settings and validation data, such as OrderInput with Checked or Endpoint with Setting, are models: they live in models/ without a role (ADR 0092). So Tachyon does not treat their validation and configuration fields as injected dependencies. The compiler adds their behavior metadata. But it does not register them for dependency injection. In dependency injection, Tachyon creates the objects a class needs and gives them to it. Tachyon does not discover files with no framework annotations as providers. A Rust struct and all impl blocks for that same type form one class. A Go type and the methods on it also form one class. In other languages, nested types stay inside their owner. Violations fail with TY1310 before the compiler composes (joins) the generated units. The compiler joins separately checked files that you write into a generated program. That generated program may contain several behavior types. Modifiers such as Needs, Named, Table, WhenProfile, Settings, Checked and Setting do not add suffix or folder requirements. Both realms share every role except the controllers: RequestRoute and SocketRoute classes exist only in Yon (ADR 0048). StreamRoute is a method marker inside a controller, not a role. A Tac service is client/services/<Name>Service, and a view addresses it as {name.field}. A Yon service is server/services/<Name>Service, and Tachyon injects it into a controller. A Yon controller is server/controllers/<Name>Controller, and its annotations declare its URLs. These are strict Tachyon conventions. Spring Boot does not require them.

`server/gateways/` is reserved. Tachyon writes the generated units of `@Gateway` class targets there, inside its own snapshot. A file that you write in that folder fails with `TY1310`.

This rule does not add a module linker (a tool that connects separate modules). A Yon role file that the compiler includes, such as a service, may not use a relative import or `require` (`TY2101`). Use the standard-library and realm-root import forms, such as `/models/Guide.ts`, or no import at all: role classes of the same realm and language find each other by name. A Tac JavaScript or TypeScript file may import a file of its own realm with a relative path. No file imports a file of the other realm (`TY1369`). A worker Handler can keep its supported ordinary imports.

services/MoneyService.ts                @Service
services/billing/InvoiceService.ts      @Service (a nested folder is fine)
controllers/MoneyController.ts          @RequestRoute("/money") + @Public
controllers/AppIdentityProvider.ts      @IdentityProvider
roles/Admin.ts                          (a role type, no annotation)
stores/MoneyStore.ts                    @Store
remotes/MoneyClient.ts                  @HTTPClient
helpers/MoneyHelper.ts                  @Helper
converters/MoneySummaryConverter.ts     @Converter
setups/MoneySetup.ts                    @Setup
entities/MoneyEntity.ts                 @Entity + @Table
models/OrderInput.ts                    @Checked (data, no role)

sections.heading: File names follow the class
sections.body:
Every class file is named after its one class, as in Java. The file name without the extension is the class name, with the same spelling and the same capital letters, both in client/ and in server/. Rust is the one exception: a Rust file may also use the snake_case form of the name, so `http_reader_service.rs` and `HTTPReaderService.rs` both hold `HTTPReaderService` (ADR 0067). The class name still decides the role and the injection name, and a snake_case file and a PascalCase file with the same class are duplicates. Some examples: `client/services/CartService.ts` holds `CartService`, `server/models/Order.py` holds `Order`, `server/models/Order.rb` holds `Order = Data.define(...)`, and `client/tests/CartServiceTest.go` holds `type CartServiceTest struct`. It covers role files, models, test units, test setups, utilities, error types and every other file in client/ or server/ that declares a class, a struct, a record or another type. A models file holds one model, and it is named after that model. A models file with a second model, for example `Order.ts` with `Order` and `Status`, also fails with `TY1318`. Some files keep the name that Tachyon gives them: views and component files (`tac.html` and its `tac.*` companions) in client/pages/ and client/components/, plain code in client/shared/ and server/shared/, workers in server/workers/ (their class is `Handler`), and the root `middleware.<ext>` file (its class is `Middleware`). A file that declares no type, such as a Python script with functions only, has no class to follow.

Next to its one class and its imports, a file may hold a few lines that run no code: a shebang line and a `"use strict";` line at the top in JavaScript and TypeScript, a module docstring at the top in Python, `declare(strict_types=1);` in PHP, a `package` line in Java and Kotlin, one `namespace` and `#nullable` lines in C#, a `library;` line in Dart, and inner attributes such as `#![allow(dead_code)]` in Rust. A Rust file may also gate an import with `#[cfg(...)]` or `#[cfg_attr(...)]` lines directly above `use`, for example `#[cfg(unix)]` above `use std::os::unix::net::UnixStream;`. A `cfg` line above any other top-level item fails with `TY1310`: put platform code inside the class and gate it there. Code that runs when the file loads fails with `TY1310`: a JavaScript or TypeScript `static { ... }` block, a base class that is computed, such as `extends mixin(Base)`, and a decorator argument that calls or builds something, such as `@Cacheable(options())` (ADR 0044).

A file with another name fails with `TY1318` before the app runs. The message names both fixes: rename the file after the class, or rename the class after the file. `ty migrate fix --write` renames the file when it declares exactly one type. It splits a models file with several models into one file per model: each new file keeps the imports and the comments of its model, and the files that import a moved TypeScript or Dart model import it from its new file. When other files use the old file name, for example in a relay command, it renames the class instead, or lists a manual step (ADR 0067).

sections.heading: Strict role folders and file names
sections.body: A role type has a domain prefix and a standard suffix. Its file name matches the type name exactly, including case. Rust also accepts the snake_case form of the name, so `money_service.rs` may hold `MoneyService` (ADR 0067). The file sits in the folder with the plural role name, or in a folder nested inside it, such as `services/billing/InvoiceService.ts` (ADR 0091). A nested folder only organizes files: it does not make a new namespace, so two classes with the same name in one realm and language are still an error. Each class in a role folder carries the marker of its role, such as `Service` in `services/`; a class without it fails with `TY1363`, and the message shows the spelling for its language. Examples are MoneyService in services/MoneyService.ts, MoneyStore in stores/MoneyStore.ts and MoneySetup in setups/MoneySetup.ts. Each annotated file holds exactly one class and its imports. Helper types and functions belong in their own files. Each realm has shared role folders, and the two realms use the same folder names. Yon uses server/services, server/stores, server/remotes, server/setups, server/entities, server/helpers and server/converters. Tac uses the same seven under client/. Controllers live in server/controllers, one class in each file. A role file in the wrong folder fails with TY1310. The error names the shared folder where the file belongs. The compiler validates the selected files from the snapshot of the source, which cannot change, and puts them together. Role annotations register validated declarations inside that entry scope. Modifiers such as CacheSettings, Setting and Table add no naming rules. Data types without a role, including the Settings and Checked classes that hold settings and validation rules, live in models/ (ADR 0092). Native Tac keeps its service type first and uses only public client modules. See the Strict annotation layout guide for every supported language.
sections.code:
server/controllers/MoneyController.ts
server/services/MoneyService.ts
client/pages/money/tac.html                     <money-panel hydrate="load" />
client/components/money/panel/tac.html          {money.amount}
client/services/MoneyService.ts
client/entities/MoneyEntity.ts

sections.heading: Models: types without a role
sections.body:
Data types that several files share live in client/models/ or server/models/. A models folder is not a role folder. A models file holds data, not behavior (ADR 0041, ADR 0043). Choose a language below. TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, C#, F#, Dart, Kotlin, Go, Java, Ruby, Lua and Python models work in both realms. Swift models live only in client/models/, because Swift is not a Yon language. PHP and Groovy models live only in server/models/, because those languages run only in Yon. The PHP and Groovy tabs show only a route that returns the guide, and the page is not part of them. A Python model is a `@dataclass`, and a Python page service also needs the Python runtime in `client/manifest.json` (see Your first app). A controller returns a model, or takes one with FromBody, and Yon turns it into JSON and back, like Spring.

A JavaScript models file holds one JSDoc `@typedef` comment and `export {}`, such as `client/models/CartTotal.js` for `CartTotal`. Every JavaScript file of the realm uses a JavaScript model by its name, with no import. JavaScript also reads the TypeScript models of its realm: write `/** @import { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts' */` above the class. Routes, events and `/api.json` read these models like the models of any other language. A `@typedef` in another JavaScript file of client/ or server/ is a model outside its folder. The build refuses it with `TY1310`, and `ty migrate fix --write` moves it to the models folder. The fix keeps one file for identical copies. When a copy matches a model that the realm already has, in JavaScript or TypeScript, the fix removes the copy and imports that model. It reports a copy that differs, and leaves that file for you.

A TypeScript models file holds interfaces, type aliases and import type statements. TypeScript removes a type-only import, so the browser never loads the models file. In the other languages, a models file holds structs, records, data classes, enums and type aliases with fields only. It also holds the imports they need. A PHP array has no item type, so a doc comment gives it: `/** @var list<Guide> */` on a property, or `@param list<Guide> $guides` and `@return list<Guide>` on a controller method. A Ruby model is a Data.define record whose fields have YARD @!attribute types. A Lua model is a table whose fields have `---@field` types.

Every models file holds one model: one interface, type alias, JSDoc `@typedef`, struct, record, class, enum or Ruby record, and the file is named after it, such as `Guide.ts` for `Guide` (ADR 0067). Put a second model, even a small enum, in its own file next to the first. A models file with two models fails with `TY1318`, and `ty migrate fix --write` splits it into one file per model.

Other files import a model in the usual way of their language: `import type { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts'`, `use crate::models::Guide;`, `using Models;`, `import 'models/Guide.dart';`, `import models.Guide`, `import models.Guide;`, `open Models`, `from models import Guide` or `use Models\Guide;`. JavaScript, Swift, Go, Ruby and Lua use the type name with no import. A C++ model is a `struct` or an `enum class` in a header-only file such as `client/models/Guide.hpp`, and other C++ files may write `#include "../models/Guide.hpp"` so that an editor finds it; C++ models live only in `client/models` (`TY1372`). A Go models file holds one type, because Tachyon compiles it as another file of the program's package main. The framework adds the realm's models files of that language to every program it builds in that language. A JavaScript or TypeScript page service is the exception: its module gets only the models that it names, and the models that those name, so a route does not load the others (ADR 0043). It never routes a models file and never ships one on its own. A Rust model declares its type and fields pub, because the models files become the module crate::models. Each Rust models file is its own module inside it, so a model that uses another model writes `use crate::models::Item;`. When a models file does not compile, the error names that file.

A role annotation in a models folder fails with TY1310. The message names the role folder where the type belongs. A method, a function, a constant or a service marker also fails with TY1310. So does any other statement, or a language in the wrong realm. A model may carry configuration and validation data: Settings, Setting, Checked, Required, NotEmpty, Length, Min, Max and Description (ADR 0092). Every Tac and Yon language reads such a model except Lua and C++, which refuse these markers in a model. A Swift schema model is a struct, and a Rust schema model is `pub`.

sections.heading: Yon: every language implementation
sections.body: Choose one language below for GET /money. Each implementation returns {"amount":42}. Copy the controller from server/controllers and the shared server/services role file. The compiler finds only role files in the same language as the controller. It orders them by their definition dependencies, and this order is always the same. Needs infers the controller's dependency from the field it marks, so you do not write a constructor. JavaScript names the field moneyService to match the exact lowerCamel name of MoneyService, Ruby names its attr_reader money_service, the snake_case name, and Lua names its table field money_service in the same way. The other languages use its concrete type, which is Arc<MoneyService> in Rust and *MoneyService in Go. Types in the discovered role files are available by name in the assembled unit. So do not import these role files into each other. You do not need a runtime annotation package or an HTTP method decorator. RequestRoute on the class and GetRoute on the method declare GET /money. The controller role, the route and error handler markers, StreamRoute, Gateway and Schedule exist only in Yon. Tac mirrors Service, Lifetime, Store in its bare and entity-bound forms, HTTPClient, Helper, Needs, Named, OnStart, OnStop, OnEvent, Order and InBackground. In Tac, a service is what a view addresses. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, C#, F#, Java, Ruby and C++, a Tac HTTPClient can use the browser transport that Tachyon manages. Python and Lua refuse a Tac HTTPClient (TY1308). In native app services, the Setup gives the client an HTTP adapter. Swift is not a Yon endpoint language. Needs selects each field it marks that is not static and has no initial value, in declaration order. Fields with a default value and static fields are not injected. Named names the provider when the field does not. Missing or ambiguous providers fail closed: Tachyon rejects them and does not guess. Unsupported optional, generic, interface or function field types also fail closed. Discovery covers only the realm's shared role folders. Other controllers are not part of the program. Each invocation still owns its instance graph (the objects it creates), and Tachyon adds no global container.

sections.heading: Tac: every service language
sections.body: Tac supports shared role modules in every Tac language: JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Ruby and Python. The example declares a MoneyEntity mapping in the required client/entities folder. Table is a modifier and does not change that path. The view shows local service state, not the result of a database query. Declaring an entity does not connect to a database and does not fetch data. To run queries, explicitly supply an authorized public client adapter and own its behavior context. Select one language tab and copy its service file and entity file. The shared page client/pages/tac.html places <money-panel hydrate="load" />, and the view reads {money.amount}. Annotation discovery selects that language automatically. The native application opens that page, because the manifest's start_url is /. JavaScript, TypeScript and Dart run on every target. Rust links on macOS, Windows and Linux, C# links on Windows, and both reach every other target, including the web, as WebAssembly. Go reaches every target as WebAssembly (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045). F# runs on the same .NET browser runtime as C# on every target. Java reaches the page as WebAssembly through TeaVM, and Ruby through Tachyon's mruby WebAssembly runtime (ADR 0049). Swift links on macOS and iOS and Kotlin on Android. Both reach every other target as WebAssembly, where the built-in Store keeps its rows in IndexedDB, as it does for the other WebAssembly languages (ADR 0059, ADR 0078, ADR 0082). Keep the native MoneyService type first in the file. The compiler appends the discovered entity declarations after it. Tac stays client-rendered. It uses only public TAC_ configuration, never private Yon credentials. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Entity in Lua Tac code with TY1308. A Python entity builds, and its markers are snake_case, such as `@entity`, `@table` and `Annotated[int, id]`. But Python has no Store (the build refuses it with TY1308), so a Python service cannot save these records yet. Python runs on its pinned runtime in the page on every target (ADR 0093). C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Entity in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Moving role types and compiler checks
sections.body: A type that has a role cannot stay inline in a controller file or in a Tac service. For each role type, do these steps. Rename it. Update the typed dependency fields, or the lowerCamel field names in JavaScript. Update any Named provider names, Store entity classes and behavior factory references. Move the type into the matching shared plural role folder of its realm. Controllers go in server/controllers. Remove old module manifests. The compiler works on an immutable snapshot (a copy of the files that does not change). It checks the original source paths before annotation lowering, the step that turns annotations into ordinary code. Missing files, wrong languages or realms, unsafe paths, duplicate declarations, conflicting roles and invalid names fail closed: the compiler rejects them. Only files with a role annotation register, within their entry scope. Helpers without annotations do not register, and there is no global DI (dependency injection) container. In Yon, an included role file may not use a relative import (`TY2101`); standard-library imports and realm-root imports such as `/models/Guide.ts` are allowed. A Tac JavaScript or TypeScript file may import a file of its own realm with a relative path, and no file may import a file of the other realm (`TY1369`). Annotations need no import. Helpers without annotations keep the ordinary rules of their language. Existing per-invocation scopes, ownership that you state in code and adapter authorization do not change.

sections.heading: One structure check before the build
sections.body:
Before Tachyon writes any output or starts a compiler such as `dart`, `cargo`, `go` or `dotnet`, it checks the structure of the whole project. It reads every file in every role folder of both realms, at any depth, and it reports the problems of all files in one run. Each message names the file, points at the class or the import, and gives the fix in the spelling of your language.

| The check | Code | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A class in a role folder has the marker of that folder. | `TY1363` | Add the marker, such as `@Service`, `#[Service]`, `[<Service>]`, `-- @Service` or `// @yon::Service`, or move a plain class to `models` or a utility folder. |
| A marked class ends with its role name and sits in its role folder: `Service`, `Store`, `Client`, `Helper`, `Converter`, `Setup`, `Entity` or `Controller`. | `TY1310` | Rename the class `Mail` to `MailService` and the file to `MailService.rb` in a `services` folder. |
| The file has the name of its class, in the file name style of its language. | `TY1318` | Rename `Order.ts` that declares `Invoice`; Rust may write `mail_service.rs`. |
| A role file holds one class: in Go a struct with its methods, in Lua a class table, in F# a type, in Rust a type with its `impl` blocks. | `TY1310` | Move the second class to its own file. |
| Dependencies point down, nothing needs a controller, and a utility class names no role class. | `TY1327` | Give the utility the value it needs as a parameter, or move the code into a service. |
| A file never imports a file of the other realm. | `TY1369` | Call the server through an HTTPClient in `client/remotes`, and give each realm its own model, utility or service. |

Some files keep their own rules, so they need no role marker: models, which only hold data; utility classes in `client/shared/utils` and `server/utils`; test units and test setups; generated files; the native Go module in `server/packages`; and the data, styles, scripts and assets in `client/shared`. A folder that is not a role folder, such as `server/commands`, never needs a marker.

`ty migrate check` lists missing markers, imports of the other realm and dependency problems, and `ty migrate fix --write` renames a file whose class has another name.

preview-and-build.title: Preview and build
preview-and-build.summary: `ty preview` runs your app while you work, and it builds the app again when you save a file. `ty bundle` builds the files that you publish. `ty start` serves those files.

sections.heading: One program for pages and server
sections.body: Tac and Yon do not run as two servers. One process builds the client and serves the routes. A project may have only client/pages, only server/controllers, or both. `ty preview` builds again when a source file changes. `ty start` serves what you published and never builds again.
sections.code:
ty preview
ty start --port 8080

sections.heading: Run on a name under .localhost
sections.body:
`ty preview --host shop.localhost` serves your app at `http://shop.localhost:3000/`. `--hostname` is another name for `--host`. `ty serve`, `ty start` and `server.host` in `server/application.json` accept the same names. A name works when it is `localhost` or ends in `.localhost`, in upper or lower case, with or without one dot at the end. Each part of the name has 1 to 63 letters, digits or hyphens. Tachyon binds `127.0.0.1` for the name without asking the operating system (RFC 6761), so the name needs no setup, and it never opens the server to the network. Another name stops with `TY1302`.

A name helps in three ways. Chrome and Firefox treat `http://shop.localhost` as a secure context, so browser APIs that need HTTPS work on plain HTTP; the Tachyon browser gate measured the same in WebKit on macOS. Cookies ignore the port, so two apps on `localhost:3000` and `localhost:3001` overwrite each other's session cookie; `shop.localhost` and `admin.localhost` keep their cookies apart. And the address says which app it is. Safari asks the operating system for the name, which works on macOS. Do not use `Domain=localhost` cookies to share a cookie between two names; keep each cookie on its own name.

A server on a loopback address answers a request only when its `Host` name is a localhost name, an IP address, the host of `tac.origin`, or a name in `server.hosts`. Any other name gets `403` with `TY1366` (see Isolation and security). When you open the app through a tunnel or a reverse proxy that sends its own name, add that name to `server.hosts`, such as `["preview.example.com", "*.tunnel.example"]`. The port is not checked, because a proxy may change it. With `--allow-non-loopback`, the server checks `Host` only when `server.hosts` is set. ADR 0094 explains the choices.
sections.code:
ty preview --host shop.localhost
ty start --host admin.localhost --port 8080

sections.heading: When the project has a problem
sections.body:
`ty preview` keeps running when your project has a problem that you can fix in your files, such as a broken `server/application.json` (`TY2010`), a view that does not compile, or a rule that the build checks.

When a save breaks the build, the preview keeps serving the last good build. Open pages show a box with each problem: its code, a plain message, the file and line, and help. The terminal prints the same list. Press Dismiss or Escape to hide the box. Tools can read the same list as JSON from `/.tachyon/diagnostics`. When a later save builds, the box goes away and the page updates.

When the project has a problem at start, the preview serves an error page with the list at the same address, with status `503`, and it keeps watching your files. When a save fixes the problem, the real site starts and the error page reloads into it.

When `ty` changes on disk, the preview restarts with the new `ty` (`TY1320`). Before that, it asks the new `ty` to load the project. If the new `ty` refuses the project, the old server keeps running and the box shows the reason. After your next save, the preview asks again, and it restarts once the new `ty` accepts the project. `--no-self-restart` keeps the old `ty` running.

When a method has no test, or a test fails, the preview still starts, and the box lists the untested methods (`TY2023`) or the failed test (`TY2020`).

Only a problem with the process stops the preview: the address is not allowed (`TY1301`) or the port is in use (`TY1302`). `ty bundle`, `ty start`, `ty serve --no-watch` and `ty test --coverage` still stop on every error, so CI does too. ADR 0077 explains the choices.

sections.heading: Preview on a device
sections.body: Preview accepts exactly one target. If you do not pass --target, Tachyon previews web. A native preview serves the web bundle inside a target that you already built with `ty bundle --target <target>`, so it checks no toolchain. With `--watch` it builds that target first and rebuilds it when a source changes; that build checks the platform SDK, compiler and WebView and reports any missing dependency.
sections.code:
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos
ty preview --target android

pages.title: Pages and URLs
pages.summary: Each folder under `client/pages` is one part of a URL. The `tac.html` file in a folder is the page for that URL. A folder whose name starts with `_`, such as `_topic`, matches any value in that part of the URL.

sections.heading: Folders become URLs
sections.body: client/pages/tac.html serves /. client/pages/docs/tac.html serves /docs. client/pages/docs/_topic/tac.html serves /docs/:topic. The page you are reading uses this dynamic segment. A page that contains a slot element becomes a reusable shell (a shared layout) for every page below it.
sections.code:
client/pages/
  tac.html          -> /
  docs/tac.html     -> /docs (shell with <slot />)
  docs/_topic/
    tac.html        -> /docs/:topic

templates.title: Templates
templates.summary: A template is the `tac.html` file of a page or a component. It is HTML with a few additions. Braces show values. `on:` attributes run a method when an event happens. The `loop`, `logic` and `switch` elements repeat or hide parts of the page. A component is a part of a page that you can use again.

sections.heading: Values in braces and events
sections.body: Braces evaluate a limited expression. Braces work only in text. An attribute gets a value through a name that starts with `:`, such as `:title="shell.name"`. For a true-or-false attribute such as `hidden` or `disabled`, the expression gives true or false, such as `:hidden="!shell.open"`. When the value is false, Tachyon leaves the attribute out. The build refuses braces in a plain attribute, such as `title="{shell.name}"`, with `TY1313`. The expression can use the services that the view names. It can also use the properties that its parent passed. A view refers to ShellService as shell. An event handler contains one method call or one assignment, such as shell.refresh() or shell.name = $event.target.value. The compiler turns the handlers into one delegated listener for each event type. It registers each listener on the document. The listener activates after the most important loading work (off the critical path). Tachyon replays the events that happen before that, so no event is lost.
sections.code: {shell.headline}

sections.heading: Accessible views
sections.body: Every view must work with a screen reader and a keyboard. The build checks each `tac.html` file in `client/pages` and `client/components` and stops with `TY1336` when a view breaks one of these rules: An `` has an `alt` text that says what the picture shows. A picture that only decorates the page takes `alt=""` together with `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"`. A `

sections.heading: Control flow
sections.body:
Loops, conditionals and switches are elements, so you can see the structure in the markup. A conditional is always `<logic>`: `<logic :if>`, then `<logic :else-if>`, then `<logic else>`. A loop is always `<loop :for="item of items">`. `<switch>` and `<case>` choose one part by a value. There is no `<if>`, `<else>` or `<for>` element: the build stops with `TY1367` and names the form to use. `ty migrate check` lists these old elements, and `ty migrate fix --write` rewrites them, so `<for :each="item in items">` becomes `<loop :for="item of items">`.

A loop binding (the name of the current item) exists only inside the loop. In `<loop :for="topic of documentation.topics()">`, the binding `topic` has the name of a service. Inside the loop, `topic` reads the item. It does not load `TopicService`.

sections.heading: Components
sections.body:
Each component folder under client/components becomes a tag with hyphens: components/panel/users becomes panel-users. You pass props (the values a component receives) as attributes. The lazy attribute waits to load the component until it scrolls into view. To use a component outside your Tac app, list it in `tac.elements` (see Components in other apps).

A component shows the children that it receives in a slot. `<slot>` holds every child without a `slot` attribute. A named slot, such as `<slot name="title">`, holds the children whose `slot` attribute has that name, such as `<page-title slot="title" />`. A slot name is fixed text that is not empty (`TY1302`). A child for a slot that the component does not declare stops the build with `TY1404`, and so do children without a `slot` attribute when the component has no `<slot>`.

The markup of a component belongs in its `tac.html`, and its styles belong in its `tac.css`. A client script changes text, classes and service state, but it does not build markup or write styles (`TY1364`). The build refuses `innerHTML` and `outerHTML` writes (also with `||=`, `??=` or `+=`), `document.write`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `setHTML`, `setHTMLUnsafe`, inserting nodes made with `document.createElement`, writes to `element.style` or its fields, `setAttribute('style', ...)` and style sheet changes. It follows them through aliases, fields of objects such as `refs.list`, `bind`, `call` and `apply`. The check reads the source when you build. It checks a convention and is not a sandbox, so a computed name such as `element[name]` is not followed. A third-party script that builds its own markup is declared in `tac.scriptSources` (`TY1365`).

sections.heading: Markup and styles stay in the view
sections.body:
Write the markup of a view in its `tac.html` and its styles in its `tac.css`. A script changes text, classes and service state. It does not build markup or write styles. The build stops with `TY1364` when a JavaScript or TypeScript file under `client/` writes `innerHTML` or `outerHTML`, calls `document.write`, `insertAdjacentHTML` or `document.createElement`, inserts nodes with `append`, `appendChild`, `insertBefore` or a similar method, writes `element.style` or changes a style sheet. This covers services, component scripts and every script in `client/shared/`. It also refuses `setHTML` and `setHTMLUnsafe`, compound writes such as `innerHTML ||= html`, and these methods called through `call` or `apply`, such as `document.write.call(document, html)`. The check follows a document or a node that a variable holds, and a node kept in an object field, such as `const refs = { list: document.querySelector('#l') }`, also when another function reads the field. An object that holds only literal values is data, so `theme.style = 'light'` passes. A CSS variable is a value, not a style, so `style.setProperty('--accent', color)` and `style.removeProperty('--accent')` pass when the name is written as text that starts with `--`; a name held in a variable is refused, because the check cannot see it. The check reads the source text, so it is a guard for mistakes, not a sandbox: computed names such as `element[name]`, `Reflect.set` and `Object.assign` are not followed. HTML that comes as data, such as the body of an email or rich text pasted into an editor, goes in through `:safe-html`. Write `
`, and Tachyon parses the text, keeps a fixed list of formatting elements (paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, links, images, bold and italic text and similar), and drops everything else: scripts, styles, frames, forms, SVG, event attributes, `id`, `name` and `class`. A link keeps only an `http`, `https`, `mailto` or `tel` address and opens in a new tab with `rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow"`, an image keeps only an `http` or `https` address or an inline PNG, GIF, JPEG or WebP, and a `style` attribute keeps only text, color, spacing, border and size properties without `url()`. sections.heading: Shared data and the page
sections.body: Content that is only data needs no service. A view reads client/shared/data/<name>.json as data.<name>. The file loads once per page as a JSON module. If no file exists for a name, the build fails with TY1311. page.path is the page's own path. page.development is true while ty preview serves the page. A view passes these values to a service as properties. So a service does not need to read location or the document itself. Every view has data and page built in. So no service can use either name as its instance name (ADR 0036; an ADR is an architecture decision record).

sections.heading: What an update keeps
sections.body:
When a service value changes, the browser renderer renders the view again. It keeps every element that is still at the same place in the template and has the same loop item. It changes only the attributes, text and children that are different. So the element keeps its DOM node, its focus, its caret and its scroll position. In the example, a click on a card changes `graph.selected`. The scrolling `div` and the three buttons stay the same nodes, so the view does not jump back to the start.

A loop item keeps its element when it is the same object, or a plain object or array with the same values. So a list that a getter or a method builds again on every render keeps its elements, the focus, the caret and an open native `<select>` inside them. A loop item whose values changed gets a new element. A `<select>` shows the option that its `:value` or its options' `:selected` choose after every update, also when the options come from a loop and change. A `<select>` without either keeps the option that the user chose. A custom element, for example one from a component library, stays only when its children and its light-DOM `slot` elements are as the renderer left them. If the library moved them, or an attribute that the element observes changes, the renderer creates the element again. When the focus was inside it, the new element gets the focus and the same selection.

sections.heading: When a component starts
sections.body:
Tac has no server-side rendering mode (the server does not build the HTML of a view). The browser renderer creates the first DOM (the tree of elements on the page) and does every rerender. The document that a route serves contains no rendered view subtree. So `hydrate` does not say when the browser takes control of HTML from the server. It says when a component activates. A component activates when the services that its view names are initialised.

`load` activates at once. `idle` waits until the browser is free. `visible` waits until the component is in the viewport (the visible part of the page). `interaction` waits for the first event. `never` keeps the component inactive. A component that only displays the values it received names no service at all.
sections.code: <product-card hydrate="visible" :sku="sku" />

sections.heading: Write the start time in the markup
sections.body:
`hydrate` must be one of `load`, `idle`, `visible`, `interaction` or `never`. Write it as a static literal (a fixed value written in the markup). It cannot be an expression. The compiler puts the schedule into the render plan (the compiled steps that build the page). A value known only at run time would come too late. It would come after the moment when the schedule must decide.

Properties are ordinary values passed to the component. The browser evaluates them like everything else. So the served document contains nothing about them.

services.title: Services
services.summary: A service is a class in `client/services` that holds the data and the actions of a view. The view names the service, and Tachyon creates it. For example, a view refers to `BasketService` as `basket` and shows `{basket.count}`. When a field changes, the page updates.

sections.heading: Fields that update the page
sections.body: Fields and methods belong to the service instance. A view reads them by the instance name: {counter.count}, on:click="counter.increment()". Template handlers and OnEvent methods refresh the view when they finish. Background work injects taskScheduler (Tachyon gives it to a field) and calls its render(). Fields marked @SessionState are saved to sessionStorage. Fields marked @LocalState are saved to localStorage. The Python, Lua and C++ tabs have only plain fields, because the build refuses SessionState and LocalState in Python, Lua and C++ Tac code with TY1308. Their `theme` starts again after a reload. A Python service also needs the Python runtime in `client/manifest.json` (see Your first app). To save a change inside an array or object, assign a new value to the field.

sections.heading: Start, stop and events
sections.body: OnStart marks a method with no arguments that initializes the service. It runs after Tachyon injects resources and attaches the DOM. OnStop stops and cleans up the work that the service owns. To publish, a class declares an applicationEventPublisher field with no value. Then it calls publishEvent(model[, retain]) with a value of a model type. OnEvent registers a local listener that belongs to its owner, and the model type of its one parameter is the event it hears. Order sets the order of listeners. InBackground detaches a listener (it runs in the background). Retention and replay are off unless you turn them on. When a service is removed or hot-replaced (replaced with new code while the page runs), Tachyon unregisters its listeners automatically. A Lua service writes each marker as a comment above its function, such as `-- @OnEvent({"replay":true})`. Its field `application_event_publisher = nil` is the publisher, and an event is a model table, such as `setmetatable({ release = "TACHYON" }, ReleaseChanged)` (ADR 0085). A Python service writes `@on_event` above a synchronous method, and its field `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher` is the publisher (ADR 0093).

sections.heading: One per page, or one per component
sections.body: By default, a service is a page singleton: the page has one instance of it. Tachyon creates it when the first view that names it renders. Tachyon initialises it once, and every component that names it shares it. Tachyon disposes of it (cleans it up) when the user leaves the page. A service built from its component's properties is different. It has one instance for each component instance. Tachyon constructs it with those properties and disposes of it with the component. You write no constructor for it. @NeedsAll takes no arguments, and a class with it has no constructor. It takes every field that has no initial value, like Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor, and the properties with the same names fill those fields. Each such field is required: the build refuses a component tag that does not pass it (`TY1407`), and the page refuses a missing or `null` value. A field with an initial value is plain state. This works the same in every Tac language except C++, which has no tab here: the build refuses NeedsAll in C++ Tac code with TY1308 for now (ADR 0099). A Go field that a property fills is marked // @Required. A Python field is a typed class attribute with no value, such as `files: list[str]`, under `@needs_all`. In Lua, every field in the class table has a value, such as files = {}, and the property with the same name replaces it. A field can hold text, a number, a list, or a model from client/models (a list of models and nested models too). In F#, @NeedsAll marks the primary constructor, so its parameters are the properties (ADR 0073). No Lifetime is needed, because a page singleton is constructed with no properties at all (ADR 0039; an ADR is an architecture decision record). Use Lifetime({"value":"prototype"}) for a service that keeps state for each component but takes no properties. A view reads those fields directly, not through a method that returns them. Tachyon injects collaborators (other services that this service uses). It does not pass them as constructor arguments. In the view, properties from a parent and loop bindings have no service name in front of them. A service field can be declared, left undefined and named after another service. That field receives that singleton, in the same way a Yon service receives its collaborators.

browser-storage.title: Saving data in the browser
browser-storage.summary: A service can keep data in the browser. A field marked `@LocalState` or `@SessionState` keeps its value after a reload. A browser Store keeps records, and a cache keeps answers so that the page does not ask for them again.

sections.heading: Saved service fields
sections.body: A service field marked @SessionState is saved in sessionStorage for the life of the tab. A field marked @LocalState is saved in localStorage, so it comes back in later visits on this device. Both markers work in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go and Ruby services. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses both markers in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Python has no tab here either: the Python runtime has no browser storage, so nothing would save the field. One field takes one of the two markers, and never together with Needs. The old `$` and `$$` field prefixes are refused, and the message names the marker to write. `ty migrate fix --write` changes the fields, their uses in the class and in the views, and a value saved under the old key moves to the new key once. Tachyon restores saved values before OnStart runs. Each assignment stores JSON of up to 64 KiB. When a service method changes its own saved field, the new value is saved as the method returns; this is also true for a Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java or Ruby service that runs as WebAssembly. To save a change inside the value, assign the field again. Template handlers and OnEvent methods render the view again automatically. Background work uses an injected taskScheduler. If the browser denies storage or its quota (storage limit) is full, the UI still works. Never save secrets. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses SessionState in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).
