sections.heading: Records and caches in the browser
sections.body:
A browser Store keeps records, such as a list of products, in IndexedDB. IndexedDB is a database that is built into the browser. Mark the record type with `Entity` and `Table`, and mark the class that saves and finds records with `Store`. When the Entity names the adapter "indexeddb", you write no adapter code. This works in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart and Ruby services, and in Go, Rust, C#, Swift, Kotlin and Java services that run as WebAssembly. A native Swift, Kotlin, Rust or C# app service names its own adapter in its Setup. Tachyon keeps one IndexedDB object store for each Table. The data never leaves the browser.

A cache keeps the answer of a method, so the next call with the same arguments does not run the method again. Mark the method with `Cached`, and name its cache with `CacheSettings`. In the browser, Tachyon keeps the cache in the Cache API, the storage for answers that is built into the browser. The cache has limits: ttlMs (how long an answer stays), maxBytes (the size of one answer) and maxEntries (the number of answers). On an insecure origin, such as a plain http address that is not localhost, the browser has no Cache API, so the cache lives in memory only and is gone after a reload.

For complete examples in every language, read Data access: Tac and Caching: Tac on the Annotations A–Z page. Never save secrets in the browser.

application-events.title: Events between services
application-events.summary: An event is a message that one service publishes and other services receive. The publisher does not need to know who listens. This page also shows the start and stop methods of a service (lifecycle hooks), in the browser and on the server.

sections.heading: Signals between components
sections.body: An injected applicationEventPublisher and OnEvent connect services that have no shared parent. To publish, call publishEvent(model) or publishEvent(model, retain) with a value of a model type. The name of the model type is the event name. Retain and replay are false by default. Payloads (the data an event carries) are finite JSON of up to 64 KiB. Each listener receives its own copy. A listener whose return type is a model publishes the value it returns as that model. Disposal (cleanup of a service) unregisters its listeners. In Lua, the publisher is the field `application_event_publisher = nil`, the call is `publish_event`, and `-- @OnEvent` above a function makes it a listener. In Python, the field is `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher`, the call is `publish_event`, and `@on_event` marks a synchronous listener. In C++, the field is `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` and `[[OnEvent]]` marks the listener. A page's events stay in the page: Tachyon does not send them to the server. A listener for a Topic model also receives the server's events of that model (see Topics).

sections.heading: Based on Spring, owned by Tachyon
sections.body: OnStart marks the initialization method, and OnStop marks the cleanup method. An OnEvent method receives one payload (the value that comes with the event). Publishing works as in Spring. A class declares an applicationEventPublisher field with no initial value. Then it calls publishEvent(model) or publishEvent(model, retain). The event is the model: the name of its type is the event name, so a model named OrderPlaced in one language reaches a listener of the model OrderPlaced in any other language. The EventPublisher annotation is removed, and any use of it fails with TY1308. The reason: a method's return value is its answer to its caller, not an event. In Tac, Tachyon injects the field by its name, with or without Needs. In Yon, the field is a provider token that the container (the Tachyon part that creates providers) constructs. Needs binds it in exactly the same way as dataSource. A listener hears the model type of its one parameter. JavaScript reads that type from the JSDoc @param line. Before a listener runs, Tachyon checks the payload against its model with the same rules as a request body, and a payload that does not fit is not delivered. A listener can take replay, condition and id, but no event names (ADR 0055). ty migrate fix --write converts a listener whose event name matches a model. The Order(n) and InBackground modifiers go on the method. Each of these markers is compiler syntax on its own line. It is not a Spring package that runs at run time. The markers add no class-name or folder suffix beyond the existing role rules. A model marked Topic works like a Spring Cloud Bus remote event: its events also reach the listeners in other Yon languages and in open pages (see Topics).

sections.heading: Browser services: JavaScript and TypeScript
sections.body: Tachyon registers listeners and injects resources before OnStart runs. OnStart runs after the element exists. After listeners and template actions run, the view renders again automatically. Tachyon injects a resource by the field's name. Each name is the one Spring gives to its closest equivalent (ADR 0038; an ADR is an architecture decision record). The names are view (the element), lifecycle, taskScheduler, resourceLoader and applicationEventPublisher. The cacheManager resource was removed with the IndexedDB fetch cache (ADR 0087), and a field with that name is refused: mark the client method that changes the data ClearCache or UpdateCache instead. lifecycle is an AbortSignal that is aborted on disposal, which means cleanup. An applicationEventPublisher field with no initial value receives that resource even without the annotation. Use lifecycle for cancellation. Use taskScheduler.render() for external callbacks (callbacks from code outside Tachyon). Use resourceLoader.precache(urls) and its clearAssetCache() method for offline assets. Constructors must not use these resources. Retention and replay are off unless you turn them on. Hooks apply to services and to the providers that Tachyon manages for them. They do not apply to other instances that you create yourself. A Dart service is a browser service too. But its only resource is the ApplicationEventPublisher. Its example is under Compiled services below.

sections.heading: Listener options: condition, Order and InBackground
sections.body: A listener hears one model, the type of its parameter. It can also have a condition. A condition is a small, limited expression that uses value and event. Tachyon compiles it once into a matcher, and every runtime evaluates that matcher. Order(n) runs the listeners of one event from the lowest number up. Listeners with the same number run in the order you declare them. A listener without Order has the number 0. A listener publishes again when its return type is a model: the value it returns, or each of up to 32 values in a returned list, is published as that model. Tachyon ignores any other return value. InBackground makes a listener run later, after the current delivery pass. Such a detached listener never publishes again, as in Spring. In Tac, InBackground works in every language, because the page's event bus delays the delivery itself. In Yon, it needs a language with asynchronous methods: JavaScript, TypeScript and Python accept it. The other Yon languages reject it at compile time: PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua. An id names a listener in diagnostics (error and warning messages).

sections.heading: Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Dart, C++ and Ruby services
sections.body: Each example injects the publisher and publishes a CatalogCount model during initialization. The model lives in client/models in the language of the service. A listener updates the count, and cleanup resets it. The prelude (code that Tachyon adds before your code) constructs any member of type ApplicationEventPublisher. That member is not in the page's member table. Each activation has a new owner. Tachyon rejects old callbacks. Listener work waits in a queue until the active callback returns. Native and Go service hooks and event methods are synchronous. A Go service is not native: it runs as WebAssembly in the web view on every target, with the same rules. A Dart service compiles to WebAssembly (WasmGC) and follows the same shape. A C++ service compiles to WebAssembly with Emscripten and follows the same shape: it declares `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` and marks its hooks and listeners with `[[OnStart]]`, `[[OnEvent]]` and `[[OnStop]]` (ADR 0099). A Kotlin service links into the Android app and compiles to WebAssembly (WasmGC) for every other target. A Swift service links into the macOS and iOS apps. On the other targets it runs as WebAssembly. There, as for Kotlin and Rust, its events go through the page's event bus: its listeners hear events from every service and component on the page, and a listener for a Topic model reads the topic stream (ADR 0082). A Java service runs as WebAssembly on every target and uses the same page event bus: it publishes client/models records and classes with ApplicationEventPublisher, its OnEvent listeners take one model, and a listener for a Topic model reads the topic stream (ADR 0083). The same example works in both. It declares the publisher with Needs, and its hooks are synchronous. A Ruby or F# service also runs as WebAssembly on every target and uses the page event bus: Ruby creates its publisher with ApplicationEventPublisher.new, and F# takes it as a constructor parameter. Helper types cannot own events. You cannot publish from background work that has no owner. You still configure native HTTP clients manually. Only JavaScript and TypeScript services receive the browser resources.

sections.heading: Yon: every supported language
sections.body: Choose one language. The roles below live in the shared server/services folder. The controller lives in server/controllers. Tachyon finds both automatically. PublishService injects the applicationEventPublisher provider through Needs. JavaScript matches it by field name. Every other language matches it by type: F# takes it as a constructor parameter. A Ruby service creates its publisher itself with ApplicationEventPublisher.new. A Lua service declares the field `application_event_publisher = nil` with the type comment `---@type ApplicationEventPublisher`. PublishService publishes a ProbeReady model during OnStart. ProbeService listens for ProbeReady and keeps the result, and GET returns it as JSON. Events belong only to this invocation (this one run of the route), unless the model is a Topic. A Topic event is also saved in the topic log, and Tachyon calls its listeners in the other files and languages once (see Topics). JavaScript, TypeScript and Python support async hooks, async listeners and InBackground. PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua use synchronous event listeners. They reject InBackground at compile time. Tachyon rejects compiled async methods, streaming event containers and transient event providers. The initialization and endpoint queues finish before serialization (turning the result into JSON). Then cleanup runs in reverse order, within the supervisor deadline (the time limit of the process that runs the route).

sections.heading: Delivery and migration
sections.body: Payloads are model values that travel as finite JSON of at most 64 KiB. Each listener gets its own copy. Delivery has limits on listeners, queues and cycles. A republished event has the same limits. Events are not transactional, and they are not a background-job API. Tachyon saves only the events of a Topic model, in the topic log (see Topics); other events are not durable. The EventPublisher annotation, the this.tac object, the TacRuntime type and the implicit mount hook are removed. Instead, inject the applicationEventPublisher. Use HTTPClient and request annotations, the lifecycle and listener markers and the injected resources. ty migrate reports an EventPublisher method as Changed. It names the injected publisher that replaces it. Cleanup runs once. It runs when the user leaves the page, on hot replacement, or when the document is really removed. In hot replacement, the development server swaps in changed code. A prototype-scoped service gets a new instance each time it is injected. For such a service, cleanup runs when its component is removed. When the browser suspends the page in its back-forward cache (bfcache), Tachyon keeps the owner. String event names are removed (ADR 0055): OnEvent takes no event or events, and publishEvent takes no name. ty migrate fix --write converts listeners, and JavaScript and TypeScript calls, whose event name matches a model, and lists the rest as manual steps. Ruby listeners name their model in a YARD tag, # @param order [PlacedOrder], and the fix converts a Ruby listener that already has that tag.

web-components.title: Components in other apps
web-components.summary: A component can leave your Tac app. List it in `tac.elements`, and the build makes it a custom element: a standard HTML tag that a plain HTML page, React, Angular, Vue or another Tac app can use. Values go in as attributes or properties, events come out as DOM events, and the children of the tag show in its slots. Each element comes with TypeScript declarations, and a project can export elements without having a page.

sections.heading: Export a component
sections.body:
List the component in `tac.elements` in `client/manifest.json`. Write its tag, as a page writes it: the folder `client/components/shop/counter` is `shop-counter`. `ty bundle` and `ty preview` then write `.tachyon/elements/shop-counter.js`, beside the runtime and the services that a Tac page already loads. `ty bundle` puts it in `dist/web/.tachyon/elements/`. A custom element is a tag that JavaScript defines, and the HTML standard says that its name must contain a hyphen. So a component in a folder with one part, such as `client/components/counter`, cannot be exported: the build stops with `TY1358`. `TY1358` also stops a name that is not a component (ADR 0086).

The element accepts a prop (a value that it receives) for each name that the template reads, except service names, loop names, `data` and `page`. Here the prop is `label`. It also accepts each field that a service fills with `NeedsAll` (see One per page, or one per component). When a service publishes an event, the element also sends it to the page as a DOM event. The event name is the model name in kebab case (words in small letters, joined by hyphens): `CountChanged` becomes `count-changed`. The component still works on your own Tac pages, such as `/shop` here.

The service can be written in any Tac service language. A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby, Lua, Python or C++ runs as WebAssembly inside the element, in the same way as on a Tac page. A Python service also needs the pinned Python runtime in `tac.python`, as the manifest shows; the other languages ignore that member (ADR 0093). Choose a language above the code.

A project does not need a page to export elements. When `tac.elements` lists a component, `ty bundle` and `ty preview` work without `client/pages` and without a controller, so a project can hold only the components that it gives to other apps. The build stops with `TY1002` only when it finds no page, no controller and no exported element.

sections.heading: TypeScript declarations
sections.body:
Beside each element module, the build writes a TypeScript declaration file (a `.d.ts` file, which describes types and holds no code): `.tachyon/elements/shop-counter.d.ts`. A TypeScript page that imports the element gets these types:

`document.querySelector('shop-counter')` and `document.createElement('shop-counter')` return a `ShopCounterElement`, because the file adds the tag to `HTMLElementTagNameMap`.

`ShopCounterElement` has a property for each prop, such as `label`. A prop has the type `unknown`, because a template does not declare types, so it takes any value.

`addEventListener('count-changed', ...)` gives a `CustomEvent<CountChanged>`, so `event.detail.count` is a `number`. The file copies each event model as an interface. The events are the models that the component's JavaScript or TypeScript services pass to `publishEvent`. A service in another language also sends its events to the page, but the file does not list them, so the listener gets a plain `Event` type.

The second listener below does not compile: `event.detail.count` is a number, not a string. Helpers for React and Vue types are planned.

controllers.title: Controllers
controllers.summary: A controller is a class in `server/controllers` that answers HTTP requests. Each method with a route annotation, such as `GetRoute`, answers one kind of request on one path. An argument marked `FromPath`, `FromQuery` or `FromBody` gets its value from the request. Every route also says who may call it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`; the build stops without it.

sections.heading: What a controller method is
sections.body: A controller method is an instance method with a route annotation, such as `GetRoute`. Your code does not read standard input or write an envelope (the wrapper around the response). It does not declare main, import a Tachyon symbol or extend a framework class. Tachyon does that work. The server answers `OPTIONS` and `HEAD` for you. A request for a verb that no method on that path answers gets 405, with an `Allow` header.

sections.heading: Routes and paths
sections.body: A controller is a class in `server/controllers/<Name>Controller.<ext>`. `RequestRoute("/items")` on the class gives the base path of its routes. `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class or on a method says who may call a route, and a route without one stops the build with `TY1322` (see Who may call a route). `GetRoute`, `PostRoute`, `PutRoute`, `PatchRoute` and `DeleteRoute` on a method make it answer that HTTP verb. They can add to the path, such as `GetRoute("/{id}")`. A part in braces is a path variable (a part of the path that can change). The method name must start with its verb, such as `getItem` or `postItem`. Argument annotations say where each value comes from: `FromPath`, `FromQuery`, `FromBody`, `FromHeader` or `FromCookie`. One argument without an annotation gets the request in the language's own type: Fetch `Request` in JavaScript and TypeScript, `urllib.request.Request` in Python, a `Net::HTTP` request in Ruby, `HttpExchange` in Java, Groovy and Kotlin, `HttpRequestMessage` in C# and F#, `http::Request` in Rust, a shelf `Request` in Dart, `*http.Request` in Go and a table with `method`, `path`, `headers` and `body` in Lua. PHP has no request object: it reads `$_SERVER`, `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_COOKIE` and `php://input`. You can write a controller in any Yon language. You need no runtime annotation package. The glossary explains each annotation name in plain words. See the [routing annotation glossary](/docs/routing-annotations) for each name.

sections.heading: Route rules
sections.body: A route is a path that `RequestRoute` on the controller class and `GetRoute`, `PostRoute` and the other verb annotations on a method declare together. A part in braces, such as `{id}`, is a path variable (a part of the URL that can change). The method reads it with a `FromPath` argument, and its declared type is checked. A fixed path part uses only lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, such as `order-items`. A path variable name uses only lowercase letters, digits and underscores, such as `{order_id}`. The build refuses other characters. A page folder `_id` and a path variable `{id}` name the same route, so a page and a controller can share a path. On a shared path, a browser that opens the address gets the page, and a fetch from the page gets the controller's answer: Tachyon serves the page to a GET or HEAD with `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`, or with no `Sec-Fetch-Mode` and an `Accept` that names `text/html`. The controller's access rule still guards every other request, and both answers carry `Vary: Sec-Fetch-Mode, Accept`. Two controllers cannot answer the same verb on the same path. This works the same way in every language that Yon runs. Every route also says who may call it: `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the controller class or on the method, and the method wins.

sections.heading: Annotated controllers and providers
sections.body: GET /products returns [{"id":1,"name":"Anvil"}]. GET /products/42 returns {"id":42,"name":"Anvil"}. Both answers are Product models (data types in server/models/), and Yon turns them into JSON. A controller is a class that answers HTTP requests. Put each controller in server/controllers/, one class in each file, and end its name with Controller. Mark the class with RequestRoute and a base path, such as RequestRoute("/products"), and say who may call its routes: Public here, because anyone may read the products (SignedIn and Allow(Role) are the other choices). Mark each route method with GetRoute, PostRoute, PutRoute, PatchRoute or DeleteRoute. A method marker can add a path part, such as GetRoute("/{id}"). The full path is the class path plus the method path. The method name must start with its verb. So write getProducts, GetProducts in C#, F# and Go, or get_products in Python, Rust, Ruby and Lua. A method named GET no longer answers requests by its name. Route methods are instance methods: Python takes self, Rust takes &self, Go uses a method with a receiver, Ruby uses an ordinary def, and Lua uses a function with a colon, `function ProductsController:get_products()`. Parameter markers say where each value comes from: FromPath, FromQuery, FromBody, FromHeader and FromCookie. One parameter without a marker receives the request in the language's own type: Fetch Request in JavaScript and TypeScript, urllib.request.Request in Python, a Net::HTTP request in Ruby, HttpExchange in Java, Groovy and Kotlin, HttpRequestMessage in C# and F#, http::Request in Rust, a shelf Request in Dart, *http.Request in Go and a request table in Lua. PHP has no request object: it reads $_SERVER, $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE and php://input. The parameter types check the input. Bad input gets a 400 answer before the method runs. ResponseStatus(201) sets the status of a normal answer. A generator method (a method that yields values one at a time) answers with a stream, and StreamRoute marks it: a generator under GetRoute is refused. Tachyon rejects ResponseStatus on a method without a route marker. The role markers are RequestRoute, Service, Store, HTTPClient, Helper and Converter. Put Needs on each field that the class requires. In Ruby, Needs stands above an attr_reader line. Its `# @return [ProductsService]` type comment names the provider, or the field name does when there is no type comment. The compiler finds the dependency from the field and writes the assignment for you. When the field does not name the provider, use Named to name it. Here the field catalog uses Named("ProductsService"). In F#, the field is a settable property, `[<Needs>] member val Catalog : ProductsService = Unchecked.defaultof<ProductsService> with get, set`, and a primary constructor parameter, `type ProductsController(catalog: ProductsService) =`, is the other F# form. Lifetime selects singleton, request or transient. The same marker on a Tac service selects singleton or prototype. Singleton and request instances are shared only inside one invocation (one run of a route for one request). Transient instances are new each time something asks for them. These problems fail before the invocation: missing tokens, cycles, two methods for one path and verb, and singleton dependencies on request instances. A token is a name that identifies a provider. A cycle is a group of providers that need each other. For automatic discovery, put each role in a file named after its type. Put that file in the shared plural role folder of its realm (the Tac side or the Yon side). On the Yon side, these are server/controllers, server/services, server/stores, server/remotes, server/setups, server/entities, server/helpers and server/converters. Each controller file is compiled with the shared roles in the same language. Guards, interceptors and filters are not supported. Plain imported helpers and existing root middleware (code at the project root that runs around every request) still work. Each annotation is on its own line. You need no framework imports.

sections.heading: Native requests and responses
sections.body: A Yon method that needs the whole request, or an answer with its own status and headers, uses the types of its own language (ADR 0062). The request is a Fetch `Request` in JavaScript and TypeScript, `urllib.request.Request` in Python, a `Net::HTTP` request in Ruby, `HttpExchange` in Java, Groovy and Kotlin, `HttpRequestMessage` in C# and F#, `http::Request<Vec<u8>>` in Rust, a shelf `Request` in Dart, `*http.Request` in Go and a table with `method`, `path`, `headers` and `body` in Lua. PHP has no request object: it reads `$_SERVER`, `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_COOKIE` and `php://input`. The answer is a Fetch `Response`, an `(HTTPStatus, headers, body)` tuple in Python, a `[status, headers, body]` array in Ruby and a `{ status, headers, body }` list in Lua, `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo` in PHP, a write on the same `HttpExchange` in Java, Groovy and Kotlin, `HttpResponseMessage` in C# and F#, `http::Response<Vec<u8>>` in Rust, a shelf `Response` in Dart and `*http.Response` in Go. A Go `*http.Response` body may hold binary bytes, such as an image or a file: Tachyon sends them unchanged. `YonRequest` and `YonResponse` are removed, and the build refuses them with a message that names the native type (TY2015). Tachyon itself uses private names that start with `__Yon` for the code it writes, so a `__Yon` name in your code is refused too. The server computes `content-length`, `transfer-encoding` and `connection`, so a handler answer does not set them. A Rust handler builds with Cargo and the `http` crate, offline first, so `ty doctor` checks for `cargo`. A Dart handler needs the `shelf` package: Tachyon writes a pubspec and runs `dart pub get`, which reads the pub cache or the network. PHP runs with `php-cgi`, the PHP program in which `header()` works. Homebrew's `php` includes it, Debian and Ubuntu have the `php-cgi` package, and the Windows PHP zip file has `php-cgi.exe`. `ty doctor` tells you when it is missing. The request ID is in the header `x-tachyon-request-id`. The client address is in `X-Real-IP`, and Go `RemoteAddr`, `HttpExchange.getRemoteAddress()` and PHP `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']` hold it too (see The client address and forwarding headers).
sections.code:
Moving from YonRequest and YonResponse (ADR 0062)

1. Run ty migrate fix to see the plan, then ty migrate fix --write.
   It removes every YonRequest parameter that the method does not read,
   and lists every other use with the native type to write.
2. Change each listed use by hand:

  Language     Read the request              Answer with
  JavaScript   request.headers.get('x-a')    new Response(body, { status, headers })
  TypeScript   await request.text()          Response.json(value, { status: 400 })
  Python       request.get_header('X-a')     (HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST, headers, body)
               request.data
  Ruby         request['x-a'], request.body  [400, { 'content-type' => 'application/json' }, [body]]
  PHP          $_SERVER['HTTP_X_A']          http_response_code(400);
               file_get_contents('php://input')  header('Content-Type: application/json'); echo $body;
  Java         exchange.getRequestHeaders()  exchange.sendResponseHeaders(400, bytes.length);
               exchange.getRequestBody()     exchange.getResponseBody().write(bytes);
  Groovy       exchange.requestHeaders       exchange.sendResponseHeaders(400, bytes.length)
  Kotlin       exchange.requestHeaders       exchange.sendResponseHeaders(400, bytes.size.toLong())
  C#           request.Headers               new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest)
  F#           request.Headers               new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest)
  Rust         request.headers().get("x-a")  http::Response::builder().status(400).body(bytes)
  Dart         request.headers['x-a']        Response(400, body: body)
  Go           request.Header.Get("X-A")     &http.Response{StatusCode: 400, Body: ...}
  Lua          request.headers["x-a"]        { 400, { ["content-type"] = "application/json" }, body }

3. Middleware that let the request pass with an empty 204 answer can
   answer nothing instead: return undefined, None, nil or null, or
   write nothing in PHP, Java, Groovy and Kotlin.
4. relay(command, request) now takes the native request. PHP calls
   Yon::relay(command); Java, Groovy and Kotlin call Yon.relay(command, exchange).
   The program no longer receives path parameters: read them from route.

models.title: Models and JSON answers
models.summary: A model is a data type in `server/models`. A controller method takes models and returns them. Yon turns the value that a method returns into a JSON answer.

sections.heading: How return values become responses
sections.body: An ordinary return value becomes JSON. A response in the language's own type controls status, headers and body, such as a Fetch `Response` in JavaScript, `http::Response` in Rust, `HttpResponseMessage` in C# or an `(HTTPStatus, headers, body)` tuple in Python. Java, Groovy and Kotlin write the answer on the `HttpExchange` argument, PHP uses `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo`, and Ruby and Lua return a `[status, headers, body]` list. Yon sends HTML only when the controller method itself selects `Content-Type: text/html`. Yon passes those bytes through unchanged. It does no interpolation (filling values into text), no component expansion, no control-tag evaluation and no server-side rendering. Tachyon rejects a `yon.html` file with TY1008.

sections.heading: JSON in every language
sections.body: In every Yon language, Yon turns an ordinary return value that is compatible with JSON into JSON text. It does this once, with status 200 and application/json. You do not build a response object. To encode and decode JSON yourself, use the JSON APIs of the language. Java and Kotlin give Json.parse and Json.stringify. Rust gives Json::parse and Json::stringify, which can fail. C# can use System.Text.Json directly. Dart can use dart:convert. Go can use encoding/json. Tachyon reads the fields of Go types in `server/models/` only. A Go type from another package, such as `json.RawMessage`, `http.Header`, `time.Time` or `spec.Document` from your native packages in `server/packages/`, is an open JSON value in a model field, a route parameter or a route result: Go's `encoding/json` reads and writes it, and Tachyon accepts any JSON there. A field tagged `json:"-"` is not part of the JSON at all. A `*http.Request`, a `context.Context` or a multipart file is not JSON data, so a model field of that type fails with `TY2015`: read it from the `*http.Request` parameter of the route method instead, like an `HttpServletRequest` or `MultipartFile` parameter in Spring. A returned model is written with the names of its fields. C# writes its PascalCase properties in camelCase, so `Name` becomes `name`, in normal answers and in streams. A model that extends another model keeps the fields of its parent, such as a Java class that extends a model or a Dart model that passes `super.name` to its parent. JSON that is not valid is rejected. A returned string stays a JSON string, even if its contents look like JSON. To send a custom status, headers, cookies or a raw body, answer with the language's own response, such as a Fetch Response, an http::Response or a Go `*http.Response` with `Set-Cookie` in its `Header`; this is the role of Spring's `ResponseEntity`.

sections.heading: Route contracts
sections.body:
Tachyon makes the API schema of each route from the controller method: its argument types, its return type, its `ResponseStatus` and the models they name. You write no schema file. `OPTIONS` on a route answers with the schema of that path. `/api.json` lists every controller route and every model. The server checks requests and answers against the same types, so the schema and the checks always agree. The example is a shortened `/api.json`.

A model record accepts only its declared fields, also in nested records and in lists, so its schema says `"additionalProperties": false`. A request body with a field that the model does not declare gets 400. Required fields must be present, and optional fields may be missing. Fields of a parent model join the record: Java and Groovy `extends`, a Python base class, a Dart `super` field, a Go embedded struct and a TypeScript `&`. A record stays open, without `"additionalProperties": false`, when Tachyon cannot see all of its fields: its parent is not in `server/models/`, it uses a PHP trait or a TypeScript index signature, or a field has a type that Tachyon cannot read. A field typed as any JSON value stays open too. A stream route says `"stream": true` and `"produces": "text/event-stream"`. A socket path says `"socket": true`, and its `request.body` names the message model.

checking-values.title: Checking values
checking-values.summary: Yon checks the values that a caller sends before your method runs. A wrong value gets an error answer, and your method never sees it.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: The types in a controller method decide what a caller may send and what it gets back. A model is a data type in `server/models/`. A JavaScript model is a JSDoc `@typedef` in its own file, such as `server/models/Product.js`. The server checks each argument before the method runs. A value of the wrong type gets a 400 answer that names the part and the field. An answer that does not match the return type becomes a 500 error. Fields that the model does not name are allowed. The same types make the API schema: `OPTIONS` on a route answers with it, and `/api.json` lists every route.

sections.heading: Checking values and method arguments
sections.body: Checked defines JSON rules for direct fields. Required rejects a missing or null value. NotEmpty requires a string that is not empty. The string must contain at least one Unicode scalar (one Unicode character) that is not whitespace. Its whitespace set is U+0009 to 000D, 0020, 0085, 00A0, 1680, 2000 to 200A, 2028, 2029, 202F, 205F and 3000. Length counts UTF-8 bytes for strings, elements for arrays and keys for objects. Length, Min and Max ignore a missing or null value unless a separate rule requires it. Min and Max require finite numbers, never numeric strings. Behaviors.validate(Type, value) needs no context. It checks a plain value, so the caller does not build a DTO first. Check validates its parameter before pagination, cache authorization, cache reads, HTTP or application code. Errors use validation plus a limited field.rule path, and they do not repeat the input. Unknown fields are still allowed. Tachyon does not support nested validation or validation groups. Lua has no tab here: a Lua model cannot carry `Checked` yet, so the build stops at the model file with `TY1310` (ADR 0092). Tac form validation improves the user experience (UX), but it is not the final check. Validate again in Yon. Also check authorization there, and check which fields a caller may assign.

error-handlers.title: Error handlers
error-handlers.summary: An error handler turns an error that your code throws into a clear answer for the caller. You write it once, and it works for every controller of its language.

sections.heading: Error handlers in every Yon language
sections.body: An error handler turns a typed error into a public answer, in one place for all routes (ADR 0051). Choose a language below. GET /orders throws OrderNotFound. The handler answers 404 with {"code":"order-not-found"}. The error type lives in server/errors/ and has no annotation. The handler class lives in server/controllers/ and its name ends with ErrorHandler. HandlesError takes no argument: the type of the first parameter says which error the method handles. Ruby names that type in a YARD tag, # @param error [OrderNotFound]. An optional second parameter receives the request in the language's own type; a PHP handler reads the superglobals instead. ResponseStatus sets a status from 400 to 599. Tachyon checks the answer against the Problem model, and OPTIONS and /api.json list OrderNotFound with status 404 and the Problem shape. The nearest type wins: a handler for a subclass runs before a handler for its base class. Go matches with errors.As, so a wrapped error matches too. Rust matches the error type of the controller method's Result. An error that no method handles, or an error thrown inside a handler, keeps the fixed 500 answer. Nothing from the error reaches the client unless the handler returns it. The order is: controller, then error handler, then middleware after.

route-access.title: Who may call a route
route-access.summary: Every route says who may call it: anyone, any signed-in user, or only some roles. One identity provider class tells Tachyon who is signed in, and Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before your code runs.

sections.heading: Every route says who may call it
sections.body: Tachyon refuses every route until you say who may call it, like Spring Security when it denies by default. Write `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow` on the controller class or on a route method. `Public` means anyone may call the route. `SignedIn` means any signed-in user may call it. `Allow(Admin)` means only a signed-in user with the role `Admin` may call it; name more roles with commas. The rule on a method wins over the rule on its class. A route without a rule stops the build with `TY1322`, and no setting turns this check off.
sections.code:
Who may call a route (ADR 0068)

  Annotation       Who may call the route               Answer to anyone else
  @Public          anyone, also a caller who is not     (none)
                   signed in
  @SignedIn        any signed-in user                   401 when nobody is signed in
  @Allow(Admin)    a signed-in user with the role       401 when nobody is signed in,
                   Admin (list more roles with commas)  403 for another role

- Write the rule on the controller class, on a route method, or on both.
  The rule on the method wins.
- A route with no rule stops the build with TY1322. There is no switch to
  turn this off.
- A role is a type: an empty class in server/roles/<Role>.<ext>.
  Java writes Admin.class, Kotlin and PHP Admin::class, C# typeof(Admin).
- @SocketRoute classes take the rule on the class. @StreamRoute methods take
  it like any other route.

sections.heading: Tell Tachyon who is signed in
sections.body: A project with `SignedIn` or `Allow` routes has exactly one class marked `IdentityProvider`, in `server/controllers/<Name>IdentityProvider.<ext>`. It is like a Spring `AuthenticationProvider`. Its one method, `identify` (`Identify` in C# and Go), takes the request in the language's own type and returns the signed-in user with the names of their roles, such as `{ "user": "ada", "roles": ["Admin"] }`, or no value when nobody is signed in. It may also read one header or cookie with `FromHeader` or `FromCookie`. Tachyon calls it before every `SignedIn` or `Allow` route, in any Yon language. When `identify` returns no value, Tachyon answers 401. When the user has none of the roles, Tachyon answers 403. In both cases the route method never runs. When `identify` fails, Tachyon answers 500 and the route method does not run either. A `SignedIn` or `Allow` route without an identity provider, a second identity provider, or an `Allow` role with no type in `server/roles/` stops the build with `TY1322` or `TY1323`. A test unit calls a controller method directly, so no identity is needed there. To test the identity provider itself, a test unit builds it and fakes its collaborators with `@Fake`.

sections.heading: Who may call a route in every Yon language
sections.body: Choose a language below. The controller class says `SignedIn`, so any signed-in user may call its routes. `getOrders` says `Public`, so anyone may call it: the rule on a method wins over the rule on its class. `deleteOrders` says `Allow(Admin)`, so only a user with the role `Admin` may call it. A role is a type: an empty class in `server/roles/`, named after the role. The one class marked `IdentityProvider` says who is signed in. Its method `identify` reads the request in the language's own type and returns the user and the names of their roles, or no value when nobody is signed in. PHP has no request object, so its `identify` reads `$_SERVER`. Lua reads the request table, `request.headers["authorization"]`, with the header name in lower case. With the header `authorization: ada-token`, every route answers. With `bob-token`, `DELETE /orders` answers 403. Without the header, `POST /orders` and `DELETE /orders` answer 401. The example keeps its sessions in a constant; a real app checks a token or a session store.

#[IdentityProvider]
class AppIdentityProvider {
    private const SESSIONS = [
        'ada-token' => ['user' => 'ada', 'roles' => ['Admin']],
        'bob-token' => ['user' => 'bob', 'roles' => []],
    ];

    public function identify(): ?array {
        return $this->session($this->token($_SERVER));
    }

    /** @param array<string, mixed> $server */
    private function token(array $server): string {
        return strval($server['HTTP_AUTHORIZATION'] ?? '');
    }

    private function session(string $token): ?array {
        return self::SESSIONS[$token] ?? null;
    }
}

open System.Net.Http
open Models

[<IdentityProvider>]
type AppIdentityProvider() =
    static let sessions =
        dict [
            "ada-token", { User = "ada"; Roles = [| "Admin" |] }
            "bob-token", { User = "bob"; Roles = [||] }
        ]

    member this.Identify(request: HttpRequestMessage) : Identity option =
        this.Find(string request.Headers.Authorization)

    member private this.Find(token: string) : Identity option =
        match sessions.TryGetValue(token) with
        | true, identity -> Some identity
        | _ -> None

application-configuration.title: Settings and configuration
application-configuration.summary: Server settings live in `server/application.json`. Page settings live in `client/manifest.json`. Secrets, such as passwords, live in `.env` and never reach the browser. A class marked `Settings` gets its field values from these files.

sections.heading: Configuration and secrets are separate
sections.body: Tachyon uses two configuration files, one for each realm (Tac for the client, Yon for the server). client/manifest.json is the web app manifest. A browser uses it to install the app. Its tac member is the public configuration for Tac. The whole file goes to every visitor. server/application.json belongs only to Yon. The file itself is the yon namespace. Yon reads its members as yon.* paths, with no root key. For example, server.port is yon.server.port. If this file still contains a tac section or a yon wrapper, the build stops. Its message says what to do. JSON keys use lowercase letters and digits. In a TAC_ or YON_ name, each underscore stands for one level of nested key. For example, YON_CATALOG_PAGE_SIZE maps to yon.catalog.page.size. The JSON files refuse secret fields and URLs that contain credentials. Runtime secrets go in .env. They use only YON_ names and stay literal strings (Tachyon does not change them). They never enter client bundles. The tac member of the manifest follows the same key rules. It also refuses names that look like secrets. When yon.datasource or yon.redis is configured, Yon starts that managed resource before it accepts requests. The PostgreSQL example needs a running database and the .env credentials below. You create the schema and run migrations yourself. Tac never receives database connections. The build refuses a value that looks like a password, a token or a key in the code, a template or either public file (`TY1324`), and it names .env instead.

sections.heading: Reading settings and choosing configuration
sections.body: Settings declares a name prefix. The class's own fields are the settings: each field's type and initial value give the type and default, and @Min and @Max on a field give its limits. Rust and Go fields have no initial values, so their defaults go in Settings({"defaults":{...}}). Standard snapshots that you give yourself use the tac and yon namespaces. Every underscore becomes a nested key, so YON_APP_SIZE means yon.app.size. Flat in-memory maps are still an optional adapter input. They are not server/application.json syntax. Binding fails for unknown keys under the selected prefix. It also fails for missing fields and for fields with the wrong type. Setting binds standard paths of the same framework: tac.* for Tac and yon.* for Yon. Its ${path:default} form is annotation syntax. It does not insert values into JSON files. WhenProfile and WhenSetting read context values that cannot change and that you give yourself. Error messages are redacted: they hide the values. Binding does not create a DTO (data transfer object), give environment permissions or publish server secrets. Lua has no tab here: a Lua model cannot carry Settings or Setting yet, so the build refuses it with TY1310.

use Models\Settings;

#[RequestRoute("/settings")]

class SettingsController {
    #[GetRoute]
    public function getSettings(): Settings {
        $application = json_decode(getenv('YON_APPLICATION_JSON'), true, 512, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);

        $endpoint = Behaviors::values(Endpoint::class, $application);
        $profile = $endpoint['profile'];
        $signal = new BehaviorSignal();

            'partition' => 'public-catalog',

sections.heading: client/manifest.json, field by field
sections.body:
The manifest is a standard web app manifest. A browser reads its standard members to install the application. Tachyon reads some of the same members for a native build. It also adds one member of its own, tac, and a browser ignores it. The whole file is public, because the build publishes it at /manifest.webmanifest. Do not put anything private in it. The file is plain JSON: if you compute a value, write the generated client/manifest.json before you run ty bundle. There is no tac.config.js and no tachyon.json, and a top-level tachyon member is refused: a build refuses each one and says where its values moved (ADR 0052).

tac holds two kinds of members. Your own members, such as tac.api.url, are the public configuration that services bind with Settings and Setting (TAC_ names and tac. paths). Tachyon's own members are settings for the build and the native host, not values for services: application, origin, scripts, blockingScripts, styles, styleSources, scriptSources, cache, metadata, sitemap, browserApis, nativeCapabilities, elements, python, budgets, outgoing, go, dotnet, implicitmembers, simplify, accessibility and the check switches below. Do not bind them in a service.

The standard `theme_color` member also becomes `<meta name="theme-color" content="...">` in every page head, HTML-escaped, when it is a text value that is not blank; a number or another JSON value writes no tag. The manifest has one theme color, so there is no light and dark pair. A web build reads the members it needs: scripts, blockingScripts and styles with their sources, cache rules, metadata, the origin, the sitemap, browserApis, outgoing hosts, budgets and python. `browserApis` lists the browser APIs that need the user's consent and that the services may use: any of `clipboard`, `share`, `notifications`, `geolocation` and `preferenceStrings`, each once, for example `"browserApis": ["clipboard", "geolocation"]`. Any other name stops the build (`TY1601`). The page refuses an API that is not listed. `nativeCapabilities` grants native capabilities separately: `["filePicker"]` is the only name today, and without it the file picker answers denied (see the feature Inject an OS file picker into a service). `outgoing.hosts` lists the other hosts that page code may send requests to; the page's `connect-src` allows only these, and the build refuses a request URL with any other host (`TY1326`). Each `scripts` entry is a deferred module that runs after the Tac runtime. Each `blockingScripts` entry is a classic script placed before the runtime, so it runs before the first paint, for example to apply a saved theme; the page waits for it, so keep it small and free of `import` and `export`. A native build takes its name, entry route, identifier, version, window and menus from this file only. `tac.application.menus` adds your own items to the File, View and Help menus of a macOS, Linux or Windows app; iOS and Android refuse it (`TY1601`; see Native menus). `tac.application.window.titleBar: "integrated"` draws the page under the macOS title bar, and `titleBarButtonInset` moves the window buttons (see Window controls).

These `check` settings each turn one build rule off while you migrate, for Tac code only: `tac.cohesion.check`, `tac.duplication.check`, `tac.dependencies.check`, `tac.names.check`, `tac.signatures.check`, `tac.constants.check`, `tac.visibility.check`, `tac.types.check` and `tac.tests.check`, each `false` (`tac.types.check` is off until you set it to `true`; see Cohesive services, Utilities, Dependencies point down, Plain-English names, Small signatures, Named values, Public only when used, Types in every language and Test units). `tac.accessibility.check: false` turns off the accessible-view check (`TY1336`, see Templates). `tac.budgets.script` and `tac.budgets.webassembly` set the size budget of every route in kilobytes (defaults 200 and 3584; without `tac.budgets.script`, a route that loads more than one web runtime gets a measured allowance for each runtime after the largest one), and `tac.budgets.check: false` turns that check off (`TY1337`, see Route size budgets). With `tac.python` and no `tac.budgets.script`, a route that uses a Python service gets a 512 KiB script budget. `tac.elements` lists the components that the build also exports as custom elements, such as `"elements": ["shop-counter"]`; a name without a hyphen or a name that is not a component stops the build (`TY1358`, see Components in other apps). `tac.simplify.suggest` set to `false` hides the simpler-form suggestions for Tac code, and `tac.implicitmembers.suggest` set to `true` shows the receiver suggestions too (off by default; see Simpler forms). `tac.names.words` lists words of your domain, such as a product name, that Tac names may use. `tac.go.compiler` chooses the Go compiler for Go web services: `"tinygo"` or `"go"`; without it a release build tries TinyGo first and falls back to Go (see WebAssembly compilers per language). `tac.dotnet.aot: true` compiles C# and F# web services ahead of time in a release build: faster for heavy computing, but a larger download.

`tac.application.rust` declares crates and helper executables for the Rust companion of a macOS, Linux or Windows app. Its `dependencies` and `platformDependencies` use exact Cargo versions, with optional `features` and `defaultFeatures`; platform keys are `macos`, `linux` and `windows`. Its `executables` maps up to eight program names to Rust class files under `client/`. A packaged desktop build compiles from the project's `vendor/rust/` folder offline and places each helper beside the app executable. The declaration needs a Rust service and does not add crate dependencies to a WebAssembly service. See Rust crates and helper executables under Native services.
sections.code:
name                                          browser, native
  The application's name. A native build names the app and its
  executable after it (short_name when name is absent). 1 to 64
  printable characters.

short_name                                    browser, native
  The label a launcher shows where name is too long.

start_url                                     browser, native
  The route the application opens at, and the entry route of a
  native build. A canonical local route, such as "/".

icons                                         browser, native
  [{ "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512" }], local bundle
  paths. A native build uses the largest raster icon; an SVG-only
  manifest gets no native icon rather than a blurry one.

theme_color                                    browser, build
  Published as written. Text that is not blank also becomes
  <meta name="theme-color" content="..."> in every page head,
  HTML-escaped. One color: there is no light and dark pair.

display, background_color, ...                        browser
  Standard members for a browser's install, published as written.

tac                                              Tac services
  Tac's public configuration (ADR 0034): any nested object, bound
  with TAC_ names and tac. paths, so tac.api.url is TAC_API_URL.
  Lowercase keys, and no secret-shaped names such as password.

tac.application.id                                     native
  Reverse-DNS bundle identifier, such as com.example.catalog.
  Derived from the project folder when absent.

tac.application.version                                native
  A portable version, such as 1.4.0 (1.0.0 when absent).

tac.application.window                                 native
  width and height the window opens at (1024 by 768 unless set,
  each 64 to 16384), minWidth and minHeight, and controls: which
  window controls a service may use through WindowControls (close,
  fullscreen, maximize, minimize, resize, title). None are granted
  unless listed. titleBar "integrated" lets a macOS page reach the
  top edge under the real window buttons ("standard" unless set;
  other targets keep the standard bar and the build prints a
  note), and titleBarButtonInset { "leading", "top" }, 0 to 200
  points each, moves those buttons (see Window controls).

tac.application.menus                           native desktop
  Your items in the File, View and Help menus of a macOS, Linux
  or Windows app: { "help": [{ "id": "guide", "label": "Guide",
  "route": "/guide", "shortcut": { "key": "g", "modifiers":
  ["command"] } }] }. Each item has a route (a static page) or an
  action { "service", "method", "event" } on a Rust application
  service. At most 64 items; iOS and Android refuse them (see
  Native menus).

tac.application.rust                            native desktop
  Rust companion crates and helpers. dependencies lists exact
  versions, or { "version", "features", "defaultFeatures" }.
  platformDependencies has macos, linux and windows tables.
  executables maps up to 8 names, such as "catalog-event", to
  client class paths, such as "/shared/native/EventEmitterMain.rs".
  Each class has pub fn run() -> i32. Crates come from vendor/rust
  at the project root; packaged builds run Cargo offline. Helpers
  go beside the app executable (see Rust crates and helper
  executables). These settings require a native Rust service.

tac.nativeCapabilities                                 native
  ["filePicker"]: native capabilities a native service may use.
  The only name today; without it the picker answers denied.

tac.origin                                              build
  The public address, such as https://example.com, without a path.
  It turns on the built-in sitemap.xml and robots.txt.

tac.scripts, tac.styles                                 build
  Up to 8 local paths each, linked into every page. A style is
  foundation CSS (colors, fonts, resets) unless styleSources says
  it is a pinned vendor file (TY1403). Each script is a deferred
  module that runs after the Tac runtime.

tac.blockingScripts                                     build
  Up to 8 local paths, each linked as a classic script before the
  Tac runtime, such as "/shared/scripts/ThemeDefault.js". It runs
  before the first paint, so it can apply a saved theme. The page
  waits for it: keep it small, with no import or export.

tac.styleSources, tac.scriptSources                     build
  Where each listed file comes from, keyed by its path:
  { "kind": "foundation" } for your own style, or a pinned vendor
  file with package, version, license and sha256 (styleSources
  adds "kind": "vendor"). A vendor script must also be in
  tac.scripts (TY1365). Tachyon publishes vendor files unchanged.

tac.outgoing.hosts                                      build
  Other hosts that page code may send requests to, such as
  ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example"]. The page's connect-src
  allows only these; any other request host stops the build
  (TY1326).

tac.python                                              build
  Exactly { "runtime": "pyodide-314.0.7", "profile": "offline" }
  to run Python services; other values are refused. The build
  copies the pinned Pyodide files from the Tachyon cache.

tac.elements                                            build
  Components to export as custom elements, such as
  ["shop-counter"]: one module each in .tachyon/elements/.

tac.cache                                               build
  Service-worker rules: [{ "path": "/api/*", "policy":
  "network-first" }]; cache-first, network-first or no-store.
  They answer navigations, assets and Cached HTTPClient GETs.

tac.metadata                                            build
  defaults, and routes keyed by route: title, description,
  canonical, image, siteName, lang, noindex.

tac.sitemap                                             build
  Values for a dynamic page route, read from a shared data file:
  { "/docs/_topic": { "data": "/shared/data/docs.json",
  "values": "/order" } }.

sections.heading: server/application.json, field by field
sections.body: This file is the configuration of Yon, and the file itself is the yon namespace. Its members are yon.* paths with no root key, so server.port is yon.server.port. Tachyon reads server, datasource, redis, topics and outgoing. server takes only host, port, hosts, proxies, environment and maxbody; with any other member of server the server does not start, and its message names the members it accepts. (server/packages/ is a folder for the native Go packages of Go Yon code, not a key; see Native Go packages.) server.hosts lists the extra names that a loopback server answers (`TY1366`), server.proxies lists the reverse proxies whose forwarding headers count (see The client address and forwarding headers), server.environment lists the variables of `ty`'s environment that handler processes may see, as names or prefix patterns such as `HD_*` (see Environment variables for handlers), topics.directory names the folder of the topic logs (data/topics unless set), and outgoing.hosts lists the hosts that Yon code may send requests to, and every other host is refused when Tachyon builds and when it runs (`TY1326`). Every other member belongs to the application, which reads it with Setting or Settings. A profile (a set of settings for one environment) is a file server/application-<profile>.json that YON_PROFILE selects. It has the same shape and merges over the base file, so its values win over the base values. Secrets never go in this file. A password is a YON_ name in the .env file at the project root. The file refuses names that look like secrets and URLs that contain credentials. Tachyon also reads the migration settings `cohesion.check`, `duplication.check`, `dependencies.check`, `names.check`, `signatures.check`, `constants.check`, `visibility.check`, `types.check` (off until you set it to `true`) and `tests.check` (the test-case rule `TY1339`, see Test units): `false` turns that build rule off for Yon code while you migrate. `simplify.suggest` set to `false` hides the simpler-form suggestions for Yon code (see Simpler forms). `implicitmembers.suggest` set to `true` shows the receiver suggestions for Yon code too (off by default). `names.words` lists words of your domain that Yon names may use.
sections.code:
server.host
  The address ty serve and ty start bind; 127.0.0.1 unless set.
  localhost or a name under .localhost (shop.localhost) binds
  127.0.0.1 and prints the name. Anything but loopback also needs
  --allow-non-loopback, and --host overrides it.

server.hosts
  Extra names that a loopback server answers, such as
  ["preview.example.com", "*.tunnel.example"]: names without
  scheme, port or path. Localhost names, IP addresses and the
  tac.origin host always work; other names get 403 (TY1366).

server.proxies
  The reverse proxies whose forwarding headers count, as IP
  addresses or CIDR ranges: ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.0.2.10"]. Empty
  unless set, so ty replaces Forwarded, X-Forwarded-* and X-Real-IP
  from every other peer with the real client address (ADR 0096).

server.environment
  The variables of ty's environment that handlers may see, beyond
  PATH, LANG, LC_ALL and TMPDIR: names or prefix patterns, such as
  ["HOME", "AWS_*", "HD_*"]. Empty unless set. "*" and entries
  that cover ty's own TAC_*, TACHYON_*, YON_* or proxy variables
  are refused (TY2010).

server.maxbody
  The largest request body that a route reads, in bytes: 1 MiB
  (1048576) unless set, at most 12 MiB (12582912). A larger body
  gets 413. Tachyon reads the rest of a larger body, up to 16 MiB,
  before it answers, so the sender sees the 413.

server.port
  The port, 0 to 65535. ty serve and ty start use 8080 unless
  set, ty preview uses 3000, and ty preview --static ignores it.
  0 picks a free port, and --port overrides it.

datasource.driver
  postgresql, mysql, mariadb, sqlserver, sqlite or fylo.

datasource.url
  Where the database is, without credentials:
  postgresql://db:5432/catalog, sqlite:///var/lib/catalog.db,
  sqlite::memory:, or fylo:///absolute/root for a FYLO store
  whose root folder already exists (a page reads at most the
  first 10,000 matching documents).

datasource.username
  The database user, usually YON_DATASOURCE_USERNAME in .env beside
  YON_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD, which only .env may hold. SQLite and FYLO
  take neither.

datasource.tls.ca
  Absolute path of a CA certificate to trust.

redis.url
  The Redis server: redis://, or rediss:// for TLS.

redis.username
  The Redis user, usually YON_REDIS_USERNAME in .env beside
  YON_REDIS_PASSWORD, which only .env may hold.

topics.directory
  The folder of the topic logs; data/topics unless set. A plain
  path inside the project or an absolute path with no symbolic
  link. Never inside .tachyon, which holds only generated files.

anything else
  The application's own settings. catalog.page.size is
  yon.catalog.page.size, and YON_CATALOG_PAGE_SIZE names it in
  Settings.

With any other member of server, the server does not start.

Limits: keys are lowercase letters and digits; at most 128 keys,
16 levels deep and 64 KiB per file. A tac section or a yon root key
stops the build and says where it belongs.

sections.heading: Profiles, paths and which value wins
sections.body: When the Yon server starts, YON_PROFILE selects server/application-<profile>.json. Objects merge recursively (at every level of nesting). An array in the profile replaces the base array. Tachyon does not join the two arrays. For the server host and port, the source with the highest priority wins. From highest to lowest, the sources are: CLI --host and --port flags that you pass, the profile file, the base server/application.json, and the command defaults. So a flag that you pass overrides yon.server.host and yon.server.port. Values from the parent application environment no longer override configuration or provide secrets. .env names map to paths by underscores. They are not interpolated (Tachyon does not replace references inside them). They cannot overwrite configuration paths. A .env file that sets a name Tachyon keeps for its own transport, profile, endpoint, runtime or isolation policy is refused: YON_PROFILE, YON_HOST, YON_HOSTNAME, YON_PORT, YON_ISOLATION, YON_SKIP_BUNDLE, YON_APPLICATION_JSON, YON_RESOURCE_ENDPOINT, YON_RESOURCE_TOKEN, YON_HANDLER_PROTOCOL, YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME, YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME, YON_RUBY_RUNTIME, YON_SERVER, and every name that starts with YON_SERVER_ or YON_FIRECRACKER_. Empty path segments, duplicate names, and a name that is both a scalar (a single value) and an object fail. Their errors are redacted, which means they hide the values. To expose the server beyond the local machine (non-loopback), you still need --allow-non-loopback. In production, a secret manager may mount the .env file. Tac builds read only the tac member of client/manifest.json. No profile is merged over it.

sections.heading: Access from every Yon language
sections.body: Code in every language reads the private YON_APPLICATION_JSON snapshot. Your code passes it to behavior binding; this does not happen automatically. Settings turns its prefixed names into nested paths. Setting names the full standard path directly. Return data, not a response object or a JSON string that you serialized yourself. This example returns only some fields, and none of them are secret. Never return the complete snapshot. Lua has no tab here: a Lua model cannot carry Settings or Setting yet, so the build refuses it with TY1310.

sections.heading: Swift: public configuration in native Tac
sections.body: Swift runs as native Tac on macOS and iOS, and as WebAssembly in the browser. It is not a Yon language. Only the public tac configuration may enter client code. The build publishes client/manifest.json, including its tac member, at /manifest.webmanifest. In the browser, a Swift service loads it through an HTTPClient (see Public Tac output and private Yon lifetime). A native service uses a loader that it owns, or public input. This short Swift service binds a public snapshot that it gets as input. The Settings and Setting classes are structs in `client/models/` (ADR 0092), and the service carries Service. It does not touch the private Yon configuration or .env. Nothing is injected here: the service binds the snapshot in its init.

sections.heading: Public Tac output and private Yon lifetime
sections.body: The build checks the tac member of client/manifest.json. It publishes the whole manifest at /manifest.webmanifest for web bundles and staged native bundles. A browser also finds it there to install the app. The manifest can have other members beside tac, and it still binds without changes. Only the tac member is configuration. Bind only the members that your application adds, such as tac.api.url here. Tachyon's own members, such as application, scripts, budgets or browserApis, are settings for the build, not values for services. The build never opens .env, never resolves production secrets and never publishes the Yon configuration. A browser service loads the published manifest through an HTTPClient and binds it with Behaviors.values and the PublicSettings model in client/models, whose Setting reads tac.api.url. Every compiled Tac language can read such a model (ADR 0092). In this example the service loads the manifest when you press the button. JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, C# and Ruby inject the client with Needs. F# builds it with ApplicationClient(). In these languages except Java, Tachyon's browser transport sends the GET request to the server of the page: the compiled languages need an ApplicationSetup, and it gives the client no adapter. In Java, the HTTP adapter of ApplicationSetup answers it in the page with the public tac member, as in Outgoing HTTP: Tac. A native service loads the manifest itself with its SDK, and it owns that loader (see Swift: public configuration in native Tac). The browser transport is network-only (no-store) unless a read is marked Cached. It is not an offline cache loader. A change to client/manifest.json causes a development reload for Tac. A change to Yon settings or .env secrets needs a server restart. The deployment controls runtime executables, isolation policy, environment allowlists and capabilities. They are not options in the application files. YON_APPLICATION_JSON is reserved output of the supervisor. An operator cannot use it as an override. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. C++ has no tab either, because the build refuses Setting in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

calling-the-server.title: Calling the server from a page
calling-the-server.summary: A page gets data from the server through a client class. Mark the class with `HTTPClient` and its methods with `GetRequest`, `PostRequest` and the other request annotations. A service gets the client with `Needs` and calls its methods. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java and Ruby, a client whose Setup gives it no adapter sends its request through the browser to the server of the page, without cookies. A C++ client has no Setup, so it always uses this transport. This browser transport refuses every other origin. Python and Lua cannot use `HTTPClient` (`TY1308`). A request to another host goes through a Setup adapter, and that host must be listed in `tac.outgoing.hosts`.

sections.heading: Client classes that call the server
sections.body: Use HTTPClient on a client class whose methods have empty bodies: a client is a contract with no implementation, and Tachyon writes each request. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. C++ has no tab here either, because a C++ client has no Setup adapter yet: it always sends its requests through the browser (see the C++ section of Calling the server; ADR 0099). Use GetRequest, PostRequest, PutRequest, PatchRequest or DeleteRequest on its methods. Needs injects the client into a service without a constructor. Browser JavaScript and TypeScript clients send bounded JSON to the same origin. They reject redirects, send no credentials and cancel when their owner is disposed. Other languages declare the client as a contract (an interface, trait, protocol or abstract interface class), and its Setup may give it an explicitly configured HTTP adapter. Tachyon builds the client and its context from the Setup that the `setup` option names; without the option it uses `<Name>Setup`, such as `CatalogSetup` for `CatalogClient`. In Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby, C# and F#, a client whose Setup gives it no adapter sends its request through the browser to the server of the page, without cookies (see the sections below). A Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby or C# service can inject the client with Needs too. In Ruby, `#[Needs]` stands above `attr_reader :catalog_client`, with `# @return [CatalogClient]` between them. A service in the other languages builds the client itself. In this example, CatalogSetup's adapter answers with two product names. Like a Spring @Configuration, a Setup is configured once per page: every client, store and service context built from it shares the same adapters until the last of them is disposed. In Yon it is configured once per server process. For now, the browser services in Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust and Dart each still get their own copy of a Setup, so two of these services that use the same client do not share its adapters yet. The Go services of a page build into one Go package with one Setup, so they share it (ADR 0045). JavaScript and TypeScript services import one Setup class from the shared behavior runtime module, so they share its definition, its static fields and its adapters (ADR 0022). The clients inside one service already share them. A Service cannot also be an HTTPClient (TY1308). A Tac service never calls fetch itself (TY1361). A read is sent no-store by default, so it is always fresh. To keep a read, use the cache annotations on the client: CacheSettings on the class, Cached on the read, and ClearCache or UpdateCache on the write that changes it. In JavaScript and TypeScript a Cached GET is also a public read, so the service worker may answer it by the manifest's tac.cache rules. HTTPClient takes no cache option: the build refuses `{"cache": ...}` and names CacheSettings and Cached (ADR 0087). See the [routing annotation glossary](/docs/routing-annotations). Another host needs its name in `tac.outgoing.hosts` or `outgoing.hosts`; Tachyon refuses every other host when it builds and when it runs (`TY1326`).

#[Service]
class CatalogService
  #[Needs]
  # @return [CatalogClient]
  attr_reader :catalog_client

  # @return [Array<String>]
  attr_reader :products
  # @return [String]
  attr_reader :error

  def initialize
    @products = []
    @error = ""
  end

  # @return [void]
  def load
    show(fetch)
  end

  private

  # @return [Array<String>, nil]
  def fetch
    catalog_client.all
  rescue StandardError
    nil
  end

  # @param answer [Array<String>, nil]
  # @return [void]
  def show(answer)
    return show_failure unless answer.is_a?(Array)

    @products = answer
    @error = ""
  end

  # @return [void]
  def show_failure
    @error = "Products could not be loaded. Please retry."
  end
end

files.code:
open System.Threading.Tasks

[<Service>]
type CatalogService() =
    let catalog = CatalogClient()
    member val products : string list = [] with get, set
    member val error : string = "" with get, set

    member this.Load() : Task =
        task {
            let! names = this.Fetch()
            this.Show(names)
        }

    member private this.Fetch() : Task<string list option> =
        task {
            try
                let! answer = catalog.All()
                return Some(answer.Items |> Array.map (fun item -> item.Text) |> List.ofArray)
            with _ ->
                return None
        }

    member private this.Show(names: string list option) : unit =
        match names with
        | Some list ->
            this.products <- list
            this.error <- ""
        | None -> this.ShowFailure()

    member private this.ShowFailure() : unit =
        this.error <- "Products could not be loaded. Please retry."

The empty GreetingSetup uses Tachyon’s default same-origin asynchronous browser transport; the typed Greeting answer is rendered after Yon replies. Credentials are omitted. sections.heading: Rust awaits a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A Rust service gets its HTTPClient with `Needs` and awaits it with `.await`. The client trait declares `async fn read(&self) -> BehaviorResult<Greeting>`, and Tachyon writes the method. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. The answer becomes the typed `Greeting` model from `client/models`; an answer of another shape fails with the error code `HTTP_RESPONSE`. A failed request gives the error code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`, and the `?` operator passes it on. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. While an `async` method waits, the page reads the fields as they were when the method started, and other calls to the same service wait for it. Removing the component cancels the request. `Retry`, `MaxAtOnce` and `AllOrNothing` belong on a service method; the build refuses them on a client request method. In a native app and in a test unit there is no browser transport: the request fails with `HTTP_MISSING` unless the Setup gives the client an adapter. In a test, a Fake field `std::cell::RefCell<Option<std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>>>` can supply the client; while it is empty, the service gets a client whose requests the TestSetup adapter answers. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby or Lua answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.

sections.heading: Go waits for a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A Go service gets its HTTPClient with `// @Needs` above a field such as `greetingClient *GreetingClient`, and calls it like any Go function: `greeting, err := service.greetingClient.Read()`. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own goroutine, so the call waits for the server while the page keeps working; a method that waits returns a promise to the page. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. The answer is read into the `Greeting` model from `client/models` with its `json` tags, and a request body model is written with them as `encoding/json` writes it: `omitempty` leaves out an empty string or a nil pointer instead of sending `""` or `null`, `omitzero` leaves out a zero value (an `IsZero` method decides when there is one), `string` sends a number or a bool as text, and `json:"-"` leaves the field out; an answer of another shape gives an error whose code is `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and a failed request gives the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`; `BehaviorErrorStatus(err)` gives the status number of an `HTTP_STATUS` answer, such as 404. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. Removing the component or leaving the page cancels the request: the page stops the service at once and runs its `OnStop`, the method gets the error code `CANCELLED` afterwards, and a call the method makes after that also gets `CANCELLED` without reaching the server. A getter, a setter or an `OnStart` method cannot wait for the server: the call fails with `HTTP_REQUEST`. A test unit has no browser transport (`HTTP_MISSING`). In a test, `test.construct(service)` fills the `Needs` fields from the `// @Fake` fields of the test; an empty Fake client field gets a client made with `NewGreetingClientWith`, so the TestSetup adapter answers. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby or Lua answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.

sections.heading: Kotlin suspends for a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A Kotlin HTTPClient is an interface whose methods are `suspend fun` without a body, such as `suspend fun read(): Greeting`. Tachyon writes the method and reads the answer into the `Greeting` data class from `client/models`; an answer of another shape gives a `Behaviors.Failure` whose code is `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and a failed request gives the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`. A service gets the client with `@Needs private val greetingClient: GreetingClient` and calls it from a `suspend fun`. sections.heading: Swift awaits a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A Swift HTTPClient is a protocol whose methods are `async throws` and have no body, such as `func read() async throws -> Greeting`. Tachyon writes the method and decodes the answer into the `Greeting` struct from `client/models`, which is `Codable`.
