While the method waits for the server, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. Removing the component cancels the request, and the promise is rejected with the code `CANCELLED`. In a Swift test unit, a Fake field `var greetingClient: GreetingClient? = nil` can supply the client to `let service: GreetingService = try construct()`; while it is `nil`, the service gets a client whose requests the TestSetup adapter answers. In a native macOS or iOS app and in a test unit there is no browser transport: the request fails with `HTTP_MISSING` unless the Setup gives the client an adapter, and a native app runs an `async` method to the end before it answers, as before. sections.heading: Ruby waits for a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A Ruby HTTPClient is a class whose methods have empty bodies, such as `def read` with `end` on the next line. Tachyon writes each method. The `# @return [Greeting]` comment above the method names the answer: Tachyon reads the answer into the model `Greeting` from `client/models`. `# @return [Array<Greeting>]` reads a list of models, and `String`, `Integer`, `Float` or `Boolean` read a plain value. `Hash` and `Object` keep the answer as it is. An answer of another shape raises a `BehaviorError` whose `behavior_code` is `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and a failed request raises the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`. A service gets the client with `#[Needs]` above `attr_reader :greeting_client`, with `# @return [GreetingClient]` between them, and calls it from an ordinary method. Ruby has no async keyword, so Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own Ruby fiber. When the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once. When it waits for the server, the fiber pauses, the page keeps working, other calls to the service run, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. `OnStart` cannot wait: a request there fails with `HTTP_REQUEST`. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again; a failed `ClearCache` keeps the cached answer. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. Removing the component cancels the request, and the promise is rejected with the code `CANCELLED`. A Ruby test unit runs in CRuby and has no browser transport: there a client without an adapter fails with `Required behavior adapter is missing.` The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. #[Service]
class GreetingService
  #[Needs]
  # @return [GreetingClient]
  attr_reader :greeting_client

  #[Needs]
  # @return [OverrideClient]
  attr_reader :override_client

  # @return [String]
  attr_reader :message, :custom
  # @return [Integer]
  attr_reader :loads, :clears

  def initialize
    @message = ""
    @custom = ""
    @loads = 0
    @clears = 0
  end

  # @return [void]
  def ask
    @loads += 1
    @message = greeting_client.read.message
  end

  # @return [void]
  def clear
    greeting_client.clear
    @clears += 1
  end

  # @return [void]
  def ask_custom
    @custom = override_client.read.message
  end
end

files.name: client/services/HttpProbeService.fs
files.code:
open System.Threading.Tasks

[<Service>]
[<Lifetime({"value":"prototype"})>]
type HttpProbeService() =
    static let clientName: string = "greeting"
    static let requestPath: string = "/api/greeting"
    static let messageField: string = "message"

    let signal: BehaviorSignal = new BehaviorSignal()
    let context: BehaviorContext = Behaviors.create(typeof<BrowserHttpSetup>, "fsharp-greeting", signal)

    member val Last: string = "" with get, set

    member this.Read() : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
        task {
            let! answer = context.restClient(clientName).get(requestPath).retrieve()
            this.Last <- answer.Get(messageField).Text
            return answer
        }

    [<OnStop>]
    member this.Close() : unit =
        context.Dispose()
        signal.Dispose()

sections.heading: C++ awaits a real Yon endpoint
sections.summary: A C++ service gets its HTTPClient with `[[Needs]] GreetingClient& greetingClient;` and waits for it with `co_await`. A method that returns `Task<void>` or `Task<T>` is a C++20 coroutine; the page awaits it like any asynchronous service method. The client class in `client/remotes` declares `Task<Greeting> read();` under `[[GetRequest("/greeting")]]`, and Tachyon writes the method. The request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies, through the browser transport that Rust and C# use. The answer becomes the typed `Greeting` model from `client/models`, read by the codec that Tachyon generates for it. A failed request throws `tachyon::http::HttpRequestException`, whose `code()` is the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`; when the exception leaves the method, the page's promise rejects with that code. `{id}` in a request path takes the parameter of the same name, `[[RequestBody]]` sends a parameter as the JSON body, `[[RequestParam]]` adds it to the query and `[[RequestHeader("X-Name")]]` sends it as a header. The client types follow .NET's System.Net.Http: `tachyon::http::HttpClient`, `HttpRequestMessage`, `HttpResponseMessage` and `HttpContent` (ADR 0099). Cached, ClearCache and Setup adapters are not in C++ yet; the build refuses Cached in C++ Tac code with TY1308. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby or Lua answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.

sections.heading: What the browser transport allows
sections.body:
The browser transport of Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby, C#, F# and C++ clients has fixed limits, so one page cannot flood the server or read too much:

A request, with its path, query, headers and body, may hold at most 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes); a larger one fails with `HTTP_REQUEST`. An answer may hold at most 1 MiB. A larger answer fails with `HTTP_LIMIT`.

A page may have at most 64 requests waiting at the same time; one more fails with `HTTP_CAPACITY`. A request waits at most 60 seconds.

The request must go to the origin of the page. Another origin fails with `HTTP_ORIGIN`. A redirect fails too.

The browser sends no cookies and no other credentials. The transport refuses the headers `Cookie`, `Host`, `Origin`, `Referer`, `Connection`, `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`, and every header that starts with `Sec-` or `Proxy-`, with `HTTP_HEADER`.

A request is not kept in the browser cache, except a public read marked `Cached`. A request with an `Authorization` header is never kept.

An answer that does not have the shape of the model fails with `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and an answer with an error status fails with `HTTP_STATUS`. The transport gives the page the status number with that code but never the body of the answer; in Go, `BehaviorErrorStatus(err)` reads it, such as 404. Removing the component that started a request cancels it (ADR 0090).

server-data.title: Server data
server-data.summary: Yon can connect to a SQL database, to the FYLO document store and to Redis for you. You name them in `server/application.json`, and a Store class gets them with `Needs`. Values always go in as parameters: Tachyon refuses query text built from pieces. With FYLO, DataSource also reads and changes documents by id, scrolls through any number of them with a cursor, manages collections and runs a durable queue.

sections.heading: Yon-managed SQL and Redis
sections.body: Configure resources as datasource and redis in server/application.json. Yon reads them as the yon.datasource and yon.redis paths. Yon creates the connections and manages them. Needs injects (gives) DataSource and RedisTemplate into stores and services in every Yon language except Lua: a Lua class that needs them stops the build with `TY2015` (ADR 0085). Browser Tac code never receives these resources or their secrets. Tachyon never creates or migrates (changes) a database schema (the tables and their columns) by itself. SQL over the network uses verified TLS (an encrypted connection with a checked certificate). A configured driver must connect successfully before the server starts. You still configure native Tac clients manually. Pass every value as a parameter, such as `query("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name = $1", [name])`: query text built by joining values stops the build with `TY1325`. Redis keys and values are always parameters.

sections.heading: DataSource in a service, in every Yon language
sections.body: Choose one language. Lua has no tab here: Lua Yon classes have no server resources yet, so the build refuses DataSource in Lua with `TY2015` (ADR 0085). Copy server/application.json and that language's service and controller. GET /catalog queries the managed in-memory SQLite datasource. It returns [{"amount":42}]. In the controller language, you need no constructor of your own, no module manifest and no database library. The same query works with each SQL dialect. For real tables, bind values as parameters (do not paste them into the SQL text). Use the driver's placeholder syntax shown above. Run database schema migrations (changes to tables) outside controllers. The service asks for DataSource with Needs, like a Spring service that asks for a JdbcTemplate, and the controller asks for the service. F# takes the DataSource, and the controller takes the service, as primary constructor parameters. Raw SQL belongs in a service because a Store has no implementation: a Store names an Entity, and Tachyon writes each of its queries (see Data access). The query text is one literal, and values go in the parameter list; Tachyon refuses query text built from pieces (`TY1325`). Lua has no tab here: DataSource is a resource, and a Lua class that needs it stops the build with `TY2015` (ADR 0085).

sections.heading: FYLO documents and queue, in every Yon language
sections.body:
Configure the `fylo` driver and every Yon language except Lua can use the FYLO document store and its queue through the injected DataSource. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses a DataSource in Lua Yon code with `TY2015` (ADR 0085): write the class that needs it in another Yon language. Choose one language and copy server/application.json with that language's service and controller (Go also needs its three models). GET /events answers {"found":"deploy","patched":7,"pages":2,"seen":3,"job":{"app":"web"},"gone":true,"dropped":true}.

Collections: `createCollection(name)` creates a collection and does nothing when it already exists, `dropCollection(name)` answers false when there was nothing to drop, and `collectionExists(name)` answers true or false. A collection name has 2 to 64 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starts and ends with a letter or digit, and is not a FYLO reserved word, so `hd-events` works and `../etc`, `hd_events` and `Events` are refused with `TY2160`. Store tables on FYLO follow the same rule.

Documents: `insert(collection, document)` stores a document and answers it with the `id` that FYLO assigned (Go answers the id itself). FYLO assigns identifiers, so a document that already has an id is refused. `findById(collection, id)` answers the newest version of the document, or null when there is none, like `findById` in Spring Data. `patch(collection, id, fields)` changes only the named top-level fields and keeps every other field, like `Update.set` in Spring Data MongoDB: a null value stores null, and a nested object replaces the old one. The change and the read of the result happen in one step, so patches that run at the same time never lose each other's fields. It answers the patched document, or null when the id does not exist, and it cannot change the id. `deleteById(collection, id)` answers true, or false when the document was already gone.

Scrolling: `scroll(collection, where, cursor, size)` reads one page of at most `size` documents (1 to 100, 20 by default) in id order, which is the order FYLO created them in. `where` is null or an object of field values that must all be equal. Pass a null cursor (an empty string in Go and Rust) for the first page, and then the `nextCursor` of the page before; `nextCursor` is null on the last page. There is no offset and no 10,000 limit, like the scroll API (`Window`) of Spring Data. The first page takes a snapshot of every match, so later inserts and changes do not move documents between pages; it may take up to 30 seconds, and the matches of one scroll must fit in 8 MiB. A cursor is opaque text that lasts 15 minutes in the server that made it; reading the same cursor again reads the same page. A server keeps at most 8 scrolls open: a ninth scroll ends the oldest one, and its cursor then counts as expired. After a cursor expires or the server restarts, start again from the first page.

Queue: FYLO has a durable queue, and DataSource reaches it with no broker. `publish(topic, payload, key)` adds a message and answers its id; publishing again with the same key and payload answers the first id instead of adding a copy. `claim(topic, group, maxMessages, leaseMs)` hands out up to `maxMessages` deliveries (1 to 100), each with `id`, `receipt`, `attempt` and `payload`, and hides them from other workers of the same group for `leaseMs` milliseconds. `ack(topic, group, delivery)` finishes a delivery; `nack(topic, group, delivery, delayMs)` gives it back to be claimed again after `delayMs`. A delivery that is not acknowledged before its lease ends is claimed again, so delivery is at least once: write handlers that can safely run twice. After the third attempt FYLO keeps the message as a dead letter. A receipt from an expired lease is refused. Topic and group names have 1 to 127 ASCII letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores.

These methods need the FYLO datasource; the SQL drivers refuse them with `TY2160`. In Go, `FindById` and `Patch` decode into a model and answer whether the document exists, `Scroll` answers a `DocumentWindow`, and `Claim` answers `QueueDelivery` values; `Decode` turns their JSON into your models.

@service
class EventService:
    _COLLECTION = "hd-events"
    _DEPLOYS = {"kind": "deploy"}
    _CHANGE = {"count": 7}
    _PAGE_SIZE = 2
    _TOPIC = "app.render"
    _GROUP = "renderers"

    def report(self) -> dict[str, object]:
        collection = self._COLLECTION
        self.data_source.create_collection(collection)
        event_id = self.data_source.insert(collection, self._DEPLOYS)["id"]
        self.data_source.insert(collection, self._DEPLOYS)
        self.data_source.insert(collection, self._DEPLOYS)
        found = self.data_source.find_by_id(collection, event_id)
        patched = self.data_source.patch(collection, event_id, self._CHANGE)

        job = self._run_job()
        self.data_source.delete_by_id(collection, event_id)
        gone = self.data_source.find_by_id(collection, event_id) is None
        dropped = self.data_source.drop_collection(collection)
        return {"found": found["kind"], "patched": patched["count"], **scrolled, "job": job, "gone": gone, "dropped": dropped}

    def _count_pages(self) -> dict[str, int]:
        pages, seen, cursor, more = 0, 0, None, True
        while more:
            window = self.data_source.scroll(self._COLLECTION, self._DEPLOYS, cursor, self._PAGE_SIZE)
            pages += 1
            seen += len(window["content"])
            cursor = window["nextCursor"]
            more = cursor is not None
        return {"pages": pages, "seen": seen}

        topic = self._TOPIC
        self.data_source.publish(topic, {"app": "web"}, "render:web")
        delivery = self.data_source.claim(topic, self._GROUP, 1, 30000)[0]
        self.data_source.ack(topic, self._GROUP, delivery)

@Service
class EventService {
  private static final String COLLECTION = "hd-events"
  private static final Map DEPLOYS = [kind: "deploy"]
  private static final Map CHANGE = [count: 7]
  private static final int PAGE_SIZE = 2
  private static final String TOPIC = "app.render"
  private static final String GROUP = "renderers"

  @Needs
  DataSource dataSource

  Map<String, Object> report() {
    dataSource.createCollection(COLLECTION)
    String id = (String) ((Map) dataSource.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)).id
    dataSource.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)
    dataSource.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)
    Map found = (Map) dataSource.findById(COLLECTION, id)
    Map patched = (Map) dataSource.patch(COLLECTION, id, CHANGE)
    Map<String, Object> report = countPages()
    report.found = found.kind
    report.patched = patched.count
    report.job = runJob()
    dataSource.deleteById(COLLECTION, id)
    report.gone = dataSource.findById(COLLECTION, id) == null
    report.dropped = dataSource.dropCollection(COLLECTION)
    return report
  }

  private Map<String, Object> countPages() {
    int pages = 0
    int seen = 0
    String cursor = null
    boolean more = true
    while (more) {
      Map window = (Map) dataSource.scroll(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS, cursor, PAGE_SIZE)
      pages += 1
      seen += ((List) window.content).size()
      cursor = (String) window.nextCursor
      more = cursor != null
    }
    return [pages: pages, seen: seen]
  }

  private Object runJob() {
    dataSource.publish(TOPIC, [app: "web"], "render:web")
    Map delivery = (Map) ((List) dataSource.claim(TOPIC, GROUP, 1, 30000)).get(0)
    dataSource.ack(TOPIC, GROUP, delivery)
    return delivery.payload
  }
}

[<Service>]
type EventService(dataSource: DataSource) =
    static let collection = "hd-events"
    static let deploys = {| kind = "deploy" |}
    static let change = {| count = 7 |}
    static let pageSize = 2
    static let topic = "app.render"
    static let group = "renderers"

    member this.Report() : obj =
        dataSource.CreateCollection(collection) |> ignore
        let id = dataSource.Insert(collection, deploys).GetProperty("id").GetString()
        dataSource.Insert(collection, deploys) |> ignore
        dataSource.Insert(collection, deploys) |> ignore
        let found = dataSource.FindById(collection, id)
        let patched = dataSource.Patch(collection, id, change)
        let pages, seen = this.CountPages()
        let job = this.RunJob()
        dataSource.DeleteById(collection, id) |> ignore
        let gone = dataSource.FindById(collection, id).ValueKind = System.Text.Json.JsonValueKind.Null
        let dropped = dataSource.DropCollection(collection).GetBoolean()
        box (dict [
            "found", box (found.GetProperty("kind").GetString())
            "patched", box (patched.GetProperty("count").GetInt32())
            "pages", box pages
            "seen", box seen
            "job", box job
            "gone", box gone
            "dropped", box dropped ])

    member private this.CountPages() : int * int =
        let mutable pages = 0
        let mutable seen = 0
        let mutable cursor : string = null
        let mutable more = true
        while more do
            let window = dataSource.Scroll(collection, deploys, cursor, pageSize)
            pages <- pages + 1
            seen <- seen + window.GetProperty("content").GetArrayLength()
            cursor <- window.GetProperty("nextCursor").GetString()
            more <- not (isNull cursor)
        (pages, seen)

    member private this.RunJob() =
        dataSource.Publish(topic, {| app = "web" |}, "render:web") |> ignore
        let delivery = dataSource.Claim(topic, group, 1, 30000).[0]
        dataSource.Ack(topic, group, delivery) |> ignore
        delivery.GetProperty("payload")

class EventService {

    $this->dataSource->insert(self::COLLECTION, self::DEPLOYS);
    $this->dataSource->insert(self::COLLECTION, self::DEPLOYS);
    $found = $this->dataSource->findById(self::COLLECTION, $id);
    $patched = $this->dataSource->patch(self::COLLECTION, $id, self::CHANGE);
    $scrolled = $this->countPages();
    $job = $this->runJob();
    $this->dataSource->deleteById(self::COLLECTION, $id);
    $gone = $this->dataSource->findById(self::COLLECTION, $id) === null;
    $dropped = $this->dataSource->dropCollection(self::COLLECTION);

    $pages = 0;
    $seen = 0;
    $cursor = null;
    $more = true;

      $seen += count($window['content']);
      $cursor = $window['nextCursor'];

#[Service]
class EventService
  COLLECTION = "hd-events"
  DEPLOYS = { "kind" => "deploy" }.freeze
  CHANGE = { "count" => 7 }.freeze
  PAGE_SIZE = 2
  TOPIC = "app.render"
  GROUP = "renderers"

  #[Needs]
  # @return [DataSource]
  attr_reader :data_source

  # @return [Hash]
  def report
    data_source.create_collection(COLLECTION)
    id = data_source.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)["id"]
    data_source.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)
    data_source.insert(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS)
    found = data_source.find_by_id(COLLECTION, id)
    patched = data_source.patch(COLLECTION, id, CHANGE)
    scrolled = count_pages
    job = run_job
    data_source.delete_by_id(COLLECTION, id)
    gone = data_source.find_by_id(COLLECTION, id).nil?
    dropped = data_source.drop_collection(COLLECTION)
    { "found" => found["kind"], "patched" => patched["count"], "job" => job, "gone" => gone, "dropped" => dropped }.merge(scrolled)
  end

  private

  # @return [Hash]
  def count_pages
    pages = 0
    seen = 0
    cursor = nil
    more = true
    while more
      window = data_source.scroll(COLLECTION, DEPLOYS, cursor, PAGE_SIZE)
      pages += 1
      seen += window["content"].length
      cursor = window["nextCursor"]
      more = !cursor.nil?
    end
    { "pages" => pages, "seen" => seen }
  end

  # @return [Hash]
  def run_job
    data_source.publish(TOPIC, { "app" => "web" }, "render:web")
    delivery = data_source.claim(TOPIC, GROUP, 1, 30_000).first
    data_source.ack(TOPIC, GROUP, delivery)

  end
end

sections.heading: Redis in a store
sections.body: Redis is another server resource that Yon can inject. It is not a SQL dialect. On a managed Store, declare a redisTemplate field with no value and mark it with Needs. This field is Spring's RedisTemplate. Your application source does not need to install a driver. get(key) returns a JSON value or null. set(key, value, ttlSeconds) stores limited JSON. It requires an expiry time. delete(key) returns whether it removed a key. Rust methods return Result<Json, YonResourceError>, and Go methods return (any, error). C# also offers Get, Set and Delete. Keep session and cache authorization in your application. Each operation has a time limit of five seconds. If a change times out, the change may still have happened. Keys and values are always passed as parameters, so no Redis command text is ever built from input.

streams.title: Streams
streams.summary: A stream keeps one HTTP answer open and sends many messages on it. On the server, mark the method with `StreamRoute`. In the page, a client method marked `StreamRequest` receives the messages. A stream route says who may call it like any other route.

sections.heading: Streaming
sections.body: StreamRoute marks a controller method that answers GET requests with a stream. The method yields values from a private generator that holds the loop. Each value becomes one limited server-sent event, a message that the server pushes over an open HTTP response. When the method finishes, the server sends an end event, so the browser does not reconnect. The method name starts with stream. A generator under GetRoute is refused, so one marker says that a route streams. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin, C#, F#, Dart, Ruby, Lua and Go support this. Lua sends each value with `coroutine.yield`, because Tachyon runs the route in a coroutine. A Go stream method returns `iter.Seq[Tick]`, Go's own generator: its function calls `yield` once for each value and stops when `yield` returns false. Return `iter.Seq2[Tick, error]` when the stream can fail; an error ends the stream with an error event. Java, Groovy and Rust have no generator, so they refuse StreamRoute with TY2015 and return once. A stream has the same time limit as every request. At the limit, Tachyon stops the process and sends an error event, and the browser opens the stream again. When the reader goes away, Tachyon stops the process at once. A Go method that takes the `*http.Request` can read the time limit from `request.Context()`. The context ends just before the limit, so a stream that should finish there, such as a log follow, returns and sends the end event instead.

sections.heading: Streaming: Yon
sections.body: StreamRoute marks a controller route method that answers GET requests with a stream of server-sent events. It replaces GetRoute with Stream: one marker says that the route streams. The method name starts with stream, such as streamEvents, StreamEvents or stream_events. The server sends text/event-stream headers before it invokes the route. Then it sends each yielded value as one SSE (server-sent events) data frame, and an end event when the method finishes. The route method only passes on the values; a private generator method holds the loop. StreamRoute is Yon-only and takes an optional path, like the other route annotations. A generator under GetRoute or another route annotation is refused, and so is Stream: `ty migrate fix --write` turns GetRoute with Stream into StreamRoute and renames a get method to stream when that is safe. In one controller, either every GET route is a StreamRoute or none is. Python supports only synchronous generators. These Yon languages stream: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin, C#, F#, Dart, Ruby, Lua and Go. A Lua stream method, like its private helper, sends each value with `coroutine.yield(value)`, because Tachyon runs the route in a coroutine (ADR 0085). An F# stream member returns `seq<'T>` or `IAsyncEnumerable<'T>`. A Go stream method returns `iter.Seq[Ticket]`, or `iter.Seq2[Ticket, error]` when the stream can fail, and its function stops when `yield` returns false. Java, Groovy and Rust stay single-response. They reject StreamRoute with TY2015 "@StreamRoute needs JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin, C#, F#, Dart, Ruby, Lua or Go". In those languages, return the whole collection once as ordinary JSON instead. A stream has the request time limit. At the limit the server stops the process and sends an error event. When the reader goes away, the server stops the process group at once (ADR 0058). A Go route that takes *http.Request gets a request context that ends at that deadline. /api.json marks a stream route with "stream": true and "produces": "text/event-stream". In the browser, StreamRequest on an HTTPClient method in JavaScript, TypeScript or Go receives the stream. The browser event bus opens it. After an error it reconnects after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds and then stops, and sixty seconds without a message count as an error.

sockets.title: Sockets
sockets.summary: A socket (a WebSocket) is a connection that stays open, so the browser and the server can both send messages at any time. On the server, mark a controller with `SocketRoute`. In the page, a client method marked `SocketRequest` connects to it. The socket class also says who may connect: `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class.

sections.heading: Sockets
sections.body: SocketRoute marks a controller that keeps a WebSocket open at its path. Put the class in server/controllers/ in any Yon language (.js, .ts, .py, .go, .java, .groovy, .kt, .cs, .fs, .php, .rb, .rs, .dart or .lua). Tachyon makes one object for each connection, as Jakarta's @ServerEndpoint does. OnOpen runs when a browser connects, OnMessage runs for each message, OnClose runs when the socket closes, and OnError runs when OnOpen or OnMessage fails; the socket stays open, as in Jakarta. The session sends messages back, closes the socket, and lists the open sessions of the same path with openSessions() (each language uses its own style, such as open_sessions() in Python). Each message is JSON text of at most 64 KiB, and Tachyon checks it against the model type of the OnMessage parameter. In Lua, a message that is not JSON or is nested more than 64 levels deep goes to OnError, and the socket stays open. When the browser closes the socket, Tachyon answers with the same close code, so the browser sees a clean close. SocketRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the messages in the browser, and the client's send(message) sends one. In Go, the client is an interface method, the service receives the messages with `// @OnEvent`, and `Send(message any) error` sends one. Public, SignedIn or Allow(Role) on the SocketRoute class says who may connect. Tachyon checks it before it opens the socket, and answers 401 or 403 instead. The socket path has no {variables}. Tachyon guards every socket: a message that is not JSON or does not fit the model closes it with code 1007, a binary message with 1003, and a message larger than 64 KiB with 1009. Five minutes without a message closes it with 1001, and a socket lasts at most one hour. At most 32 sockets are open at once in the whole server, and the next one gets 503. A browser page from another origin gets 403. A plain HTTP request to the path gets 426 Upgrade Required. /api.json marks the path with "socket": true and names the message model.

topics.title: Topics
topics.summary: A topic is a model marked `Topic`. When one part of the app publishes a value of that model, Tachyon sends it to the listeners in the Yon languages that have topics and in open pages.

sections.heading: Topics
sections.body:
A topic is a model marked Topic. Write @Topic above the model in a models folder: `@topic` in Python, `@Topic` in Java, Groovy, Kotlin, Dart and Swift, `#[Topic]` in Rust, PHP and Ruby, `[Topic]` in C#, `[<Topic>]` in F#, `// @Topic` in Go, `-- @Topic` in Lua and `/** @Topic */` in TypeScript. JavaScript writes ` * @Topic` inside the model's @typedef block. The topic name comes from the model's type name only: InventoryRecord becomes the topic inventory-record.

When a Yon class calls publishEvent(model) with a Topic model, its own listeners hear the event first, as with any event. Then Tachyon adds the value as one line to the topic log, an append-only file (new lines are only added at the end) at `data/topics/inventory-record.jsonl`. The server then calls every OnEvent listener of that model in the other Yon files and languages once. The listeners that already ran in the publishing request are not called again. This works like Spring Cloud Bus: delivery is at most once, the server keeps no position for a Yon listener, and a listener that fails is not called again. An event that a listener publishes again travels at most 8 times. Each language declares its own model and marks it Topic; a listener hears other processes only when its own model is a Topic. A Yon listener runs when its class is part of a controller (through a Needs field), like every Yon provider.

In a page, an OnEvent listener for a Topic model opens the stream `/.tachyon/topics/inventory-record` by itself. This address is a server route, not a folder: the server reads the log from the topic log folder. No HTTPClient or StreamRequest is needed. The same is true for an OnEvent listener in a Dart service and in a service that runs as WebAssembly in the page. All listeners of one topic share one stream. The stream replays the kept records, and after a lost connection it resumes after the last record it received. It reconnects after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, like StreamRequest. A page's publishEvent stays in the page: to send a value to the server, call a Yon route that publishes it, as InventoryController does here.

Tachyon refuses Topic outside a models folder and Topic that is not written above a model. The server accepts a publication only for a Topic model of the publishing file's language, only a model value, and at most 64 KiB; a log holds at most 16 MiB. Every Yon language sends and receives Topic events, and a page service in every Tac language listens to them, Lua and Python included. Lua has no network client, so a Lua route gives its publications to the server in its answer. The server adds them to the topic log after the route ends and before the browser gets the response, so the order is the same as in the other languages (ADR 0085).

The topic logs are saved data, so they live outside the generated `.tachyon` folder, which you can delete at any time. The folder is `data/topics` in the project unless `topics.directory` in `server/application.json` names another one: a plain path inside the project, such as `storage/events`, or an absolute path with no symbolic link in it. Tachyon refuses a path with `..`, a path inside `.tachyon`, and a folder that a symbolic link leads out of the project (`TY1303`). Back up this folder like a database. Commit it only when the events are sample data for everyone; `ty init` does not ignore it in `.gitignore`. An app that saved topic logs in `.tachyon/topics` before keeps them: when the server starts and the topic log folder has no logs yet, it moves the old logs there once and prints a notice. `ty migrate check` lists old logs that are still in `.tachyon/topics`.

A route that streams its own values is a different feature. That is a StreamRoute method in Yon (a method that gives its values one at a time). C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Topic in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

service-languages.title: Choosing a service language
service-languages.summary: You can write a Tac service in JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart or Ruby. Lua, Python and C++ work with limits. "Which languages can I use?" lists every language, what it can do, and the languages that Tachyon does not support. A service runs in the page on every target, also inside a native app. Some native hosts link Rust, Swift, Kotlin or C# services instead.

sections.heading: Which languages can I use?
sections.summary: You can write a Tac service in the supported languages below. Lua, Python and C++ are supported with limits. Other WebAssembly languages are not supported.
sections.body:
A Tac service is a class in `client/services`. Tachyon reads that class, connects its fields, methods, events and storage to the page, and runs its test units. A language is a Tac service language only when Tachyon does all of this for it. A compiler that makes WebAssembly is not enough. Each language below is in one of four groups.

Supported and tested: JavaScript and TypeScript run in the page as JavaScript. Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart and Ruby run in the page as WebAssembly. Tachyon tests each of these languages with its own test units and in a real browser. The feature pages show examples in them, and the site build checks those examples. When one of these languages cannot use a feature, the feature page says so and names the build error.

Supported with limits: Lua, Python and C++ work, but some features are not ready in them yet. Each feature page says when Lua, Python or C++ cannot use the feature.

Lua runs on Tachyon's Lua 5.4 WebAssembly runtime (ADR 0085; an ADR is an architecture decision record). A Lua service has fields, methods, `OnStart` and `OnStop`, events with `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `OnEvent`, topics, test units, and Tachyon's browser APIs except `WindowControls` and `FilePicker`. A `WindowControls` or `FilePicker` field in a Lua service stops the build with `TY2015`. The build refuses these in Lua with `TY1308`: behavior annotations such as `Cached`, `Retry` and `AllOrNothing`, `HTTPClient`, `Store`, `LocalState`, `SessionState`, `Helper` and `Fake`.

Python runs on Pyodide 314.0.7, a Python runtime for WebAssembly (ADR 0093). A Python service has fields, methods, models, `Needs`, `NeedsAll`, `Named`, helpers, synchronous `on_start` and `on_stop`, synchronous `on_event` listeners, an `ApplicationEventPublisher` field, topics and test units. Every call is synchronous. An `async def` method, a stream or a browser API stops the build with `TY1605`. The build refuses these in Python with `TY1308`: `HTTPClient`, `Store`, `LocalState`, `SessionState`, `PageDefaults`, the caching annotations, `Retry`, `MaxAtOnce` and `AllOrNothing`. ADR 0093 covers web builds; Tachyon does not test Python services in native apps.

C++ runs as WebAssembly that Emscripten builds from header-only `.hpp` files, one class in each file (ADR 0099). A C++ service has fields, methods, `Needs`, `OnStart` and `OnStop`, events with `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `OnEvent` (with `Order` and `InBackground`), models in `client/models`, `HTTPClient` clients in `client/remotes`, and test units. A method that returns `Task<T>` is awaited by the page. The build refuses most other annotations in C++ with `TY1308`, for example `Setup`, `Cached`, `Retry`, `Store`, `Entity`, `LocalState`, `SessionState`, `Topic`, `Helper`, `Converter`, `Setting`, `NeedsAll`, `Named` and `Lifetime`. A `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient`, so C++ has no browser APIs such as `Clock` yet (`TY1372`). A C++ test unit uses `Fake`, `ValueSource` and HTTP answers from its TestSetup, and `ty test --coverage` records the C++ methods that each case runs. C++ links into no native host. Yon handlers in C++ are not ready yet.

In progress and planned: you cannot use these languages today, and the plan can change. Zig is planned. Scala, through the WebAssembly output of Scala.js, and MoonBit, after its version 1.0, are under consideration.

Not supported: many other languages can reach a browser through WebAssembly, for example Haskell, OCaml, Grain, Nim, D, Odin, Crystal, AssemblyScript, Elixir, PHP, Perl and R. Tachyon does not support them as Tac service languages, and you cannot write a Tac service in them. Some languages compile to JavaScript, not to WebAssembly, for example Gleam, Elm and ClojureScript. Tachyon does not support them as Tac service languages either. A server language such as PHP can still be a Yon language (see The Yon languages).

The first table shows how each language runs and which tools build it.

| Language | Runs as | Toolchain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript | JavaScript in the page | none |
| TypeScript | JavaScript in the page, after `tsc` | TypeScript 6 or newer |
| Rust | WebAssembly (`wasm32-unknown-unknown`) | rustc 1.97.1 |
| Go | WebAssembly (`GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm`) | Go 1.27 or newer; TinyGo 0.42 or newer is optional and makes release modules smaller |
| C# | WebAssembly on the trimmed .NET browser runtime | .NET SDK 9.0.317 (`net9.0`) with the `wasm-tools` workload |
| F# | WebAssembly on the same .NET browser runtime as C# | the same .NET SDK as C# |
| Swift | WebAssembly (`wasm32-unknown-wasip1`) | Swift 6.3.3 from swift.org and its Swift SDK for WebAssembly, found through `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_SDK` |
| Kotlin | WebAssembly with garbage collection (WasmGC) | kotlinc 2.1.10 and kotlin-stdlib-wasm-js 2.1.10, found through `TAC_KOTLIN_WASM_STDLIB` |
| Java | WasmGC, made by TeaVM | JDK 21 or newer and TeaVM 0.15.0 |
| Dart | WasmGC (`dart compile wasm`) | Dart SDK 3.13 or newer |
| Ruby | Tachyon's mruby WebAssembly runtime | Ruby and Emscripten 6.0.10 build the pinned mruby once on your machine |
| Lua (with limits) | Tachyon's Lua 5.4.9 WebAssembly runtime, about 170 KB | Emscripten 6.0.10 builds it once on your machine |
| Python (with limits) | Pyodide 314.0.7 (CPython 3.14.2), about 13 MB before compression | the five pinned Pyodide files, which you put in the Tachyon cache |
| C++ (with limits) | WebAssembly, compiled by Emscripten | Emscripten 6.0.10 (`em++`) |

The second table shows how each language behaves. Calls says whether the page waits for a method. Native host says where a native app links the service in; everywhere else the service runs in the page, also inside a native app. `HTTPClient` says how a client in that language sends requests (see Calling the server from a page). Example names a working service in Code examples on the home page; the site build compiles and checks each one.

| Language | Calls | Native host | HTTPClient | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript | Synchronous or `async` | none | sent by the browser | `TallyService.js` |
| TypeScript | Synchronous or `async` | none | sent by the browser | `TallyService.ts` |
| Rust | Synchronous; an `async fn` runs on Tachyon's task runner in the module | macOS, Windows and Linux | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.rs` |
| Go | Each call runs in a goroutine; a call that waits finishes later | none | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.go` |
| C# | Synchronous; a `Task` method is awaited | Windows | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.cs` |
| F# | Synchronous; a `Task` method is awaited | none | sent by the browser | `TallyService.fs` |
| Swift | Synchronous; an `async` method runs as a task in the module and the page gets a promise (in a native app it runs to the end before the call returns) | macOS and iOS | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.swift` |
| Kotlin | Synchronous; a `suspend fun` waits in the module and the page gets a promise | Android | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.kt` |
| Java | Each call runs in a TeaVM fiber; a call that waits finishes later | none | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.java` |
| Dart | Synchronous; a `Future` method is awaited | none | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.dart` |
| Ruby | Each call runs in a Ruby fiber; a call that waits finishes later; `sleep` is refused | none | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.rb` |
| Lua | Synchronous | none | no; the build refuses it (`TY1308`) | `TallyService.lua` |
| Python | Synchronous only; `async def` stops the build (`TY1605`) | none | no; the build refuses it (`TY1308`) | `TallyService.py` |
| C++ | Synchronous; a `Task<T>` method is awaited | none | sent by the browser, through `Needs` | `TallyService.hpp` |

Kotlin, Java and Dart need a browser with WasmGC: Chrome or Edge 119, Firefox 120, Safari 18.2 or newer. An older browser shows a clear error instead of these services. `ty doctor` lists the tools that your project needs and says which ones are missing. A page loads the runtime of a language only when one of its views uses a service in that language.

sections.heading: Choose a service language
sections.body:
A service is a file client/services/<Name>Service.js, .ts or .dart. You can also write it as <Name>Service.rs, .go, .rb, .lua, .py, .swift, .kt, .java, .cs, .fs or .hpp (C++) in the same folder. A component holds only its tac.html and tac.css. A page holds only its own tac.html, which places components. JavaScript and TypeScript run on every target. Dart compiles to WebAssembly with garbage collection (WasmGC), which ships wherever that bundle ships (ADR 0033; an ADR is an architecture decision record). WasmGC needs Chrome or Edge 119, Firefox 120 or Safari 18.2 and newer; an older browser shows a clear error instead of the Dart, Kotlin or Java services.

A Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin or Java service with no browser sibling compiles to WebAssembly. It runs as WebAssembly on the web and on any target that does not link it (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045, ADR 0073, ADR 0078, ADR 0082, ADR 0083). Kotlin compiles to WasmGC, like Dart, so it needs the same browsers. Java compiles to WasmGC too, with TeaVM (a compiler from Java bytecode to WebAssembly); no host links Java, so a Java service runs as WebAssembly on every target. A Java web service has fields, methods with arguments, @OnStart and @OnStop, saved @LocalState and @SessionState fields, models from client/models (records, classes with fields, and enums), events with ApplicationEventPublisher and @OnEvent, Topic streams, the built-in browser cache and Store (Cached, UpdateCache, ClearCache and AllOrNothing), Tachyon's browser APIs (Clock, SecureRandom, Connectivity, PageVisibility, Preferences, Clipboard, Share, Notifications and Geolocation) with their built-in events, and the behavior annotations such as Retry, MaxAtOnce, configuration binding and validation. Groovy stays a Yon language only, because its runtime cannot be compiled to WebAssembly.

When a service has files in several languages, a JavaScript, TypeScript or Dart file wins, and so does a native service that the target links. Otherwise Tachyon uses the first WebAssembly file in this order: Rust, Go, C# or F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Ruby, Lua, Python. An F# file takes the place of C#.

A release build makes the Kotlin program about three times smaller with Binaryen, as Kotlin's own production build does. Every other WebAssembly language also gets the compiler and settings that make the smallest download: TinyGo for Go, a size-tuned rustc for Rust, -Osize and Binaryen for Swift, TeaVM and Binaryen for Java, a trimmed .NET interpreter for C# and F#, and -O4 for Dart (see WebAssembly compilers per language). A Swift program holds the Swift standard library, about 3.4 MB (0.9 MB with Brotli), so a Swift web service should not import Foundation, which would make it more than ten times larger. It does not need it: models in client/models cross the page boundary through Codable, with an encoder and decoder that Tachyon ships in the Swift program.

No target links Go, so a Go service runs as WebAssembly on every target. A C++ service is a header-only .hpp file with one class, compiled with Emscripten; no target links C++ either, so it runs as WebAssembly everywhere. Its markers are standard attributes, such as `class [[Service]] OrderService`, and Tachyon ships C#-shaped JSON and HTTP types for it (`tachyon::json`, `tachyon::http`; ADR 0099). A Ruby service runs on Tachyon's mruby WebAssembly runtime on every target (ADR 0054). Your machine builds that runtime once with Ruby and Emscripten. A Lua service runs on Tachyon's Lua 5.4 WebAssembly runtime on every target (ADR 0085). Your machine builds that runtime once with Emscripten. Native services link on their supported targets: Rust on desktop, Swift on Apple, Kotlin on Android and C# on Windows. On every other target they run as WebAssembly, so every service language reaches every target. A Python service runs in the page on Pyodide 314.0.7, a Python runtime for WebAssembly (ADR 0093). Lua, Python and C++ services have limits; "Which languages can I use?" lists them. PHP and Groovy are not Tac service languages.

This site is a complete example of the web mix. Rust holds the contents list and page links. Go holds the feature catalogue and the inline code in prose. Ruby holds the navigation drawer. C# holds the documentation index. F# holds counts such as "1 feature" or "12 features". Java holds the choice of install command and the saved platform choice. Dart holds the sidebar and pager. Kotlin holds the feature pages and the place of each guide in the reading order. Swift holds the word and group filters of the feature list. Lua holds the reading time. TypeScript holds the clipboard, the guide pages, the list of Yon examples and the code showcase. JavaScript holds search and the code examples. A page loads the runtime of a language only when one of its views uses a service in that language, so the Swift program (about 0.9 MB with Brotli) loads only on the feature list.

A unit test in the same language tests each service. Content that is only data is not a service at all. Examples are the pillars, FAQ, footer and quickstart. This content lives in client/shared/data, and a view reads it as data.<name> (ADR 0036).

sections.heading: Contracts stay on the server
sections.body: The argument and return types of a Yon controller method are the route contract (the agreed shape of the data) for incoming requests and outgoing responses. Browser services call normal HTTP endpoints through HTTPClient + GetRequest. Native services may use their platform's networking APIs. Neither one declares a second protocol for server routes.

sections.heading: What Tachyon trusts and checks
sections.body:
A `CatalogService.js` runs everywhere and uses browser APIs. A `CatalogService.swift` runs on Apple targets. It uses the platform SDK with the operating system permissions of the host process. Native service code is trusted application code. Tachyon does not sandbox it (run it in a restricted area). The bridge between the page and the service is a separate boundary. Before the host runs a supported member operation, it checks three things. They are the local origin, the main frame and the canonical route (the one official form of the route). The page names the operation by the instance name of the service. Manifest grants still control which window API the page can use, and which browser APIs that need consent (clipboard, share, notifications, geolocation) the page gives to services (`tac.browserApis`).

At build time, Tachyon also checks that a service which runs as WebAssembly does not call the browser itself. A Swift service that imports JavaScriptKit fails with TY1317. The error names the file and the word to remove.
sections.code:
error[TY1317]: Swift services cannot call browser APIs. Put this code in a JS or TS service and send the result to this service with an event.
  --> client/services/CatalogService.swift
  help: Remove `JavaScriptKit`. Browser work lives in a JavaScript or TypeScript service. That service publishes a typed event, and this service receives it with @OnEvent.

yon-languages.title: The Yon languages
yon-languages.summary: Yon runs controllers written in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, PHP, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua. Every language uses the same annotations and the same folders.

sections.heading: Languages Yon runs
sections.body:
Yon supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, PHP, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua directly. Each controller can also use provider annotations (annotations on the classes that other classes need). Tachyon turns all annotations into plain code before the route runs. Tachyon starts each process and adapts the protocol. You need no annotation package at run time. To call a class in another of these languages, declare a `@Gateway` method. To reach other programs, call `relay(command, request)` yourself, or name the program in a `@Gateway` command. The list below shows the program that runs each language. `ty doctor` checks that these programs are installed. A Rust handler builds with Cargo and the `http` crate, offline first. A Dart handler needs the `shelf` package in the pub cache, or the network, because Tachyon runs `dart pub get`.

Groovy (ADR 0072) writes the annotations as Java does: `@RequestRoute('/orders')`, `@GetRoute`, `@Service`, `@Needs`. Tachyon reads Groovy with the Java rules, and a semicolon at the end of a line is optional. Every field and method has a declared type, such as `String name` or `List<Order> findOrders()`; a member declared with `def` stops the build (TY1334), and a local variable inside a method may still use `def`. A model is a record, an enum or a class with typed fields, and code reads it with `import models.Order`. Groovy uses the Java protocol runtime, so the request is `HttpExchange` and `Yon.relay(command, exchange)` works as in Java. Tachyon compiles your Groovy together with that Java runtime (joint compilation) into one jar with the Groovy core library and runs it on the JDK. Tachyon finds Groovy 4 or newer through `GROOVY_HOME` or `groovyc` on `PATH`. Two Groovy rules matter for Tachyon code: `1.5` is a `BigDecimal`, so write `1.5d` for a `double`, and a closure that you put into a map needs its type, such as `{ request, execution -> ... } as Behaviors.HttpAdapter`. Groovy also reads a single map argument to a record constructor as named arguments, so write `new CatalogSummary(summary: summary)`.

F# (ADR 0073) writes the annotations as F# attributes, each on its own line: `[<RequestRoute("/orders")>]`, `[<GetRoute>]`, `[<Service>]`. A type takes the roles it needs as the parameters of its primary constructor, `type OrderService(orderStore: OrderStore) =`, the way Spring injects a class with one constructor. This is the recommended form. A settable property with `[<Needs>]` receives a role too, like a Spring field: `[<Needs>] member val OrderStore : OrderStore = Unchecked.defaultof<OrderStore> with get, set`, and `[<Named("...")>]` chooses another provider. Members that Tachyon reads write their types, for example `member this.GetOrder(id: int64) : Order =`. A model is an F# record, and code reads it with `open Models`. An F# file holds one type and no `module` or `namespace` line, and it has no file-level `let` (TY1335). F# runs on .NET with the same protocol runtime as C#, so F# code uses `Yon.Relay`, `DataSource`, `HttpRequestMessage` and `HttpResponseMessage` as C# does. Behavior annotations work in F# through the C# behavior runtime: a member whose body Tachyon writes, such as a query or a Convert method, is an F# `abstract` member, and the behavior context is a `behaviors` member of the class. Events and lifecycle hooks work as in C#, and a class takes its ApplicationEventPublisher as a primary constructor parameter. F# controllers hold SocketRoute and StreamRoute as C# does: a socket member takes the SocketSession, and a stream member returns `seq<'T>` or `IAsyncEnumerable<'T>`. An F# TestSetup declares `static member configure`, as in C#, and each case of an F# test unit reads its behavior context as `this.behaviors`. ty test counts the F# members that a case really called.

Lua (ADR 0085) has no annotation syntax, so an annotation is a comment on its own line: `-- @RequestRoute("/orders")`, `-- @GetRoute`, `-- @Service`, `-- @Needs`. Lua ignores the comment, so the file runs unchanged. A Lua class is one global table in its own file, `OrderService = {}`, and its methods are `function OrderService:list()`. The fields of the class sit in the table, one field on each line, such as `order_service = nil,` under `-- @Needs`. Types are LuaCATS comments, which the Lua language server also reads: `---@param id integer`, `---@return Order[]`, `---@type OrderService`, and a model is a `---@class` with `---@field` lines. `local Name = {}`, `return Name`, `require`, a second table or code outside a method stops the build (TY1357), because Tachyon joins the class files of one realm into one program. A route parameter without a marker and root middleware receive a request table with `method`, `path`, `headers` and `body`, and middleware answers with a `{ status, headers, body }` list. An error is a table whose metatable is its error type, `error(setmetatable({ message = "order 42" }, OrderNotFound))`. Tachyon runs Lua 5.4 or newer with the `lua` program. Events and lifecycle hooks work in Lua: `-- @OnStart`, `-- @OnStop`, `-- @OnEvent` and `-- @Order` above a method, and an event is a model table that `ApplicationEventPublisher:publish_event(value)` publishes. Behavior annotations work in Lua too. A class opens its context with `self.behaviors = Behaviors.create(Setup, { partition = "orders", signal = BehaviorSignal.new() })`. Tachyon wraps each behavior method, such as a `-- @Cached` or `-- @Retry({...})` method. A Lua `-- @StreamRoute` method sends each value with `coroutine.yield(value)`, and a `-- @SocketRoute` class gets a session with `session:send(message)` and `session:open_sessions()`. A model marked `-- @Topic` is a topic: a Lua route publishes it and a Lua `-- @OnEvent` method hears it from other languages. `@InBackground` is not available in Lua yet: a Lua file that uses it stops the build with `TY1308` (the annotation is not available in Lua). Resources are not available in Lua either: a Lua class that needs `DataSource` or `RedisTemplate`, calls `relay`, or declares `@HTTPClient` or `@Gateway` stops the build and names the resource. A Lua model cannot carry `Settings`, `Setting` or `Checked` yet (`TY1310`, ADR 0092), and a Lua `Store` is not yet a provider that another class can inject (`TY2015`). Lua is also a Tac language: a page service written as a Lua class table runs on Tachyon's Lua WebAssembly runtime. ty test counts the Lua methods that a case really called, in both realms.

Go (ADR 0045) writes each annotation as a `// @Name` comment on its own line, and its files use `package main`. Your own Go packages and vendored third-party modules live in the Go module in `server/packages/` (ADR 0095). A Go `// @StreamRoute` method returns `iter.Seq[Model]`, or `iter.Seq2[Model, error]` when the stream can fail, and a method that takes the `*http.Request` reads the time limit from `request.Context()`.

native-services.title: Rust, Go and C# in the browser
native-services.summary: A service written in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart or Ruby can run in the browser as WebAssembly, a compiled format that browsers run. Lua and Python services run there too, on runtimes that Tachyon ships, and C++ services that Emscripten compiles, all with limits. In a desktop or mobile app, Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services can run as native code instead.

sections.heading: Rust, Go and C# on the web
sections.body: A service written only in Rust, only in Go or only in C# needs no browser sibling on the web. Rust links on the three desktops, C# links on Windows, and Go links on no host. Where a host links the service, it runs natively. Everywhere else, including the web, it runs as WebAssembly: in the browser, or in the web view of a native target (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045; an ADR is an architecture decision record). Rust compiles with rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown into one small module. The page script tachyon-rust.js carries that module as hexadecimal text, so a page opened from file: loads it too. Brotli and gzip make hexadecimal text about a sixth smaller than base64. Go compiles into one module for all the Go services of the application. A release build compiles it with TinyGo, which leaves out most of the Go runtime, so a small service is about 360 KB (115 KB as sent with Brotli). Without TinyGo, or when TinyGo cannot compile the services, the standard Go compiler (GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm) builds a module that carries the whole Go runtime and starts at about 2.7 MB. The page loads the module with the wasm_exec.js of the compiler that built it (see WebAssembly compilers per language, ADR 0081). C# publishes onto the .NET browser runtime. That runtime is about 3 MB, and the service worker caches it once. F# services compile into a small F# library that runs on the same .NET browser runtime, so a page with C# and F# services loads that runtime once; no host links F#, so an F# service runs as WebAssembly on every target, Windows included (ADR 0073). So when a service has several of these versions, Tachyon uses Rust, then Go, then C#, then F# (Choose a service language gives the full order). The page speaks the same companion protocol as a native host, so the service is the same file. Its fields render, and so does a model from client/models, a list of models and a model inside a model. Its methods take JSON arguments. In Rust, these are String, &str, bool, numbers, TacValue, models, and Vec or Option of them. In Go, they are string, bool, numbers, slices, maps or structs. In C# and F#, they are string, bool, numbers, object, models and lists of models. The page reaches only these members. A Rust field or method of another type, such as the HTTPClient a service holds, stays inside the service. A C# member reaches the page only when it is public or internal. A Rust model derives Clone, because the page reads a copy of the field. A model field named with a Rust keyword uses a raw identifier, such as `pub r#type: String`; the page and the JSON see it as `type`. An F# service shows its `member val` properties and its public members. A view reaches the exported Go members with a lower-case first letter, so Count is {tally.count}. Only the first letter changes, so OAuthNotice is {settings.oAuthNotice}. A view that writes the same name in another case, such as {settings.oauthNotice}, would render nothing, so the build stops with TY1311 and names the member to write. Service and NeedsAll sit on their own lines above the type. Rust spells Service as #[Service], Go spells it as // @Service, C# spells it as [Service], and F# spells it as [<Service>]. A bare constructor lets every field take the property with the same name, and it makes the service one per component. In F#, [<NeedsAll>] marks the primary constructor, so its parameters take the properties. A WebAssembly service has no DOM and no platform. It is state and logic over the properties its tag passes. It also runs on the page thread, like the page's own JavaScript (ADR 0084). A long computation in a method blocks clicks and keys until it ends, and the .NET runtime blocks the page while it starts. Move heavy work to the server. Those properties may carry a data file: the start-up request may carry up to 1 MiB (1048576 bytes) in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Ruby, Lua and Python. Every later request, such as a method call, may carry up to 64 KiB (65536 bytes). A bigger request fails, and the error names the service, the size and the limit, for example: Web service documentation: The request is 1072202 bytes. The limit is 1048576 bytes. Pass less data to the service. A method call names the method too: The request to add is 70121 bytes. ty doctor checks for the wasm32-unknown-unknown target, Go 1.27 and the .NET wasm-tools workload. It also lists TinyGo and Binaryen's wasm-opt as optional tools: release builds use them to make the modules smaller.

sections.heading: What each service language can use in the browser
sections.body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby, Lua, Swift, Python or C++ runs in the page, but it does not call the browser itself. It reaches the browser only through Tachyon: the view reads its fields and calls its methods, events carry values in and out, and the storage annotations keep its data. Tachyon also gives every language but Python and C++ a small set of browser APIs: `Clock`, `SecureRandom`, `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences`, `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation`. Every language but Lua, Python and C++ also gets `WindowControls` (see the next sections and the feature "What a page may do to its window"). Python and C++ services do not have these browser APIs yet: a Python browser API stops the build with `TY1605`, and a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or `HTTPClient` (`TY1372`). A Lua service has no `WindowControls` and no `FilePicker`: such a field in a Lua service stops the build with `TY2015`. Other browser work lives in a JavaScript or TypeScript service. That service publishes a typed event, and the service in the other language receives it with `OnEvent`.

The table shows what each language can use in the page.

| What | Rust | Go | C# | F# | Kotlin | Dart | Ruby | Lua | Swift | Java | Python | C++ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fields and methods for the view | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `publishEvent` and `OnEvent` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, synchronous listeners | Yes |
| `Store` and caches | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (ADR 0085) | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (`TY1308`) | No, not yet (`TY1308`) |
| `LocalState` and `SessionState` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (ADR 0085) | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (`TY1308`) | No, not yet (`TY1308`) |
| `HTTPClient` sent by the browser | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with its own `BehaviorContext` | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with `Needs` | No | Yes, with `Needs` | Yes, with `Needs` | No (`TY1308`) | Yes, with `Needs` |
| `HTTPClient` sent by the Setup's HTTP adapter, with `Cached`, `ClearCache` and `UpdateCache` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (ADR 0085) | Yes | Yes | No (`TY1308`) | No, not yet (`TY1308`) |
| `StreamRequest` and `SocketRequest` | No | Yes, with `Needs`; messages arrive through `OnEvent` | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No (`TY1605`) | No (`TY1308`) |
| `Clock` and `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (`TY1605`) | No, not yet (`TY1372`) |
| `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences` and their change events | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (`TY1605`) | No, not yet (`TY1372`) |
| `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation`, after a grant | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, not yet (`TY1605`) | No, not yet (`TY1372`) |
| `WindowControls`, after a grant in `tac.application.window.controls` (a native window only) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No (`TY2015`) | Yes | Yes | No | No, not yet (`TY1372`) |
| The current time from the language itself | No, use `Clock` | Yes | Yes | Yes, `System.DateTime.UtcNow` | Yes, `System.currentTimeMillis()` | Yes | Yes | No `os` library, use `Clock` | No `Date` (no Foundation), use `Clock` | Yes, `System.currentTimeMillis()` | Yes, `time.time()` | Not checked yet |
| Random numbers from the language itself | No, use `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes, `System.Random` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, `math.random` | Yes, `Int.random(in:)` | Yes, `java.util.Random` | Yes, `random` | Not checked yet |
| Wait (sleep) | No | Yes, the page waits | Yes, the page waits | Yes, `Thread.Sleep` makes the page wait | Yes, `Thread.sleep` makes the page wait | Yes, in an `async` method | No | No | Yes, `Task.sleep` in an `async` method makes the page wait | No; only the wait of a `Retry` or a blocking `MaxAtOnce`, which makes the page wait | No; `async def` stops the build (`TY1605`) | Not checked yet |
| Console output | No | Yes | Yes | Yes, `printfn` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, `print` | Yes, `print` | Yes, `System.out` | Yes, `print` | Yes, `std::cout` |

A Swift, Rust, C# or Kotlin service that a native app links in has no page, but it can still get `WindowControls`: it declares an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `Needs` or `NeedsAll`, and Tachyon calls the host directly, with the same grants (ADR 0089).

Send requests from a JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby or C++ client (see "Calling the server from a page"). In Lua and Python, a JavaScript or TypeScript client sends them. Its answers, and the messages of a stream or a socket, reach the other languages as typed events. In Rust, `std::time::SystemTime::now()` and `std::thread::sleep` stop the service with an error, and `println!` prints nothing. Use Tachyon's `Clock` and `SecureRandom` instead (see "Clock and secure random numbers"). Ruby refuses `sleep`: a Ruby call waits only for a request to the server. The Lua runtime has no `io`, `os` or `package` library, so a Lua service reads the time from `Clock`.

Tachyon refuses code that calls the browser directly, and the build stops with `TY1317`: Go `syscall/js`; Dart `dart:js_interop`, `dart:js_interop_unsafe`, `dart:js`, `dart:js_util`, `dart:html`, `package:web` and `package:js`; C# and F# `System.Runtime.InteropServices.JavaScript`, `JSImport`, `JSExport` and `JSHost`; Rust `wasm_bindgen`, `web_sys`, `js_sys` and `wasm_import_module`; Kotlin `external`, `@JsFun`, `@JsExport`, `@JsModule`, `@JsName`, `js(…)`, `kotlinx.browser`, `org.w3c` and `kotlin.js`; Java `org.teavm`, `native` methods and TeaVM's `JS…` annotations such as `JSBody`, `JSObject` and `JSExport`; Ruby `TachyonWeb` and `JS`; and Swift `JavaScriptKit`, `JavaScriptEventLoop`, `JSObject`, `JSValue`, `JSClosure`, `JSPromise`, `@_extern` and `@_expose`. Such code breaks the test units of the language, and a native target has no browser. Tachyon's own code on the page is not checked.

Two smaller browser APIs exist only in some languages. `PreferenceStrings` reads and writes short texts in the browser's `localStorage` with `read(key)` and `write(key, value)`; JavaScript, TypeScript and Java services have it after the grant `preferenceStrings` in `tac.browserApis`, and a refused or failed call gives back `null` or `false`. `DocumentTitle` sets the title of the page with `set(title)`; JavaScript, TypeScript and Kotlin services have it.

In the example, `PlaceService` in JavaScript or TypeScript reads the browser and publishes a `PlaceFound` event. `MapService` receives the event with `OnEvent`, and the view shows its fields. Write `MapService` in any service language: the tabs show each one. A Python listener is a synchronous `@on_event` method. The same pattern works for any browser API outside Tachyon's set.

sections.heading: Clock and secure random numbers
sections.body:
Tachyon gives every Tac service except Python and C++ two small browser APIs: `Clock` and `SecureRandom`. Tachyon writes them once in the page, and each language reaches them through a small client.

| Language | How the service gets them | Clock | SecureRandom | A failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript, TypeScript | `@Needs clock` and `@Needs secureRandom` | `now()`, `monotonic()`, `timeZone()` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | an error is thrown |
| Rust | fields `clock: Clock` and `secure_random: SecureRandom`, which `Default` fills | `now_ms()`, `monotonic_ms()`, `time_zone()` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | an `Err` value |
| Go | `// @Needs` above `clock Clock` and `secureRandom SecureRandom` | `NowMs()`, `MonotonicMs()`, `TimeZone()` | `Bytes(count)`, `UUID()` | an `error` value |
| C# | `private readonly Clock clock = new();` | `NowMs()`, `MonotonicMs()`, `TimeZone()` | `Bytes(count)`, `Uuid()` | an `InvalidOperationException` |
| F# | `let clock = Clock()` and `let secureRandom = SecureRandom()` in the type | `NowMs()`, `MonotonicMs()`, `TimeZone()` | `Bytes(count)`, `Uuid()` | an `InvalidOperationException` |
| Kotlin | `private val clock = Clock()` and `private val secureRandom = SecureRandom()` | `nowMs()`, `monotonicMs()`, `timeZone()` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | an `IllegalStateException` |
| Java | `private final Clock clock = new Clock();` and `private final SecureRandom secureRandom = new SecureRandom();` | `nowMs()`, `monotonicMs()`, `timeZone()` | `bytes(count)`, which gives a `byte[]`, `uuid()` | an `IllegalStateException` |
| Swift | `private let clock = Clock()` and `private let secureRandom = SecureRandom()` | `nowMs()`, `monotonicMs()`, `timeZone()` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | an error is thrown; call with `try` |
| Dart | `@Needs()` above `final Clock clock;` | `nowMs()`, `monotonicMs()`, `timeZone()` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | a `StateError` |
| Ruby | `Clock.new` and `SecureRandom.new` | `now_ms`, `monotonic_ms`, `time_zone` | `bytes(count)`, `uuid` | a `RuntimeError` |
| Lua | the tables `Clock` and `SecureRandom`, called with `:` | `Clock:now_ms()`, `monotonic_ms()`, `time_zone()` | `SecureRandom:bytes(count)`, `uuid()` | a Lua error; catch it with `pcall` |

`now` is the time in milliseconds since 1970 (UTC). `monotonic` only goes up, so it measures how long something takes. `timeZone` is the time zone of the browser, such as `Europe/Paris`. `bytes` gives 0 to 65,536 random bytes from `crypto.getRandomValues`, and `uuid` gives a random version 4 UUID.

The page answers at once, so no call waits. These two APIs need no permission, so the manifest grants nothing for them. A service that is linked into a native app has no page, so the build refuses these APIs in it (`TY1317`). A test unit has no page either: give the calls fake answers (see "Browser APIs in test units"). The fields are not shown to the view. In Swift, Tachyon's `Clock` hides the standard library's `Clock` protocol; write `Swift.Clock` when you need the standard one. Python has no tab: a Python service has no browser APIs yet, and a Python service that uses one stops the build with `TY1605`. C++ has no tab either: a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient`, so a C++ service has no browser APIs yet (`TY1372`).

sections.heading: Connectivity, page visibility and preferences
sections.body:
Three small browser APIs tell a Tac service about the browser: `Connectivity` (is the browser online?), `PageVisibility` (is the page shown?) and `Preferences` (the color scheme, the motion setting and the language). A service reads the current value with a call, and hears each change as a built-in event model.

| API | JavaScript, TypeScript | Rust | Go, C#, F# | Dart, Java, Kotlin, Swift | Ruby | Lua | Event model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Connectivity | `@Needs connectivity`, `online()` | `connectivity: Connectivity`, `online()` | `Online()` | `online()` | `Connectivity.new.online` | `Connectivity:online()` | `ConnectivityChanged { online }` |
| PageVisibility | `@Needs pageVisibility`, `visible()` | `page_visibility: PageVisibility`, `visible()` | `Visible()` | `visible()` | `PageVisibility.new.visible` | `PageVisibility:visible()` | `VisibilityChanged { visible }` |
| Preferences | `@Needs preferences`, `scheme()`, `motion()`, `language()` | `preferences: Preferences`, same names | `Scheme()`, `Motion()`, `Language()` | same as JavaScript | `Preferences.new.scheme` | `Preferences:scheme()`, `motion()`, `language()` | `PreferencesChanged { scheme, motion, language }` |

`scheme` is `light` or `dark`, `motion` is `reduce` or `no-preference`, and `language` is the language of the browser, such as `fr-FR`. The service fields are created the same way as `Clock` (see above): Rust fields that `Default` fills, Go `// @Needs` fields, C# `new()` fields, F# `let connectivity = Connectivity()` bindings, Kotlin `Connectivity()` fields, Java `private final Connectivity connectivity = new Connectivity();` fields, Swift `private let connectivity = Connectivity()` fields and Dart `@Needs()` fields. Lua calls the global tables with `:`, such as `Connectivity:online()`, and needs no field. In Swift, a call can throw, so call it with `try`. In F#, the event models are F# records with the C# names, so a listener reads `changed.Online`.

The event models are built in: do not declare them in `client/models/`. Write a listener with a parameter of the model type, like any `@OnEvent` listener. The page publishes the current values when it starts and keeps them, so a listener with `replay` hears the current value first and then every change. These APIs need no permission, so the manifest grants nothing for them. Python has no tab: a Python service has no browser APIs yet, and a Python service that uses one stops the build with `TY1605`. C++ has no tab either: a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient`, so a C++ service has no browser APIs yet (`TY1372`).

sections.heading: Clipboard, share, notifications and geolocation
sections.body:
Four browser APIs need the user's consent, so a project must grant them first. List them in `tac.browserApis` in `client/manifest.json`. A call to an API that is not granted fails at once with a message that names the grant. Tachyon adds nothing to a page that grants nothing.

| API | Calls (JavaScript names) | Needs a click or key handler | The answer arrives as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Clipboard` (grant `clipboard`) | `writeText(text)`, `readText()` | Yes | `ClipboardTextRead { text }` after `readText` |
| `Share` (grant `share`) | `open(title, text, url)` | Yes | `ShareFinished {}` |
| `Notifications` (grant `notifications`) | `permission()`, `requestPermission()`, `show(title, body)` | `requestPermission` only | `NotificationPermissionChanged { permission }` |
| `Geolocation` (grant `geolocation`) | `currentPosition()` | No | `PositionFound { latitude, longitude, accuracy, timestamp }` |

JavaScript and TypeScript get them with `@Needs clipboard`, `@Needs share`, `@Needs notifications` and `@Needs geolocation`. Rust fields such as `clipboard: Clipboard` are filled by `Default`, Go uses `// @Needs` fields, C# `new()` fields, F# `let clipboard = Clipboard()` bindings, Dart `@Needs()` fields, Swift `private let clipboard = Clipboard()` fields, Java `private final Clipboard clipboard = new Clipboard();` fields, and Ruby `Clipboard.new`. Lua calls the global tables with `:`, such as `Clipboard:write_text(text)`, and needs no field. The names follow each language: `write_text` in Rust, Ruby and Lua, `WriteText` in Go, C# and F#, `writeText` in Dart, Java, Kotlin and Swift. A Java call that the page refuses at once throws an `IllegalStateException`, and a C# or F# call an `InvalidOperationException`. A Lua call raises a Lua error; catch it with `pcall`. Swift names its arguments: `open(title:text:url:)` and `show(title:body:)`, and every call is used with `try`.

The browser answers these calls later, so the call itself only starts the work. The answer is a built-in event model, and Tachyon sends it to the service that made the call, not to every listener. Write an `@OnEvent` listener for the model. When the browser refuses or fails after the call started (the user says no, or no position is found), the service gets `BrowserCallFailed { api, call, message }` instead. `permission()` and `show(title, body)` answer at once; `show` fails until the user has allowed notifications.

The browser allows the clipboard, sharing and the notification question only right after the user clicks or presses a key. Call them from a method that the view runs on a click. Every call to the page is synchronous, so a Rust, Go, C#, F#, Dart, Ruby, Lua or Swift method that a click runs still counts as the click. A call without a user action fails at once with "The clipboard browser API needs a user action. Call it from a click or key handler." A call made after an `await` in Dart may no longer be tied to its service; its answer then goes to every listener of the model. Python has no tab: a Python service has no browser APIs yet, and a Python service that uses one stops the build with `TY1605`. C++ has no tab either: a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient`, so a C++ service has no browser APIs yet (`TY1372`).

type PlaceService() =
    let geolocation = Geolocation()
    let clipboard = Clipboard()
    member val Place : string = "" with get, set
    member val Problem : string = "" with get, set

    member this.Locate() : unit = this.KeepProblem(fun () -> geolocation.CurrentPosition())

    member this.Copy() : unit = this.KeepProblem(fun () -> clipboard.WriteText(this.Place))

    [<OnEvent>]
    member this.Found(found: PositionFound) : unit =
        this.Place <- string found.Latitude + ", " + string found.Longitude

    [<OnEvent>]
    member this.Failed(failed: BrowserCallFailed) : unit =
        this.Problem <- failed.Message

    member private this.KeepProblem(call: unit -> unit) : unit =
        try
            call ()
        with :? System.InvalidOperationException as refusal ->
            this.Problem <- refusal.Message
