#[Service]
class PlaceService
  # @return [String]
  attr_reader :place
  # @return [String]
  attr_reader :problem

  def initialize
    @geolocation = Geolocation.new
    @clipboard = Clipboard.new
    @place = ""
    @problem = ""
  end

  # @return [void]
  def locate
    keep_problem { @geolocation.current_position }
  end

  # @return [void]
  def copy
    keep_problem { @clipboard.write_text(@place) }
  end

  # @param found [PositionFound]
  # @return [void]
  #[OnEvent]
  def found(found)
    @place = "#{found.latitude}, #{found.longitude}"
  end

  # @param failed [BrowserCallFailed]
  # @return [void]
  #[OnEvent]
  def failed(failed)
    @problem = failed.message
  end

  private

  # @return [void]
  def keep_problem
    yield
  rescue RuntimeError => refusal
    @problem = refusal.message
  end
end

---@param call function
---@param api table

sections.heading: Browser APIs in test units
sections.body:
A test unit runs without a page, so Tachyon's browser APIs cannot reach a browser there. Give them fake answers instead.

JavaScript and TypeScript: declare the API as a `@Fake` field of the test unit and assign the fake object. `construct` gives it to the service's field of the same name, like a `@Fake` for a service. For example, `@Fake clock;` and then `this.clock = { now: () => 1000 };` before `this.construct(StampService)`.

Go: give each call an answer with `BrowserFakes`, for example `BrowserFakes{}.Answer("clock", "now", 1000)` and `BrowserFakes{}.Answer("connectivity", "online", false)`. The first argument is the API, the second is the call (its JavaScript name), and the third is the value that the call returns.

Ruby: `BrowserFakes.answer("clock", "now", 1000)` works the same way.

Lua: `BrowserFakes.answer("clock", "now", 1000)` works the same way.

Swift: `BrowserFakes.answer("clock", "now", 1000)` works the same way. `Clock().nowMs()` and `monotonicMs()` cannot throw, so without an answer they read the computer's clock.

C# and F#: `BrowserFakes.Answer("clock", "now", 1000)` works the same way. The unit sees the same `Clock`, `Connectivity` and other API classes as the page, and the built-in event models: C# records such as `new ConnectivityChanged(true)`, and F# records such as `{ Online = true }`.

A call without an answer fails with a message that names `BrowserFakes`. To test a listener, call it with a value of the built-in event model, for example `service.HearConnectivity(ConnectivityChanged{Online: false})` in Go or `service.hearConnectivity(ConnectivityChanged(online: false))` in Swift. Rust and Dart test units cannot use these APIs yet, because their test programs do not include the page's clients. Kotlin and Java have no `BrowserFakes` yet. Test such services in the browser for now. Python services have no browser APIs, so their test units need no fakes.

sections.heading: What a native service reaches
sections.body:
Native services use their platform SDK (software development kit). They inject an ApplicationEventPublisher for local events that they own. They use OnEvent, and OnStart and OnStop for the lifecycle. Each example initializes the service and publishes a CatalogCount model. A listener updates the count, and cleanup resets it. Old callbacks from an earlier activation cannot change the owners that replaced it. A native service has no page, so it cannot use Tachyon's browser APIs (such as `Clock`, `Clipboard` or `Geolocation`) or listen for their built-in event models (such as `ConnectivityChanged`). The build refuses them in a service that is linked into the app (`TY1317`). Use them in a JavaScript, TypeScript or WebAssembly service, and send the result to the native service with an event. `WindowControls` is the one exception: a linked service gets it from the host through an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `Needs` or `NeedsAll` (ADR 0089; see the feature "What a page may do to its window"). Only Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services are linked into a native app. JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Go, Ruby, Java, F#, Lua, Python and C++ services always run in the page, also inside a native app, so this section has no tab for them.

On macOS, Linux and Windows, a page call sends a JSON request and waits for a reply. The Rust method runs synchronously on the host's user interface thread: the macOS main actor, the Linux GTK main loop, or the Windows window thread. Windows sends one call at a time with a 10 second timeout. Keep these methods short and put long work in an application-owned background task. Arguments are positional; a model argument uses its Rust field names as JSON keys. Same-named methods in mutually exclusive `#[cfg]` implementation blocks pass the class-layout checks, and the target compiler selects the matching implementation.

A desktop bridge request is at most 64 KiB. Linux and Windows also cap the encoded reply at 64 KiB and answer an oversized reply with a paging hint. macOS currently has no reply-size cap. Application code owns paging and its total-transfer limit, for example 2 MiB; these are not fields of the Tachyon bridge. Keep each text page at most 24 KiB and check that the complete escaped JSON reply fits the host limit: quotes and backslashes double in JSON, and control characters can expand further. The Linux bridge fixture verifies quote/backslash, multibyte and plain-text pages, plus oversized request and reply refusal.

Tachyon imposes no sandbox root on Linux or Windows. Apps choose their own per-user paths, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<app>` on Windows and `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or `$XDG_STATE_HOME` on Linux. MSIX and Flatpak packaging are not planned.

sections.heading: Services are compiled in
sections.body:
Tachyon compiles a `<Name>Service.swift`, `.kt`, `.cs` or `.rs` file in client/services for a supported target and includes it in the host. A Rust, C#, Swift or Kotlin service may have no browser sibling. Then it also compiles to WebAssembly. The browser runs that WebAssembly, and so does the web view of any target that does not link the service: iOS and Android for Rust, every target except Windows for C#, Windows, Linux and Android for Swift, and every target except Android for Kotlin (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0078, ADR 0082; an ADR is an architecture decision record). A Go or Java service links into no host, so it always compiles to WebAssembly and runs in the web view on every target (ADR 0045, ADR 0083). Swift and Rust use native compilation. A Swift method marked `async`, such as a `@Cached` method, runs on macOS and iOS too: the host waits for it on the main thread and keeps the main run loop turning, so work that the method sends to the main actor can finish. Kotlin uses the Android toolchain. C# uses the Windows .NET host. In all other cases, the browser runs the `.js`, `.ts` or `.dart` file next to them. Native service code reaches the platform SDK with the operating system permissions of the host process. So every service reaches every target.

A Swift or Kotlin service with `NeedsAll` can declare a field without a value, such as `let title: String`. Tachyon generates the constructor that fills it from the props of the component (ADR 0057). When a prop is missing or has the wrong type, Tachyon does not create the service, and the page gets the error code `TY_NATIVE_REQUIRED`.

sections.heading: Rust crates and helper executables
sections.body:
A desktop app can declare the crates its native Rust companion needs in `tac.application.rust` in `client/manifest.json` (ADR 0019). `dependencies` applies to every desktop, and `platformDependencies` has `macos`, `linux` and `windows` tables. Each version is exact, written `=MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A dependency can also set `features` and `defaultFeatures` (true unless set to false). Git, path and registry dependencies and unknown declaration fields are refused at build time (`TY1601`). The app needs at least one native Rust service. These declarations do not supply crates for a service compiled as WebAssembly.

Tachyon builds declared crates offline from `vendor/rust/` at the project root, beside `client/`. Stage the selected host first, for example `ty bundle --target windows --arch arm64 --native`. This writes `dist/windows/project/rust-companion/Cargo.toml` without invoking the platform packager. To prepare the vendored folder, run `cargo vendor --manifest-path dist/windows/project/rust-companion/Cargo.toml vendor/rust` yourself with the sources you intend to use. That preparation step may download crates; a Tachyon bundle never does. Then run the same bundle command without `--native` to package it. Change the staged path when you choose another target or `--out-dir`. Cargo runs with `--offline`, `net.offline=true` and registry source replacement. A missing folder stops the build before Cargo (`TY1605`), and a missing crate fails offline resolution.

`executables` maps a program name to a Rust class file under `client/`. Names use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, and there may be at most eight. The name must not match the app executable. The entry class is named after its file and has `pub fn run() -> i32`; Tachyon generates a main function that calls it and uses its result as the exit code. A helper can reach exported companion items through `crate::models` and `crate::<Type>`.

Helpers have stable paths beside the main executable: `<App>/bin/<name>` on Linux, `<App>\bin\<name>.exe` on Windows, and `<App>.app/Contents/MacOS/<name>` on macOS. A helper can resolve that folder from `std::env::current_exe()?.parent()`. macOS helpers are signed ad hoc before the app bundle is signed. Tachyon packages these programs; the app chooses when to start them. No service, login item, autostart entry or elevated helper is registered.

devices.title: Targets
devices.summary: A target is the kind of app that you build: web, macos, windows, linux, ios or android. You write the pages once. The web target runs in a browser. The other targets put the same pages in a desktop or mobile app.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.body: The bundle targets are web, macos, windows, linux, ios and android. The web target writes browser assets. Every other target prepares a host that contains the platform WebView. Native packaging needs the SDKs (software development kits) and host tools for that platform. The windows target also needs the WebView2 SDK: restore the `Microsoft.Web.WebView2` package and set `TAC_WEBVIEW2_SDK` to the folder where you extracted it, or the build stops with `TY1605`. Build a Windows app on Windows, from a Visual Studio developer prompt, so that `cl` and the Windows SDK are on the PATH. The app is built for x64. On a Windows on Arm PC, open the prompt for ARM64 host and x64 target (`vcvarsall.bat arm64_amd64`); the x64 app runs there under emulation. There is no ARM64 target yet. A Windows app shows its page only in a signed-in desktop session. Started from a service or an SSH session, the window opens but WebView2 cannot attach to it, so the page stays empty. The all target builds every target. It writes one folder for each target under dist/. You must still test on each platform.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target web
ty bundle --target macos
ty bundle --target windows
ty bundle --target linux
ty bundle --target ios
ty bundle --target android
ty bundle --target all

sections.heading: One bundle, every target
sections.body:
Every non-web target contains the platform's own WebView and loads the application's own bundle (its built files). Tachyon does not turn tags into native controls. So there is no fallback (a second way to show a tag) to think about. The bundle renders the same way on every target.

In the past, Tachyon converted a Tac view into SwiftUI, Compose and WinUI controls. Where it had no adapter for a tag, it used a web view instead. In real designs, the web view showed almost everything. The other parts looked very different from the rest. Tachyon removed this approach. It also removed the `--render-mode` flag and `TAC_RENDER_MODE`. Tachyon rejects them if you pass them.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos
ty bundle --target android
ty bundle --target windows

sections.heading: What the page knows about its host
sections.body: Native hosts mark the body with data-platform="native". The capability manifest (client/manifest.json) still limits the window controls and the browser APIs that need a grant (`tac.browserApis`). Tachyon does not inject (add) a platform, environment, os or target variable for you. To reach its own element, a JavaScript or TypeScript service injects view. This works only in the browser. A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby, Python, Lua or C++ has no DOM (the tree of page elements), so it cannot read this mark, and this section has no tab for those languages. The application itself is responsible for native capabilities.

native-hosts.title: Native hosts
native-hosts.summary: A native host is the desktop or mobile app that Tachyon builds for a target. It shows your pages in the WebView, the browser view that is built into the operating system. So the app shows exactly what the browser shows.

sections.heading: The same page on every device
sections.body:
`web` is a browser target. Native hosts serve the built application bundle inside the platform WebView. They serve it from a restricted local origin. An origin is the scheme, host and port that a page comes from. The WebView is WKWebView on macOS and iOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux, and Android WebView on Android. The same DOM, CSS and client runtime render the application. Browser engines still differ, so test on each target.

To match the look of a platform, make that choice in the UI layer. Use the UI kit that the application already uses. The framework does not make this choice by turning tags into controls.

sections.heading: One HTML file for every target
sections.body: An application writes `tac.html` once. The control elements `logic`, `loop`, `switch` and `case` compile into a render plan (the compiled steps that build the page). The shared client runtime runs that plan. It mounts components (adds them to the page) to create the DOM. A published route document starts that renderer. It does not contain a view subtree rendered on the server. Native hosts use the same plan and runtime. They do not build a second tree of platform widgets.

sections.heading: The platform's own JavaScript engine
sections.body: Tachyon does not build or include its own JavaScript engine. Each host uses the engine that its platform already includes. This is the same engine that runs the WebView inside the host.
sections.code:
macOS, iOS   WKWebView      system WebKit and JavaScriptCore
Linux        WebKitGTK      system WebKit and JavaScriptCore dependencies
Windows      WebView2       requires the WebView2 runtime
Android      WebView        uses the installed system WebView provider

sections.heading: What the host adds
sections.body:
The host adds three things. First, `data-platform="native"` on the document body. With it, a page can behave differently without checking the user agent string (the text that names the browser). Second, the list of window controls that the manifest granted, and nothing else. A service reaches them through the injected `WindowControls` browser API. Third, the service channel, which works in both directions.

On macOS, the host also builds the standard menu bar, with the items that `tac.application.menus` declares. On Linux and Windows, it shows a menu bar when the manifest declares at least one item (see Native menus). A menu item opens a page or calls a service method; it gives the page no new capability. These three desktop hosts also run application services: Rust services with `#[Lifetime({"value":"application"})]` that start with the app and stop when it quits.

On macOS, `"titleBar": "integrated"` in `tac.application.window` lets the page reach the top edge of the window. The host then sets the CSS custom properties `--tac-titlebar-height`, `--tac-titlebar-leading-inset` and `--tac-titlebar-trailing-inset`, and it moves the window when a person drags an element marked `data-tac-drag-region` (see Window controls). This is a window setting, not a new capability.

On purpose, Tachyon adds no other capability vocabulary (a fixed list of platform actions). A compiled service can use its platform's SDK because it was compiled in that language for that target. A list of verbs between them would contain only the part that Tachyon had built.

sections.heading: What the host does not do
sections.body:
The host has no managed surface (a view that the host controls) for remote content. It has no always-on-top or opacity control beyond what the manifest grants. It has no global shortcut registry and no system tray API. These features were once a fixed list of verbs compiled into each host. A fixed list limits what an application can do. If an application needs one of these features, it uses the feature from its service. It uses it in the language of the platform it runs on.

The host also does not pass platform errors to the page. When a native service throws an error, the page gets only the fixed message "Native companion operation failed.", on every native host. The exception text stays in the app.

platform-apis.title: Platform APIs
platform-apis.summary: A platform API is a feature of the device, such as the tray or the file system. In a native host, the page is the same as in the browser. A service that is compiled for the platform uses the platform API directly.

sections.heading: No fixed list of platform actions
sections.body:
Tachyon does not put a list of verbs (fixed platform actions) between an application and its platform. A tray, a notification and a file dialog belong to the platform. A service written in the platform's own language can already use them. A fixed list in the middle could contain only the part that Tachyon had built. That part would have to exist in three hosts, for every platform at once. An application would be limited to that part.

So in the browser, a JavaScript or TypeScript service uses web APIs. A service in another language uses Tachyon's small set of browser APIs (`Clock`, `SecureRandom`, `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences`, `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation`), or gets other browser values from a JavaScript or TypeScript service through an event. Python services do not have Tachyon's browser APIs yet (see "What each service language can use in the browser"). A service that is linked into a native app has no page, so the build refuses these browser APIs in it (`TY1317`). The native side uses AppKit, UIKit, the Android framework or Win32, each from the language that already works with it.

sections.heading: What the host injects
sections.body:
On purpose, the host injects three things and no more. First, the document body carries `data-platform="native"`. With it, a page can style itself or behave differently without checking the user agent string. The user agent string is the text that names the browser. Second, the list of window controls that the manifest granted. Tachyon's page runtime reads it, and a service reaches the controls only through the injected `WindowControls` browser API. Third, the service channel runs in both directions. A service publishes to the page, and the page calls the service by its instance name.

The publish stub (a small function that the host injects) puts values in a queue. It does not deliver them at once. A service may publish from its own thread before the page's modules have run. Without the queue, that value would be lost. This loss is a race condition, and the application cannot see it. A race condition is a bug that depends on which code runs first.

The example shows the JavaScript form of the injected `WindowControls`. TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Java, C# and F# get the same controls in their own syntax, so this section has no tab for them; the feature "What a page may do to its window" shows the service in every language that has `WindowControls`. Lua, Python and C++ services do not get `WindowControls`: the field stops the build with `TY2015` in Lua and `TY1605` in Python, and a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient` (`TY1372`).

A native capability is not a fourth thing in the page. `tac.nativeCapabilities: ["filePicker"]` in `client/manifest.json` lets the host answer the calls of a service's `FilePicker` field. Only a macOS app opens a panel; every other host answers `unsupported` (see the feature "Inject an OS file picker into a service").

sections.heading: The same service shape in every language
sections.body: A service is written in its own language and uses its own platform directly. So there is no portable verb list to learn. All languages share the same shape. A class has the same name as its file. Its fields are state and its methods are behaviour. It has the two persistence lifetimes (how long saved fields last) that the browser gives a page. It has an injected applicationEventPublisher and OnEvent for local events that it owns. Each language writes these parts in its own normal syntax. Lua and Python do not have every part yet: Lua has no saved fields, and Python has no saved fields and no event listeners (see "Which languages can I use?").

sections.heading: What the host records
sections.body: A packaged host writes `tachyon.host.json` next to its bundle. The file names the target the host was built for. It also names the one capability that the bridge (the channel between the page and the service) offers: `companion.invoke`. The file is one line because it holds very little information. An application uses everything else through its own language.
sections.code: { "hostCapabilities": ["companion.invoke"] }

window-controls.title: Window controls
window-controls.summary: In a desktop or mobile app, `client/manifest.json` describes the window that the app opens. It lists the window controls that a page may ask for; by default, a page may ask for none. On macOS, it can also let the page reach the top edge of the window, with an integrated title bar.

sections.heading: Window controls need permission
sections.body: client/manifest.json declares the window that a native target opens and the controls that a service may use, under `tac.application.window.controls`. By default, the manifest grants nothing. A service gets the controls by injection, like the other browser APIs: `@Needs windowControls` in JavaScript and TypeScript, and a `WindowControls` field in every language that runs in the page. Lua and Python services do not get `WindowControls`. A service that the native app links in has no page, but it can still get the controls: a Swift or Rust service in a macOS app, a C# service on Windows and a Kotlin service on Android declare an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `Needs` or `NeedsAll`, and Tachyon calls the host directly, with the same grants (ADR 0089). A service never reads `globalThis` (`TY1360`). `granted(control)` answers whether a control is granted; ask it before you offer a control. A call to a control that is not granted fails at once, and the message names the grant to add. In a browser tab nothing is granted, because the page has no native window. The host checks the manifest grants again before it runs a request. A test unit fakes the controls like any browser API: a `@Fake windowControls` field in JavaScript and TypeScript, and `BrowserFakes` in Go, Ruby, Swift, C# and F#. These controls do not sandbox (restrict) the native service code that the application owns. That code runs with the operating system permissions of the host process. See the feature "What a page may do to its window" for the service in every language.

sections.heading: Integrated title bar
sections.body:
With `"titleBar": "integrated"` in `tac.application.window`, a macOS app shows one continuous surface: the page reaches the top edge of the window, and the real close, minimize and full screen buttons sit on the page. The window keeps its title for VoiceOver, Mission Control and the Window menu; only the text is hidden. The optional `titleBarButtonInset` moves the buttons, in points from the leading and top edges (0 to 200 each). The default is `"standard"`. Any other `titleBar` value, a `titleBarButtonInset` without `"titleBar": "integrated"`, a value above 200 or an unknown key in the inset stops the build with `TY1601`.

The host tells the page how much room the buttons need with three CSS custom properties: `--tac-titlebar-height`, `--tac-titlebar-leading-inset` and `--tac-titlebar-trailing-inset`. It updates them when the window is resized, enters or leaves full screen, or changes appearance. In full screen they are `0px`, because macOS shows the title bar over the page only when the pointer reaches the top of the screen. A browser sets none of them, so always write a fallback, such as `max(16px, var(--tac-titlebar-leading-inset, 0px))`. Draw the page in both light and dark colors (for example with `light-dark()`); the title bar area shows the page background, so there is no strip of another color.

The page now covers the area that moves the window, so mark that area with `data-tac-drag-region`. Dragging it moves the window, and a double-click does what System Settings says for a title bar double-click (fill, zoom, minimize or nothing). Links, buttons, form fields, focusable elements and anything marked `data-tac-no-drag` inside the region keep their clicks. The rest of the page is never a drag area. Windows, Linux, iOS and Android keep the standard title bar; the build prints a note. See ADR 0098.

native-menus.title: Native menus
native-menus.summary: A macOS, Linux or Windows app that Tachyon builds has a menu bar. `tac.application.menus` in `client/manifest.json` adds your own items to the File, View and Help menus. An item opens a page of the app, or it runs a menu action: a method of a service that lives as long as the app.

sections.heading: The standard menus
sections.body:
The macOS host builds the menu bar itself, so every app has the menus that a Mac user expects. The app menu has About, Hide (Command-H), Hide Others (Option-Command-H), Show All and Quit (Command-Q). Quit is the normal macOS quit, so the app cleans up once. The File menu has Close Window (Command-W). The Edit menu has Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste and Select All; they act on the field that has the focus. The View menu has Enter Full Screen, the Window menu has Minimize (Command-M), Zoom and Bring All to Front, and the Help menu has the system search.

The host adds no New, Open, Save or Print item, because a Tachyon app has no document type. Your own items cannot take a shortcut of these standard commands.

On Linux and Windows the host shows a menu bar only when the manifest declares at least one item, so an app without menus keeps its plain window. That menu bar has File (your File items, then Close Window, Ctrl+W, and Quit, Ctrl+Q; Windows calls it Exit), and View and Help when they have items. There is no Edit menu: the web view handles Cut, Copy, Paste and Select All itself. iOS and Android have no menu bar, so they refuse declared menu items at build time (`TY1601`).

Linux menus and application services are tested by building and running the real GTK 4 and WebKitGTK 6.0 host. Windows menus and application services were built with MSVC and run on Windows 11: the service starts once before the window, menu actions run, and Close Window stops the service once. The page inside WebView2 was not yet tested on Windows, because that needs a signed-in desktop. The Windows app is built for x64; there is no ARM64 target yet.
sections.code:
Monitor   About Monitor, Hide Monitor (Command-H), Hide Others (Option-Command-H),
          Show All, Quit Monitor (Command-Q)
File      your File items, then Close Window (Command-W)
Edit      Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All
View      Enter Full Screen, then your View items
Window    Minimize (Command-M), Zoom, Bring All to Front
Help      system search, then your Help items

Reserved shortcuts: Command-Q, Command-W, Command-H, Option-Command-H,
Command-Z, Shift-Command-Z, Command-X, Command-C, Command-V, Command-A,
Command-M and Control-Command-F.

sections.heading: Menu items that open a page
sections.body:
An item with a `route` opens a page of the app in the same window. Each item has an `id`, a `label`, the `route` and an optional `shortcut`. An item has exactly one of `route` or `action`. The `route` must be a static page of the app, without a query or a fragment, such as `/help`. A shortcut has one lowercase letter or digit and always includes `command`; it may add `control`, `option` and `shift`. On Linux and Windows, `command` is Ctrl, `option` is Alt and `shift` is Shift. A shortcut that uses `control` has no keyboard shortcut there, because Ctrl is already `command`; the item still works from the menu. There are at most 64 items in all menus, and ids and shortcuts must be unique. A wrong item (a bad id, label or shortcut, both `route` and `action`, or neither) stops the build with `TY1601`.

Opening a page loads a new document. The services of the old page stop, and the new page starts with fresh services. Use a menu action when the item must keep the state of the page.

sections.heading: Menu actions
sections.body:
An item with an `action` calls a method of an application service. Such a service is a Rust service in `client/services/` with `#[Lifetime({"value":"application"})]`. It starts with the app and stops when the app quits, so the method also works when no page is open. It lives only inside the app: Tachyon never installs a system service or starts it at login. Application services work in native macOS, Linux and Windows apps. The browser, iOS and Android cannot own one, so the build stops with `TY1406` there. The `action` names the `service` (its type name) and the `method` (a method that takes only `&self`). The return value of the method is ignored. Selecting the item never loads a page, so the page keeps its state: its fields, the text in its inputs and its scroll position.

To change the page, the application service forwards an event. It gets `CurrentPageEvents` by injection and calls `publish_event` with a model from `client/models`. Every live Rust page service with an `OnEvent` listener for that model receives it, as with any other event. A page service that two components share receives it once, and each prototype instance receives it once. `publish_event` answers `false` when the page has no listener. Only Rust page services receive the event directly, because only they can inject an application service. A JavaScript or TypeScript page service can listen to an event that a Rust listener returns. A listener cannot publish to the page again while it receives the event.

The optional `event` names the model that the method forwards. Tachyon uses it to decide when the item is enabled (see the next section). The build checks each action: the service must be a client Rust service with an application lifetime, the method must exist and take only `&self`, and the event must be a Rust model in `client/models`. Otherwise the build stops with `TY1370`.

Menu actions are Rust only. The host calls the generated Rust service module, and only a client Rust service can have the application lifetime. So this section has no JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Go, Ruby, Python, Lua, Swift, Kotlin, Java, C# or F# tab: a service in one of these languages cannot be the `service` of an action (`TY1370`), but it can still run on the page that the action changes. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Lifetime in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: When an item is enabled
sections.body:
One rule decides when a menu action item is enabled. An action with an `event` is enabled only while the window shows a page that has a live Rust page service with an `OnEvent` listener for that event. When there is no such listener, the item is disabled. This happens when no window is open, when another page is shown (such as the Help page), and while a page loads. If a shortcut arrives while the item is disabled, the host refuses it with the system beep and does not call the service.

An action without an `event` belongs to the app, not to a page. It is enabled while the app runs, also when no window is open. A route item is enabled while its window is open.

Linux and Windows follow the same rule. A refused item or shortcut beeps and does not call the service.
sections.code:
Item                         Enabled when
action with "event"          the shown page has a live OnEvent listener for the event
action without "event"       the app runs (also with no window)
route                        the window is open
Close Window, Minimize,      a window is open
Zoom, Enter Full Screen

sections.heading: Close Window and reopening
sections.body:
On macOS, File > Close Window (Command-W) closes the app's own window, like the red close button. The services of that page stop, as when the page changes. The app keeps running, as Mail and Notes do on a Mac: application services keep their state and their work, such as a collector that reads data in the background. With no window open, the window commands and the page actions are disabled, and the actions that belong to the app still work.

Click the app in the Dock to open the window again. The new window shows the start page with fresh page services and new menu items, so nothing from the closed window can receive an action. Quit stops the application services once, whether a window is open or not.

Linux and Windows follow their own convention: closing the last window quits the app. Close Window and Quit both end the app, and the application services stop once. There is no reopen step, because the app is no longer running.
sections.code:
Close Window (Command-W)   page services stop; application services keep running
Click the Dock icon         new window at the start page, fresh page services and menu items
Quit (Command-Q)            application services stop once

dependency-injection.title: Dependency injection
dependency-injection.summary: Dependency injection means that Tachyon creates the objects that a class needs and puts them into its fields. Mark a field with `Needs`, or mark the class with `NeedsAll`. `Lifetime` says how long one object lives.

sections.heading: Fields that Needs fills
sections.body: Put Needs on each field that the container fills, and write no constructor. The container is the part of Tachyon that creates providers and fills fields. The spelling is @Needs in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Dart. It is [Needs] in C#, [<Needs>] on a settable property in F# (an F# primary constructor parameter works too), #[Needs] in PHP, Rust and Ruby, // @Needs in Go and -- @Needs in Lua, where the field is written `order_store = nil,` in the class table. Put it above a field of the managed class or struct. The field must be direct, uninitialized (it has no starting value) and non-static. It must not be nullable either, because the container never fills it with null: the build refuses `store?: OrderStore`, `store: OrderStore | None`, `Optional[OrderStore]`, `?OrderStore $store`, `Option<Arc<OrderStore>>` and a Kotlin, Dart or C# `OrderStore?` with TY1331. Write `store!: OrderStore` in TypeScript, `lateinit var store: OrderStore` in Kotlin and `late final OrderStore store;` in Dart. The same rule holds for every field of a NeedsAll class that has no starting value. The field name uses the language's own variable case, not the class name. It is `orderStore` in JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, Dart and Go, and `$orderStore` in PHP. It is `order_store` in Python, Ruby, Lua and Rust. In C#, a private field is `_orderStore`, and a property or a public field is `OrderStore`. The build refuses `OrderStore OrderStore;` or a Python `orderStore` with TY1332. Only the case is checked, so a field `ledger` with Named("OrderStore") stays allowed. Tachyon assigns the marked fields in the order you declare them. Tachyon leaves an unmarked field alone. Typed languages require the exact concrete provider type. Rust requires Arc<Provider> or std::sync::Arc<Provider>. Go requires *Provider or Provider. JavaScript matches the field to the exact lowerCamel name of the provider (MoneyService becomes moneyService, CatalogClient becomes catalogClient). It rejects any match that is ambiguous. Fields with a starting value and static state stay unchanged. There is no hidden Setting or configuration binding. When the field itself does not select a provider, Named("Provider") names it directly. If that name matches no provider in the entry scope, the build fails. Lifetime still chooses singleton, request or transient. Controllers use request by default, and providers use singleton by default. All of them are local to one invocation. This feature does not give Tac a dependency injection (DI) container. Tac keeps its behavior contexts, which your code owns and creates.

sections.heading: Injection: Yon
sections.body: GET /ledger returns {"total":42}. Three annotations connect every class to the classes it needs. Service, Helper, Needs, Named, NeedsAll and Lifetime work in every Yon language, Lua included. In Tac, Helper has a shorter language list (see Injection: Tac). Needs marks each field that the framework fills. The field must be an instance field, not static, and it must have no starting value. The framework fills the fields in the order that you declare them. The field itself decides which provider it gets. LedgerService declares one LedgerAmountsHelper field. It writes no constructor and nothing else. F# has two forms. A type can take a dependency as a parameter of its primary constructor, which is Spring's constructor injection and the recommended form: LedgerHelper takes its LedgerAmountsHelper this way. Or a Needs property can receive it: a settable `member val` with a written type, as in LedgerService, `[<Needs>] member val Amounts : LedgerAmountsHelper = Unchecked.defaultof<LedgerAmountsHelper> with get, set`. Tachyon sets the property right after the constructor runs, like a Spring field, so a test can set it too. Its type selects the provider, and Named selects another one, as for Settlement in LedgerController. A type may not take the same role both ways, or twice (TY2015). `[<NeedsAll>]` on an F# type only states what the constructor does. When the field does not decide the provider, Named gives the provider's name directly. So you can give a field any words you want, written in the language's variable case (TY1332): lowerCamel case in most languages, snake_case in Python, Ruby and Rust, and an underscore with lowerCamel case for a private C# field, such as `_service`. In LedgerController, the fields service and settlement have Named("LedgerService") and Named("LedgerHelper"). If a name matches no provider in the entry scope, the build fails. Without Named, the field selects its provider in the way its language allows. JavaScript uses the lowerCamel field name. Ruby and Lua use the type comment above the field, such as `# @return [LedgerService]` or `---@type LedgerService`, and the snake_case field name when there is none. Every other language uses the declared type. Lifetime takes one literal string: singleton, request or transient. A singleton is one instance that everything shares. A request-scoped instance lives for one request. A transient instance is new each time something needs it. Without Lifetime, a controller is request-scoped and everything else is a singleton. So you write Lifetime only to change that. Tachyon rejects a singleton that would depend, directly or through other providers, on a request-scoped provider.

<?php
use Models\Ledger;

#[RequestRoute("/ledger")]
#[Public]
class LedgerController {
  #[Needs]
  #[Named('LedgerService')]
  private LedgerService $service;
  #[Needs]
  #[Named('LedgerHelper')]
  private LedgerHelper $settlement;

  #[GetRoute]
  public function getLedger(): Ledger {
    $subtotal = $this->service->subtotal();
    $total = $this->settlement->settle($subtotal);
    return new Ledger($total);
  }
}

sections.heading: Injection: Tac
sections.body:
Tac accepts the same annotations in its browser services, with two differences. First, Lifetime is a literal object, not a string. {"value":"prototype"} gives every component instance its own service. {"value":"singleton"} is the default and shares one service. {"value":"application"} works only for a client Rust service in a native macOS, Linux or Windows app (not in the browser, iOS or Android): one instance starts with the app and stops when it quits, and page services and menu actions reach it (see Native menus). In the browser and on other native targets the build refuses it with TY1406.

A service with NeedsAll already has one instance for each component, because it takes its component's properties. NeedsAll follows Lombok's RequiredArgsConstructor: every field without an initial value is required, and a field with an initial value is plain state. NeedsAll takes no field list, and its class declares no constructor; the build refuses both (ADR 0056). A required collaborator is injected, and every other required field must come from the component's props. A collaborator is a field marked Needs or Named, a field that names a service or provider, or, in every language except JavaScript and TypeScript, a field whose type is a browser resource such as Clock, PreferenceStrings or DocumentTitle. JavaScript and TypeScript mark a browser resource field with Needs. PreferenceStrings has `read(key)` and `write(key, value)` for plain string preferences, in JavaScript, TypeScript and Java services. DocumentTitle has `set(text)` for the page title, in JavaScript, TypeScript and Kotlin services. The build refuses both in other languages and in linked native services. Setting, LocalState and SessionState fields are filled by Tachyon as well. Any other annotation on a field, such as JsonProperty in Java or Published in Swift, leaves it a prop.

The build refuses a page that does not pass a prop, and the browser refuses a missing or null value. So a required field and a Needs field are never null when a method runs, and the build refuses one that is declared nullable with TY1331. Write the language's non-null form: `open!: boolean` in TypeScript, `late final String path;` in Dart, `val path: String` or `lateinit var path: String` in Kotlin, `let path: String` in Swift (or `var store: Store!` for a Needs field), `public required string Path;` in C#, and `path: String` in Rust instead of `Option<String>`. A field that may stay empty is plain state: give it a starting value, such as `note: string | null = null`. `ty migrate fix --write` rewrites the simple cases. A required field in a Swift or Kotlin service can be a let or val with no value. Tachyon writes the constructor for it and fills the field from the props.

A required field whose name is the instance name of a service, such as documentation next to DocumentationService, is that service and never a prop. So the build also refuses a page that passes :documentation to that component, with TY1407: rename the field, for example to documents, to receive the value, or mark it Needs and stop passing it if you meant the service. Lifetime is for a service like CartService, which keeps state for each component without those properties.

Second, Needs finds a Tac provider from the field name in lowerCamel case, or in snake_case in Rust and Python. So CartService declares cartPricesHelper and cartHelper. A field that copies the class name, such as `CartPricesHelper`, stops the build with TY1332, because an injected field uses the language's variable case. The service writes no constructor at all. AuditService calls its field ledger, so it gives the provider's name with Named("CartHelper") instead. Python writes both markers inside the field's type: `ledger: Annotated[CartHelper, needs, named("CartHelper")]`. Dart marks each injected field final, and it also writes no constructor.

Helper works in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust and Python, where Needs injects it. C# and F# use Helper too, but Tachyon does not inject it there: the caller builds it with `new`, as the C# and F# tabs show. CartService and AuditService create their helpers in their constructors (in F#, in `let` bindings), and CartHelper creates its own CartPricesHelper. On a C# or F# Helper the build refuses Needs, NeedsAll, Lifetime, OnStart, OnStop and OnEvent with TY1308, and it also refuses an F# class whose constructor takes a Helper. A C++ web service has a graph of injected services too: `[[Needs]] CounterService& counter;` injects another C++ service or a C++ HTTP client of the same page program, and every C++ service is one shared instance (ADR 0099). A Go web service needs another Go service the same way, with `// @Needs` above a field such as `counter *CounterService`, and the field holds the instance that the page uses (see A service that needs another service: Tac, below). Swift, Kotlin, Go, Ruby, Lua, Java and C++ have no tab here, because the build refuses Helper in those languages with TY1308. Their services use the other roles instead.

An entity Store is the exception: it has no dependencies and opens the context of its own Setup, so a service in every Tac language that has a Store asks for one with Needs, and an F# service takes it as a constructor parameter (see Data access: Tac). A Converter is the other exception: it has no dependencies and needs no context, so a service asks for it the same way (see Mapping: Tac). Roles: Tac above shows where native roles go. client/manifest.json turns on the pinned Python runtime that the Python tab needs (ADR 0093).

sections.heading: A service that needs another service: Tac
sections.body:
A service can need another service. Mark a field with Needs and give it the type of the other service. The field holds the same instance that the page uses. The view below shows {counter.count}, and TallyService changes that count when it calls increment on its counter field. So a click on Bump changes both lines. In JavaScript and TypeScript, the field name is the instance name of the other service: counter for CounterService.

In Go, `// @Needs` sits on the line above a field such as `counter *CounterService` (ADR 0045). All Go services of a page build into one Go package, so TallyService names CounterService without an import and calls its methods directly. The field holds a pointer, so TallyService and the page share one CounterService. The field stays inside the service: the page never reads it. Tachyon creates the needed service first and runs its OnStart first, so the OnStart of TallyService can already use counter. When TallyService calls counter.Increment() and CounterService publishes an event there, the event reaches every listener on the page, as if the page had called the method. Tachyon stops the services in the opposite order: OnStop of TallyService runs before OnStop of CounterService. If the page disposes of its CounterService first, TallyService keeps it until TallyService stops. The OnEvent methods of a needed Go service run when the page uses that service too, as this view does with counter.

A needed Go service is a page singleton: it keeps its state when the components that use it come and go, and it stops when the last Go service of the page is disposed. The build refuses these Go fields with TY1406, at the field: a field that holds the service by value, such as `counter CounterService`, because a copy is not shared; a field whose service has one instance for each component, because it is Lifetime prototype or NeedsAll; services that need each other in a circle, which you break with an event; and a field whose type the page has under two instance names, unless the field name is one of them.

Python writes the marker inside the field's type: `counter: Annotated[CounterService, needs]`. The field holds the CounterService that the page uses, so it is never a property of the component. A Dart service takes no Needs marker here. TallyService declares `late CounterService counter;`, a field typed with the other Dart service and named after its instance, and the page fills it with that same instance (ADR 0033). With `@Needs` on that field, the build stops with TY1009, because Needs in Dart builds a collaborator class from the service's own file. A C++ service needs another C++ service with `[[Needs]] CounterService& counter;`. Every C++ service of a page program is one shared instance, and Tachyon compiles CounterService before TallyService (ADR 0099).

The other Tac languages have no tab here, because their browser services cannot need another service yet. The build refuses the field in Rust with TY1406, in Java and F# with TY1405, and in C# with TY1308: Needs there takes only the providers that the language's browser build supplies, such as a client or a browser resource. Kotlin and Swift build each browser service in its own scope, so the compiler cannot find CounterService from TallyService, and the build stops with TY1605. In Ruby and Lua, the build refuses a Needs field whose type is another service with TY2015, at the field: `#[Needs]` with `# @return [CounterService]` on `attr_reader :counter` in Ruby (ADR 0054), and `-- @Needs` with `---@type CounterService` on `counter = nil,` in Lua (ADR 0085). In these languages Needs takes a Store, a Converter or an HTTPClient in Ruby, and a Converter in Lua. To reach CounterService from Ruby or Lua, let the view call it, or publish an event that CounterService handles with OnEvent. Injection: Tac above shows Needs with helpers, and One per page, or one per component explains Lifetime.

behavior-annotations.title: Behavior annotations
behavior-annotations.summary: Behavior annotations add common work to a method without extra code, such as caching, retries, value checks, stores and settings. The same annotations work in Tac and in Yon, in every service language except Lua and Python in Tac: Lua Tac code refuses them, and Python Tac cannot run them yet.

sections.heading: Shared behavior annotations: all supported languages
sections.body: Every Yon language supports the shared behavior annotations: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua. Lua has two limits: a Lua model cannot carry `Settings` or `Checked` yet (`TY1310`), and a Lua `Store` is not yet a provider that another class can inject (`TY2015`). Tac supports the annotations in JavaScript, TypeScript and Dart browser services. It also supports them in native Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services and in Go web services. Swift is not a Yon language. Native ports have typed execution adapters, not an embedded JavaScript runtime. The names need no import in any language, because Tachyon annotations and types are global. JavaScript and TypeScript write @Name. Other languages use these forms: @Name for Java, Groovy, Kotlin, Swift and Dart; @snake_case for Python; [Name] for C#; [<Name>] for F#; #[Name] for PHP, Ruby and Rust; -- @Name for Lua. A Python parameter or field marker goes inside the type, `Annotated[ProductInput, check]`, so the file stays valid Python; the old decorator form is refused, and ty migrate fix --write converts it. Rust also accepts the namespaced forms #[yon::snake_case] and #[tac::snake_case]. Go uses standalone // @Name comments, with one space after //. The comments are valid Go syntax and keep their spelling under gofmt (ADR 0050). The examples on this site leave out the package line, so add one, such as package main, before you run gofmt on a copied example. Type checking still needs the framework declarations that Tachyon generates. Put a marked Go parameter on its own line, followed by a comma. A comment marker that is close to a Tachyon name, such as // @GetRote, fails the build and suggests the right name. Other comments such as the // @Summary lines of swag stay ordinary comments. Run ty migrate fix --write to convert the old Go bracket markers. Ruby writes each marker as a #[Name] comment line, alone on its line, so an annotated Ruby file stays ordinary Ruby (ADR 0054). A bare @Name line and # [Name], with the space that RuboCop's Layout/LeadingCommentSpace adds, are refused with the right spelling, so turn that RuboCop rule off for marker lines. Ruby has every shared behavior annotation, in Yon and in Tac services. A parameter marker such as #[Check(ProductInput)] stands on its own line inside a parameter list written over several lines, and YARD tags give the types. Each marker is on its own line. Object options are strict JSON literals. You need no annotation package, no reflection scanner and no global decorator registration. A reflection scanner is code that inspects classes while the program runs. The Cache import is local to the source file. It does not replace the Cache constructor of the browser. Invalid declarations fail with TY1308.

sections.heading: What the behavior annotations do
sections.body: Setup gives factories (functions that create objects) that you write yourself. On managed Yon roles, Needs finds the provider dependencies and writes the field assignment. Unmanaged behavior types and Tac still create objects in code that you write. CacheSettings, Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache manage cache operations that are authorized and limited. PageDefaults normalizes input (puts it into a standard form). It does not fetch a collection or slice it. Entity, Table, object-form Store and Query give mappings and read-only structured queries. They are not an ORM (object-relational mapper), and they do not give migrations (scripts that change the database structure). HTTP request annotations are for outgoing requests. It is never a route decorator. Settings, WhenProfile and WhenSetting bind (copy values into typed fields) and select configuration that you give yourself. Checked, Check, Required, NotEmpty, Length, Min and Max validate the direct fields of JSON values. RequestRoute and the method route annotations define Yon endpoints. Put cache policies on services, after request authentication. AllOrNothing names the entities adapter (code that connects Tachyon to a data store) that handles begin, commit and rollback. Every Store command inside a transaction (a group of changes that all succeed or all fail) carries that adapter. `Gateway` is a Yon-only marker outside this set. It declares a method that another language answers (see Calling a method in another language).

sections.heading: Cache changes run after success
sections.body: UpdateCache and ClearCache accept {method: 'find', arguments: [0]}, written in strict JSON in annotations. The target is a Cached method in the same class. arguments maps the parameter positions of the mutation method to the raw arguments of the target. The mutation method is the method that changes data. The mutation reuses the pagination, key selection, Cache namespace, TTL (time to live) and limits of the target. Tachyon checks authorization (cache:put or cache:evict), adapter availability and keys before application code runs. The set or delete happens only after the output succeeds within its limits. The output must also pass the cancellation and deadline checks. Put never reads the cache. A failure does not change the cache. This is not an atomic (all or nothing) transaction across the database and the cache. If a database change succeeds and the cache adapter then fails, the application must still fix the difference. A mutation cannot have its own @PageDefaults. It can combine with an HTTP request annotation, which provides its successful result.

sections.heading: Limited Store and Query
sections.body: Store names an Entity class from the same source, like Store(ProductEntity, {...}), and at most 64 allowed fields. A Store is a contract with no implementation, like a Spring Data repository interface: Tachyon builds its behavior context from its Setup (ProductSetup for ProductStore, or the setup option), and a controller or service injects it with Needs. A Store with no Entity is refused with TY1308. Each method is a query without a body, and it compiles to a find, findOne, count, exists or delete operation. In JavaScript and TypeScript they declare their answer with | void, such as Promise<ProductEntity[] | void>, because an empty body returns nothing to the type checker. They use either a structured Query or derived names: findByStatus, countByStatus, existsByStatus, deleteByStatus and the same names in snake_case. A Store that extends Repository<Entity, Id>, like Spring Data's CrudRepository, also gets findById (a findOne on the Id field), findAll (a find with no predicate), save and deleteById without declaring them. Derived predicates (conditions) support Equals, NotEquals, LessThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqual, In, IsNull and IsNotNull, joined by And. The structured operators are eq/ne/lt/lte/gt/gte/in/isNull/isNotNull. Tachyon does not accept SQL text, expressions, OR, joins, nested paths or bulk updates; a delete removes exactly the records that its predicates match. The entity adapter receives a query command with bound values (values sent apart from the query text). The adapter must have authorizeEntity(command, execution). That method must return true before execute runs. The limits are eight predicates, 100 In values, 64 KiB of bindings and 1 MiB of results. Find returns at most the requested page size, and the maximum is 100. The annotation sets the order. When two results have the same order, the ID decides. The caller's page.sort must be empty. FindOne returns the first matching record or null. Count and delete return a nonnegative safe integer. Exists returns a boolean. Query cannot combine with other method policies. The examples run queries through an explicit, authorized in-memory adapter. Every language declares the same store and controller route. In Lua the store is a class table marked `-- @Store(ProductEntity, {...})` whose methods have empty bodies, and the Setup's entity adapter is a table with an `execute` method, here CatalogRowsHelper.

files.name: server/helpers/CatalogAdapterHelper.php
files.code:
<?php

#[Helper]
class CatalogAdapterHelper {
    public static function execute(array $command, mixed $execution): array|int {
        $rows = [['id' => 1, 'status' => 'active'], ['id' => 2, 'status' => 'retired']];
        $query = $command['query'];
        $condition = $query['where'][0];
        $keepUnequalRows = $condition['operator'] === 'ne';
        $matchingRows = [];
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            $isEqual = $row[$condition['field']] === $condition['value'];
            $isMatch = $keepUnequalRows ? !$isEqual : $isEqual;
            if ($isMatch) $matchingRows[] = $row;
        }
        if ($query['kind'] === 'count') return count($matchingRows);
        return array_slice($matchingRows, 0, $query['page']['size']);
    }

    public static function authorize(array $command, mixed $execution): bool {
        return $command['entity'] === 'ProductEntity';
    }
}

files.name: server/helpers/CatalogAdapterHelper.fs
files.code:
open System.Threading.Tasks

[<Helper>]
type CatalogAdapterHelper() =
    let rows = BehaviorJSON.Parse("[{\"id\":1,\"status\":\"active\"},{\"id\":2,\"status\":\"retired\"}]")

    interface BehaviorEntityAdapter with
        member this.execute(command: BehaviorJSON, execution: BehaviorExecution) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
            let query = command.Get("query")
            let condition = query.Get("where").Items[0]
            let keepUnequalRows = condition.Get("operator").Text = "ne"
            let isMatch (row: BehaviorJSON) =
                let isEqual = row.Get(condition.Get("field").Text).ToString() = condition.Get("value").ToString()
                if keepUnequalRows then not isEqual else isEqual
            let matchingRows = rows.Items |> Array.filter isMatch
            if query.Get("kind").Text = "count" then
                Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.From(matchingRows.Length))
            else
                Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.Array(matchingRows))

files.code:
#[Setup]
class CatalogSetup
  ROWS = [{ "id" => 1, "status" => "active" }, { "id" => 2, "status" => "retired" }].freeze

  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Hash]
  def self.configure(execution)
    { entities: { catalog: { execute: method(:find_rows) } }, authorizeEntity: method(:product_entity?) }
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Object]
  def self.find_rows(command, execution)
    return [] unless command["operation"] == "query"
    query = command["query"]
    matching_rows = ROWS.select { |row| matches?(row, query["where"][0]) }
    return matching_rows.length if query["kind"] == "count"
    matching_rows.first(query.dig("page", "size") || matching_rows.length)
  end

  # @param row [Hash]
  # @param condition [Hash]
  # @return [Boolean]
  def self.matches?(row, condition)
    is_equal = row[condition["field"]] == condition["value"]
    condition["operator"] == "ne" ? !is_equal : is_equal
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Boolean]
  def self.product_entity?(command, execution)
    command["entity"] == "ProductEntity"
  end
end

}

function CatalogRowsHelper:execute(command, execution)
  local condition = command.query.where[1]
  local matching = {}
  for _, row in ipairs(self.ROWS) do
    if (row.status == condition.value) == (condition.operator == "eq") then
      matching[#matching + 1] = row
    end
  end
  if command.query.kind == "count" then
    return #matching
  end
  return matching
end

  return command.entity == "ProductEntity"
end

sections.heading: Helper calls in each language
sections.body: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and Ruby use Behaviors.properties(CatalogSettings, values) and Behaviors.validate(Input, value). PHP uses Behaviors::properties(CatalogSettings::class, $values) and ::validate(Input::class, $value). Java, Groovy and Kotlin use string names that Tachyon generates from the same source, for example Behaviors.properties("CatalogSettings", values). They do not use reflection. C# passes typeof(CatalogSettings). Swift passes CatalogSettings.self with try. Rust uses Behaviors::properties::<CatalogSettings>(&values)? and ::validate::<Input>(value)?. Go uses BehaviorsProperties[CatalogSettings](values) and BehaviorsValidate[Input](value). These factories are synchronous. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, C#, Dart and Swift, the cache, HTTP and query methods are async. In Java, Groovy, Kotlin, PHP, Rust and Go, these remotes are synchronous, with cooperative limits. With cooperative limits, the running code checks the limits itself. C# and Swift use BehaviorJSON. Rust uses BehaviorValue with BehaviorResult, and Go uses BehaviorValue with (BehaviorValue, error). The JVM (Java virtual machine) languages use strict native values that are compatible with JSON. Context creation keeps its current API, with optional profiles and properties. See docs/BEHAVIOR_ANNOTATIONS.md for the exact typed forms and for fixtures you can run.

sections.heading: Context ownership and cache permission
sections.body: Call Behaviors.create(ConfigurationClass, { partition, signal, timeoutMs }) yourself. Assign the returned context to the behaviors field of each service. The partition (a separate area of data for one owner) is required. Base it on authenticated ownership. Never base it on caller input that was not validated. Use fixed public partitions only for data that is meant to be public. In Yon, create and dispose of the context inside the invocation. There is no global container, and no object is reused across requests. For a shared cache, the application must select an external adapter. By default, each operation has a 10-second deadline, and at most 64 operations run at the same time. You can set timeouts from 1 ms to 60 seconds. The authorize hook receives the operation, cache, type, method and selected keyArguments. The authorize hook is a function that Tachyon calls to ask for permission. It must return the literal value true for every cache access, including hits and eviction (removing entries). Put every argument that changes the result into the cache key. The limits are 4 KiB for keys and 1 MiB for values. The limits are also 24 hours for TTL and 10,000 entries for each policy. The storage adapter must enforce the given quota and replace entries atomically. Tachyon does not control the physical capacity of an external database. A failure never runs side effects again without telling you.

sections.heading: Saved data, outgoing calls and types
sections.body: context.repository(EntityClass) offers find(page), save(value) and delete(id). They return limited JSON, not class instances filled with the data. Adapters own parameterized operations, authorization and tenancy (keeping the data of each tenant separate). Request methods are signatures of an HTTPClient contract: their parameter annotations say where each argument goes, and Tachyon builds the request. The adapter owns a trusted base origin. A literal path cannot select another authority (another host). Transport requests carry redirect: 'error', credentials: 'omit', a signal, a deadline and a 1 MiB response limit. The adapter must enforce that limit while it reads. There are no automatic retries, and no credentials are added without your code. A managed Yon role gets its stores, converters and HTTP clients with Needs fields, so it needs no constructor call. To build a NeedsAll class yourself, for example a plain helper outside the container, TypeScript decorators cannot add constructor signatures, so declare the fields and call Behaviors.construct(Type, { behaviors: context, ...fields }). The runtime checks that the fields are exactly the required set. Request methods should declare the return type Promise<BehaviorJsonValue>, because decorators cannot change the return types that TypeScript infers. A method with an empty body, which Tachyon writes, declares Promise<Hello | void> instead, because an empty body returns nothing to TypeScript; check the value before you use it. This holds for request methods, Gateway methods, Store queries and Convert methods. An entity adapter's execute receives a BehaviorEntityCommand, or a BehaviorTransactionCommand (begin, commit or rollback) for an AllOrNothing method. Generated projects include tachyon-behaviors.d.ts, and ty writes .tachyon/types/client/composed.d.ts and .tachyon/types/server/composed.d.ts, so a test or role file uses a composed class such as a service without an import. A class is composed when its file exports it (export default class) from a role folder, server/errors or server/roles. tachyon-env.d.ts also declares process.env and relay for Yon. Each @Test class also gets behaviors and construct(Type), the members that ty test adds. Each realm's jsconfig.json turns on experimentalDecorators for parameter annotations such as @FromBody and maps imports such as /models/Hello.ts, so tsc -p client/jsconfig.json checks the whole realm. See the repository's docs/BEHAVIOR_ANNOTATIONS.md for the full adapter contract.

sections.heading: Shared browser behavior annotations
sections.body: Tac supports the shared behavior annotations: Setup, Needs, Named, Description, CacheSettings, Cached, UpdateCache, ClearCache, PageDefaults, Retry, MaxAtOnce, Entity, Table, Store, Query, HTTP request annotations, Settings, WhenProfile, WhenSetting, Setting, Checked, Check, Required, NotEmpty, Length, Min and Max. Every language uses these names without an import. They work in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java and Ruby services. Lua refuses them with TY1308 (ADR 0085). Python has no behavior runtime yet (ADR 0093): write these annotations in a service of another language. Native Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services, Go web services and Dart services use typed native adapters. Tac stays client-only. Validation only helps the user fill in forms (UX, the user experience). Queries call adapters (code that connects an annotation to real storage or a real network) that you choose yourself. Setup receives only TAC_ values that you made public on purpose. There is no server-side rendering (SSR), no hidden database connection, no environment snapshot and no package scanner. Native owners dispose of contexts in their own code. Synchronous adapters cannot interrupt blocking work. Setup, Entity and object-form Store declarations have roles, so they follow strict rules. Their folder names are plural, and each file name matches its type exactly. Tachyon finds them automatically in client/setups, client/entities and client/stores, next to the service. The selected sources in the same language form one metadata unit.

sections.heading: Create the behavior context in OnStart
sections.body: Create the context in OnStart. In JavaScript and TypeScript, inject lifecycle and pass this.lifecycle as the context's signal (the object that tells work to stop). The other languages pass a BehaviorSignal that they create. Then give the context to behaviors yourself. When the user leaves the page or a hot replacement happens, Tachyon aborts the operations that are still waiting. For lifetimes that you manage separately, use context.dispose(). The complete service below needs no storage or network adapter. PageDefaults only puts limited input into a standard form. It does not fetch a collection or cut it into parts. The application is responsible for more advanced adapters. The Yon guide describes their shared contracts. docs/BEHAVIOR_ANNOTATIONS.md is the full reference. Python has no tab here: Behaviors.create is asynchronous in Python, and the build refuses asynchronous methods in Python Tac code with TY1605. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup in Lua Tac code with TY1308. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

middleware.title: Middleware
middleware.summary: Middleware is code that runs before every request and after every response. Put it in a `middleware.<ext>` file at the project root. Who may call a route is not middleware work: routes say it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`.

sections.heading: Middleware
sections.body: Tachyon calls a `middleware.<ext>` file at the project root before every request and after every response. The file holds one class named `Middleware`. Tachyon calls its `before(request)` before the route and its `after(request)` after the route. It does this for every request, whatever its HTTP method. `request` is the request in the language's own type, such as a Fetch `Request`, `HttpExchange` or `http::Request`. PHP has no request object and reads `$_SERVER`, `$_GET`, `$_COOKIE` and `php://input`. If the class has no `before` or no `after`, that phase lets the request pass. A method that answers nothing lets the request pass too. A 204 answer continues, and in the after phase its headers are added to the response. Any other status answers the request or replaces the response. The answer is the language's own response, such as a Fetch `Response`, an `(HTTPStatus, headers, body)` tuple in Python, `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo` in PHP, or a write on the `HttpExchange` in Java and Kotlin. You can write root middleware in any Yon language. In Lua, `middleware.lua` holds the class table `Middleware = {}`, its functions take no `self`, such as `function Middleware.before(request)`, `request` is a table with `method`, `path`, `headers` and `body`, and an answer is a `{ status, headers, body }` list. The Middleware feature page shows one middleware file in each language. Any other class in a middleware file fails with `TY1310`. Middleware does not decide who may call a route: every route says it with Public, SignedIn or Allow(Role), and one IdentityProvider class says who is signed in (see Who may call a route).

relays-and-gateways.title: Relays and gateways
relays-and-gateways.summary: A gateway lets a method in one language call a class that is written in another language. A relay sends a request to a program that Yon does not run itself.

sections.heading: Calling a method in another language
sections.body:
`@Gateway` declares a method that another language answers. Write it like a request method: a method without a body in an `HTTPClient` contract. In JavaScript and TypeScript its answer is `Promise<BehaviorJsonValue | void>`. The annotation names one of two targets.

`{"class":"server/services/ReportService.java","method":"summarize"}` names a role file in another Yon language. `method` is optional. By default, it is the name of the annotated method. Tachyon builds a small unit in the language of the target. The unit puts together the role files of that language. It creates the class with its own dependencies. It calls only the methods that callers declared. The target runs like a route: it has the same environment and its own managed storage.

`{"command":["python3","server/helpers/forecast.py"]}` names a program. The first entry is a program on the `PATH` of the server. Every entry that contains a slash is a file under `server/helpers/`. No shell runs, and the arguments of the call never go on the command line. The program reads `{"method": "forecast", "arguments": [3]}` on stdin (standard input) and writes only the JSON result on stdout (standard output). Exit status 0 means success. Any other status is a failure. The program gets only the baseline environment (`PATH`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL` and `TMPDIR` on Unix; `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SYSTEMROOT`, `WINDIR`, `COMSPEC`, `TEMP` and `TMP` on Windows) and the names you add to the allowlist (`server.environment`, see Environment variables for handlers). It never gets `YON_APPLICATION_JSON` or the `YON_RESOURCE_*` values.

The positional arguments of the method travel as JSON. The return value of the other side becomes the result of the method. Typed languages use their JSON value type: `Object` in Java, `Any?` in Kotlin, `BehaviorJsonValue` in TypeScript, `BehaviorValue` in Go. These are the limits: at most 32 arguments; 1 MiB of JSON each way, at most 32 levels deep and 10,000 values; 64 calls and 4 calls at the same time per request; and the time left in the request. Each call starts a new process, so a JVM or .NET target spends its start-up time again on every call.

A failure reaches the caller as a `BehaviorError`. Its code is `invalid`, `timeout`, `capacity` or `adapter`, and its message is always `Gateway call failed.`. The messages of the target and its stderr (error output) never reach the caller. The server logs only a `handler.gateway_failed` event with the code. Only one hop (one call from one language to another) is allowed. Tachyon refuses a target class that declares its own gateway.

The build checks every target. It fails with `TY1312` when the file is missing or outside `server/`. It also fails when the file is in the caller's own language. In that case, inject it instead. It also fails when it is not a Yon language. It fails when the target has no concrete instance method of that name. It also fails when the method takes a different number of arguments. It fails when the method uses a type that is not the JSON value type of the language. Tachyon selects Java, Groovy, Kotlin and C# overloads by argument count and JSON types, not by source order. Overloads are methods with the same name but different parameters. Ambiguous signatures also fail with `TY1312`. So do callers that ask for different argument counts for the same target method. Rust target methods use `&self`. Tachyon refuses a method that consumes `self` or borrows `&mut self`. A Go target method is exported. So Tachyon calls the method whose name starts with an upper-case letter (`summarize` calls `Summarize`). A misused annotation fails with `TY1308`. This happens in Tac, on an HTTP verb method, or together with another method annotation. `server/gateways/` is reserved for the generated units (`TY1310`). A missing program fails at start-up with `TY2112`, and Firecracker isolation refuses gateways (`TY2010`).

Every Yon language below calls a class in another language. The examples also show an explicit Python command target. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Gateway in Lua Yon code with TY1308.

sections.heading: Relaying to other languages
sections.body:
A program that Yon does not run directly can still use Handler Protocol v1. Call `relay(command, request)` yourself from a controller method that takes the request argument. `request` is the request in the language's own type, and `relay` answers with the language's own response. In PHP, `Yon::relay(command)` forwards the current request and writes the answer with `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo`. The program reads the request as JSON on its standard input: `route` (the path and query), `method`, `headers`, `body` and `deadline_ms`, the time left in milliseconds. It writes one JSON answer on its standard output: `status`, `headers` (each name with a list of values) and `body`. The example relays every language to one Perl program, `server/relays/report.pl`: Perl is not a Yon language, but any program that reads and writes this JSON can answer. Yon starts the program without a shell and limits its output. The deadline of the program is the time left in the request. Tachyon counts it after the wait for a process slot and the start of the route. Every relay in the request shares that deadline. The program gets the baseline environment (`PATH`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL` and `TMPDIR` on Unix; `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SYSTEMROOT`, `WINDIR`, `COMSPEC`, `TEMP` and `TMP` on Windows). The allowlist is the list of allowed names. It also gets the names you add to the allowlist (`server.environment`, see Environment variables for handlers), `YON_HANDLER_PROTOCOL` and the `NO_PROXY` values of the route process. Yon removes the other values, so the program does not inherit them by accident. This is not a sandbox (a closed space that blocks access). A program that runs as the same user can still read the environment of its parent. It can also read the files of the project. Every relay failure reaches the controller as HTTP 502. The message is always the same: `Component invocation failed.` Yon removes sensitive details from failures. At the end, it cleans up (reaps) the whole process group. When a PHP controller relays, the program does not inherit the files that the PHP handler opened: every file descriptor above 2 goes to `/dev/null`, so the program cannot write into the response of the handler. PHP warnings go to standard error, not into the answer.

Breaking change: a relay program no longer receives `YON_APPLICATION_JSON` or the `YON_RESOURCE_*` values, even when they are on the allowlist. If a relay program read its configuration from `YON_APPLICATION_JSON`, that must change. The program must now read it from its own files or from a variable on the allowlist.

To call one method in another language and get a value back, use `@Gateway` instead of forwarding the request. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses relay in Lua Yon code with TY2015.
