modules-and-lifecycle.title: Modules and lifecycle
modules-and-lifecycle.summary: This page explains how Tachyon groups your files into programs, and how it starts and stops the process that answers a request.

sections.heading: Application modules
sections.body: Helpers without annotations stay ordinary code. Types with role annotations follow strict rules instead: plural role folders, and file names that match the type. Tachyon finds them automatically in the shared role folders of the realm. Every Yon language supports annotation modules in the same language, and Tachyon finds them automatically. Tachyon adds no folder scan at run time, no dependency injection across languages and no automatic package resolution. Automatic package resolution means finding packages for you. Tachyon rejects relative imports inside included modules (it fails closed: when it is not sure, it refuses). Annotations and framework types need no import. Supported non-relative imports of native or standard-library modules are also still allowed. Go is the one language with its own module folder: your Go packages and vendored third-party modules live in `server/packages/` (see Native Go packages).
sections.code:
server/controllers/MoneyController.ts       HTTP entry
server/services/MoneyService.ts             managed service
server/shared/MoneyFormat.ts                ordinary imported helper class
server/models/Money.ts                      data type

JavaScript and TypeScript import helpers normally, including from a service. Go shared files join package main; native Go packages with their own package names live in the server/packages/ module and are imported by module path. All other Yon languages compose server/shared/ classes before the managed roles and controller; F# helpers are declared before code that calls them. Shared files hold one class and its imports, no annotations or file-level variables.

sections.heading: Native Go packages
sections.body:
A Go app often has its own packages: a git client, a JSON schema checker, a repository layer. These are plain Go packages, not Tachyon roles. Put them in `server/packages/`. This folder holds one Go module. `server/packages/go.mod` names the module, and each folder under it is a normal Go package with its own package name. Controllers, services and other role files import a package with the module path, for example `import "example.com/shop/packages/pricing"`. The packages can import each other the same way. A route can take or return a type from these packages, such as `spec.Document`. Tachyon reads fields only from `server/models/`, so such a type is an open JSON value that Go's `encoding/json` reads and writes.

Tachyon does not treat code in `server/packages/` as roles. It is like a library on the Spring classpath: it is not a bean, because nothing registers it. So these files need no role marker, and the role folder, file name, one-class, cohesion, duplicate and visibility rules do not apply to them. The secret and code safety checks still run, except in `vendor/`. Tachyon builds every Go handler inside this module, in a folder of its own, so the import works with no download. Handler code is therefore compiled with the Go version that the module's `go` line names.

The folder has a few limits. `server/packages/go.mod` may hold only `module`, `go`, `toolchain` and `require` lines. A required third-party module must be vendored, as the next section shows. A second `go.mod` inside the folder is refused. Go code there cannot carry a Tachyon annotation, because an annotated type belongs in its role folder. Other Yon languages' source files are refused there. The folder `server/packages/yonhandler/` is reserved, because Tachyon builds each handler program there. Other files, such as JSON schemas for `go:embed`, are allowed. Each of these mistakes fails with `TY1310`. A Go file in `server/packages/` without `server/packages/go.mod` also fails with `TY1310`.

Use the folder for code that is not a role. A type with a role marker stays in its role folder, such as `server/services/`. A plain helper of package main can stay in `server/shared/`. When `TY1363` reports a Go file in a role folder without its marker, decide what it is: mark a real role, or move a native package to `server/packages/` (ADR 0095).

The folder is for Go only, so this section has one language. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Ruby and Lua keep their own module rules (see Application modules), and their source files in `server/packages/` fail with `TY1310`.

sections.heading: Vendored Go modules
sections.body:
The native module can use third-party Go modules, such as `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` or a cloud SDK. Tachyon never downloads a module: it builds every Go handler offline, with `-mod=vendor`. So the app keeps its modules in its own repository. Add each module with a `require` line in `server/packages/go.mod`, then run `go mod tidy` and `go mod vendor` in `server/packages/`. Commit `go.sum` and the `vendor/` folder that `go mod vendor` writes, including `vendor/modules.txt`. Controllers, services and native packages then import the module by its usual path. The example vendors a small module, `example.com/greet`. Vendoring belongs to the Go module in `server/packages/`, so this section has one language: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Ruby and Lua do not use that folder.

Run `go mod vendor` again after every change to a `require` line. When `go.mod` requires a module but `go.sum` or `vendor/modules.txt` is missing, the project fails with `TY1368`. When `vendor/` no longer matches `go.mod`, or Go code imports a module that is not vendored, the Go build fails with `TY1368` and Go's own explanation. Without `server/packages/go.mod`, a Go handler cannot import a third-party module at all.

Tachyon treats `vendor/` as third-party code that you do not edit, because the next `go mod vendor` rewrites it. The role folder, file name, cohesion, duplicate and design rules skip it. The secret and code safety checks skip it too: an SDK carries example keys, its own service addresses and process calls that are not your app's choices, and you could not fix a finding there. Review vendored code when it changes instead: read the `vendor/` diff in code review, and run `go mod verify` and `govulncheck` in CI, where the Go module cache is available.

Every vendored file is part of the handler build key, so a change to `go.sum`, `vendor/modules.txt` or any vendored file rebuilds the Go handlers. The `vendor/` folder counts toward the source snapshot limits of `server/`: 4,096 files and 64 MiB. For scale, an app that uses the AWS, Azure and Google Cloud SDKs vendors about 2,500 files and 37 MB.

sections.heading: Process lifecycle
sections.body: In the default process mode, Tachyon starts one process for each request, and a supervisor watches it. The process reads the request, writes its response or its limited stream, and then exits. Tachyon caches prepared sources and compiled artifacts by their content (content-addressed caching). Execution uses a private runtime staging area (a folder where Tachyon prepares code to run). Cache locations are internal details. They are not paths in your application to import or edit. The source, the prelude and the compilation identity decide when Tachyon reuses a cached item. The prelude is code that Tachyon adds before your source. Java still starts from source. It is not compiled ahead of time into a native executable. The supervisor enforces deadlines, concurrency limits and frame limits. When all process slots are busy, a request waits for one. If its deadline passes while it waits, it fails with `TY2110` and its process never starts. Optional isolation drivers are a separate deployment policy.

isolation-and-security.title: Isolation and security
isolation-and-security.summary: Tachyon refuses four dangerous mistakes when it builds, runs each request in its own process, and adds security headers to every answer. This page explains these rules and limits, and the rules for code that runs in the browser.

sections.heading: Safety rules that stop the build
sections.body: Tachyon refuses four common and dangerous mistakes when it builds, the way it refuses a file with two classes (ADR 0068). No setting turns them off. First, every route says who may call it (see Who may call a route). Second, no password, token or key is written in the code, a template or public settings: Tachyon recognizes the usual shapes of AWS, Google, Azure, GitHub, Stripe and Slack keys, private keys, JSON Web Tokens, and a long random text given to a name such as `password`, `secret`, `token` or `apiKey`. Put the value in `.env` with a `YON_` name and read it through the Yon settings; code that runs in the browser gets no secrets at all. Third, code never runs a text as code (`eval`, `new Function`, Python `exec`, Ruby `instance_eval` with a text, PHP `eval`, a Java `ScriptEngine`, C# scripting), and it never joins values into query text: write the query as one text or an UPPER_CASE constant and pass the values in the parameter list. Redis keys and values are always parameters. Fourth, code sends requests only to the hosts that you list, `tac.outgoing.hosts` for page code and `outgoing.hosts` in `server/application.json` for Yon code. This stops server-side request forgery (SSRF): a caller cannot make your app call an address that they choose. At run time the browser refuses other hosts, because Tachyon adds the listed hosts to the page's `connect-src` security rule, and Yon code sends its requests through a local guard that refuses other hosts. The guard also refuses a listed name that resolves only to a loopback or private address, unless the name is a localhost name; list an IP address to reach a private service (see Host names and local addresses). The guard works for every HTTP client that reads the standard proxy settings (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`): JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Ruby, PHP with cURL, Go, C# and Rust with reqwest. The Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Dart clients read them only when you ask them to (`ProxySelector.getDefault()`, `HttpClient.findProxyFromEnvironment`); for a hard limit on every language, run Yon with Firecracker isolation and its egress setting.
sections.code:
Safety rules that stop the build (ADR 0068)

  Code     The build stops when                         Do this instead
  TY1322   a route does not say who may call it         @Public, @SignedIn or @Allow(Role)
  TY1323   @SignedIn or @Allow has no identity          one @IdentityProvider class
           provider, or there are two
  TY1324   the code, a template or public settings      put the value in .env as YON_<NAME>
           hold a password, token or key                and read it through the settings
  TY1325   code runs text as code (eval, exec,          call the code directly; pass values
           new Function ...) or joins values into       as query parameters:
           query text                                   query("... WHERE name = $1", [name])
  TY1326   code sends a request to a host that is not   list the host:
           listed                                       client/manifest.json
                                                          { "tac": { "outgoing": { "hosts": ["api.example.com"] } } }
                                                        server/application.json
                                                          { "outgoing": { "hosts": ["api.example.com"] } }

An obvious example secret in a test or a guide may stay when the file has the
comment `tachyon: example secrets` and the value says that it is an example,
such as sk_live_example.

sections.heading: Isolation
sections.body: `YON_ISOLATION=process` is the default. It runs one child process for each request, and Tachyon watches that process directly. `YON_ISOLATION=firecracker` instead gives each request to a control program for microVMs (small virtual machines). `YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER`, `POOL`, `VCPUS`, `MEMORY_MIB` and `EGRESS` configure it. Tachyon reads this setting from the environment, not from a config file. The reason is that the right isolation depends on where a deployment runs, not on the source code. Firecracker mode supports only JavaScript and Python controllers. A controller in another language, TypeScript included, fails with `TY2010` before the driver starts, so it needs process mode. For supported languages, the handler protocol and the build do not change. If the policy is invalid or only half declared, it fails with TY2010 before any route runs.

sections.heading: Security
sections.body:
Every response carries defensive security headers. One of them is a strict content security policy. This header tells the browser which content the page may load. The policy is `script-src 'self'`, no inline script, `object-src 'none'` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`. There are two inline scripts. The speculation rules block lets the browser fetch a linked page before the click. A one-line view transition guard keeps the browser quiet when a fast click skips the animation between two pages; without it, Chromium reports `AbortError: Transition was skipped`. The policy allows both by the SHA-256 hash of their text, which every browser understands. Chrome's own keyword for it, `'inline-speculation-rules'`, made Safari warn on every page and refuse the block. The Windows and Linux desktop hosts build their policy from the same source, so their web views allow the same scripts, the hashes included; their policy also allows images, fonts and connections over `https:`. A controller call runs as one process with limits: a deadline and a concurrency limit (the most requests it runs at the same time). Its protocol frames (the messages it exchanges with the server) are limited to 16 MiB. The server checks each argument against the types of the controller method. This happens before Tachyon calls the method.

Every route says who may call it (`Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`), and one `IdentityProvider` class says who is signed in. The server answers 401 or 403 before the method runs (see Who may call a route). How users sign in stays with the application: the identity provider reads a session or a token in the language's own request type. Tachyon has no CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) layer; a middleware runs its `before` method before every request, and that policy goes there. The policy's `connect-src` allows the page's own origin and the hosts in `tac.outgoing.hosts` only.

sections.heading: Host names and local addresses
sections.body:
`ty preview`, `ty serve` and `ty start` bind `127.0.0.1` unless you choose another address. A server on a loopback address answers a request only when its `Host` name is `localhost`, a name under `.localhost`, an IP address, the host of `tac.origin`, or a name in `server.hosts` in `server/application.json`. Any other name gets `403` with `TY1366`, and a `Host` that the server cannot read gets `400`. This stops DNS rebinding: a web page on another name points its name at your computer, and the browser then lets the page read your local app as if the app were its own. Because the page still sends its own name, the server refuses it, in every browser. The check runs before routing, so it covers pages, controller routes, the hot-update stream and WebSocket upgrades. It reads `Host` itself and ignores `X-Forwarded-Host`. A server opened to the network with `--allow-non-loopback` checks `Host` only when `server.hosts` is set, so a reverse proxy keeps working; set `server.hosts` there too.

Yon code reaches a local service only through a name or address in `outgoing.hosts`. A localhost name such as `api.localhost`, or `*.localhost` for every such name, reaches `[::1]` and then `127.0.0.1` on every operating system: the guard answers the name itself and ignores `/etc/hosts`. This works for the clients that read the proxy settings: JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Ruby, PHP with cURL, Go, C# and Rust with reqwest. The Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Dart default clients and raw sockets ask their own runtime, so a name under `.localhost` works there only where the operating system answers it, such as macOS and Linux with systemd-resolved.

The guard resolves an allowed name once and connects to that address. It refuses a name that resolves only to loopback, private, link-local (such as the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254`) or shared addresses. So an allowed wildcard such as `*.example.com` cannot be pointed at your own services. To reach a private service, list its IP address. While the guard runs, handler processes get no `NO_PROXY`, so no client can go around it, and Go's standard client sends its requests to the guard too. ADR 0094 explains the choices.

sections.heading: The client address and forwarding headers
sections.body:
`ty` stands in front of every Yon handler, like a proxy, so it decides what a handler learns about the client. A browser can send any `X-Forwarded-For`, `Forwarded` or `X-Real-IP` header, so `ty` does not trust them. When the client connects to `ty` directly, `ty` removes `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Port`, `X-Forwarded-Prefix` and `X-Real-IP`. Then it writes its own: `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` hold the address of the client, `Forwarded` holds `for=<address>;proto=http`, and `X-Forwarded-Proto` is `http`. A handler in any Yon language reads the client address from `X-Real-IP`, and a back end for front end can pass these headers on to its own services as they are.

Behind a reverse proxy, list the proxies in `server.proxies` in `server/application.json`, as IP addresses or CIDR ranges such as `10.0.0.0/8`. For a request from a listed proxy, `ty` keeps the headers that the proxy sent and adds its own hop: the proxy address goes at the end of `X-Forwarded-For` and `Forwarded`. `X-Real-IP` becomes the client: the nearest address in `X-Forwarded-For`, read from the right, that is not a listed proxy. The list is empty unless you set it, so even `127.0.0.1` is not trusted, and a host name is refused when the server starts. This is how Spring's `ForwardedHeaderFilter` and Tomcat's `RemoteIpValve` work: forwarding headers count only when a known proxy sent them.

Where the native request has a field for the peer, Tachyon fills it with the same client address: `RemoteAddr` of Go's `*http.Request` (`203.0.113.9:0`), `getRemoteAddress()` of `HttpExchange` in Java and Kotlin, and `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']` in PHP. The port is always `0`, because the port of the client is not passed on. The other native request types have no peer field, so they read `X-Real-IP`.

`ty` serves plain HTTP and does not end TLS, so Go's `Request.TLS` is `nil` and there are no verified client certificate chains (`VerifiedChains`) to pass on. End TLS, and mutual TLS with client certificates, at the reverse proxy, list the proxy in `server.proxies`, and read `X-Forwarded-Proto` for the scheme the client used. ADR 0096 explains the choices. The example controller is written in Go because Go's request has a peer field. A controller in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Dart, Ruby or Lua gets the same headers, so this section shows Go only.

sections.heading: Environment variables for handlers
sections.body:
`ty` clears the environment of every handler process, so a handler cannot read the variables of the shell that started `ty`. It gets only a small baseline: `PATH`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL` and `TMPDIR` on Unix, and `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SYSTEMROOT`, `WINDIR`, `COMSPEC`, `TEMP` and `TMP` on Windows. Configuration, not code, decides what else a handler sees.

Cloud SDKs and many tools read their credentials and settings from the environment. List those variables in `server.environment` in `server/application.json`. An entry is a name, such as `HOME`, or a prefix pattern that ends in `*`, such as `AWS_*` or `HD_*`. With the list below, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `HD_REGION` reach handlers in every Yon language as ordinary environment variables: `process.env` in JavaScript, `os.environ` in Python, `os.Getenv` in Go, `System.getenv` in Java, and so on. A variable that the list does not name, such as `OTHER_SECRET`, does not reach them. Gateway commands, relay programs and Yon test units under `ty test` get the same list. The list is empty unless you set it. This is Spring's externalized configuration, bound explicitly: the application says which variables it uses, and it reads nothing else.

`*` alone would pass every variable, so the server refuses to start with `TY2010`. It also refuses any entry that names or covers a variable that `ty` itself owns: `TAC_*`, `TACHYON_*`, `YON_*`, and the proxy variables that the outgoing request guard sets (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`). So `T*` and `NO_*` are refused too. Names are compared without regard to case.

The configuration holds names, never values. The values stay in the environment of `ty`; `ty` never writes them to the configuration, to its logs or to a diagnostic, and a refused entry is reported by its name only. Every handler of the application can read an allowed variable, so list only what the handlers need. Settings that belong to the application, such as a database password, still go in `.env` as `YON_` names (see Settings and configuration). ADR 0026 explains the choice. The example controller is written in Go. A handler in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Dart, Ruby or Lua reads an allowed variable with its own environment API in the same way, so this section shows Go only.

sections.heading: Security rules for browser code
sections.body: Never put server credentials (passwords, keys or tokens for the server) in Tac configuration or adapters. Browser HTTP still follows origin and CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) rules. HTTP request annotations require these things: no credentials sent, redirects rejected, cancellation, a deadline and a limited response. Behavior caches are separate from two other caches. These are the limited JSON response cache of HTTPClient and the read cache of the service worker. Divide the cache by the signed-in user who owns the data. Authorize every cache access, including hits (reads that find an entry) and eviction (removal of an entry). Choose an adapter that enforces the declared limit on entries (the entry quota). Browser code cannot replace authorization on the server. The API must still check access to sensitive data. An annotation grants no native capability, database connection, environment access or server-side rendering (SSR) mode. The build refuses a secret in page code or in `client/manifest.json` (`TY1324`), `eval` and `new Function` (`TY1325`), and a request to a host that `tac.outgoing.hosts` does not list (`TY1326`); the page's `connect-src` enforces the same list in the browser (ADR 0068). A JavaScript or TypeScript client script, such as a service or a script in `client/shared`, does not build markup or write styles: `innerHTML`, `document.write`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.createElement`, `append` or `appendChild` of new nodes, `element.style` and style sheets fail with `TY1364`. Put markup in the component's `tac.html` and styles in its `tac.css`; a script changes text, classes and service state. A pinned vendor script loads through `tac.scripts` and `tac.scriptSources`.

cohesive-services.title: Cohesive services
cohesive-services.summary: A public method of a service or a controller only coordinates. Each private method holds at most one decision or one loop. The build checks this with TY1314.

sections.heading: Public methods coordinate
sections.body:
A service or a controller has two kinds of methods. A public method is an entry point: a page, a route or another class calls it. A private method is a helper that only its own class calls. Tachyon asks each kind of method to do one job.

A public method only coordinates. It calls injected services and private methods, it stores or returns their results, and it builds models and values from them. It holds no `if`, `else`, `switch`, `match`, `when`, `guard` or ternary (`? :`). It holds no loop, no `&&`, `||`, `??`, `and` or `or`, and no `try` or `catch`. This includes the code of a lambda that the method writes. Kotlin's `?:` counts as a decision. Optional chaining such as `order?.total` and Rust's `?` operator are allowed.

A private method holds at most one decision or one loop. An `else if` chain is one decision, and an `&&` or `||` inside its condition is part of that decision. A private method that makes a decision does not call another private method that also makes a decision. A call such as `items.map(item => item.id)` is not a loop, because its lambda holds no decision. `items.filter(item => item.ready && item.shown)` is a loop. In a Go iterator, the stop check `if !yield(item) { return }` is not a decision: it is part of `yield`, which stops by itself in the other languages.

The build refuses a service or a controller that breaks these rules with `TY1314`. The message names the method and the construct, and it shows how to write a private method in that language. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change.

| Language | Private method |
| --- | --- |
| JavaScript | A name that starts with `_`, such as `_pick(items)` |
| TypeScript | `private pick(items)` |
| Python | A name that starts with `_`, such as `def _pick(self, items)` |
| Ruby | A method below `private` |
| PHP, Java, Kotlin, C# | A method with the `private` keyword |
| Swift | A method with `private` or `fileprivate` |
| Dart | A name that starts with `_` |
| Go | A method with a lowercase name |
| Rust | A method without `pub`. The methods of `impl Trait for Type` are public. |

In every language, a method whose name starts with `_` is private.

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac services, set `tac.cohesion.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon services and controllers, set `cohesion.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration.

utilities.title: Utilities
utilities.summary: Tachyon refuses a block of code that repeats (TY1315). Move it into a static method of a utility class in client/shared/utils (Tac) or server/utils (Yon), and call it from both places.

sections.heading: One place for repeated code
sections.body:
When two places hold the same block of code, a fix in one place misses the other. So Tachyon refuses duplicated code, with the same rules as SonarQube's copy-paste detection. Tachyon checks your code itself and sends nothing to another service.

A duplicate is a block of at least 100 tokens (words, names, values and signs) that spans at least 10 lines and appears twice or more. The two copies are in the same language and the same realm, in one file or in two files. Names and values may differ: `total(order)` and `total(invoice)` are the same code. Whitespace and comments do not count, and neither do imports, annotation lines, test units, models, entities, generated files, lists of values and constants that hold one literal value, such as `static _GAP = 24` in JavaScript or `private static readonly _GAP: number = 24` in TypeScript.

The build refuses a duplicate with `TY1315`. The message names both places, for example `client/services/OrderService.js:12-40`, and tells you where to move the code. `ty migrate check` lists every duplicate.

Move the repeated code into a utility class. A Tac utility class lives in `client/shared/utils/`, and you may group utilities in nested folders, such as `client/shared/utils/text/TitleUtils.js`. A Yon utility class lives in `server/utils/`. The name of a utility class ends with `Utils`. The build refuses a file in `client/utils/` with `TY1310`, and `ty migrate fix --write` moves it to `client/shared/utils/` and changes the paths that import it. It holds only static methods and no state: no field, no stored value, no constructor and no instance method (`TY1316`). A Rust utility may hold associated `const` values, but no `static` value, not even inside a method, and its file may be named `price_utils.rs` (ADR 0064, ADR 0067). It has no annotation, and it names no role class: no service, store, client, helper, converter, setup or controller (`TY1327`). Every class of its realm may call it, so it cannot depend on one of them; give it the value it needs as a parameter. Every class of the same realm and language can call it with no import, and a test unit can test it. Its methods follow the cohesion rule: a public static method only coordinates, and private static methods hold the decisions. The design checks read every utility file, in nested folders too: plain-English names (`TY1328`), named values (`TY1330`) and public members that nothing outside the class uses (`TY1333`).

| Language | Utility class | Static method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript, TypeScript | `export default class PriceUtils` | `static label(cents)`; private: `static _dollars(cents)` or TypeScript `private static` |
| Python | `class PriceUtils:` | `@staticmethod` above `def label(cents)`; private: `_dollars` |
| Ruby | `class PriceUtils` | `def self.label(cents)`; private: `def self._dollars(cents)` |
| Lua | `PriceUtils = {}` | `function PriceUtils.label(cents)`; private: `PriceUtils._dollars` |
| PHP, Java, C#, Dart | `class PriceUtils` (C#: `static class`) | a `static` method; private: `private static` (Dart: a name that starts with `_`) |
| F# | `type PriceUtils =` | `static member Label(cents: int)`; private: `static member private` |
| Kotlin | `object PriceUtils` | `fun label(cents: Int)`; private: `private fun` |
| Swift | `struct PriceUtils` | `static func label(_ cents: Int)`; private: `private static func` |
| Go | `type PriceUtils struct{}` | `func (PriceUtils) Label(cents int) string`; private: a name that starts with a lower-case letter |
| Rust | `pub struct PriceUtils;` | `pub fn label(cents: u32) -> String`, with no `self`; private: no `pub` |

C++ has no tab here: C++ utility classes are not supported yet, and a C++ file in `client/shared/utils/` stops the build with `TY1310` (ADR 0099).

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac code, set `tac.duplication.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `duplication.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration.

helpers.title: Helpers, utilities and private methods
helpers.summary: One question decides where shared code goes: a helper when it needs other classes, saved state, lifecycle hooks or a Fake in tests; otherwise a utility, a private method or a service.

sections.heading: Helpers, utilities and private methods
sections.body:
GET /checkout returns {"total":42}. When two classes share code, or one class has a long job, ask one question: does this code need other classes (stores, clients, settings or other helpers), saved state, OnStart or OnStop, or a Fake in tests? If the answer is yes, write a helper. A helper is a class that other classes use for part of their work. Mark it with Helper, put it in client/helpers or server/helpers, and end its name with Helper. Tachyon creates it and gives it to each class that asks for it with Needs. A view or a controller does not call a helper directly: it calls a service, and the service calls the helper.

Two kinds of helper are owned by the class that creates them. In Tac, a helper works in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Python, C# and F#. A C# or F# Tac helper is created by its caller with `new`, and the caller owns it: these two languages refuse an injected helper, a helper lifetime and helper hooks (ADR 0091). Go, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Ruby and Lua Tac code has no helper yet (TY1308, and TY1405 in Java). In Yon, a helper that its caller builds with `new` stays owned by that caller: Tachyon does not inject it, so its OnStart, OnStop and OnEvent methods never run. To get those hooks, let Tachyon create the helper through Needs or NeedsAll.

If the answer is no, you do not need a helper:

| The code | Write it as |
| --- | --- |
| needs other classes, saved state, OnStart or OnStop, or a Fake in tests | a helper: Helper, in helpers, with a name that ends with Helper |
| has only static methods and no state | a utility: a class named like PriceUtils in client/shared/utils or server/utils, with no annotation (see Utilities) |
| is used by one class only | a private method of that class |
| is called by a view or a controller | a service |

The layers go in one order: a view or a controller calls a service, a service calls a helper, and a helper calls a store or a client. Any layer can call a utility. The build refuses a dependency that points up, such as a helper that needs a service (TY1327, see Dependencies point down).

In this example, CheckoutService adds the tax through TaxHelper. TaxHelper is a helper because it needs another class, TaxRateHelper. Only CheckoutService uses the subtotal, so the subtotal is a private method of CheckoutService, not a helper and not a utility. The controller calls the service, never the helper.

Helper was called Component before. The name changed because client/components holds views. The build refuses Component with its new name (TY1308) and a file in a delegates folder with the helpers folder (TY1310). `ty migrate fix --write` moves the files from delegates to helpers, renames each class from a name that ends with Component to a name that ends with Helper, and changes the Needs fields and types that use it.

dependency-direction.title: Dependencies point down
dependency-direction.summary: A class needs only the classes below it, and no chain of classes loops back. The build checks this with TY1327.

sections.heading: Dependencies point down
sections.body:
A class needs another class when it names it: the type of a field, a `Needs` list, or the field name that `NeedsAll` reads, such as `orderStore` in JavaScript or `order_store` in Ruby and Python. Tachyon draws these needs as a graph for each realm and checks two things.

First, the needs point down, the same way in every app:

| Layer | Folder | May need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry point | `server/controllers`, and Tac views | Services, and the layers below |
| Service | `client/services`, `server/services` | Other services, helpers, stores and HTTP clients |
| Helper | `@Helper` classes in `client/helpers`, `server/helpers` | Other helpers, stores and HTTP clients, never a service |
| Data access | `stores`, `client/remotes`, `server/clients` | Other data access, never a service or a helper |
| Utility | `client/shared/utils`, `server/utils` | No role class (`TY1327`); every layer may call it |

Nothing may need a controller, because only a request calls a controller. A store must not need a service or a helper, because they use data access, not the other way round.

Second, no chain of needs loops back to where it started, even when each step points down. If `OrderService` needs `PaymentService` and `PaymentService` needs `OrderService`, neither can be built first, and neither owns the rule they share. This is the same as Spring Boot, which refuses circular references.

The build refuses either problem with `TY1327`. For a loop, the message names the whole loop, for example `Circular dependency: OrderService -> PaymentService -> OrderService`. To break a loop, move the code that the classes share into a new service that each of them uses, or let one class publish an event instead of calling back. To fix a store that needs a service, move the code that needs the service up into a service that uses the store.

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac code, set `tac.dependencies.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `dependencies.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

plain-english-names.title: Plain-English names
plain-english-names.summary: Every word of a class, method, field or parameter name is an English word, a short technical word or a word of your domain. The build checks this with TY1328.

sections.heading: Names are whole English words
sections.body:
A reader should understand a name without guessing, even when English is not their first language. So Tachyon splits every class, method, field and parameter name into words, at capital letters, `_`, `-` and digits: `calcTotal` is `calc` and `total`, and `order_id` is `order` and `id`. Each word must be one of these:

A word in the English word list that `ty` ships (American and British spellings, with their endings, such as `orders`, `created` or `colour`).

A short technical word: `id`, `url`, `uri`, `html`, `css`, `json`, `api`, `http`, `https`, `ui`, `db`, `sql`, `jwt`, `uuid`, `io`, `os`, `xml`, `csv`, `pdf`, `svg`, `config`, `utils`, `async`, `sku` and a few more.

A word of your domain that you list: `tac.names.words` in `client/manifest.json` for Tac and `names.words` in `server/application.json` for Yon, such as `["fylo"]` for a product name.

Two English words written as one, such as `username` or `webhook`.

A clipped word is refused even when a dictionary knows it, and the help gives the whole word:

| Write | Not |
| --- | --- |
| `user` | `usr` |
| `config` | `cfg` |
| `calculate` | `calc` |
| `total` | `tot` |
| `button` | `btn` |
| `message` | `msg` |
| `context` | `ctx` |
| `request`, `response` | `req`, `res` |
| `index` | `idx` |
| `error` | `err` |
| `temporary` | `tmp` |
| `value` | `val` |
| `number` | `num` |
| `text` | `str` |
| `documents` | `docs` |

Local variables are not checked, and neither are names that the language or a base type chooses for you: constructors, Python `__init__`, methods marked `override`, and the methods of `impl Trait for Type` in Rust.

The build refuses a name with `TY1328`, for example: The parameter name `itemIdx` in CartService is not plain English: `idx` is short for `index`. Rename it to `itemIndex`.

One trap in Tac: do not name a service field after the instance name of another service. A field `documentation` next to a `DocumentationService` is read as that service, not as a property. Pick another word, such as `documents`.

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac code, set `tac.names.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `names.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

small-signatures.title: Small signatures
small-signatures.summary: A method takes at most four parameters, and a class needs at most five other classes. The build checks this with TY1329.

sections.heading: Few parameters and few dependencies
sections.body:
A long list of parameters hides a missing model: the values belong together, but the code passes them one by one. A class that needs many other classes does more than one job.

So a method takes at most 4 parameters. When it needs more, put the values that belong together in a model, a class in `client/models` or `server/models`, and take that model as one parameter. These do not count:

`self`, `this` and `cls`.

A parameter that Tachyon fills from the request: `FromPath`, `FromQuery`, `FromBody`, `FromHeader` and `FromCookie`. Each one names one part of the request.

The parameters of a constructor. The next rule covers them.

A class needs at most 5 other classes. The classes it needs are the ones it names (see Dependencies point down), plus the `DataSource`, `Redis` and `ApplicationEventPublisher` resources. When a class needs more, split it into smaller classes that each need fewer, and let each caller use the part it needs.

The build refuses either problem with `TY1329`, for example: The method `place` in OrderService takes 5 parameters; the limit is 4.

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac code, set `tac.signatures.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `signatures.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

named-values.title: Named values
named-values.summary: A text or number used twice, or a number in a condition, gets a name: a class constant. The build checks this with TY1330.

sections.heading: Give values a name
sections.body:
A value written in several places changes in one place and stays old in the others. A bare number such as `20` does not say what it means. So Tachyon asks you to give such values a name.

The build refuses, with `TY1330`:

A text or a number, other than 0, 1 and -1, that appears twice or more in one class.

A number, other than 0, 1 and -1, in a condition: next to `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`, `<=` or `>=`, or inside the condition of `if`, `while`, `unless`, `until` or `guard`.

A value is named when it is the whole value of a declaration: a class constant, a field, a local variable or a default value, also inside a list or a map. A method that only returns the value names it too. The empty text, annotation arguments, imports, models and entities (their defaults are data) and test code are not checked, and text that you use once, such as a log message, is fine.

The help shows a class constant in your language:

| Language | Class constant |
| --- | --- |
| JavaScript | `static CART_CHANGED = 'cart:changed';` |
| TypeScript | `static readonly CART_CHANGED = 'cart:changed';` |
| Python, Ruby | `CART_CHANGED = 'cart:changed'` in the class body |
| PHP | `private const CART_CHANGED = 'cart:changed';` |
| Java | `private static final String CART_CHANGED = "cart:changed";` |
| Kotlin | `companion object { const val CART_CHANGED = "cart:changed" }` |
| C# | `private const string CartChanged = "cart:changed";` |
| F# | `static let cartChanged = "cart:changed"` in the type |
| Swift | `static let cartChanged = "cart:changed"` |
| Dart | `static const cartChanged = 'cart:changed';` |
| Rust | `const CART_CHANGED: &str = "cart:changed";` in the `impl` block |
| Go | `func (CartService) cartChanged() string { return "cart:changed" }` |

Often there is a shorter fix. When two methods build the same map, move the map into one private method. When one method passes the same value three times, put it in a local variable first.

This check is new, so you can turn it off for one side of the app while you move code. For Tac code, set `tac.constants.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `constants.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. Use these settings only for migration. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

public-only-when-used.title: Public only when used
public-only-when-used.summary: A method or field of a class is public only when a view, another class or Tachyon uses it. Everything else is private. The build checks this with TY1333.

sections.heading: Public only when used
sections.body:
A public member promises that other code calls it. When nothing calls it, a reader must search the whole project to learn that it is only a helper. So Tachyon keeps a member public only when something outside the class uses it.

The build refuses, with `TY1333`, a public method or field of a class in `services`, `helpers`, `controllers` or `utils` when nothing outside the class uses it. A member stays public when:

The view uses it: a Tac view reads or calls `cart.total()` for `CartService`. Case and `_` do not matter, so `cart.itemCount` also matches `ItemCount` in C# and Go and `item_count` in Ruby, Python and Rust.

Another class uses it: a class of the same realm needs the class and calls the member, such as `this.priceService.total()` or `PriceUtils.label(total)`.

Tachyon uses it: the member or one of its parameters has an annotation (`OnEvent`, `GetRoute`, `OnStart`, `Cached`, `Check` and the others); it is a field that Tachyon fills (a field without a starting value, or a field that `Needs` or `NeedsAll` fills); a setup hands the class to Tachyon; a `Gateway` names the class file, such as `{"class":"server/services/ReportService.java"}`; it is `identify` of the `IdentityProvider`; or it is a name that the runtime or the language calls, such as `hotState`, `toString` or Go `String`.

A call from a test does not keep a member public. Test the member through the public member that uses it. Models, entities, errors and test files are not checked. A private member that nothing calls is dead code: delete it, because the coverage check refuses it too.

Make a member private in the form of your language:

| Language | Private form |
| --- | --- |
| TypeScript, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, Swift, PHP | `private total()` |
| C# | `private int Total()`, or no access modifier: `int Total()`. `public` and `internal` members are public |
| JavaScript | `_total()`, a name that starts with `_` |
| Dart, Python | `_total`, a name that starts with `_` |
| Ruby | `private def total`, or the method below a `private` line |
| Go | `total`, a name that starts with a lowercase letter |
| Rust | `fn total(&self)`, without `pub` |

`ty migrate fix --write` makes the simple cases private for you: it writes `private`, removes `pub`, or renames the member and its uses in the class. It leaves a member alone when the new name is taken or a use is not clear.

The check is on by default, like the other design rules. While you migrate, you can turn it off for one side of the app: for Tac code, set `tac.visibility.check` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`; for Yon code, set `visibility.check` to `false` in `server/application.json`. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

types-in-every-language.title: Types in every language
types-in-every-language.summary: Every field, parameter and return value of a class states its type: a type comment where the language has no type syntax, the native type where it has one. The build checks this with TY1356.

sections.heading: Every member states its type
sections.body:
Tachyon reads types to check routes, models, events and injection, and each language's checker reads them to find a mistake before a request does. A member without a type is invisible to both. So every field, method parameter and return value of a class states its type, in public and private members alike. Local variables do not need one.

Where the language's syntax has no types, a type comment carries the type. It is the one kind of comment that Tachyon keeps, because a tool reads it: it holds a type, never an explanation. Where the language has optional types, write the native types.

| Language | Parameter | Return value | Field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript | `@param {number} amount` | `@returns {Price}` | `/** @type {PriceService} */` |
| Ruby | `# @param amount [Integer]` | `# @return [Price]` | `# @return [PriceService]` above `attr_reader` |
| Lua | `---@param amount integer` | `---@return Price` | `---@type PriceService` above the field in the class table |
| Python | `amount: int` | `-> Price` | `price_service: PriceService` |
| PHP | `int $amount` | `): Price` | `private PriceService $priceService` |
| TypeScript | `amount: number` | inferred | `priceService!: PriceService` |
| Groovy | `int amount` | `Price priceFor(...)`, never `def` | `private PriceService priceService` |

JavaScript, Ruby and Lua type comments stand in the comment block right above the member; an annotation line such as `@Needs`, `#[Needs]` or `-- @Needs` may stand between them. Lua writes LuaCATS comments, which the Lua language server reads too, and a model lists its fields as `---@field amount integer` under `---@class Price`. A JavaScript method that gives back nothing needs no `@returns`; Python and PHP still write `-> None` and `: void`. A JavaScript or Python field whose starting value is one number, text or boolean, such as `static _CURRENCY = 'EUR'`, already shows its type. Groovy members need a declared type instead of `def` (`TY1334`), and the typed languages need nothing more: their tabs below use the native types. The tabs show Yon classes, but the same rule holds for Tac services when `tac.types.check` is on. Swift is a Tac service language only, so it has no tab here.

The build refuses, with `TY1356`, a member of a class in a role folder that has no type. The message names the member, and the help shows the exact comment or annotation to add. The types must also be right: `tsc` checks JavaScript types (with `checkJs` and `strict`, as in the `jsconfig.json` of `ty init`), Python and PHP check their own, and for Ruby and Lua the build checks that every name in a YARD or LuaCATS type is a Ruby class or a LuaCATS built-in type (`string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `table`), a class or model of your project, a Tachyon class, or `Boolean`, `nil` or `void`.

One `tsc` check is off for JavaScript: `strictPropertyInitialization`. TypeScript writes `priceService!: PriceService` to say that Tachyon fills the field after it makes the object. JavaScript has no `!`, so with this check `tsc` would refuse every `@Needs` field. The `jsconfig.json` that `ty init` writes for JavaScript code therefore sets `strictPropertyInitialization` to `false`, and the build checks the fields instead: in a JavaScript class, every field has a starting value, such as `labels = []`, the constructor or an `@OnStart` method sets it, or Tachyon fills it. Tachyon fills a field marked `@Needs` or `@Setting`, every field of a class marked `@NeedsAll`, the fields of an `@Entity`, and `applicationEventPublisher`. Any other field stops the build with `TY1356`, and the help shows the fixes. A side of the app that uses only TypeScript keeps the full `strict` check.

A class file may not switch the type checker off. `// @ts-nocheck`, `// @ts-ignore` and `// @ts-expect-error` in JavaScript and TypeScript, and `# type: ignore`, `# mypy: ignore-errors` and `# pyright: ignore` in Python, stop the build with `TY1356` too: remove them and fix the type errors they hid. A test file may still use `@ts-expect-error` to show that a wrong call does not compile.

`ty migrate fix --write` adds the types it can know: the type of an injected field, such as `/** @type {PriceService} */` or `# @return [PriceService]`, and `-> None` or `: void` for a method that gives back nothing. It lists every other member with the comment to add.

This check is new. It is off by default until the last examples and test projects of Tachyon pass it. Turn it on for one side of the app: for Yon code, set `types.check` to `true` in `server/application.json`, as the example below does; for Tac code, set `tac.types.check` to `true` in `client/manifest.json`. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

simpler-forms.title: Simpler forms
simpler-forms.summary: When a piece of code has a simpler form that reads more plainly, `ty preview` and `ty test` suggest it with codes TY1340 to TY1355. A suggestion never stops the build, and `ty migrate fix --write` applies it.

sections.heading: Suggestions, not errors
sections.body:
Some code does its job, but a reader needs a moment to see what it does. `if (total > limit) { return true; } return false;` only returns the result of the comparison, so `return total > limit;` says the same thing more plainly. Tachyon knows a short list of these patterns. Each one is easier to read for a reader who learns English as a second language, and none of them is only shorter. A long line with many parts is not simpler: when code is hard to read because it does several things, move a part into a named private method instead (see Cohesive services).

`ty preview` and `ty test` print a suggestion for each pattern that they find. A suggestion is not an error: the command goes on and the app builds. Each suggestion names the file and the line, and its `help:` line shows the code in its simpler form:

```text
suggestion[TY1340]: This `if` only returns true or false. Return the condition itself.
  --> server/services/CartService.js:14
  help: return total > limit;
```

`ty migrate fix` lists every suggested change, and `ty migrate fix --write` applies them. A simpler form never changes what the code does. When a rewrite could change the result, Tachyon does not suggest it. For example, in JavaScript, Python and Ruby `if (user) { return true; } return false;` returns `true` or `false`, but `return user;` would return the user, so this pattern is suggested only when the condition is already a comparison or another true-or-false value.

Suggestions are on for both sides of the app. To hide them for Tac code, set `tac.simplify.suggest` to `false` in `client/manifest.json`. For Yon code, set `simplify.suggest` to `false` in `server/application.json`.

Members without this is a separate optional suggestion (TY1362). Java, Kotlin, C#, Groovy, Swift and Dart can read class members by their bare names. Enable tac.implicitmembers.suggest in client/manifest.json or implicitmembers.suggest in server/application.json to see these suggestions or apply them with ty migrate fix --write. Both switches default to false. The scan preserves possible parameter/local shadowing, nested scopes, Swift closures, Dart initializing formals, qualified outer receivers, strings and comments. Required receivers in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, PHP and Lua stay unchanged; F# member declarations retain their self identifier.

sections.heading: Every simpler form
sections.body:
Each pattern has its own code, so you can search for it. Tachyon suggests each one only where the simpler form does exactly the same thing.

| Code | Pattern | Before | After | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TY1340` | An `if` that only returns true or false | `if (a > b) { return true; } return false;` | `return a > b;` | All languages. In JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, Python and Ruby only when the condition is a comparison, a `!` or another true-or-false value. |
| `TY1341` | A comparison with true or false | `ready == true`, `ready == false` | `ready`, `!ready` | Java and Rust, where the value is always a boolean. Not in Go, where a value of type `any` can be compared with true but cannot be a condition by itself. |
| `TY1342` | A choice between true and false | `a > b ? true : false`, `True if a > b else False` | `a > b` | Languages with `? :`, Python, and `if` expressions in Kotlin and Rust. `? false : true` becomes `!(a > b)`. |
| `TY1343` | Keep the matches only to see if there is one | `items.filter(isReady).length > 0` | `items.some(isReady)` | JavaScript and TypeScript (`some`), Java (`anyMatch`), Kotlin (`any`, `none`), C# (`Any`), Ruby (`any?`, `none?`), Dart (`any`), Swift (`contains`). |
| `TY1344` | Find a position only to see if a value is there | `names.indexOf(name) !== -1`, `text.find(word) != -1` | `names.includes(name)`, `word in text` | JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, Dart, Go (`strings.Contains`), PHP (`str_contains`, `in_array`), Python, Ruby (`include?`), Swift. Not C#: its `IndexOf` compares text by culture. |
| `TY1345` | `else` after `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue` | `if (a) { return 1; } else { b(); }` | `if (a) { return 1; }` then `b();` | All languages. Not when the `else` code declares a name that could clash with another name in the same block. |
| `TY1346` | Two `not` operators | `if (!!user)`, `if not not user:` | `if (user)`, `if user:` | In conditions. In Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, Swift and Dart everywhere. |
| `TY1347` | A negated equality | `!(a === b)`, `not a == b` | `a !== b`, `a != b` | All languages. Not for `<` and `>`: `!(a < b)` and `a >= b` differ when a value is not a number. |
| `TY1348` | A `return` with no value at the end of a method | `save(); return;` | `save();` | All languages except Ruby (the last value is the result) and Go. |
| `TY1349` | An `if` that holds only another `if` | `if (a) { if (b) { run(); } }` | `if (a && b) { run(); }` | All languages. Not when either `if` has an `else`. |
| `TY1350` | A variable set from its own value | `total = total + price;` | `total += price;` | All languages. In Python and Kotlin only when the variable started as a number or text, so that `+=` cannot change a shared list. |
| `TY1351` | Check for a key, then read it | `cache[key] if key in cache else None` | `cache.get(key, None)` | Python (`get`), Ruby (`fetch`), Java (`getOrDefault`), C# (`GetValueOrDefault`), PHP (`??`). Only when the default is a plain value, so that nothing extra runs. |
| `TY1352` | A loop that only joins or adds up items | `text = ""` then `for part in parts: text += part` | `text = "".join(parts)` | Python and C#, Dart, Swift (join), Kotlin and PHP (join and sum). Not Python or Ruby sums: their `sum` adds decimal numbers more exactly than a loop. |
| `TY1353` | A size compared with zero | `items.length == 0`, `items.size > 0` | `items.empty?`, `items.isNotEmpty()` | Ruby, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Swift and Rust, which have an `empty` method. |
| `TY1354` | An index loop that only reads each item | `for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) { const item = items[i]; ... }` | `for (const item of items) { ... }` | All languages except Rust. Only when the loop uses the index for nothing else. |
| `TY1355` | An `if` that only sets true or false | `if (a > b) { big = true; } else { big = false; }` | `big = a > b;` | All languages, with the same rule as TY1340. |

Tachyon does not suggest some forms on purpose. `len(items) == 0` in Python stays as it is, because `not items` asks the reader to know that an empty list counts as false. `if !ready` in Ruby stays as it is, because `unless` is a harder word than `if` and `not`. Reduce and fold chains, nested `? :` choices and comprehensions are never suggested, because they are harder to read than a plain loop.

test-units.title: Test units
test-units.summary: A test unit is a class in `server/tests` or `client/tests` whose name ends with `Test`. `ty test` finds and runs every test unit. `ty preview` does not start while a public method of an annotated class has no test.

sections.heading: Test units
sections.body:
ty test finds every server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> and client/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> file in the project. Each of these files is a test unit. ty test compiles each one like any other entry. Then it runs the driver (the code that runs the test cases) that the compiler wrote for it. It prints one line per case, then a total. It exits with a non-zero code if a case fails. CI (continuous integration) can use that exit code. A Yon unit runs through the same supervisor that serves a route. That is why all Yon languages report through one path. A Tac unit runs in its own realm. JavaScript and TypeScript units run under Node, Bun or Deno: ty tries `TAC_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME` first, then `node`, `bun` and `deno`. When the project has `@happy-dom/global-registrator` installed, these units get a browser DOM. Dart units run on the Dart VM. Swift, Kotlin, C#, F# and Rust units run as a compiled binary. Java units are compiled with `javac --release 21` and run with `java -ea`. Go units run with go run, Ruby units run under CRuby, Lua units run with the `lua` program, Python units run with `python3` (`python` on Windows, or `YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME`), and C++ units compile with clang++ (or `TAC_CPP_TEST_COMPILER`) and run as a binary. A unit that declares no case (a method whose name begins with `test`) fails with that reason.

Every public method of an annotated class needs a test case that calls it, and the development server checks this rule. A Setup and an HTTPClient are not in this list: Tachyon calls a Setup itself, and Tachyon writes the methods of a client. When no test* case called one of these methods, ty preview still starts, and it lists the missing ones in the terminal and in the error box of open pages (`TY2023`), for example `no test case called GreetingService.message`. A class-level marker says that the type has behavior the framework owns. So its public methods are the contract (the promised behavior) of the application. It costs the least to find an untested contract while you work. ty serve and ty start do not run tests or check this record. Use ty test --coverage as the CI gate before serving a release: it fails. TAC_ALLOW_UNTESTED=1 skips the check for one run. ty test prints the same report. With --coverage it fails on that report (`TY2022`), which is the form CI needs.

A method is covered only when a test case really called it while ty test ran. A test that only writes the name of the method does not cover it. In a test build, and only there, the compiler adds one line at the start of each public method of an annotated class, and of each public static method of a utility class. That line records the call. A Tac JavaScript or TypeScript utility that another file imports by its path, or that uses `import.meta`, loads as its own module. So ty test gives each JavaScript or TypeScript unit a copy of every script in client/shared/utils with that line, and an import of the utility loads the copy, under Node, Bun and Deno. Its calls count like any other. A production build has no such line, so the recording costs nothing in production. Each case reports the methods that it called, and ty test keeps the first case that called each one. A call inside the real class counts, also when the test calls another method or a real Needs dependency that calls it. A call on a Fake does not count, because a Fake is not the real class. So a controller test that fakes GreetingService does not cover GreetingService.message: a unit for the service must call it. ty test --coverage lists every class with its called methods, the first case that called each one, and the methods that no case called.

ty test writes the calls to `.tachyon/coverage/calls.json`. ty preview reuses this record only when its test run succeeded and no role file or test is newer. Before a new test run, ty marks the old record unsuccessful. If it cannot write that change, it stops before running any cases. This means that a failed or interrupted run cannot leave an older success in place. A record with no successful run, including an older record without this field, makes ty preview run the test units once before it starts. A failing test shows `TY2020` in the error box, even when it called every required method. Successful automatic tests are quiet: the first stdout line is still the server-ready message. Run ty test explicitly to see each case and its total. A write error on the record is `TY2024`. If the test units of a language cannot run on this machine, for example Swift units where swiftc is missing, ty cannot record their calls. Then, for that language only, it uses a name check: a case in a unit that names the class must also name the method. The report marks these classes with `[name check]`. This fallback describes coverage only: it does not make a failed run successful. Methods that the compiler writes are exempt (they need no test), because they contain no logic that a person wrote. A derived Store query, a declared HTTP request method and a Convert are all only a signature without a body. A signature is a name and types. ty init creates a service, a controller, a Setup in each tests folder and the units that call the service and the controller. So a new project starts with all checks passing.

A service that uses Tachyon's browser APIs, such as `Clock` or `Geolocation`, gets fake answers in a unit: a `@Fake` field in JavaScript and TypeScript, and `BrowserFakes` in Go, Ruby, Swift, C#, F# and Lua (see "Browser APIs in test units").

Controller methods count too, because a test can reach them. A unit in server/tests can use every controller in server/controllers, in the same way that it uses a service. In JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby, construct(GreetingController) makes the controller and gives it the fakes for its Needs fields, and in Lua `self:construct(GreetingController)` does the same. In the other Yon languages, the unit makes the controller directly, for example GreetingController() in Python. The test then calls the controller method directly, without HTTP. Step 5 of Your first app shows a controller test.

Before it runs, the command checks the runtimes that its units need, as the development server does. A TypeScript unit may be under a runtime that supports only JavaScript. Then it reports the readiness diagnostic, not the runtime's own error message. If you are not sure that a toolchain works, run ty doctor first.
sections.code:
ty test
ty test --coverage
ty preview
TAC_ALLOW_UNTESTED=1 ty preview

sections.heading: Assert and ValueSource
sections.summary: Check a result with Assert.equals, Assert.isTrue or Assert.throws, like JUnit. List the inputs of a case in ValueSource and Tachyon runs one case per input. A test case asserts and holds no logic (TY1339).
sections.body:
A test case prepares values, calls the code and checks the result. Tachyon gives every test unit a class `Assert` for the checks, named like JUnit 5's `Assertions`:

| Language | Equal | True | Throws |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript, TypeScript | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `Assert.throws(action)` |
| Python | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.is_true(condition)` | `Assert.throws(action)` |
| Rust | `Assert::equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert::is_true(condition)` | `Assert::throws(action)` |
| Java, Groovy | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `Assert.throwsError(action)` |
| Kotlin | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `Assert.throws { action }` |
| C#, F# | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `Assert.throws(action)` |
| Go | `Assert.Equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.IsTrue(condition)` | `Assert.Throws(action)` |
| Ruby | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.is_true(condition)` | `Assert.throws { action }` |
| Lua | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.is_true(condition)` | `Assert.throws(action)` |
| C++ | `Assert::equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert::isTrue(condition)` | `Assert::throws(action)` |
| PHP | `Assert::equals($expected, $actual)` | `Assert::isTrue($condition)` | `Assert::throws($action)` |
| Dart | `Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `await Assert.throws(action)` |
| Swift | `try Assert.equals(expected, actual)` | `try Assert.isTrue(condition)` | `try await Assert.throws { action }` |

Each check takes an optional last message. Rust has no optional arguments, so it writes `Assert::equals_with_message(expected, actual, "the total")` and the other `_with_message` forms. When a check fails, the case fails with the message and what it expected, like `the total ==> expected: <3> but was: <2>`. `equals` compares values: two lists or two objects are equal when their items are equal. `throws` returns the error, so the case can check its message. When the action is asynchronous, `throws` returns a promise (JavaScript, TypeScript) or an awaitable (Python), and the case writes `await Assert.throws(...)`. In C#, `throws` also takes an `async` lambda, and in F# an action that returns a task; both wait for the task to finish. In Rust, `throws` passes when the closure returns an `Err` or panics. Java and Groovy name it `throwsError`, because `throws` is a reserved word in both. In Java, Kotlin, Groovy, C# and F#, `equals` treats two whole numbers of different sizes as equal when their values are equal, so `Assert.equals(1200, total)` passes for a `long` total. In F#, a case that does not read the error of `throws` passes it to `ignore`, as in `Assert.throws(fun () -> parse "x") |> ignore`. Go writes the names with a capital letter, like every exported Go name. In Go, a failed check stops the case, and `Assert.Throws` takes a `func() error` and passes when it returns an error or panics. A Go case returns nothing, or `error` as before. In Ruby, `throws` takes a block. In Lua, `throws` takes a function, and `equals` compares two tables by their keys and values. In Dart, `throws` always returns a future, so the case writes `await Assert.throws(...)`. In Swift, a check throws when it fails, so the case writes `try`, and `try await` for `throws`. In Go, `Equals` treats two numbers of different types as equal when their values are equal. In Ruby, PHP and Dart, two lists or two maps are equal when their items are equal.

The assert of your language counts too, when it always runs: the Python `assert` statement, the Rust macros `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!`, the Java and Groovy `assert` statement, the Kotlin functions `check` and `require`, the PHP `assert` function, the Dart `assert` statement and the Swift `precondition` function. Tachyon runs Java test units with assertions turned on (`java -ea`), PHP test units with `zend.assertions=1` and Dart test units with `--enable-asserts`, and Groovy always runs its `assert`. A failed Swift `precondition` stops the whole unit, so prefer `Assert` in Swift; the Swift `assert` does not count, because optimized builds leave it out. Go and Ruby have no assert of their own. The Kotlin `assert` function does not count, because it runs only when assertions are turned on. A Rust case that panics fails as one case, and the other cases still run. `console.assert` does not count, because it only writes a message. The C# `Debug.Assert` and the F# `assert` do not count either, because Tachyon builds .NET test units in Release mode, which leaves them out.

`ValueSource` lists the inputs of a test case, like JUnit's `@ValueSource`. Tachyon runs the case once for each input and passes the input as the one argument. `ty test` names each run with its position, such as `testNeverLowersAPrice[2]`, so one failing input does not hide the others. The list holds literal values, at most 256. In Rust, Java, Kotlin, Groovy, C#, F#, Go, Dart, Swift and C++ it holds numbers, strings and booleans. A C++ Tac case writes `[[ValueSource([0, 5, 1000])]]` with JSON commas and takes the input as its one parameter, such as `void testNeverLowersAPrice(int cents)`. A Swift case names its input without a label, as in `func testNeverLowersAPrice(_ cents: Int)`. F# writes the list with commas too, as in `[<ValueSource([0, 5, 1000])>]`, because Tachyon reads it as JSON. `ValueSource` goes on a method whose name begins with `test` (`Test` in Go) in a `Test` class.

A test case asserts and holds no logic: no `if`, `else`, loop, `switch`, `match`, `when`, `case`, `unless`, `until`, `guard` or `? :` choice. When a case needs a branch, write one case for each path. When it needs a loop, list the inputs in `ValueSource`. `&&` and `||` inside a check are fine, and a helper method of the unit (its name does not begin with `test`) may hold logic. `ty bundle` and `ty preview` refuse a case that breaks this with `TY1339` (ADR 0080), and `ty migrate check` lists every case to change. The check is on by default. Turn it off for Yon tests with `tests.check: false` in `server/application.json`, and for Tac tests with `tac.tests.check: false` in `client/manifest.json`. The check reads the test units of every test language.
