build-and-deploy.title: Build and deploy
build-and-deploy.summary: `ty bundle` builds the files that you publish, and `ty start` serves them. This page shows the options for a release.

sections.heading: Build and deploy
sections.body:
By default, `ty bundle` writes `dist/web`. To check a release, use `--target all`. Then preview or package the single target that you plan to release. On the server, `ty start` serves the bundle and never builds it. `ty serve` also builds and watches, unless `NODE_ENV=production` is set: then it does neither.

A build compiles the services of different languages at the same time. `TAC_BUILD_JOBS` sets how many toolchains run at once; the default is the number of CPU cores divided by 3, from 1 to 4. Set it to 1 on a small machine or a CI runner with little memory. When `ty preview` or `ty serve` starts again, it serves the last build at once and builds again in the background.

Yon compiles each Kotlin, Rust, Dart, Go and Groovy handler once. The project keeps the result in `.tachyon/handlers`, and ty keeps a copy in `TAC_CACHE_DIR/runtime/handlers-v1` (the newest 512 copies), so another project or a fresh checkout with the same handler, models and compiler reuses it instead of compiling again. `ty cache clean` removes these copies.

The Tachyon cache is `~/Library/Caches/Tachyon` on macOS, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Tachyon\Cache` on Windows and `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/tachyon` (or `~/.cache/tachyon`) on Linux. `TAC_CACHE_DIR` chooses another folder, and `ty cache status` prints the one in use with its per-language build caches (`dotnet-web`, `go-wasm`, `swift-wasm`, `kotlin-wasm`, `java-wasm`, `rust-wasm`, `dart-wasm`, `ruby-web`, `lua-web`, `cpp-wasm` and `typescript`). `ty cache clean` removes those build caches with the runtime cache; installed tools in the cache, such as the Pyodide files and TeaVM, stay. The cached web builds and handlers in this folder run in the browser and on the server, so anyone who can write to it can change your app. Keep it private to your own user account, and never share it between users. A copy is trusted by its name; `ty cache clean` repairs a damaged one (ADR 0037).

A native build writes the time from `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` and the commit from `GITHUB_SHA` into its build information. Without them it writes 0 and a commit of zeros, so the build information never depends on the clock.

`ty bundle --target windows --arch arm64` and `--arch x64` select the Windows architecture. Without `--arch`, an ARM64 build machine selects ARM64 and other machines select x64; `--arch native` uses that default. The choice sets the Rust companion target, WebView2 loader folder, C# runtime identifier and linker machine together. Build in a matching MSVC developer prompt: an ARM64 machine uses `vcvarsall.bat arm64` for ARM64 or `vcvarsall.bat arm64_amd64` for x64. A conflicting `VSCMD_ARG_TGT_ARCH` stops the build (`TY1605`), and `--arch` without a Windows target is refused (`TY1001`). Both architectures have bundle and helper execution evidence; WebView2 page rendering and interaction still need an interactive desktop qualification run.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target all
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos
TAC_BUILD_JOBS=1 ty bundle
ty cache status
ty bundle --target windows --arch arm64
ty bundle --target windows --arch x64

sections.heading: Compressed files
sections.body:
A release build of the web target (`ty bundle`) writes two compressed copies next to each script, style, page, JSON, SVG, source map and WebAssembly file of 1 KiB or more: `app.js.br` (Brotli) and `app.js.gz` (gzip). The build keeps a copy only when it is smaller than the file. It writes the same bytes every time, and it reuses the copies of files that did not change, so a second build is fast. Compressed content also survives an empty output directory or a fresh checkout in `TAC_CACHE_DIR/runtime/precompression-v1`. The cache checks the source and encoder version, then decodes a hit to verify it matches the source. Each entry is named by the hash of its content and is at most 4 MiB, and new entries replace old ones atomically. After a build the cache keeps at most 256 MiB in total and removes the entries that were used least recently first. If the cache folder cannot be written, the build still writes the compressed copies; only the reuse is lost. Inputs over 16 MiB are compressed normally without persistent caching. `ty cache clean` clears these runtime entries. Native targets get no copies.

`ty start` and `ty preview --static` read the browser's `Accept-Encoding` header and send the Brotli copy, else the gzip copy, else the plain file. A value with `q=0` turns an encoding off. The answer has `Content-Encoding`, `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, and the length and ETag of the copy that is sent, and range and HEAD requests work. The browser unpacks the copy, so pages, services and the service worker get the same bytes as before. While `ty preview` watches your sources, it sends plain files and its builds write no copies, so hot updates stay fast.

On this website the copies make the published files 73% smaller: 12.0 MB becomes 3.1 MB. The Go module (built by TinyGo) goes from 320 KiB to 101 KiB, the .NET runtime from 1.4 MB to 458 KiB, the Ruby runtime from 1.1 MB to 347 KiB, the Swift module from 3.2 MiB to 920 KiB, the Kotlin module from 88 KiB to 31 KiB and the Dart module from 59 KiB to 21 KiB. A CDN or a web server such as nginx (`brotli_static`, `gzip_static`) can send the same copies. `ty bundle` prints the totals, and ADR 0075 explains the choices.
sections.code:
ty bundle
ls dist/web/.tachyon/tac-client.js*
ty start --port 8080
curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' http://127.0.0.1:8080/.tachyon/tac-client.js

sections.heading: Route size budgets
sections.body:
A release build (`ty bundle`) checks how much script and WebAssembly each route loads. It starts at the page of the route and follows every file that the page loads: script tags, the modules of the services that the view uses, `import`s, `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` and other paths written as text in a script, and the file lists in JSON files that a script reads, such as .NET's `blazor.boot.json`. It does not count the service worker, and it cannot follow a path that a script builds while it runs.

The build writes Tachyon's own page scripts, such as `tac-client.js`, `behavior-runtime.js` and the shared script of each service language (`tachyon-rust.js`, `tachyon-go.js` and the others), without comment lines, indentation or blank lines, so a route carries less of them. The Go glue `wasm_exec.js` is written the same way, and it keeps its license notice. The code in each line stays as written, so an error in the browser still points at readable code.

The services that a route counts are the services that its views use and the services that those need. A JavaScript or TypeScript service needs another service when its file names the field that receives it, such as `middle;` or `this.middle = undefined`. When a service writes to `this` with a computed name (`this[key] = ...`, `Object.assign(this, ...)`), or hands `this` to a function from another file (`initialize(this)`, `helper.call(this)`, `const owner = this`), the build cannot know which services it needs, so every route that uses it counts every service of the project. Handing `this` to the service's own method is fine: `this.save.bind(this)` and `this.pick(id).call(this)` keep the list short. Each JavaScript or TypeScript service module also carries only the models that the service names, and the models that those name, not every models file of the project (ADR 0043, ADR 0074).

The sizes are the bytes that Tachyon sends: the Brotli copy when the build wrote one (see Compressed files), else the file itself. The build adds the `.js` and `.mjs` files and the `.wasm` files of each route and stops with `TY1337` when one total is over its budget. The error names the five biggest files, so you know what to split, drop or move to the server. Set the budgets in kilobytes in `client/manifest.json`: `tac.budgets.script` (default 200) and `tac.budgets.webassembly` (default 3584). A route with a Python service gets a script budget of 512 when `tac.python` is set and `tac.budgets.script` is not, because the copied Pyodide runtime brings its own scripts (ADR 0093). A route that loads more than one web runtime gets more script budget, but only for the runtimes it loads (ADR 0100). A web runtime is the browser side of a service language: .NET (C# and F# share it), Rust, Ruby, Lua, Java, Go, Dart, Kotlin, C++ or Swift. JavaScript and TypeScript are not runtimes; they are the page itself. Each runtime has a measured allowance, the script it adds as sent: .NET 96, Rust 92, Ruby 20, Lua 12, Java 12, Go 8, Dart 8, Kotlin 8, C++ 4 and Swift 4. The budget is 200 plus the allowance of every runtime the route loads except the largest one, because a single-language route already pays for its one runtime inside 200. So a route with C#, Rust and Go services gets 200 + 92 + 8 = 300, and a route with no runtime or one runtime keeps 200. When this budget is over, the error says how it was computed and which runtimes it counted. When you set `tac.budgets.script`, your value is the budget of every route and no allowance is added. `tac.budgets.check: false` turns the check off while a project migrates. `ty preview` does not check budgets, because it sends files without compression while it watches your sources (ADR 0074).

This website uses services in many languages, and the check counts all of them on each route, so its manifest raises the script budget to 320. It loads only the DuVay components that its views use: the full DuVay component bundle is 134 KiB as sent and put the documentation home over that budget.

sections.heading: Keep the API that callers use
sections.body:
A caller that was built against your last release sends the requests and expects the answers of that release. `ty api freeze` saves the current API, the same document as `api.json`, in `server/api-baseline.json` together with `tac.application.version`. Run it after each release and commit the file.

Every later build compares its API with the baseline and stops with `TY1338` when it breaks a caller: a route, method or model is gone; a request value or a model field is gone; a request needs a new value, or a value became required; a request value accepts fewer values than before, for example `integer` instead of `number`; an answer can hold values that the old type did not allow; a model field changed its type; or the success status changed. New routes, methods, models, optional values and fields, and wider request types are fine.

If the break is on purpose, raise the major number of `tac.application.version` in `client/manifest.json`, for example from 1.4.0 to 2.0.0. The build then accepts every change. After that release, run `ty api freeze` again. A project without `server/api-baseline.json` is not checked (ADR 0074).
sections.code:
ty bundle
ty api freeze
git add server/api-baseline.json
git commit -m "API baseline of release 1.4.0"

sections.heading: Serve a built app
sections.body: ty start serves a built bundle. It sends the Brotli or gzip copy of a file that ty bundle wrote when the browser accepts it (see Compressed files). Set the host and port with `server.host` and `server.port` in `server/application.json`, or with the CLI options `--host` and `--port`. The host is an IP address, `localhost` or a name under `.localhost`, such as `shop.localhost`, which binds 127.0.0.1 (ADR 0094). An address that is not loopback also needs `--allow-non-loopback`. A server on a loopback address answers only localhost names, IP addresses, the `tac.origin` host and the names in `server.hosts`; any other `Host` gets 403 with `TY1366`. Behind a reverse proxy, list the names that it sends in `server.hosts`, and list the proxy itself in `server.proxies` (IP addresses or CIDR ranges). Only a listed proxy may send `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-*` and `X-Real-IP`; from every other peer, `ty` removes them and writes the real client address (ADR 0096). Environment values from the parent application no longer override these settings. YON_PROFILE selects a Yon profile. The .env file holds private secrets. `YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME`, `YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME` and `YON_RUBY_RUNTIME` select the runtimes (by default `node`, or `bun` when `node` is not on `PATH`, then `python3` and `ruby`), and this choice is still deployment policy. Handler processes see only a small baseline of environment variables and the names that `server.environment` lists (see Environment variables for handlers).
sections.code:
TAC_DIST_PATH=dist/web \
YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME=node \
  ty start --port 8080

webassembly-compilers.title: WebAssembly compilers per language
webassembly-compilers.summary: A release build compiles each WebAssembly service language with the compiler and settings that give the smallest download. This page shows which compiler each language uses, why, and what it costs.

sections.heading: Which compiler each language uses
sections.body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart, C++, Ruby, Lua or Python reaches the browser as WebAssembly. A release build (`ty bundle`) compiles each of these languages with the compiler and settings that make the smallest download. `ty preview` keeps fast settings, so a change shows up in about a second. After a release build, `ty bundle` prints one line for each language: which compiler it used and why (ADR 0081; an ADR is an architecture decision record).

| Language | Release build | Why this compiler | Development build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | rustc with `opt-level=z`, LTO and one codegen unit, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | rustc already makes small modules; these settings and `wasm-opt` remove what is left | rustc with `opt-level=s` |
| Swift | swiftc with `-Osize` and the static standard library, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | swiftc makes a module without Foundation; `wasm-opt` removes what is left | swiftc with `-Osize`, no Binaryen |
| Go | TinyGo with `-opt=z` and the Boehm garbage collector, then `wasm-opt -Oz` | TinyGo leaves out most of the Go runtime, so the module is many times smaller | the standard Go compiler |
| C# and F# | the trimmed .NET interpreter, with Emscripten `-Oz` | the interpreter is the smallest .NET download and fast enough for state and logic | no native relink |
| Kotlin | the Kotlin/Wasm production build, with Binaryen | Kotlin's own production step makes the program about three times smaller | no Binaryen |
| Java | javac, TeaVM's WasmGC backend, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | TeaVM keeps only the Java classes the service uses; `wasm-opt` makes the module about half as large. Tachyon changes TeaVM's `runtime.js` so that it makes no code from text, which Tachyon's content security policy forbids, and gives the behavior runtime simple text checks instead of TeaVM's regular expressions | TeaVM, no Binaryen |
| Dart | `dart compile wasm -O4` | `-O4` also drops runtime type checks, so the module is smaller and faster | `-O2`, with the type checks |
| Ruby | the pinned mruby runtime, built with Emscripten | one runtime for every Ruby service, built once on your machine | the same |
| Lua | the Lua 5.4 runtime, from the pinned lua.org source with Emscripten `-Oz` | one runtime of about 170 KB for every Lua service, built once on your machine | the same |
| C++ | em++ (Emscripten 6.0.10 or newer) with `-Oz`, `-fwasm-exceptions` and emmalloc; `-Oz` also runs Binaryen | Emscripten links only the parts of libc++ that the services use, and Tachyon's JSON prelude avoids `std::to_chars`, so a page with one small service loads about 75 KB (29 KB with Brotli) | em++ with `-O1` |
| Python | the pinned Pyodide 314.0.7 core files, prebuilt and checked by SHA-256, copied from the Tachyon cache | Tachyon never downloads or compiles Python; one runtime of about 13 MB before compression serves every Python service | the same |

Binaryen (its `wasm-opt` program) and TinyGo are optional. Without them a release build still works; the module is larger, and the build line says what to install. `ty doctor` lists both when your project has a Rust, Go, Swift or Java web service. TeaVM itself is not optional: a Java web service needs it in every build, and `ty doctor --install` downloads it into the Tachyon cache. Kotlin needs the kotlin-stdlib-wasm-js 2.1.10 library: set `TAC_KOTLIN_WASM_STDLIB` to its `.klib` file. Swift needs the Swift SDK for WebAssembly: set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_SDK` to its `wasm32-unknown-wasip1` folder, and set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_COMPILER` to the swift.org swiftc when another swiftc, such as Xcode's, comes first on PATH. Python needs its five pinned Pyodide files in `python-web/314.0.7/` in the Tachyon cache, and `ty doctor` checks them.

Ruby, Lua and Python ship a runtime that was not written by Tachyon, so a build that copies one also writes its license notices beside it in `.tachyon/services/`: `ruby/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`, `lua/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` and `python/314.0.7/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`. The Python file holds the licenses of Pyodide (MPL-2.0, with the address of its source code), CPython (PSF License) and the libraries inside `pyodide.asm.wasm`. The Ruby and Lua files also hold the licenses of the parts of Emscripten that the runtime links in: Emscripten itself, musl and compiler-rt. Go's `wasm_exec.js` refers to its LICENSE file, so a build with a Go service also writes `go/LICENSE` beside it, taken from the Go or TinyGo installation that built the module. Deploy these files with the app. Route budgets do not count them.

$ ty bundle

Dart: dart compile wasm -O4, which runs Binaryen itself and drops runtime type checks for the smallest, fastest module; development builds keep -O2 with the checks

sections.heading: Choices and trade-offs
sections.body:
For Go, a release build tries TinyGo first. When TinyGo is not installed, or it cannot compile your services (some packages, reflection or `//go:linkname` are limited in TinyGo), the build compiles them again with the standard Go compiler and prints why. It never fails only because TinyGo failed. Each compiler ships its own `wasm_exec.js`, and Tachyon publishes the one that matches the module. A call from the page still waits for a `time.Sleep` inside it, as with the standard compiler. TinyGo builds with the Boehm garbage collector (`-gc=boehm`). Each call from the page runs in a new goroutine with its own 64 KB stack, and TinyGo's default collector swept the whole heap every few calls, so one call in four or five paused for 3 to 5 ms. With Boehm the slowest 5% of calls take under 1 ms. It costs about 47 KiB raw and 14 KiB with Brotli (ADR 0081). To choose the compiler yourself, set `tac.go.compiler` in `client/manifest.json`: `"tinygo"` uses TinyGo in every build, also in `ty preview`, with no fallback; `"go"` never uses TinyGo. Use `"tinygo"` while you develop when you want to find TinyGo limits before a release.

For C# and F#, the default is the trimmed .NET interpreter. It downloads the least and runs services that hold state and logic well. When a service does heavy computing (for example image or number work in a loop), set `tac.dotnet.aot` to `true` in `client/manifest.json`. The release build then compiles the services ahead of time (AOT). They run faster, but the download is larger and the build takes minutes. Tachyon does not guess which services need AOT; the release line reminds you of the setting.

For Dart, the release setting `-O4` assumes that the program has no type errors. Development builds keep `-O2`, which checks types while the service runs, so a type error shows up in `ty preview` first.

Most of a Swift module is the Swift standard library and its runtime, so even a small Swift service is about 3.5 MiB (about 980 KiB as sent with Brotli). Other settings do not help: after Binaryen, linker flags such as `--strip-all` save nothing, and leaving out reflection metadata saves 2 KB but changes what `String(describing:)` prints. Embedded Swift would make a small counter about 33 KB (12 KB with Brotli), but it has no `Codable`, no `Any` values, no `as?` casts and no `throws` without an error type, and Swift services use all of them. So Tachyon keeps the full standard library (ADR 0082). When the download matters most, write the service in Rust or Dart.

The table shows the WebAssembly that the page downloads for one small service (the tally from the WebAssembly services example), before and after this change, as a raw file and as sent with Brotli (see Compressed files). Route size budgets measure these smaller files.

| Language | Before, raw | After, raw | Before, Brotli | After, Brotli | Smaller (Brotli) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | 142.1 KiB | 109.2 KiB | 56.7 KiB | 48.6 KiB | 14% |
| Go | 3.09 MiB | 356.5 KiB | 678.5 KiB | 112.7 KiB | 83% |
| C# | 2.87 MiB | 2.83 MiB | 943.0 KiB | 938.7 KiB | under 1% |
| Dart | 47.0 KiB | 45.6 KiB | 16.8 KiB | 16.5 KiB | 2% |
| Kotlin | 293 KB | 101 KB | | | (ADR 0078) |
| Swift | 3.30 MiB | 3.23 MiB | | 897.7 KiB | (ADR 0082) |
| Java | 134.7 KiB | 70.8 KiB | 46.5 KiB | 29.8 KiB | 36% |

Go gains the most, because TinyGo leaves out most of the Go runtime. On this website, a release build now publishes 8.7 MB instead of 11.7 MB, and sends 2.25 MB instead of 2.86 MB with Brotli; its Go module went from 684 KiB to 101 KiB as sent. The .NET browser runtime was already trimmed, so C# gains little; most of its download is the runtime itself, which the service worker caches once.

request-ids.title: Request IDs and error reports
request-ids.summary: Every request has an ID that links its log lines. When something fails, the error report has a stable code, so you can find what happened.

sections.heading: Request IDs and error reports
sections.body: Every request carries a correlation identifier (an ID that links the log lines of one request). The server creates it in its own process and passes it through the handler protocol. So in a log, you can connect a request to the controller call it caused. A handler reads the ID from the request header `x-tachyon-request-id`; the server sets this header itself, so a client cannot choose it. Failures arrive as Diagnostics v1 with stable codes. This is the same structure that a build produces. `--diagnostic-format json` makes them machine-readable. Tracing exporters (tools that send trace data to another service) are not built in.
sections.code:
ty preview --diagnostic-format json
ty doctor

cookbook.title: Cookbook
cookbook.summary: Practical recipes for building Tachyon apps with a frontend-first workflow (you build the client first). Most recipes need only client/. When a recipe needs a server, it shows the smallest controller that answers it.

sections.heading: Frontend-only prototype
sections.body: Start with only client/. Tac renders pages and components. Services provide the reactive presentation model (the data that the page shows, which updates the page when it changes). Later you can add controllers in server/controllers, and the UI can keep the same contract (the data and actions it expects).

sections.heading: Signal-driven UI
sections.body: Signals (events that a service publishes) replace event code that you connect by hand between services. The form saves a name through UsersClient and publishes the answer, a UserSaved model from client/models, through its applicationEventPublisher. The list registers a listener for UserSaved with OnEvent and adds the name to its list. The two services do not know each other, and you can add more listeners without changing the form. The listener only changes a field. It does not call the server, because the event already carries the saved name. This keeps the listener a short synchronous method, which every language accepts: a Rust event or lifecycle method that is async stops the build with TY1405. The server half is one small JavaScript controller in server/controllers: POST /users answers the saved user. A Yon handler keeps nothing in memory between requests, so a real app stores the name first, for example in a database. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby or Lua answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows the server half only in JavaScript. JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, C#, F#, Kotlin, Swift, Ruby and C++ send the request through Tachyon's browser transport to the server of the page. In the compiled languages of this group, UsersSetup gives the client no adapter; C++ needs no Setup at all. The Java UsersSetup gives the client an HTTP adapter that answers in the page with the same shape, so this tab works before the server exists; a Java UsersSetup without the adapter would use the browser transport instead. Browser services in Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust and Dart still get their own copy of a Setup each (see Client classes that call the server), so in every tab only the form uses the client. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308.

sections.heading: Middleware in any language
sections.body: Tachyon calls a `middleware.<ext>` file at the project root before every request and after every response. The file holds one class named `Middleware` with `before(request)` and `after(request)`. Each method gets the request in its language's own type and answers with its language's own response, or with nothing to let the request pass. Tachyon calls these methods by name for every request, whatever its HTTP method. So a CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) and a form `POST` reach them like a `GET`. A CORS preflight is the check request that a browser sends before a cross-origin request. If you leave out a method, that phase passes without change. A 204 answer also lets the request pass, and the headers of a 204 answer from after are added to the response, as in this example. Any other status answers the request instead of the route (before) or replaces the response (after). The middleware may be written in any Yon language. It does not need to match the language of the controllers. Python and PHP middleware import a model from `server/models/` as a controller does, with `from models import Name` or `use Models\Name;`. TypeScript middleware uses `import type` from `/models/`.

sections.heading: Adding behavior for native platforms
sections.body: Keep the shared HTML and responsive styles. Then add platform behavior in a native service. Native hosts set a marker on the document. A stylesheet can use this marker. So it does not need template globals, and those do not exist. Use a service in the target's native language for operating system (OS) SDK calls. Handle its asynchronous results in your own code.

annotations.title: Annotations A–Z
annotations.summary: An annotation is a marker that you put on a class, a field or a method. It tells Tachyon what to do. This page first lists every annotation from A to Z with one line about what it does. Then each group of annotations has a working example in every language that accepts it. Tac is the frontend realm (one side of the app), and Yon is the backend realm. When a realm or a language does not accept an annotation, the section says so and explains why.

sections.heading: Annotations A–Z
sections.body:
Each row names one annotation, says what it does, and names the page that explains it. "Below" means a section further down this page. "Goes on" is the part of the code that carries the annotation. "Arguments" says whether it takes none, needs some, or may take some. The Tac and Yon columns name the service languages that accept it: "all" means every language of that realm, and "no" means the realm refuses it. F# follows the C# rules, and Java Tac checks its own list: it refuses Helper and Named, for example. "Python limited" means that the build accepts the annotation in Python Tac code, but Python Tac cannot run it yet (see What each realm refuses).

In the code, each language writes the annotation in its own way: `@Needs` in JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, Swift, Dart and Groovy, `[Needs]` in C#, `[<Needs>]` in F#, `#[Needs]` in Rust, Ruby and PHP, `// @Needs` in Go and `-- @Needs` in Lua. Python writes snake_case decorators, such as `@needs_all` and `@cache_settings`, and puts a field or parameter marker inside the type: `cart_helper: Annotated[CartHelper, needs]`.

| Annotation | What it does | Goes on | Arguments | Tac | Yon | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AllOrNothing` | Saves all of the method's changes, or none of them when it fails. | method | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Allow` | Lets only a signed-in user with one of these roles call the route, like `Allow(Admin)`. | class or method | required | no | all | Who may call a route |
| `Cached` | Keeps a method's answer and returns it again for the same arguments. | method | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `CacheKey` | Makes this argument part of the key of a cached answer. | parameter | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `CacheSettings` | Names the cache that this class's Cached methods use, and sets its limits. | class | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Check` | Checks the fields of this argument before the method runs. | parameter | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `Checked` | Marks a model whose fields are checked before a method uses it. | class | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `ClearCache` | Removes the saved answers of a Cached method after this method runs. | method | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Convert` | Copies the fields of one model into a new model. | method | optional | all | all | Mapping, below |
| `Converter` | Marks a class whose methods copy one model into another. | class | none | all | all | Mapping, below |
| `DeleteRequest` | Means calling this method sends a DELETE request. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `DeleteRoute` | Means this method answers DELETE requests. | method | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `Description` | Gives the class a short description for tools and documents. | class | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Entity` | Marks a model that is saved as a record. | class | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Data access, below |
| `ErrorHandler` | Marks a class whose methods answer the errors of controllers. | class | optional | no | all | Error handlers |
| `Fake` | Puts a stand-in object into this field while a test runs. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Test units |
| `FreshStart` | Builds new objects for every test instead of sharing them. | class | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Test units |
| `FromBody` | Fills this argument from the request body, read as JSON. | parameter | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `FromCookie` | Fills this argument from a cookie. | parameter | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `FromHeader` | Fills this argument from a request header. | parameter | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `FromPath` | Fills this argument from a path variable, such as {id}. | parameter | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `FromQuery` | Fills this argument from the query string, after ?. | parameter | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `Gateway` | Calls a method of a class that is written in another language. | method | required | no | all but Lua | Relays and gateways |
| `GetRequest` | Means calling this method sends a GET request. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `GetRoute` | Means this method answers GET requests. | method | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `HandlesError` | Answers one kind of error with an HTTP response. | method | none | no | all | Error handlers |
| `Helper` | Marks a class that services use for part of their work. | class | none | JS, TS, Dart, Rust, Python; C# and F# with new | all | Helpers, utilities and private methods |
| `HTTPClient` | Marks a class that sends HTTP requests and gives the path they start with. | class | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `Id` | Marks the field that identifies each saved record. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Data access, below |
| `IdentityProvider` | Marks the one class that says who is signed in and which roles they have. | class | none | no | all | Who may call a route |
| `InBackground` | Runs this listener without making the publisher wait. | method | none | all | JS, TS, Python | Events between services |
| `Length` | Limits how long the text or list in this field may be. | field | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `Lifetime` | Says how long one object of this class lives. | class | required | all | all | Dependency injection |
| `LocalState` | Keeps this field in the browser's localStorage, so its value comes back after a reload and in later visits on this device. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | no | Saving data in the browser |
| `Max` | Refuses a number in this field that is above the given value. | field | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `MaxAtOnce` | Limits how many calls of this method run at the same time. | method | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Min` | Refuses a number in this field that is below the given value. | field | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `Named` | Chooses which object fills a Needs field when there are several. | field | required | all | all | Dependency injection |
| `Needs` | Asks Tachyon to supply an object that this class uses. | field or class | optional | all | all | Dependency injection |
| `NeedsAll` | Requires every field that has no initial value: collaborators are injected and the other fields come from the component's props. | class | none | all | all | Dependency injection |
| `NotEmpty` | Refuses a value when this field is empty. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `OnClose` | Runs the method when the socket closes. | method | none | no | all | Sockets |
| `OnError` | Runs the method when opening the socket or handling a message fails. | method | none | no | all | Sockets |
| `OnEvent` | Runs the method when an event of its parameter's type is published. | method | optional | all | all | Events between services |
| `OnMessage` | Runs the method for each message that the browser sends on the socket. | method | none | no | all | Sockets |
| `OnOpen` | Runs the method when a browser opens the socket. | method | none | no | all | Sockets |
| `OnStart` | Runs the method once when the object starts. | method | none | all | all | Services |
| `OnStop` | Runs the method once when the object stops. | method | none | all | all | Services |
| `Order` | Sets when this listener runs compared with the other listeners of the event. | method | required | all | all | Events between services |
| `PageDefaults` | Gives the page size and sort order that a page argument uses when the caller leaves them out. | parameter | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Data access, below |
| `PatchRequest` | Means calling this method sends a PATCH request. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `PatchRoute` | Means this method answers PATCH requests. | method | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `PathVariable` | Puts this argument into the request path. | parameter | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `PostRequest` | Means calling this method sends a POST request. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `PostRoute` | Means this method answers POST requests. | method | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `Public` | Lets anyone call the route, also a caller who is not signed in. | class or method | none | no | all | Who may call a route |
| `PutRequest` | Means calling this method sends a PUT request. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `PutRoute` | Means this method answers PUT requests. | method | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `Query` | Turns an empty method into a query of the Store's records. | method | optional | all but Lua, Python | all | Data access, below |
| `RequestBody` | Sends this argument as the request body, written as JSON. | parameter | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `RequestHeader` | Sends this argument as a request header. | parameter | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `RequestParam` | Adds this argument to the query string of the request. | parameter | optional | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Calling the server from a page |
| `RequestRoute` | Marks a controller and gives the path that its routes start with. | class | optional | no | all | Controllers |
| `Required` | Refuses a value when this field is missing. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Checking values |
| `ResponseStatus` | Sets the HTTP status of a normal answer. | method | required | no | all | Controllers |
| `Retry` | Runs the method again when it fails. | method | optional | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `Schedule` | Runs this worker again and again after a fixed delay. | class | required | no | all | Scheduling: Yon, below |
| `Service` | Marks a class that other classes can use. | class | none | all | all | Services |
| `SessionState` | Keeps this field in the browser's sessionStorage, so its value comes back after a reload in the same tab. | field | none | all but Lua; Python limited | no | Saving data in the browser |
| `Setting` | Fills this field with one setting value. | field | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Settings and configuration |
| `Settings` | Fills the class's fields from the settings whose names share a prefix. | class | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Settings and configuration |
| `Setup` | Marks a class that builds and configures shared objects. Tachyon configures it once per page in Tac and once per server process in Yon. | class | none | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |
| `SignedIn` | Lets any signed-in user call the route. | class or method | none | no | all | Who may call a route |
| `SocketRequest` | Means Tachyon keeps a WebSocket open and passes each incoming message to this method. | method | optional | JS, TS, Go | no | Sockets |

| `Store` | Marks a class that saves and finds records. | class | optional | all but Lua, Python | all | Data access, below |
| `StreamRequest` | Means Tachyon keeps a stream of server-sent events open and passes each message to this method. | method | optional | JS, TS, Go | no | Streams |
| `StreamRoute` | Means this method answers GET requests with a stream of server-sent events. | method | optional | no | all but Java, Groovy, Rust | Streams |
| `Table` | Names the table that stores this Entity. | class | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Data access, below |
| `Test` | Marks a test class and names the TestSetup class it runs with. | class | required | all | all | Test units |
| `TestSettings` | Sets setting values while this test runs. | class | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Test units |

| `Topic` | Sends each published event of this model to the listeners in every Yon language and in open pages. | class | none | all but Lua, Python | all but Lua | Topics |
| `UpdateCache` | Saves this method's answer as the new answer of a Cached method. | method | required | all but Lua; Python limited | all | Behavior annotations |

sections.heading: Roles: Yon
sections.body: GET /billing returns {"total":42}. A role is the job that a class does, such as controller, service or store. RequestRoute marks a controller (a class that answers HTTP requests) in server/controllers. It also gives the base path, and Public, SignedIn or Allow(Role) says who may call its routes. IdentityProvider is the one class in server/controllers that says who is signed in, and a role type for Allow is an empty class in server/roles. Service, Store, HTTPClient, Helper, Setup and Entity live in the realm's shared folders under server/. The compiler finds them by exact name and matching language (ADR 0031). Here is the chain. The controller injects BillingService (the framework creates the service and gives it to the controller). The service injects BillingHelper. Setup, Entity, BillingStore and BillingClient appear here only to show their folders and their names. BillingStore and BillingClient also show the form of a declarative role: each one is a contract with no implementation, like a Spring Data repository interface and a Spring @HttpExchange interface. A Store always names the Entity it keeps, and the data group shows one at work. Each language writes it in its bodiless form (an interface, a trait, a protocol, a Python Protocol, or a class with empty method bodies in JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby), and Tachyon generates each query and each request. Neither one connects to a database or configures an adapter by itself. An adapter is the code that talks to an outside system, such as a database. Needs works out every dependency from the field it marks, a field that has no starting value. So no file here writes a constructor. In Rust, a provider (a class that the framework can inject) still needs a constructor in its own impl block. That is why BillingHelper writes fn new itself, even though it has no dependencies. Go has no constructors, so Tachyon builds each Go role as &T{} and fills its marked fields. JavaScript matches a field to the name of the provider in lowerCamel case. In lowerCamel case, the first word is lowercase, and each next word starts with a capital letter. Every other language matches the concrete type. Rust matches it through Arc<T>, and Go matches it through *T. The controller and route annotations, the error handler annotations, Stream, Gateway and Schedule exist only in Yon. Swift is not a Yon language. The Lua tab has no BillingClient, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Lua Yon code with TY1308: Lua gets gateway clients in a later step (ADR 0085). A Lua Store such as BillingStore is a provider, as in the other languages, so another class can ask for it with Needs.

sections.heading: Roles: Tac
sections.body: These are the same roles, in the browser and in a native companion. A native companion is an app that runs outside the browser, such as a phone or desktop app. An entry is the file that the compiler starts from. A Tac entry is the service itself, at client/services/<Name>Service.<ext>. The page places <billing-panel hydrate="load" />. The view refers to the service instance as {billing.total} (ADR 0030). The service's role files live in the realm's shared client/ folders: stores, helpers, converters, setups and entities. The compiler finds only files in the same language as the entry. Every Tac service language runs in the browser: JavaScript and TypeScript as page JavaScript, and Dart, Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Ruby, Lua and Python as WebAssembly. Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust can also be linked into a native companion. Dart compiles to WebAssembly with garbage collection (WasmGC), behind one JavaScript module per service (ADR 0033). A service written only in Rust, only in C# or in Go compiles to WebAssembly (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045). Service, Lifetime and Needs work in every Tac language; a Java service cannot ask for another service, and the build refuses that with TY1405. Helper works in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust and Python, where Needs injects it, and in C# and F#, where the caller builds it with `new` (see Injection: Tac). Swift, Kotlin, Go, Java, Ruby and Lua refuse Helper with TY1308. BillingService reads its total through the injected helper. BillingStore shows the form of a Store: a contract with no implementation that names its Entity, and Tachyon generates each query. The Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go and Ruby tabs place Store, Setup and Entity next to a plain service type. That is why those services hold their own state. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses Store in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. HTTPClient works in every Tac language except Python and Lua, which refuse it with TY1308 (see Outgoing HTTP: Tac). Controllers (RequestRoute) do not exist in Tac at all. C++ has no tab here: it has the Service and HTTPClient roles, but the build refuses Store and the other roles in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Data access: Yon
sections.summary: Entity and Table name a table. Store names that Entity class and gives an explicit allowlist of fields and its page bounds. Method names derive the query, @Query states a query exactly, and @PageDefaults on a parameter limits a page request that the caller supplies.
sections.body:
Choose one language for GET /products. Each implementation returns {"active":[{"id":1,"status":"active"}],"count":1,"others":[{"id":2,"status":"retired"}],"first":{"id":1,"status":"active"}}. An entity is a type that describes one kind of stored record. You must declare Entity and Table together, in server/entities. Entity takes only the adapter name; the one field marked @Id is the identifier. The Store that names an Entity lives in server/stores. Its first argument is the Entity class itself: ProductEntity.class in Java, ProductEntity::class in Kotlin and PHP, typeof(ProductEntity) in C#, typeof<ProductEntity> in F#, and the bare name in the other languages. Its options are exactly fields, defaultSize and maxSize. The fields list must contain the field marked @Id. Both sizes are from 1 to 100, and defaultSize cannot be larger than maxSize.

A method name can start with findBy/countBy/existsBy/deleteBy, or with the snake_case find_by_/count_by_/exists_by_/delete_by_. That method builds its query plan from that allowlist (the fields list). A query plan describes the query that the adapter runs. The operator suffixes (name endings) are Equals, NotEquals, LessThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqual, In, IsNull and IsNotNull. And joins them. Equals is also the default when there is no suffix. @Query gives the plan directly instead. It accepts exactly operation, where and orderBy. operation is find, findOne, count, exists or delete. A find reads its page request from the parameter marked @PageDefaults. findOne answers the first matching record or null. delete removes every matching record and answers how many it removed, so deleteByStatus is a derived delete. findOne, count, exists and delete take no page parameter and need orderBy set to []. The plan must use every declared parameter exactly once. Sometimes the orderBy of a find does not include the id field. Then the compiler adds the id field at the end. This keeps the order fixed when two records have equal values. A Store is a contract with no implementation, like a Spring Data repository interface, and the compiler writes every query. Like Spring Data's CrudRepository, a Store can extend Repository<Entity, Id> and then gets four methods without declaring them: findById(id) answers the record with that id or null, findAll(page) answers one page ordered by id (pass {} for the first page), save(entity) inserts or replaces a record and answers it, and deleteById(id) answers how many records it deleted. Each language names the base in its own form: extends Repository<ProductEntity, Integer> in Java and Groovy, : Repository<ProductEntity, Int> in Kotlin, : Repository<ProductEntity, int> in C#, extends Repository in PHP, the embedded Repository[ProductEntity, int64] in a Go interface, implements Repository<ProductEntity, int> in Dart, the supertrait Repository<ProductEntity, i64> in Rust, Repository[ProductEntity, int] before Protocol in Python, and extends Repository<ProductEntity, number> in TypeScript. F# writes inherit Repository<ProductEntity, int> as the first line of its abstract type. JavaScript writes extends Repository with the JSDoc tag @extends {Repository<ProductEntity, number>}, and Ruby writes class ProductStore < Repository. The Repository must name the same Entity as the Store, and only a Store can extend it (TY1308). The controller calls findById(1) for the first field. The compiler removes the base and writes the four methods next to the other queries. Each language writes it in its bodiless form: an interface in Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C# and PHP, a Go interface, an abstract interface class in Dart, a trait in Rust, a Protocol class in Python with ... as each body, and a type with only abstract members in F#. JavaScript and TypeScript have no bodiless form that takes annotations, so there a Store is a class whose methods have empty bodies, and each query declares its answer as Promise<ProductEntity[] | void> or Promise<number | void>, because an empty body returns nothing to the type checker. A method body, a field or a constructor in a Store stops the build with TY1308, and so does a method that is neither a derived query nor a Query. The compiler reports it and does not quietly drop it. `ty migrate fix --write` rewrites a class store into its contract form.

@PageDefaults sits on the page parameter and accepts exactly defaultSize, maxSize and sort. It turns page, size, sort and offset into standard values before the call. The queries run through the store's behavior context. The behavior context is the object that Tachyon creates from a Setup: by default the Setup named after the store (ProductSetup for ProductStore), or the one that the setup option names, here CatalogSetup. The controller asks for the store with Needs, like any other provider, and never builds it. A Converter that turns rows into another shape is injected the same way, but it opens no context, because a mapping reads only its argument (see Mapping: Yon). A Store must name its Entity: a Store without one stops the build with TY1308, and code that only runs SQL belongs in a service that asks for a DataSource (see DataSource in a service). The adapter that Entity.adapter names is your application code. Every query must pass authorizeEntity. These annotations hold a query plan. They are not a database and not an authorization system.

Two language notes. C# route methods are synchronous, so the route method waits for the tasks that the behavior methods return. Synchronous means a call returns only when its work is done. Rust converts BehaviorError into YonResourceError so that the route method can use ?. Go does the same, and its route method returns (value, error). Raw SQL through a DataSource must pass its values as parameters; query text built from pieces stops the build with TY1325. Lua has no base classes, so the Lua store declares find_by_id as a derived query instead of extending Repository.

use Models\ProductReport;

#[RequestRoute("/products")]

class ProductController {
    #[Needs]
    private ProductStore $products;

    #[GetRoute]
    public function getProduct(): ProductReport {
        $activeStatus = 'active';
        $active = $this->products->findByStatus($activeStatus);
        $activeCount = $this->products->countByStatus($activeStatus);

<?php

#[Helper]
class CatalogAdapterHelper {
    public static function execute(array $command, mixed $execution): array|int {
        $rows = [['id' => 1, 'status' => 'active'], ['id' => 2, 'status' => 'retired']];
        $query = $command['query'];
        $condition = $query['where'][0];
        $keepUnequalRows = $condition['operator'] === 'ne';
        $matchingRows = [];
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            $isEqual = $row[$condition['field']] === $condition['value'];
            $isMatch = $keepUnequalRows ? !$isEqual : $isEqual;
            if ($isMatch) $matchingRows[] = $row;
        }
        if ($query['kind'] === 'count') return count($matchingRows);
        return array_slice($matchingRows, 0, $query['page']['size']);
    }

    public static function authorize(array $command, mixed $execution): bool {
        return $command['entity'] === 'ProductEntity';
    }
}

open System.Threading.Tasks

[<Helper>]
type CatalogAdapterHelper() =
    let rows = BehaviorJSON.Parse("[{\"id\":1,\"status\":\"active\"},{\"id\":2,\"status\":\"retired\"}]")

    interface BehaviorEntityAdapter with
        member this.execute(command: BehaviorJSON, execution: BehaviorExecution) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
            let query = command.Get("query")
            let condition = query.Get("where").Items[0]
            let keepUnequalRows = condition.Get("operator").Text = "ne"
            let isMatch (row: BehaviorJSON) =
                let isEqual = row.Get(condition.Get("field").Text).ToString() = condition.Get("value").ToString()
                if keepUnequalRows then not isEqual else isEqual
            let matchingRows = rows.Items |> Array.filter isMatch
            if query.Get("kind").Text = "count" then
                Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.From(matchingRows.Length))
            else
                Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.Array(matchingRows))

files.code:
#[Setup]
class CatalogSetup
  ROWS = [{ "id" => 1, "status" => "active" }, { "id" => 2, "status" => "retired" }].freeze

  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Hash]
  def self.configure(execution)
    { entities: { catalog: { execute: method(:find_rows) } }, authorizeEntity: method(:product_entity?) }
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Object]
  def self.find_rows(command, execution)
    return [] unless command["operation"] == "query"
    query = command["query"]
    matching_rows = ROWS.select { |row| matches?(row, query["where"][0]) }
    return matching_rows.length if query["kind"] == "count"
    matching_rows.first(query.dig("page", "size") || matching_rows.length)
  end

  # @param row [Hash]
  # @param condition [Hash]
  # @return [Boolean]
  def self.matches?(row, condition)
    is_equal = row[condition["field"]] == condition["value"]
    condition["operator"] == "ne" ? !is_equal : is_equal
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Boolean]
  def self.product_entity?(command, execution)
    command["entity"] == "ProductEntity"
  end
end

---@class CatalogRowsHelper
CatalogRowsHelper = {
  ---@type table[]
  ROWS = { { id = 1, status = "active" }, { id = 2, status = "retired" } },
}

---@param command table
---@param execution table
---@return any
function CatalogRowsHelper:execute(command, execution)
  local query = command.query
  local condition = query.where[1]
  local matching = {}
  for _, row in ipairs(self.ROWS) do
    if (row[condition.field] == condition.value) == (condition.operator == "eq") then
      matching[#matching + 1] = row
    end
  end
  if query.kind == "count" then
    return #matching
  end
  if query.kind == "findOne" then
    return matching[1]
  end
  return matching
end

sections.heading: Data access: Tac
sections.summary: The same five annotations in the browser and on native targets. A view addresses a service, the service owns the behavior context, and the store carries the query plan.
sections.body:
Select a language tab and copy the page, the component view and the four role files. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses Store in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart and Ruby bundle for the web. Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust stage their native hosts. Go and Java bundle for the web as WebAssembly. The view reads {product.summary} from the service. A view reads its services and the built-in `data` and `page` roots, nothing else (ADR 0036). The store is the same contract as in Yon: it has no implementation, and Tachyon generates each query. It extends Repository<ProductEntity, Id> in the same form as in Yon, so a service can also call findById, findAll, save and deleteById, and a derived deleteBy method removes the matching rows from IndexedDB. The service asks for the store with Needs, as a Yon service does, and never builds it. A service asks for a Converter the same way; the converter opens no context (see Mapping: Tac). The store creates its own context from the Setup that its setup option names, here CatalogSetup. Without a setup option, a store uses the Setup with its own stem: ProductStore would use ProductSetup. Tachyon configures a Setup once per page, so this context shares the Setup's adapters with every other context built from the same Setup (see Declarative HTTP clients for the compiled languages that do not share them yet). In JavaScript and TypeScript the service's owner creates that context before the service starts, because a browser creates a context asynchronously. Dart builds the store with the service. A Kotlin, Swift, Java or C# service that marks a store field with Needs gets a new store in that field, a Rust service fills it with Default, a Go service gets it before it starts, and a Ruby attr_reader documented with # @return [ProductStore] builds it the first time it runs. F# has no field Needs, so an F# service takes the store as a primary constructor parameter, type ProductService(products: ProductStore) =, and Tachyon turns that parameter into a let binding that builds the store. The Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services below carry the Service marker, like every class in client/services (TY1363). The compiler finds their annotated entity, store and setup files and adds them to the same compile unit. A native companion (Android Kotlin, or a native Swift, Rust or C# app) has no page storage, so its Setup must name the entity adapter: its native build stops when a Store uses an entity adapter that no Setup in the service names (ADR 0059).

The annotations and their options are the same as in Yon. The previous section runs them in a full example. Only the realm is different. The role folders are client/entities, client/stores, client/setups and client/services (ADR 0031). Table is a modifier (an extra annotation on the entity). It does not change the entity's path. Declaring an entity does not open a database. The adapter named by Entity.adapter is usually application code. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart and Ruby, and in Go, Rust, C# and Kotlin services that run as WebAssembly, the name "indexeddb" needs no adapter code: Tachyon keeps one IndexedDB object store per Table, keyed by the Id field. A Dart, Ruby or WebAssembly service answers the page synchronously, so Tachyon loads its Tables into memory before the services start (at most 10,000 rows per Table), reads from that copy and saves changes to IndexedDB in the background. It builds an index for every field that a Store query compares or orders by, and it adds new indexes by upgrading the database version. It never deletes stored rows: if the Id field changes, it stops with a message. A query that has no usable index reads at most 10,000 rows. AllOrNothing collects the writes and saves them in one IndexedDB transaction. A Store that uses "indexeddb" needs no authorizeEntity, because the data never leaves the browser. It handles the transport, the query parameters and tenancy (keeping the data of each customer apart). authorizeEntity must approve every query. Tac stays client-rendered (the browser builds the page). It uses only public TAC_ configuration, never private Yon credentials. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Entity in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Transactions: Yon
sections.summary: AllOrNothing runs one service method inside a transaction on the entity adapter it names. The adapter decides: it answers begin, commit and rollback. The managed Yon datasource already does this.
sections.body: A transaction is a group of changes that either all happen or all do not happen. AllOrNothing goes on a service method, like Spring's @Transactional. LedgerService opens the transaction, and it injects EntryStore with Needs. EntryStore is a contract with no implementation (TY1308): Tachyon builds its behavior context from LedgerSetup. A store call made inside the method joins the open transaction when the store's entity uses the same entity adapter. Spring calls this propagation REQUIRED. So if the second query fails, the runtime rolls back the first one too. A call on another entity adapter does not join, and its commands carry no transaction. The open transaction follows the call, not the object. Each runtime keeps it in storage that belongs to one call: AsyncLocalStorage in JavaScript and TypeScript on the server, ThreadLocal in Java, Kotlin and Groovy, AsyncLocal in C# and F#, a context variable in Python, fiber storage in Ruby, a zone in Dart, a thread local in Rust, one entry for each goroutine in Go, and the request in PHP. In Go, each behavior context has its own LedgerAdapterHelper, so the Go report lists the service's commands, and each row that the store reads shows the transaction it ran in. AllOrNothing takes one key, adapter, which names an entry in configuration.entities. Before the method body runs, the runtime sends {"operation":"transaction","action":"begin"}. The adapter answers with an identifier of limited size, and the runtime reads it. The runtime adds this identifier to every Store and Query command that the body sends. In JavaScript and TypeScript, execute takes a BehaviorEntityCommand | BehaviorTransactionCommand: check operation first, because only Store and Query commands carry entity, table and query. When the method returns, the runtime commits (it saves all the changes). When the method raises an error, the runtime rolls back (it undoes all the changes). The caller sees the original failure, never a rollback error. Rust and Go do not use this command shape. Their entity command is a typed struct, so they control transactions through a separate method. In Rust, it is a trait method, and its default implementation refuses. In Go, it is a Transaction method, and an adapter without that method also refuses. So an adapter without transactions tells you so. An AllOrNothing inside another one joins the open transaction. It does not start a nested one, because there are no savepoints. A savepoint is a point inside a transaction that you can roll back to. A Retry method opens a new transaction for each attempt. So a failed attempt is undone before the next one starts. The managed datasource (the database connection that Tachyon manages) sets limits on both sides. At most four transactions are open at once. Each one holds one connection. If the connection does nothing for ten seconds, the transaction is rolled back. So a controller that crashes during a transaction cannot keep a connection. SQL that you write still cannot contain BEGIN, COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The FYLO datasource has no transactions. It refuses to open one, and it does not pretend to. In Lua the store is a class table marked `-- @Store(...)`, and a store call inside the service's `-- @AllOrNothing` method joins the open transaction in the same way.

#[Service]
class LedgerService {
    public BehaviorContext $behaviors;
    #[Needs]
    private EntryStore $entries;

    #[OnStart]
    public function open(): void {
        $signal = new BehaviorSignal();
        $this->behaviors = Behaviors::create(LedgerSetup::class, ['partition' => 'ledger', 'signal' => $signal]);
    }

    #[AllOrNothing({"adapter":"ledger"})]
    public function settle(string $status): array {
        $open = $this->entries->findByStatus($status);
        $total = $this->entries->countByStatus($status);
        return ['open' => $open, 'total' => $total];
    }
}

<?php

#[Helper]
class LedgerAdapterHelper {
    private const TRANSACTION = 'transaction';
    private const ACTION = 'action';
    private const KIND = 'kind';
    public static array $commands = [];
    public static int $sequence = 0;

    public static function execute(array $command, mixed $execution): array|int {
        $rows = [['id' => 1, 'status' => 'open'], ['id' => 2, 'status' => 'settled']];
        if ($command['operation'] === self::TRANSACTION) {
            $entry = $command[self::ACTION];
            if (isset($command[self::TRANSACTION])) $entry = $command[self::ACTION] . ':' . $command[self::TRANSACTION];
            self::$commands[] = $entry;
            if ($command[self::ACTION] !== 'begin') return ['ok' => true];
            self::$sequence++;
            return [self::TRANSACTION => 't' . self::$sequence];
        }
        $query = $command['query'];
        $transaction = $command[self::TRANSACTION] ?? 'none';
        self::$commands[] = $query[self::KIND] . '@' . $transaction;
        $status = $query['where'][0]['value'];
        $matchingRows = [];
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            if ($row['status'] === $status) $matchingRows[] = $row;
        }
        if ($query[self::KIND] === 'count') return count($matchingRows);
        return $matchingRows;
    }

    public static function authorize(array $command, mixed $execution): bool {
        return true;
    }
}

open System.Collections.Generic
open System.Threading.Tasks

[<Helper>]
type LedgerAdapterHelper() =
    let transactionKey = "transaction"

    static member val commands = List<string>() with get
    static member val sequence = 0 with get, set

    interface BehaviorEntityAdapter with
        member this.execute(command: BehaviorJSON, execution: BehaviorExecution) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
            let identifier = if command.Has(transactionKey) then command.Get(transactionKey).Text else null
            if command.Get("operation").Text = transactionKey then
                this.Transaction(command.Get("action").Text, identifier)
            else
                this.Query(command.Get("query").Get("kind").Text, identifier)

    member private this.Transaction(action: string, identifier: string) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
        LedgerAdapterHelper.commands.Add(if isNull identifier then action else action + ":" + identifier)
        if action <> "begin" then
            Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.Parse("{\"ok\":true}"))
        else
            LedgerAdapterHelper.sequence <- LedgerAdapterHelper.sequence + 1
            let started = "t" + string LedgerAdapterHelper.sequence
            Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.Object(dict [ transactionKey, BehaviorJSON.From(started) ]))

    member private this.Query(kind: string, identifier: string) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
        let transaction = if isNull identifier then "none" else identifier
        LedgerAdapterHelper.commands.Add(kind + "@" + transaction)
        if kind = "count" then
            Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.From(1))
        else
            Task.FromResult(BehaviorJSON.Parse("[{\"id\":1,\"status\":\"open\"}]"))

files.code:
#[Helper]
class LedgerAdapterHelper
  TRANSACTION = "transaction"
  ACTION = "action"
  ROWS = [{ "id" => 1, "status" => "open" }, { "id" => 2, "status" => "settled" }].freeze

  @commands = []
  @sequence = 0

  class << self
    # @return [Array<String>]
    attr_reader :commands
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @param execution [Object]
  # @return [Object]
  def self.execute(command, execution)
    return transaction(command) if command["operation"] == TRANSACTION
    query = command["query"]
    @commands << "#{query["kind"]}@#{command.fetch(TRANSACTION, "none")}"
    status = query["where"][0]["value"]
    matching_rows = ROWS.select { |row| row["status"] == status }
    query["kind"] == "count" ? matching_rows.length : matching_rows
  end

  # @param command [Hash]
  # @return [Hash]
  def self.transaction(command)
    identifier = command[TRANSACTION]
    @commands << (identifier ? "#{command[ACTION]}:#{identifier}" : command[ACTION])
    return { "ok" => true } unless command[ACTION] == "begin"
    @sequence += 1
    { TRANSACTION => "t#{@sequence}" }
  end
end

files.code:
-- @Helper
---@class LedgerAdapterHelper
LedgerAdapterHelper = {
  ---@type string[]
  commands = {},
  ---@type integer
  sequence = 0,
  ---@type table[]
  ROWS = { { id = 1, status = "open" }, { id = 2, status = "settled" } },
}

---@param command table
---@param execution table
---@return any
function LedgerAdapterHelper:execute(command, execution)
  if command.operation == "transaction" then
    return self:_transaction(command)
  end
  local query = command.query
  self.commands[#self.commands + 1] = query.kind .. "@" .. (command.transaction or "none")
  local matching = {}
  for _, row in ipairs(self.ROWS) do
    if row.status == query.where[1].value then
      matching[#matching + 1] = row
    end
  end
  if query.kind == "count" then
    return #matching
  end
  return matching
end

---@param command table
---@return table
function LedgerAdapterHelper:_transaction(command)
  local identifier = command.transaction
  self.commands[#self.commands + 1] = identifier and (command.action .. ":" .. identifier) or command.action
  if command.action ~= "begin" then
    return { ok = true }
  end
  self.sequence = self.sequence + 1
  return { transaction = "t" .. self.sequence }
end

sections.heading: Caching: Yon
sections.summary: CacheSettings declares the policy on the type. Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache then do three different jobs with the same key. Cached is rejected on a controller route method, so the policy goes on a service that the controller calls.
sections.body: A cache keeps a copy of a result, so the next read does not need to run the method again. CacheSettings takes exactly name, ttlMs, maxBytes and maxEntries. Its name selects configuration.caches.catalog. ttlMs is how long an entry lives, in milliseconds. Cached runs a read method in these steps. It checks authorization. It builds a key of limited size from the parameters marked @CacheKey, or from every parameter when none is marked. It looks up the key. On a miss (the key is not in the cache), it runs the method. Then it stores the JSON result if the method succeeded. UpdateCache goes on a method that changes data. It always runs that method, and then it writes the result under the target's key. ClearCache also goes on a method that changes data. It deletes that key, but only after the method succeeds. UpdateCache and ClearCache both name a Cached method in the same class. Their parameters are matched by name to the key parameters of that method, so a parameter named sku fills the sku key. A missing name fails the build. So reading, updating and removing an entry all use one key. Cached is not allowed on a Yon route method, and this is on purpose. Check who the user is and check the request in the controller. Then call a service that can be cached. That is why CacheSettings is on the shared server/services/CatalogService, and the controller only calls it. A Cached route method fails the build. The service reaches its adapter through a behavior context that it owns. Yon builds a new set of instances for each call, so the context that OnStart opens is request-scoped. Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache methods are asynchronous in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, C#, F# and Dart. They are synchronous in Java, Groovy, Kotlin, PHP, Rust, Go, Ruby and Lua. A Lua service writes each annotation as a comment marker, such as `-- @Cached`. It keeps its context in `self.behaviors`, which OnStart opens with `Behaviors.create(CatalogSetup, { partition = "public-catalog", signal = BehaviorSignal.new() })`. Its Setup makes the adapter object with `Behaviors.construct(MemoryCacheHelper, { entries = {} })`. An adapter is a table whose methods Tachyon calls with `:`, such as `cache:get(key, execution)` (ADR 0085). Rust cannot assign a BehaviorContext through &self, so its managed provider opens the context in new(). Go has no constructor, so its provider opens the context in an OnStart method. C# calls a route method synchronously, so its controller waits for the pipeline once. The F# service opens the context in a `member val behaviors` initializer, which runs once for each new instance (an OnStart member works too), and its F# controller also waits once. GET /catalog returns first and repeat with the same read count, because the cache answered the second call. written holds the value that UpdateCache stored, without a call to find. refreshed holds a higher count, because ClearCache removed the entry. The in-memory adapter here lives only as long as its owner. An application that needs to reuse cached values across requests must choose a shared external cache.

#[Service]
#[CacheSettings({"name":"catalog","ttlMs":30000,"maxBytes":65536,"maxEntries":256})]
class CatalogService {
    public BehaviorContext $behaviors;
    public int $reads = 0;

    #[OnStart]
    public function open(): void {
        $signal = new BehaviorSignal();
        $this->behaviors = Behaviors::create(CatalogSetup::class, ['partition' => 'public-catalog', 'signal' => $signal]);
    }

    #[Cached]
    public function find(string $sku): array {
        $this->reads++;
        return $this->entry($sku, $this->reads);
    }

    #[UpdateCache({"method":"find"})]
    public function write(string $sku, int $reads): array { return $this->entry($sku, $reads); }

    #[ClearCache({"method":"find"})]
    public function invalidate(string $sku): array { return $this->entry($sku, $this->reads); }

    private function entry(string $sku, int $reads): array { return ['sku' => $sku, 'reads' => $reads]; }
}

            values.Remove(key) |> ignore

sections.heading: Caching: Tac
sections.summary: The same four annotations in the Tac service languages. CacheSettings is a modifier, so the service keeps its name, its client/services folder and its construction without arguments. The same annotations also work on the methods of an HTTPClient: the client class names its cache with CacheSettings, Cached keeps a read's answer, and ClearCache or UpdateCache on a write removes or replaces it (see the feature "Caching public reads").
sections.body: CacheSettings selects configuration.caches.catalog from a configuration that the service creates itself. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart and Ruby, and in Go, Rust, C#, F#, Kotlin and Java services that run as WebAssembly, the Setup can leave caches out: Tachyon then keeps the cache in the browser Cache API. It loads the saved entries into memory before the services start, answers reads from memory and writes changes in the background. It enforces ttlMs, maxBytes (per value) and maxEntries (the least recently used entry goes first). Where the Cache API is missing, such as a plain-http address on a local network, the cache lives in memory only and the console says so once. In a Safari private window, and in any WebKit web view whose storage is not kept on disk, the browser drops the saved entries when the page reloads. The cache then starts empty and the next call runs the method again. Store rows stay. The Go and Java Setups leave caches out, because Go and Java run only as WebAssembly; their Cached reads come from the same memory copy through a synchronous storage host. Rust, C# and Kotlin keep an adapter in the example, because a native companion (Android Kotlin, or a native Swift, Rust or C# app) has no page storage. Its native build stops when a Cached, UpdateCache or ClearCache method uses a cache that no Setup in the service names, for example with "Android Kotlin services need a cache adapter in their Setup" (ADR 0059). The other Tac languages still name an adapter in their Setup, as shown. It adds no rule of its own about name endings or folders. Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache behave exactly as they do in Yon. UpdateCache and ClearCache name find and map their arguments onto its key. JavaScript and TypeScript open the context in an async OnStart with the injected lifecycle signal. A native service owns its own BehaviorSignal. Its lifecycle hooks (such as OnStart) must be synchronous. So Swift, Kotlin, C#, Go and Java open the context in a synchronous OnStart. A Java Cached method returns Object, and the Behaviors.Context field stays inside the service. Rust builds it in new(), because a BehaviorContext field cannot be assigned through &self. The view reads the service's local state. Declaring a cache does not contact a server. The browser keeps only the values that Cached methods return, within the limits above. It runs only with public TAC_ configuration. Its bundle must never include the private credentials that a Yon cache adapter may hold. JS/TS bundle for every target, and Rust, Go, C#, Kotlin, Swift and Java reach the web, and every target that does not link them, as WebAssembly. A Swift Cached method is async and returns BehaviorJSON; on the web the page gets a promise, which settles at once when the method does not wait for the network. In a native app Tachyon runs the method to the end before the call returns. A Dart service owns its BehaviorSignal, as a native service does. It opens its context in a synchronous OnStart. The context is not a JSON value, so it stays inside Dart and the view never sees it. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup, CacheSettings and Cached in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Python has no tab either, because the build refuses CacheSettings and Cached in Python Tac code with TY1308. So Python Tac services cannot use caching yet. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup, CacheSettings and Cached in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Retries: Yon
sections.summary: Retry runs one method again after a bounded delay, which can grow exponentially. MaxAtOnce limits how many calls to the method run at the same time. Both are method annotations on a service, never on an HTTP verb endpoint.
sections.body: Retry takes maxRetries (from 1 to 8) and the optional delayMs, multiplier, maxDelayMs and jitterMs. jitterMs adds a small random delay. Every value is a literal in milliseconds, so you do not need a TimeUnit. Tachyon never retries a framework refusal, because a refusal is a decision, not a fault. These refusals are an invalid policy, a denied authorization, a disposed (closed) context and an expired deadline. Tachyon does retry an adapter fault or an error that the method itself raised. MaxAtOnce limits how many calls run at the same time. It takes limit (from 1 to 64) and policy. With block, a call waits for a free slot until the operation deadline. With reject, the call is refused at once. A call that retries keeps its slot for every attempt. So retries cannot add more load than the limit allows. PHP, Ruby and Lua serve one call at a time and cannot pause a call, so they accept only reject. A Lua service writes `-- @Retry({...})` and `-- @MaxAtOnce({...})` above its methods and opens its context in OnStart with `Behaviors.create(OrdersSetup, { partition = "orders", signal = BehaviorSignal.new() })` (ADR 0085). Stock Lua has no clock finer than one second, so Lua waits between attempts with the operating system's sleep command, which does not use the processor, and a Lua deadline fires at most about two seconds late, never early.
