<?php
#[Service]
class OrdersService {
    public BehaviorContext $behaviors;
    private const FIRST_WORKING_ATTEMPT = 3;
    private int $attempts = 0;

    #[OnStart]
    public function open(): void {
        $signal = new BehaviorSignal();
        $this->behaviors = Behaviors::create(OrdersSetup::class, ['partition' => 'orders', 'signal' => $signal]);
    }

    #[Retry({"maxRetries":3,"delayMs":10,"multiplier":2,"maxDelayMs":200,"jitterMs":5})]
    public function submit(string $id): array {
        $this->attempts++;
        $this->failFirstTwoAttempts();
        return $this->reportOf($id);
    }

    #[MaxAtOnce({"limit":2,"policy":"reject"})]
    public function report(string $id): array { return $this->reportOf($id); }

    private function reportOf(string $id): array { return ['id' => $id, 'attempts' => $this->attempts]; }

    private function failFirstTwoAttempts(): void {
        if ($this->attempts < self::FIRST_WORKING_ATTEMPT) throw new Exception('the payment gateway is unavailable');
    }
}

sections.heading: Retries: Tac
sections.summary: The same two annotations in every Tac service language, with the same bounds and the same refusals.
sections.body: A Tac service can reach its own context, so the policy is the same in both realms (ADR 0031). The annotation, its keys and its limits do not change between realms. Only the spelling in the host language changes. A Rust behavior method takes and returns BehaviorValue, which the page cannot pass, so the Rust service gives the page a plain submit(&mut self, id: String) method and an attempts field, and calls its Retry method send from there. In a Swift service on the web, the wait between two tries and the wait of a blocking MaxAtOnce happen inside the call, so the page waits for that time, as with a sleep in Go or C#. A Java service on the web waits the same way between two tries. A blocking MaxAtOnce in Java that finds no free slot fails with timeout at once, because nothing else on the page can free the slot while the call waits. A Ruby service runs one call at a time, so its MaxAtOnce policy is reject; the build refuses block in Ruby with TY1308. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Retry and MaxAtOnce in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Python has no tab either, because the build refuses Retry and MaxAtOnce in Python Tac code with TY1308. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup and Retry in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

    member this.submit(id: BehaviorJSON) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
        this.attempts <- this.attempts + 1
        this.FailFirstTwoAttempts()
        Task.FromResult(this.ReportOf(id))

    [<MaxAtOnce({"limit":2,"policy":"block"})>]
    member this.report(id: BehaviorJSON) : Task<BehaviorJSON> =
        Task.FromResult(this.ReportOf(id))

    member private this.ReportOf(id: BehaviorJSON) : BehaviorJSON =
        BehaviorJSON.Object(dict [ "id", id; "attempts", BehaviorJSON.From(this.attempts) ])

    member private this.FailFirstTwoAttempts() : unit =
        if this.attempts < firstWorkingAttempt then
            raise (InvalidOperationException("the checkout API is unavailable"))

  # @return [Integer]
  attr_reader :attempts

    @attempts = 0
    @behaviors = Behaviors.create(OrdersSetup, partition: "orders", signal: BehaviorSignal.new)
  end

  # @param id [String]
  # @return [Hash]
  #[Retry({"maxRetries":3,"delayMs":10,"multiplier":2,"maxDelayMs":200,"jitterMs":5})]
  def submit(id)
    @attempts += 1
    fail_first_two_attempts
    report_of(id)
  end

  # @param id [String]
  # @return [Hash]
  #[MaxAtOnce({"limit":2,"policy":"reject"})]
  def report(id)
    report_of(id)
  end

  private

  # @param id [String]
  # @return [Hash]
  def report_of(id)
    { "id" => id, "attempts" => @attempts }
  end

  # @return [void]
  def fail_first_two_attempts
    raise "the checkout API is unavailable" if @attempts < FIRST_WORKING_ATTEMPT
  end
end

sections.heading: Outgoing HTTP: Yon
sections.summary: A client (a contract that sends HTTP requests to another server) is marked with HTTPClient. It lives in server/remotes/<Name>Client.<ext>, and Needs injects it into a service. Like a Spring @HttpExchange interface, it has no implementation: each method is a signature with a request marker (GetRequest, PostRequest, PutRequest, PatchRequest or DeleteRequest), and Tachyon generates the request.

sections.body: HTTPClient marks a contract: a declaration with no implementation, like a Spring @HttpExchange interface. Tachyon generates each request, the constructor and the behavior context. Declare the client in the bodiless form of your language: an interface in Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C# and PHP, a Go interface, an abstract interface class in Dart, a trait in Rust, a type with only abstract members in F#, and a Protocol class whose methods end with ... in Python. JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby have no method without a body that takes annotations, so there the client is a class whose methods have empty bodies. A method body, a field or a constructor in a client is a build error (TY1308), and `ty migrate fix --write` rewrites a class client. Put logic that works on the answer into a service that needs the client. HTTPClient can take a path that comes before every method path, like HTTPClient("/api"). It can also take an object with path, adapter, cache and setup. The adapter is the code that really sends the request. Its default name is the class name without Client, in lowerCamel case. So CatalogClient uses the catalog adapter. The setup is the Setup class that registers the adapter. Its default name is the class name with Setup instead of Client, so CatalogClient uses CatalogSetup, and this example needs no option. GetRequest("/products") on a method sends a GET request to /products. PostRequest, PutRequest, PatchRequest and DeleteRequest send the other HTTP methods. A marker on each parameter says where its value goes. PathVariable fills a {name} part of the path. RequestParam("page") is a value for the query string, after ?. RequestHeader("X-Tenant") is a value for a request header. RequestBody is the JSON body of the request. Tachyon builds the request from the arguments. The adapter holds the base origin (the scheme, host and port) and sends the request. The path is relative to that origin. Tachyon refuses headers that the transport controls. GET and HEAD have no body. The answer is JSON of limited size. RestClient makes the same adapter call from normal code, without an annotation. Use it when you know the shape of the request only at call time. RestClient is a method of the behavior context. In JavaScript, `this.behaviors.restClient("catalog").get("/products").query({ page: 1 }).header("X-Tenant", "acme").retrieve()` sends GET /products?page=1 through the catalog adapter. The builder also has post, put, patch, delete, head and options, and body sets the JSON body. GET and HEAD refuse a body. Python, Ruby and Rust write `rest_client`, and Go writes `RestClient`, which also returns an error. In Rust and Go, query takes one name and one value. retrieve sends the call with the same limits as an HTTPClient method. See the [routing annotation glossary](/docs/routing-annotations) for each name. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Lua Yon code with TY1308: Lua gets gateway clients in a later step (ADR 0085).

sections.heading: Outgoing HTTP: Tac
sections.summary: In the browser, HTTPClient is the auto-managed transport. A read is sent no-store, so it is always fresh; to keep a read, put CacheSettings on the client and Cached on the read, as CatalogClient does (see the feature "Caching public reads"). HTTPClient takes no cache option: the build refuses `{"cache": ...}` and names CacheSettings and Cached (ADR 0087). A Tac HTTPClient must declare at least one request method, such as GetRequest. Like a Spring @HttpExchange interface, a client has no implementation: JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby write a class whose methods have empty bodies. Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go and Dart write the client in their bodiless form (a protocol, an interface, an F# type with only abstract members, a trait, a Go interface or an abstract interface class). The client lives in client/remotes. Tachyon generates the client and its behavior context from the Setup with the same stem (CatalogClient uses CatalogSetup), whose HTTP adapter sends the request. A JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, C# or Ruby service injects the client with Needs; in Rust the field is `#[Needs] catalog_client: std::sync::Arc<CatalogClient>`, in Go `// @Needs` stands above `catalogClient *CatalogClient`, in Kotlin `@Needs` stands above `private val catalog: CatalogClient`, in Swift above `private let catalog: CatalogClient`, in Java above `private final CatalogClient catalog;`, in C# `[Needs]` stands above `private readonly CatalogClient _catalog;`, and in Ruby `#[Needs]` stands above `attr_reader :catalog_client`, with `# @return [CatalogClient]` between them. An F# service builds the client: CatalogClient(). A client with a method body, a field or another role, such as a service that is also an HTTPClient, fails with TY1308. A request to another origin needs its host in `tac.outgoing.hosts`: the build checks request URLs, and the page's `connect-src` lets the browser reach only these hosts. In Dart, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java and Ruby, when the Setup has no matching HTTP adapter, the browser sends the request to the same origin (ADR 0090). A C++ client has no Setup, so the browser always sends its request to the same origin (ADR 0099). See "Calling the server from a page".

sections.heading: Gateways: Yon
sections.summary: Gateway declares a method that another language answers. Declare it on an HTTPClient contract as a signature. In JavaScript and TypeScript its answer is Promise<BehaviorJsonValue | void>, because an empty body returns nothing to the type checker. It names a class in another Yon language or a program under server/helpers.
sections.body: Choose one language for GET /report. Each implementation returns {"summary":{"period":"2026-Q3","total":42,...},"forecast":{"months":2,"growth":[1.5,1.5]}}. The controller returns a `Report` model, and each of its two fields holds a gateway result. A gateway is a method that calls code written in another language. `ReportClient` declares two gateways. `summarize` names the Python class `server/services/ReportService.py`. The Python tab names the JavaScript class `server/services/ReportService.js` instead, because a gateway never calls the caller's own language. The TypeScript tab names the Go class `server/services/ReportService.go` to show a Go target. The Go tab holds that class. Tachyon calls its exported method `Summarize`. `forecast` names the program `python3 server/helpers/forecast.py`. This program reads `{"method": "forecast", "arguments": [2]}` on stdin (standard input). It writes only the JSON result on stdout (standard output). So the Python tab also holds two more things: the class that most of the other languages call, and the program that every language calls. The arguments and results use the JSON value type of each language. JavaScript and Python use none. TypeScript uses `BehaviorJsonValue`. PHP uses `mixed` or no type. Ruby uses no type. Java uses `Object`. Kotlin uses `Any?`. C# and F# use `BehaviorJSON`. Rust uses `BehaviorValue` and `BehaviorResult<BehaviorValue>`. Dart uses `Object?` and `Future<Object?>`. Go uses `BehaviorValue` and `(BehaviorValue, error)`. The C#, F# and Go methods are named `Summarize`, so their options add `"method":"summarize"`. A failure is a `BehaviorError`. Its code is `invalid`, `timeout`, `capacity` or `adapter`, and its message is always `Gateway call failed.`. Gateway exists only in Yon. The full rules are in the Yon guide, in the section Calling a method in another language. A gateway program gets only the platform variables (such as PATH) and the variables that server.environment in server/application.json lists (ADR 0026). Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Gateway in Lua Yon code with TY1308: Lua gets gateway clients in a later step (ADR 0085).

sections.heading: Configuration binding: Yon
sections.summary: One Setup role class carries the whole policy. Settings binds the YON_CATALOG_ prefix, and the Setup class's own fields are the settings, with @Min and @Max on a field. WhenProfile selects the active environment. WhenSetting turns the bean on or off based on a bound property. Setting binds a single canonical yon. path with a literal default. Its class, Endpoint, is a model in `server/models/` (ADR 0092); the Rust controller imports it with `use crate::models::{Endpoint, Settings}`. Every YON_CATALOG_ name in the snapshot must be declared. WhenProfile and WhenSetting are both decided before configure runs. The private snapshot stays private. Secrets live in .env. server/application.json holds placeholders and safe defaults. The controller returns selected fields that are not secret, never the resolved configuration.
sections.body:
Settings takes the prefix and, if you need it, "names":{"pageSize":"PAGE_LIMIT"}, which renames one variable. By default the name after the prefix is the field name in capital letters with underscores, so pageSize reads YON_CATALOG_PAGE_SIZE. With that option it reads YON_CATALOG_PAGE_LIMIT. Only Rust and Go use "defaults":{"field":value}, as the Go tab shows (ADR 0055).

The Lua tab binds the same Settings policy. Lua cannot write the Endpoint model yet: a Lua model that carries Setting stops the build with TY1310 (ADR 0092). So the Lua controller reads the profile from the application snapshot, `application.yon.active.profile`.

Settings reads server/application.json and .env. It does not read the environment of ty itself. A handler gets an outside variable, such as HOME, only when server.environment in server/application.json lists its name (ADR 0026).

    public function getSettings(): Settings {
        $application = json_decode(getenv('YON_APPLICATION_JSON'), true, 512, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        $catalog = Behaviors::properties(CatalogSetup::class, $application);
        $endpoint = Behaviors::values(Endpoint::class, $application);
        $profile = $endpoint['profile'];
        $signal = new BehaviorSignal();
        $context = Behaviors::create(CatalogSetup::class, [
            'partition' => 'public-catalog',
            'signal' => $signal,
            'profiles' => [$profile],
            'properties' => $application,
        ]);
        $context->dispose();
        $signal->abort();
        return new Settings($profile, $catalog['pageSize']);
    }
}

sections.heading: Configuration binding: Tac
sections.summary: Tac binds only values that are explicitly public. Its source is the tac member of client/manifest.json. This is the web app manifest that the build publishes at /manifest.webmanifest. server/application.json and .env belong to Yon and never reach Tac. So Settings uses a TAC_ prefix, Setting uses tac. paths and WhenSetting names a TAC_ property. A private Yon secret cannot be bound here at all. Browser services load the published manifest through an injected HTTPClient. Native services bind a public snapshot that is supplied explicitly. A native service file keeps its service type first. The class that Setting reads is a model in `client/models/` (ADR 0092), so a service reaches it like any model: C# and F# open `Models`, Rust uses `crate::models::PublicValues` and Dart imports `models/PublicValues.dart`. Every key under TAC_CATALOG_ must be a field of the Settings class, including title. Setting demonstrates binding that same title individually; it does not exempt the key from prefix validation. Every language passes the full public snapshot to both binders.
sections.body: Python and Lua have no tab here, because a browser service loads the manifest through an HTTPClient, and the build refuses HTTPClient in Python and Lua Tac code with TY1308. Lua also refuses Setup and Settings with TY1308. Python has no behavior runtime yet: it cannot await Behaviors.create, because Python Tac refuses async methods with TY1605. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup and Setting in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Validation: Yon
sections.summary: `Checked` declares a field schema on a plain type. That type is a model: a data class in its own file, `server/models/OrderInput.<ext>` (ADR 0092). Discovery composes it into the same unit as the method that names it (ADR 0044). A Rust model is `pub`, and the Rust service imports it with `use crate::models::OrderInput`. Check sits on one parameter and checks it against that schema before the annotated method body runs. It returns a checked copy; it does not construct the type. The option shapes are fixed. Checked(), Required() and NotEmpty() accept no arguments. Length takes exactly {"min","max"}. In JavaScript, TypeScript and Python, Check takes no arguments: the parameter's type names the Checked class (a JSDoc @param type in JavaScript). The other languages keep the JSON parameter type and name the class in Check: Check(OrderInput.class) in Java, Check(OrderInput::class) in Kotlin and PHP, Check(typeof(OrderInput)) in C#, and Check(OrderInput) in Dart, Rust and Go. The controller reads the body with FromBody as a plain JSON value (any in TypeScript and Go, dict in Python, array in PHP, Object in Java, Any? in Kotlin, BehaviorJSON in C#, Object? in Dart, Json in Rust) and passes it to the service. Min and Max take a bare finite number, not an object. Length, Min and Max ignore a missing or null value, so only Required makes a bound required. Choose one language below for POST /orders. Each one rejects a blank name, a level above 9 and a missing level. Otherwise it answers 200 with the checked payload. Unknown fields such as sku stay in the payload after validation. This does not make it safe to assign all of them to an object at once.
sections.body: Lua has no tab here. The Checked model must live in server/models (ADR 0092), and a Lua model that carries a schema stops the build with TY1310, so a Lua class cannot use Check yet.

sections.heading: Validation: Tac
sections.summary: The same seven markers work in Tac, on a service instead of a controller. The data transfer object (DTO) that `Check` names is a model: a data class in its own file, `client/models/OrderInput.<ext>` (ADR 0092). Discovery composes its rules into the service that it protects (ADR 0044), and the model itself compiles once, without its markers. A service reaches it the way the language reaches any model: C# and F# open `Models`, Rust uses `crate::models::OrderInput`, Kotlin imports `models.OrderInput` and Dart imports `models/OrderInput.dart`; Swift, Go and Ruby need no import. A Swift model is a struct, and a Rust model and its fields are `pub`. JavaScript, TypeScript and Dart keep Service without an import, as their Yon services do. The compiled languages mark the service with Service too: the build refuses a service in client/services without its marker with TY1363. Swift and C# take checked parameters as BehaviorJSON, Rust and Go take them as BehaviorValue, and Java takes them as Object, as its Yon service does; Check names the class, as in Yon. Tac validation protects only the user experience (UX). It is not authorization, so Yon must validate the same payload again.

Python has no tab either: Python Tac does not read a Checked model from client/models yet, so the build stops a Python Check with TY1308. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Check in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Lifecycle and events: Yon
sections.summary: One route, two shared services and a controller. CheckoutService publishes through the injected applicationEventPublisher during OnStart and releases in OnStop. AuditService holds the listeners. EventPublisher is removed (ADR 0031), and any use of it fails the build. So publishing is always a call on that field. Needs binds a Yon resource by the field's own name, which is the name Spring uses: dataSource, redisTemplate and applicationEventPublisher in every Yon language. Python and Rust write the field name in snake_case, so they bind the publisher by type. F# takes the publisher as a primary constructor parameter, so it binds it by type too. A listener takes exactly one parameter, and the model type of that parameter is the event it hears (ADR 0055). Order runs the listeners of one event from the lowest value first. condition skips delivery without an error. When a listener returns a model, Tachyon publishes that model as its own event, so the SettledOrder that settle returns reaches the next listener. InBackground appears only in JavaScript, TypeScript and Python. PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua have no asynchronous method here, and they reject it at compile time. GET /lifecycle answers with the recorded log and the final total. Ruby creates its publisher with ApplicationEventPublisher.new and names each listener's model in a YARD tag, # @param order [PlacedOrder]. Lua writes each hook as a comment marker above its method, such as `-- @OnStart` or `-- @OnEvent({"id":"audit-log"})`, names the listener's model in a LuaCATS tag, `---@param order PlacedOrder`, and publishes a model table, `setmetatable({ status = "paid", total = 25 }, PlacedOrder)`, through its `application_event_publisher = nil` field, which Tachyon binds by that name (ADR 0085). Lua has no asynchronous methods, so InBackground stops the build there too. A Lua model marked `-- @Topic` is a topic like in the other languages.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and events: Tac
sections.summary: The same two roles in the browser and on native hosts, used by one component view. A browser resource is autowired by the field's name, which is the name Spring uses: view, lifecycle, resourceLoader, taskScheduler and applicationEventPublisher. An uninitialised applicationEventPublisher field is already that resource, so its annotation is optional. Native services have no browser resources. The prelude constructs a member of type ApplicationEventPublisher. An F# service takes its ApplicationEventPublisher as a primary constructor parameter, and Tachyon passes one when it creates the service. A Needs property, `[<Needs>] member val Publisher : ApplicationEventPublisher = Unchecked.defaultof<ApplicationEventPublisher> with get, set`, receives it the same way. A listener takes one model parameter, and the type of that model is the event that it hears. Write one method for each model; there is no list of events. The listener has the same condition, id, replay and Order options as in Yon. When a listener returns a model, Tachyon publishes the returned model as a new event, as settle does with SettledOrder; a returned `{event, value}` record is not read (ADR 0055). InBackground is allowed in every Tac language, because it delays delivery and does not need an asynchronous method. Native hooks and listeners stay synchronous. JavaScript and TypeScript bundle for the web. Swift builds for macOS, Kotlin for Android, C# for Windows and Rust for desktop Linux. A Rust or C# service with no browser script reaches the web, and every native target that does not link it, as WebAssembly, and a Go, Java or F# service always runs that way. A Java service declares an uninitialised ApplicationEventPublisher field (Needs is optional), and its listeners take one model from client/models. On the web, WebAssembly listeners share the page event bus with browser services, including conditions, Order, InBackground microtasks, retained replay and cleanup. Publications from any service reach its own listeners and other services exactly once. A Dart service is a browser service compiled to WebAssembly (WasmGC). Its only resource is the ApplicationEventPublisher that it declares with Needs. This publisher publishes through the page runtime, so Dart and JavaScript listeners receive the same events. Its lifecycle and listener methods are public and take JSON values, because the runtime calls them by name across the bridge. A Lua service (ADR 0085) writes each hook as a comment marker, such as `-- @OnStart` or `-- @OnEvent`, above its method. Its field `application_event_publisher = nil` is that resource, autowired by its name, and an event is a model table such as `setmetatable({ total = 25 }, PlacedOrder)`. A Python service (ADR 0093) writes `@on_start`, `@on_stop` and `@on_event` above synchronous methods, and an `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher` field is that resource. Its events are dataclass models from client/models. A C++ service (ADR 0099) writes `[[OnStart]]`, `[[OnStop]]`, `[[OnEvent]]`, `[[Order(n)]]` and `[[InBackground]]` before its methods, and its `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` field is that resource. Its hooks and listeners may be private; its events are structs from client/models.

sections.heading: Mapping: Yon
sections.summary: Converter signatures generate mappings from a literal JSON field plan or from declared source and target model types. Explicit fields override inferred same-named model fields.
sections.body:
GET /catalog returns {"summary":{"productId":7,"title":"Anvil","absent":null,"kind":"product"}}. Converter is the role. A converter copies values from its input into a new output shape. It is a <Name>Converter type in server/converters. A controller or service asks for it with Needs, like a MapStruct mapper that Spring injects: a Needs field, a constructor parameter in F#, or Needs above an attr_reader in Ruby. In JavaScript and Ruby the field name names the provider (productConverter, product_converter). Lua names it in the type comment above the field, `---@type ProductConverter`. A converter needs no behavior context and no Setup, because a mapping reads only its argument, so Tachyon builds it with no constructor argument. Convert describes the whole method. Each entry names its target (the output field). Each entry takes either a source path of at most eight names joined by dots, or a literal constant. The method takes exactly one parameter, the value it converts, and the plan reads it. The parameter and the result keep the language's JSON value type. A source that is missing maps to null, exactly as in MapStruct. An input field that no entry names is dropped, so extra never reaches the output. A Convert has at most 32 entries. Options that are not one strict JSON object fail the build, and a note after the closing bracket is not part of the options. Writing the same target twice fails the build.

A Converter is a contract, like a MapStruct @Mapper interface: it has no implementation, and Tachyon generates each mapping. It is an interface in Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, PHP and Go, and an interface of `abstract` members in F#. It is a trait in Rust, an abstract interface class in Dart and a Protocol class in Python. Python writes the stub (the empty body) as an Ellipsis. JavaScript, Ruby and Lua have no method without a body. TypeScript cannot put a decorator on an abstract member. So these four keep an empty body. JavaScript and TypeScript declare the answer as Promise<BehaviorJsonObject | void> for the same reason. In every case, the compiler writes the class and each method, and the class has no constructor argument. So the source declares nothing else. A method body, a field, a constructor, or a class where the language has a contract form fails the build with TY1308 ("A Converter has no implementation: Tachyon generates each mapping."). `ty migrate fix --write` rewrites a class converter as a contract. `ty migrate` reports code that still builds a converter with a context, such as `new ProductConverter(context)` or `Behaviors.construct(ProductConverter, ...)`: remove it and ask for the converter with Needs.

Typed model signatures may omit Convert: Tachyon infers exact same-named target fields from models in the realm models folder and projects nested models and lists. Explicit Convert fields override their named targets; missing or incompatible target fields fail the build. JavaScript uses JSDoc parameter, return and typedef model types. JSON-value signatures keep the complete literal field plan shown here. The next sections show converters with typed models in every language, Lua included.

sections.heading: Typed model mapping: Yon
sections.summary: Model types supply same-named fields. Convert overrides only the targets it names.
sections.body:
GET /catalog returns {"id":7,"name":"Anvil","detail":{"name":"detail"},"items":[{"name":"detail"}],"kind":"product"}. The controller asks for ProductConverter with Needs. The source Product holds secret fields; the target Summary and ShortDetail do not, so those fields are dropped even inside the list. The explicit kind constant overrides that target. Every other target comes from the model signatures.

When source and target fields already match, omit Convert entirely. Missing or incompatible target fields fail the build and name the field that needs an explicit entry. One method maps one model: a parameter or result that is a list, a map, a tuple or two models fails the build. Model-valued fields and lists inside a model are projected recursively. A JSON-value signature still needs its literal field plan.

Lua declares its signatures with LuaCATS comments and asks for its provider with -- @Needs. Converter methods have empty bodies; the compiler generates each projection.

sections.heading: Mapping: Tac
sections.summary: Converter signatures generate mappings from a literal JSON field plan or from declared source and target model types. Explicit fields override inferred same-named model fields.
sections.body:
Select a language tab and copy the page, the component view and the two role files. JavaScript, TypeScript and Dart bundle for the web. Go, F#, Java, Ruby and Lua bundle for the web as WebAssembly. Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust stage their native hosts. The view reads {catalog.title} from the service. A view reads its services and the built-in `data` and `page` roots, nothing else (ADR 0036). The browser services ask for the converter with Needs: a Needs field, a `#[Needs]` `attr_reader` in Ruby, a `-- @Needs` field in Lua, or a constructor parameter in F#. A converter needs no behavior context and no Setup, so Tachyon builds it and the service only maps. The Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services carry the Service marker, like every class in client/services (TY1363), and only show the title. The compiler finds the annotated converter file and adds it to the same compile unit. Lua writes the converter as a table with an empty method under `-- @Converter` and `-- @Convert(...)`. Python has no tab here, because a Python service cannot ask for a converter yet: a Python Needs field must name a Python service or Helper, and the build stops with TY1605.

The annotation and its options are the same as in Yon. The converter is the same contract too, with a protocol in Swift, and a method body fails the build with TY1308. The previous section runs them in a full example. Only the realm is different. The role folder is client/converters (ADR 0031). A mapping reaches no adapter and needs no authorization, because it reads only the argument that it was given. It is the only data annotation that cannot leave the running process. Tac stays client-rendered. It uses only public TAC_ configuration, never private Yon credentials.

Typed model signatures may omit Convert: Tachyon infers exact same-named target fields from models in the realm models folder and projects nested models and lists. Explicit Convert fields override their named targets; missing or incompatible target fields fail the build. JavaScript uses JSDoc parameter, return and typedef model types. JSON-value signatures keep the complete literal field plan shown here. In the page, a converter runs in JavaScript, in TypeScript and in the WebAssembly of each compiled service language. The next section shows converters with typed models. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Converter in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Typed model mapping: Tac
sections.summary: A service injects the converter and uses typed models for both implicit copying and public projection.
sections.body:
Click Map to see the same Summary in every language: `product 7: Anvil, detail, 1`. The injected ProductConverter first copies Product without a Convert marker, then projects Summary using its signatures and the explicit kind override. The target models omit the secret fields in nested objects and lists, so no secret reaches the Summary.

Models belong to client/models and the converter to client/converters. A mapping needs no Setup or external adapter: it reads only its argument. Every tab runs in the page, as JavaScript or as WebAssembly. The JavaScript signatures use JSDoc types and the TypeScript signatures use model interfaces. Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F#, Rust, Go and Dart write the converter in their bodiless form: a protocol, an interface, an F# type with only abstract members, a trait, a Go interface or an abstract interface class. Ruby writes a class with empty methods. Lua uses LuaCATS signatures, a -- @Converter table with empty methods and a -- @Needs field. The compiler supplies the converter and restores typed nested models after projection. Each service asks for the converter with Needs. F# takes it as a primary constructor parameter, and the Rust service derives Default, so Tachyon can create it and fill the Needs field.

Python has no tab here, because a Python service cannot ask for a converter yet: a Python Needs field must name a Python service or Helper, and the build stops with TY1605. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Converter in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099).

sections.heading: Scheduling: Yon
sections.summary: Schedule declares how often a worker runs, next to the code that runs, instead of in .tachyonrc. The worker gets the same supervisor, deadlines and bounds that a controller already gets.
sections.body: A worker under server/workers is a Handler class that the runtime calls with POST on a timer. Like a Spring @Scheduled method, POST takes no parameter and returns nothing. Schedule takes fixedDelaySeconds (from 1 to 86400) and the optional initialDelaySeconds (from 0 to 86400). By default, initialDelaySeconds is one full interval. A .tachyonrc worker has always worked this way. There is no cron field. A cron expression is a calendar schedule written as text. It needs a parser and a time zone policy, and the runtime has neither. A limited worker really needs only a fixed delay. A source declares its cadence (how often it runs) in exactly one place: the annotation or .tachyonrc. Declaring both fails with TY1502. The annotation is removed before the worker compiles. So a worker that declares nothing else gets no extra runtime code at all. Tac has no equivalent. A browser page has no supervisor (a process that runs and watches other work) to run a separate timer. So this annotation exists in only one realm. In Lua the marker is a comment line, `-- @Schedule({...})`, above the Handler table.

sections.heading: Test units: Yon
sections.summary: A Test unit is a source file under server/tests with one Test class. It composes the realm it tests. The compiler writes the context lifecycle and the case driver. ty test invokes it through the same supervisor that serves a route. The controller calls `total`, so it stays public: a call from a test alone does not keep a member public (TY1333).
sections.body:
Select a language tab and copy the files. A test unit is a server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> file with Test on exactly one class. A test case is any method whose name begins with test. This is a naming rule, not an annotation on each method. A case checks its result with `Assert.equals`, `Assert.isTrue` or `Assert.throws` (JUnit names; Java and Groovy write `Assert.throwsError`, because `throws` is a reserved word there, Go writes `Assert.Equals`, Ruby `Assert.is_true` and PHP `Assert::equals`), and `ValueSource` runs one case for each listed input; see Assert and ValueSource in Test units. Rust has no reflection (a way for code to inspect itself while it runs) that could find an annotated method. Also, a controller route method already starts its name with its verb, which is a similar rule.

Test names the Setup that the context is built from. It also names the partition that the context is built in. UseProfiles and TestSettings go on the same class. They reach the context in the same way as the profiles and properties of a running server. FreshStart is accepted, but its behavior is already the default. The compiler starts a context before every case and disposes of it afterwards. In F#, the case reads it as `this.behaviors`, and the TestSetup declares `static member configure`, as in C#. Run the units with ty test. It runs every unit and reports one line for each case. If any case fails, it exits with a non-zero code at the end.

When a class has an annotation, it needs a test unit. ty preview does not start while any public method of an annotated class was not called by a test* case. Writing the name of the method in a test is not enough, and a call on a Fake does not count. ty test --coverage fails on the same report. Methods that the compiler writes do not need a test. A derived query, a declared HTTP request method and a Convert contain no logic that a person wrote. TAC_ALLOW_UNTESTED=1 lets one run skip the check. ty start never checks.

Fake declares a field that the test assigns. In JavaScript and TypeScript, this.construct(Role) builds the role under test. It uses those fakes (test doubles) in place of its Needs collaborators (the classes that its Needs fields point to). Ruby also gets construct(Role), because Ruby can set a field from outside the class, and Lua gets `self:construct(Role)` (ADR 0085). Java and Groovy get `construct(Role.class)`, Kotlin `construct(Role::class)`, C# `construct<Role>()` and Dart `construct<Role>(Role)`. The role can be a service or a controller: a unit in server/tests can use every controller in server/controllers, SocketRoute controllers and error handlers included, and the error classes in server/errors. It calls a controller method directly, without HTTP. The driver clears every Fake before each case: it becomes null, nil, None or undefined, a number becomes zero and a boolean false. In C# it becomes `default`, and in Go the zero value of its type. A Kotlin or Dart Fake is nullable or has a primitive type, because a `lateinit var` or a `late` field has no empty value and the build refuses it. A Rust case reads the unit through `&self`, so a Rust Fake that a case assigns is a `RefCell` or a `Cell`, and the driver resets it to its `Default`, `None` for an `Option`. F# runs every case on a new instance, so its Fakes start empty too. In F#, a Fake is a settable property, `[<Fake>] member val Names : NameService = Unchecked.defaultof<NameService> with get, set`, and the case builds the role with its Needs properties set: `StockService(Names = this.Names)`. In PHP, a Fake is a typed property with no value, `#[Fake] public CatalogCounterHelper $catalogCounterHelper;`. The driver unsets it before every case, and the case passes it to the constructor that Needs gives the role: `new CatalogService($this->catalogCounterHelper)`. Python, PHP, F#, Go and Rust units have no construct helper (a Go or Rust Tac unit has one), so they pass the Fakes to the role's own constructor or test the logic directly, not through the container. The container is the part of the framework that creates and injects roles.

The test class and its TestSetup live in separate files in the same tests/ folder. The Setup class that Test names, for example Test(CatalogTestSetup), selects the sibling file (the file next to it) by exact class name and source extension. The compiler checks both files that you wrote before it builds the test program. The test configuration is never included in a production browser or server bundle. Tachyon does not load sibling test setups that are not used. You may still select a production Setup yourself instead.

sections.heading: Test units: Tac
sections.summary: The same unit in the client realm. client/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> composes the Tac roles beside it and is lowered for the browser. It runs in the host that its language compiles to: a JavaScript runtime, or one binary, jar or assembly. The page reads `title` and `double`, so they stay public. A call from a test alone does not keep a member public (TY1333).
sections.body:
A Tac unit cannot use the Yon route plan. Its roles are Tac roles, and its context is a Tac context. So it has its own runner. ty test finds the units of both realms in one run and reports them together.

Everything that Test accepts is the same as in Yon: the same Setup, the same partition, and the same UseProfiles and TestSettings. Only the host is different. Lua accepts UseProfiles, but the build refuses TestSettings and FreshStart in Lua Tac code with TY1308. A case in every Tac test language except Python checks its result with `Assert` and can list its inputs with `ValueSource`, as in Yon; see Assert and ValueSource in Test units. A Python Tac unit checks with `Assert` too, but it refuses `ValueSource` with TY1308. Fake also works as in Yon: the Test or TestSetup class marks a field with Fake, the test assigns a stand-in to it, and every role that asks for that type receives the stand-in. Lua refuses Fake with TY1308. C++ units compile with clang++ and run as a binary. Their Test names a TestSetup class, `[[ValueSource([1, 2])]]` runs a case once for each input, and a `[[Fake]]` field reaches the service that `construct<CatalogService>()` makes. A static `configure()` method of the TestSetup returns `BehaviorAdapters`, whose `http` answers the requests of each HTTP client. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses UseProfiles in C++ Tac code with TY1308 (ADR 0099); first app step 5 shows a C++ unit.

JavaScript and TypeScript run under Bun, or under Node for plain modules. Dart runs on the Dart VM (virtual machine). The reason is that a Dart service is plain Dart until its browser build adds the bridge. Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, F# and Rust each compile to one build output that prints its report. These outputs are a binary, a jar, a folder of Java classes, and a .NET project built the way a C# controller is; an F# unit's project also holds the C# behavior runtime in a library next to the F# code. Go runs with go run, outside the browser, against the same service runtime as its WebAssembly module. Ruby runs under CRuby, with the same prelude that its mruby web runtime loads. Lua runs under the `lua` program, with the same prelude that its Lua web runtime loads. `self:construct(CatalogService)` builds the service with its own copy of its fields. Python runs under `python3`, outside the browser, and needs no Pyodide files. It writes Test, TestSetup and UseProfiles with their capital names, such as `@Test(CatalogTestSetup, {"partition":"tests"})`, as a Python Yon unit does. The Tac driver uses no Yon transport type. Every behavior runtime already has a JSON serializer with size limits. So the driver answers with its own encoded report, and the runner reads that report.

A Tac service is the entry of its realm (ADR 0030). The file that you write for it holds one class and its imports, like every other annotated file (ADR 0044). A test unit has exactly one Test class.

The test class and its TestSetup live in separate files in the same tests/ folder. The Setup class that Test names, for example Test(CatalogTestSetup), selects the sibling file by exact class name and source extension. The compiler checks both files that you wrote before it builds the test program. The test configuration is never included in a production browser or server bundle. Tachyon does not load sibling test setups that are not used. You may still select a production Setup yourself instead.

sections.heading: What each realm refuses
sections.body:
Every annotation above appears in each language that accepts it. The missing examples are not mistakes. The compiler rejects these combinations before anything runs, and its error message says why.

A native Tac service is a Swift, Kotlin, C# or Rust service that Tachyon links into a native companion. It carries the Service marker like every class in client/services (TY1363). It accepts Service, Lifetime, NeedsAll, Needs, Named, the data and behavior annotations, Setup, CacheSettings, Entity, Table, Store, Checked, Settings, WhenProfile, WhenSetting and HTTPClient. A native companion has no page storage and no page transport, so its Setup names every cache and entity adapter that the service uses, and the native build stops when one is missing (ADR 0059). Its HTTPClient sends requests through the HTTP adapter that its Setup names. A native Rust service injects a Helper with Needs, and a native C# service builds one with `new`; Swift and Kotlin refuse Helper with TY1308. A linked native service cannot use page-only APIs such as PreferenceStrings and DocumentTitle. It receives the native WindowControls and FilePicker providers instead (ADR 0089; see Native services). StreamRequest and SocketRequest clients are written in JavaScript, TypeScript or Go; the page's JavaScript holds the connection for a Go service. A client in any other Tac language fails with TY1308 at the client file, and the message names its language, for example `@StreamRequest is not available in Java Tac code`, or `[<SocketRequest>] is not available in F# Tac code` in F#.

Lua, Python and C++ are Tac service languages with limits. This table lists what each one refuses.

| Language | What the build refuses in Tac code |
| --- | --- |
| Lua (ADR 0085) | TY1308 for the behavior annotations (Setup, Settings, Setting, WhenProfile, WhenSetting, CacheSettings, Cached, ClearCache, UpdateCache, Retry, MaxAtOnce, AllOrNothing, Checked, Check and the field checks), Entity, Store, Query, HTTPClient and its request annotations, LocalState, SessionState, Helper, Fake, TestSettings and FreshStart. Lua has no WindowControls. TY2015 for a Needs field whose type is another service. It accepts Service, Lifetime, Needs, Named, NeedsAll, OnStart, OnStop, OnEvent, Order, InBackground, Topic, Converter, Convert, Test, TestSetup, UseProfiles and ValueSource. |
| Python (ADR 0093) | TY1605 for `async def` methods, streams and the browser API resources. TY1308 for Store, Query, HTTPClient and its request annotations, ValueSource, LocalState, SessionState, the caching annotations, PageDefaults, Retry, MaxAtOnce and AllOrNothing. A Python Check cannot read a Checked model from client/models yet (TY1308), and a Python Needs field cannot name a Converter yet (TY1605). Python accepts Service, Lifetime, Needs, Named, NeedsAll, Helper, synchronous OnStart, OnStop and OnEvent with their options, ApplicationEventPublisher, Topic, Test, TestSetup and UseProfiles. |
| C++ (ADR 0099) | TY1308 for every annotation that C++ does not reach yet, such as Setup, the behavior annotations, Entity, Store, Query, LocalState, SessionState, Topic, Helper, Converter, Lifetime, Named and NeedsAll. TY1372 for a `Needs` field that names anything but a C++ service or a C++ HTTPClient, so C++ has no browser APIs yet. TY1371 for a file that is not one header-only class, and for a lowercase marker such as `[[service]]`. C++ accepts Service, Needs, OnStart, OnStop, OnEvent, Order, InBackground, ApplicationEventPublisher, HTTPClient with its request annotations, Test, TestSetup, Fake and ValueSource. |

Other languages refuse fewer annotations. Swift, Kotlin, Go, Ruby and Java refuse Helper with TY1308. A Java service cannot ask for another service with Needs, and it cannot use Named; the build stops both with TY1405. A Ruby service cannot ask for another service with Needs either; the build stops it with TY2015 (ADR 0054).

The build also checks where each annotation is written (ADR 0056). It refuses an annotation on the wrong kind of member, such as Cached on a field. It refuses arguments on an annotation that takes none, such as Service, and a missing argument list on one that needs it, such as Test or Named. It refuses an annotation that needs an instance method, such as a route, a listener or Cached, on a static method, the same annotation twice on one member, and two annotations that clash, such as LocalState with SessionState, or Cached with ClearCache. It refuses an annotation without its partner: Order or InBackground without OnEvent, Named without Needs, Id outside an Entity class, and Fake or ValueSource outside a Test or TestSetup class. NeedsAll takes no field list, and a NeedsAll class declares no constructor. Each message names the annotation in your language's spelling, the member, the right place and what the annotation means. These refusals use TY1308.

InBackground listeners (methods that run when an event happens) need a language whose methods can be asynchronous. In Yon, these languages are JavaScript, TypeScript and Python. PHP, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua reject the annotation. They do not pretend to delay the call. Tac accepts InBackground in every service language that has listeners, because it only delays delivery on the page.

A StreamRoute method (ADR 0058; the old `@Stream` name is retired) returns its values one at a time, so the language needs a way to do that. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin, C#, F#, Dart and Ruby use their own generator syntax, Lua sends each value with `coroutine.yield`, and Go returns an `iter.Seq` (Go's range-over-function iterator). Java, Groovy and Rust refuse StreamRoute. They return the whole collection at once.

Both realms refuse a field that Tachyon fills, a Needs field or a NeedsAll field without a starting value, when it is declared nullable. Tachyon never leaves such a field null, so `label?: string` or `final String? path;` would only mislead the reader. The build stops with TY1331 and shows the non-null form to write instead. Both realms also refuse, with TY1332, a field that holds an injected class and does not use the language's variable case, such as `CartStore CartStore;` in Java or `cartStore` in Python.

Gateway exists only in Yon. A Tac service has no supervisor that could start another language for one call. So the annotation fails with TY1308 in every Tac language. Public, SignedIn, Allow and IdentityProvider exist only in Yon, because only a server can decide who may call a route. A Tac page cannot protect data: the server route must say who may call it.

sections.heading: Coming from Spring
sections.body:
Tachyon uses plain English names (ADR 0047). So a reader who learned English as a second language can guess what each one does. This table maps each Spring name to its Tachyon name. It also shows what Tachyon leaves out on purpose. An annotation keeps the meaning of its Spring or Lombok counterpart, and Tachyon adds its own checks at build time. When you write a Spring name that has a Tachyon name, the build stops with TY1308 and names the new annotation. `ty migrate fix --write` renames these annotations for you, and it moves files into the new role folders, such as stores/, setups/, converters/ and helpers/. Older Tachyon names fail the same way: Client is now HTTPClient, WebCall is GetRequest and the other request annotations, TachyonTest is Test, and Resource is Needs. Behaviors is not an annotation at all: it is a name that Tachyon generates for its own code.

| Spring | Tachyon | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@SpringBootApplication` | No equivalent, by design | There is no main class to annotate. The folders and files define the project. Controllers live in server/controllers, views come from client/pages, and client/manifest.json declares what a document loads. |
| `@RestController` | @RequestRoute | Yon supports only REST, so every controller is a REST controller. It lives in server/controllers. |
| `@RequestMapping` | @RequestRoute | On the class, it gives the base path, such as @RequestRoute("/orders"). The compiler refuses RequestMapping and names RequestRoute. |
| `@PermitAll`, `permitAll()` | @Public | Anyone may call the route. Tachyon refuses a route that says nothing, like Spring Security when it denies by default. |
| `isAuthenticated()`, `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` | @SignedIn | Any signed-in user may call the route. |
| `@RolesAllowed`, `@Secured`, `hasRole(...)` | @Allow(Role) | Only a user with one of these roles may call the route. Roles are types, such as @Allow(Admin), not strings. |
| `AuthenticationProvider` | @IdentityProvider | The one class that reads the request and returns the user and their roles. Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before the method runs. |
| `@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping` | @GetRoute, @PostRoute, @PutRoute, @PatchRoute, @DeleteRoute | The method answers that verb at the class path plus its own path. Its name must start with the verb, such as getOrder. The server answers OPTIONS and HEAD. |
| `@RequestParam` | @FromQuery | On a controller argument, it reads one value from the query string (the part of the URL after ?). On a client, the Spring name RequestParam stays. |
| `@PathVariable` | @FromPath | On a controller argument, it reads a path variable, such as {id}. Its declared type is checked. On a client, the Spring name PathVariable stays. |
| `@RequestHeader`, `@CookieValue` | @FromHeader, @FromCookie | On a controller argument, they read one request header or one cookie. The build refuses CookieValue and names FromCookie. On a client, RequestHeader stays and sends the argument as a header. |
| `@RequestBody`, `@RequestPart` | @FromBody | On a controller argument, it reads the request body as JSON. A method has at most one, and a GET route has none. The build refuses RequestPart and names FromBody. On a client, RequestBody stays and sends the argument as the body. |
| `@HttpExchange`, `@GetExchange`, `@PostExchange`, `@PutExchange`, `@PatchExchange`, `@DeleteExchange` | @HTTPClient, @GetRequest, @PostRequest, @PutRequest, @PatchRequest, @DeleteRequest | A client is a contract with no implementation, like an HTTP service interface, in the realm's remotes folder. Tachyon writes the client from the Setup with the same stem. A method body, a field or a constructor fails the build with TY1308. |
| `@Autowired`, `@Inject`, `@Resource` | @Needs | Goes on a field that is not static and has no starting value. The provider comes from the field's declared type, or from its lowerCamel name in JavaScript. Only field injection exists. There is no constructor or setter form, except that an F# class takes its providers as primary constructor parameters. The field is never null, so the build refuses a nullable Needs field with TY1331. |
| `@RequiredArgsConstructor` (Lombok) | @NeedsAll | Every field without a starting value is required, as with Lombok. A field that holds a provider is injected, and every other required field comes from the component's props in Tac. NeedsAll takes no field list, and the class writes no constructor, because Tachyon writes it. |
| `@Scope` | @Lifetime | Yon takes one string: singleton, request or transient (Spring's prototype). Tac takes a literal object: {"value":"singleton"}, {"value":"prototype"} for one service per component, or {"value":"application"} for one service per app in a native macOS, Linux or Windows Rust app. |
| `@Qualifier` | @Named | Gives the provider's name directly, next to @Needs, when the field itself does not select one. If a name matches no provider in the entry scope, the build fails. |
| `@Service` | @Service | The same role, in the shared services folder of the realm. |
| `@Repository` | @Store | A Spring Data repository interface: a contract with no implementation that names its Entity. Each method is a derived query (a query built from the method name) or a Query, with size limits, and Tachyon writes it. Needs injects the store. |
| `CrudRepository<T, ID>` | Repository<Entity, Id> | The base of a Store: extending it gives `findById`, `findAll` (one page), `save` and `deleteById` without declaring them. Derived `deleteBy` methods remove every matching record and answer the count. |
| `@Component` | @Helper | A class that services use for part of their work. It lives in client/helpers or server/helpers, and its name ends with Helper. The name is not Component, because client/components holds views. A class with only static methods is a utility in utils instead. |
| `@Configuration` | @Setup | The same. It is the type that holds the configuration rules. It is a singleton too: Tachyon runs its configure method once per page in Tac and once per server process in Yon, and every client, store and service context built from it shares the same adapters. Each case of a test unit still starts with a fresh Setup, as if every test had `@DirtiesContext`. |
| `@Value` | @Setting | Puts one property into a field, with the ${name:default} syntax. |
| `@ConfigurationProperties` | @Settings | Binds the properties that share a prefix, such as {"prefix":"YON_CATALOG_"}, to the fields of a Setup or a Settings model in models/. Every key under the prefix must be a field. Tac reads only public TAC_ values. |
| `@Profile` | @WhenProfile | Uses the Setup only when one of the named profiles is on. |
| `@ConditionalOnProperty` | @WhenSetting | Uses the Setup only when a setting has a value. It keeps Spring's keys: name, havingValue and matchIfMissing. |
| `@PostConstruct`, `@PreDestroy` | @OnStart, @OnStop | The method runs once when the object starts or stops. A method has at most one of these hooks. |
| `@EventListener` | @OnEvent | The listener takes one model parameter, and that model's type is the event. Spring's list of event classes is not kept: write one method for each model. The options are condition, id and replay. A returned model is published as a new event. |
| `@Async` on a listener | @InBackground | Only on an OnEvent listener. The publisher does not wait. Yon accepts it in JavaScript, TypeScript and Python; Tac accepts it in every service language that has listeners. |
| `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, `@CacheEvict` | @Cached, @UpdateCache, @ClearCache | Cached keeps a method's answer for the same arguments. UpdateCache and ClearCache name the Cached method, such as {"method":"find"}, and run only after the method succeeds. A method has only one of the three. |
| `@CacheConfig` | @CacheSettings | Names the cache that the class's Cached methods use, and also sets its limits: ttlMs, maxBytes and maxEntries. Cached needs CacheSettings on its class. |
| `@PageableDefault` | @PageDefaults | Goes on the page parameter and gives the page size and sort order when the caller leaves them out. |
| `@Validated`, `@Valid` | @Checked, @Check | Checked marks the model in models/ whose fields are checked. Check goes on the method parameter and names that model. A check in Tac only helps the user; Yon must check the same data again. |
| `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Min`, `@Max` | @Required, @NotEmpty, @Length, @Min, @Max | Field checks on a Checked model. Length takes {"min","max"}. |
| `@Bean` | The configure hook | A Setup gives named adapters from its configure method: caches, http, entities and the authorization hooks. There is no general bean container to add beans to. |
| `@Entity` | @Entity | Declares the adapter and the identifier that a Store uses. |
| `@Table` | @Table | The same. It names the table that an entity maps to. |
| `@Column` | Not supported | The field names of an entity are its column names. There is no way to rename a column. |
| `@Id` | @Id | Marks the identifier field. It must be the same field that @Entity declares. The compiler refuses a mismatch. |
| `@Mapper`, `@Mapping` (MapStruct) | @Converter, @Convert | This is not part of Spring Framework, but Spring applications often use this mapper. @Converter is the role, in converters/<Name>Converter, and it is a contract like a MapStruct interface: a method body fails the build with TY1308. Like a mapper bean, it needs no context, and a service or controller asks for it with @Needs. @Convert is the whole method. It is a fixed plan of fields, made of source paths with dots and constants, and it reads one JSON argument of limited size. There is no expression language, no `qualifiedByName` and no generated implementation class. The compiler writes the body itself. |
| `@Transactional` | @AllOrNothing | Goes on a service method and names the entity adapter that answers begin, commit and rollback. A store that the service injects joins the open transaction, like propagation REQUIRED. Every Store command inside the method is part of the transaction. There are no propagation modes and no savepoints. An inner one joins the open transaction. |
| `@TransactionalEventListener` | Not implemented | In the compiled languages, the event dispatcher and the behavior context share no handle (no shared reference). So a step that runs after the commit could work in only some Yon languages. Instead, publish the event after the transactional method returns. |
| `RemoteApplicationEvent` (Spring Cloud Bus) | `@Topic` on the model | A Topic model's events are saved in the topic log and reach the OnEvent listeners in the other Yon languages and in open pages, at most once. See Topics. |
| `@JsonComponent, @JsonMixin` | Not supported | The framework itself copies every value that crosses a boundary into JSON of limited size. An application serializer does not do this. There is no serializer registry to extend. |
| `@Lazy` | Already the behaviour | Tachyon creates a managed provider only when something asks for it. So the annotation would have nothing to turn on. |
| `@Retryable` | @Retry | The resilience annotation from Spring Framework 7, with millisecond literals instead of a TimeUnit: maxRetries, delayMs, multiplier, maxDelayMs and jitterMs. Tachyon never retries a framework refusal. |
| `@ConcurrencyLimit` | @MaxAtOnce | The same two policies, block and reject. A blocked caller waits only until its operation deadline. PHP accepts only reject. |
| `@Description` | @Description | One literal line of limited length that goes into the registration for tools to read. It goes on a class that already declares a behavior. |
| `@SpringBootTest` | @Test | A test unit is an entry. server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> puts together the role files of its realm. The annotation names the Setup that its context comes from. Nothing is found automatically, so you name the Setup. |
| `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@WebFluxTest`, `@JsonTest`, `@RestClientTest` | @Test | There is no shared container to divide into slices (smaller partial contexts). Each call owns its own set of instances, and you always select a Setup yourself. One annotation covers everything that the slices divided. |
| `@ParameterizedTest` with `@ValueSource` | @ValueSource | The test case lists its inputs; Tachyon runs one case for each input and passes it as the one argument. The case is found by its `test` name, so no `@ParameterizedTest` is needed. |
| `Assertions.assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertThrows` | `Assert.equals`, `Assert.isTrue`, `Assert.throws` | The same checks with the same failure text. Python, Rust and Ruby write `is_true`; Rust writes `Assert::equals` and PHP `Assert::equals`; Go writes `Assert.Equals`; Java and Groovy write `Assert.throwsError`, because `throws` is a reserved word there. |
| `@MockBean`, `@MockitoBean` | @Fake | A field that the test assigns. Any role that injects it receives it. There is no bean to replace, because the generated constructor already takes the classes that the role needs. |
| `@SpyBean`, `@MockitoSpyBean` | Refused, with the alternative named | There is no bean to wrap. Write Fake and assign the stub (a simple replacement) that the test needs. |
| `@AutoConfigureMockMvc` | Refused, with the alternative named | Call the controller's route method directly. There is no MockMvc. |
| `@TestConfiguration` | @TestSetup | A configuration only for tests, in tests/<Name>TestSetup.<ext>, selected by the sibling unit. |
| `@TestPropertySource` | @TestSettings | At most 64 literal properties of limited size. Each one must be in the realm's own namespace, so a Tac unit cannot reach yon.*. |
| `@ActiveProfiles` | @UseProfiles | Profiles for the unit's context, with the same limits as @WhenProfile. |
| `@DirtiesContext` | @FreshStart | Closes the context between cases. |
| `@Sql` | Seed through the entity adapter | Tachyon never creates or updates a database schema by itself, so there is no script step to attach to. The name is too common to refuse, so the compiler ignores it. |
| `@BeforeEach`, `@Disabled` (JUnit) | A naming convention | These belong to your own test runner, and other libraries may use the same names. So the compiler ignores them. In a @Test unit, a case is an instance method whose name begins with test. JUnit puts its own `@Test` on each case method. Tachyon's @Test marks the test class, so it never goes on a method. A controller route method gets its job from its route annotation, and its name starts with its verb. ty test runs the cases. |
| `@CrossOrigin` | Not supported | Responses carry a fixed set of security headers. You cannot set a cross-origin policy for each endpoint. |
| `@ControllerAdvice`, `@RestControllerAdvice` | @ErrorHandler | A class in server/controllers/<Name>ErrorHandler. Every controller of the same language uses it. The compiler refuses the Spring names and names @ErrorHandler. |
| `@ExceptionHandler` | @HandlesError | Goes on an instance method of an @ErrorHandler class and takes no argument. The declared type of the first parameter is the handled error, like Spring's form without an argument. @ResponseStatus sets its status. An unmatched error still becomes a fixed error response with a correlation identifier (an ID that links the response to the server logs). Internal error details never cross the HTTP boundary. |
| `@EnableAsync` | Not needed | @InBackground marks the listener itself, in the languages whose methods can be asynchronous. |
| `@Scheduled` | @Schedule | Goes on a worker under server/workers, with fixedDelaySeconds and initialDelaySeconds instead of cron and TimeUnit. The .tachyonrc workers object still works. A source uses one or the other. |
| `@EnableScheduling` | Not needed | A worker under server/workers that has a cadence is scheduled. There is no switch to turn the feature on. |

Most differences have one shared cause. Tachyon keeps each annotation small and checks it at compile time. Every annotation above that Tachyon accepts appears earlier on this page, with an example in each language that accepts it.

Members without this: as in a Spring service, Java, Kotlin, C#, Groovy and Dart can read a class field by its name. Swift methods can use the field name too. Keep the receiver when a parameter or local shadows the member; Swift captured closures keep self., and Dart initializing formals keep this. F# private values may use let bindings, while members retain their explicit self identifier. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, PHP and Lua retain the receivers their language requires. TY1362 is an optional suggestion, off by default, enabled per realm with tac.implicitmembers.suggest or implicitmembers.suggest.

routing-annotations.title: Routing glossary
routing-annotations.summary: Routes answer incoming requests. Clients send outgoing requests. These names explain where paths and argument values come from. Access annotations say who may call a route.

sections.heading: Controller paths
sections.body: RequestRoute marks a controller and sets its base path. Put the class in server/controllers/NameController.ext. GetRoute answers GET requests. PostRoute answers POST requests. PutRoute answers PUT requests. PatchRoute answers PATCH requests. DeleteRoute answers DELETE requests. StreamRoute answers GET requests with a stream of server-sent events: the method yields each message, and StreamRequest on a client receives them. Each method path follows the class path. Start the method name with its verb: getItem, GetItem or get_item, and streamTicks, StreamTicks or stream_ticks for StreamRoute. ResponseStatus sets a successful response status, such as 201. Public, SignedIn and Allow(Role) say who may call a route: anyone, any signed-in user, or only users with one of these roles. Write one on the class or on the method; the method wins, and a route without one stops the build. IdentityProvider marks the one class that says who is signed in.

sections.heading: Incoming values
sections.body: FromPath reads a path value, such as {id}. FromQuery reads the query string after ?. FromBody reads the JSON request body. FromHeader reads a request header. FromCookie reads a cookie. A marker may name the value, such as FromQuery("page_size"); without a name it uses the parameter name. Each parameter has one marker at most. A method has at most one FromBody parameter, because a request has one body, and a GetRoute method has none, because a GET request has no body; the build refuses both. Python writes the marker inside the type, such as `id: Annotated[int, from_path]`. The identify method of the IdentityProvider class may read a header or a cookie with FromHeader or FromCookie too. One parameter without a marker receives the request in the language's own type, such as a Fetch Request, urllib.request.Request, HttpExchange, HttpRequestMessage, http::Request, a shelf Request or *http.Request; PHP reads $_SERVER, $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE and php://input instead. Parameter types validate these values before the method runs. Model return types validate the response. OPTIONS publishes the generated schema. HEAD uses the GET route.

sections.heading: Error handlers
sections.body: ErrorHandler marks a class that answers typed errors for every controller of its language. Put it in server/controllers/NameErrorHandler.ext. HandlesError marks one of its instance methods and takes no argument. The declared type of the first parameter is the error that the method handles. JavaScript declares that type with JSDoc, such as @param {OrderNotFound} error. An optional second parameter receives the request in the language's own type, such as a Fetch Request or HttpExchange. PHP handlers take no second parameter and read the superglobals. ResponseStatus on that method sets an error status from 400 to 599; the default is 500. An error type is a normal error class or type in server/errors/Type.ext, with no annotation. The nearest type wins, so a subclass handler runs before a base class handler. Two methods that handle the same error type are refused, also when they are in different handler classes. An error that no method handles keeps the fixed 500 answer, and so does an error that a handler throws itself: handling never runs again on its own error. OPTIONS and /api.json list the error types of each route with their status and answer shape. Go matches with errors.As. Rust matches the error type of the controller method's Result. Spring's ControllerAdvice and ExceptionHandler and NestJS's ExceptionFilter and UseFilters are refused; use ErrorHandler and HandlesError. See [error handlers](/docs/error-handlers) for an example in every Yon language.

sections.heading: Outgoing requests
sections.body: HTTPClient marks a client contract (a declaration with no implementation, like a Spring @HttpExchange interface) and optionally sets its base path. GetRequest sends GET. PostRequest sends POST. PutRequest sends PUT. PatchRequest sends PATCH. DeleteRequest sends DELETE. StreamRequest keeps a stream of server-sent events open, the partner of StreamRoute: its one parameter is the message model, and Tachyon passes each message to the method and publishes it as that model's event. Each method path follows the class path. PathVariable fills a path value, such as {id}. RequestParam adds a query value after ?. RequestBody sends the JSON body; a method has at most one RequestBody parameter. RequestHeader adds a request header. A client has no implementation: each method is a signature, written in the contract form of its language (an interface, trait, protocol or Protocol class; an empty-bodied class in JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby), and Tachyon builds the request. A body stops the build with TY1308. StreamRequest and SocketRequest work on JavaScript, TypeScript and Go page clients, because the JavaScript of the browser holds the connection: for a Go client, the page holds it for the Go service that keeps the client in a field. Each message is also published as a typed event, so a page service in another language receives it with OnEvent. A Go socket client gets `Send(message any) error`. Other languages and Yon code refuse both markers with TY1308. Browser JavaScript and TypeScript, and compiled Dart, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java and C++ page clients, and Ruby page clients, use Tachyon's owner-bound browser transport. Lua and Python page clients refuse HTTPClient with TY1308. A URL with a host must name a host in tac.outgoing.hosts (page code) or outgoing.hosts in server/application.json (Yon code). Tachyon refuses other hosts when it builds (TY1326) and when it runs.

sections.heading: A typed path in every Yon language
sections.body: Each controller answers GET /items/42. The id argument is a number. GET /items/abc fails validation before the method runs.

sections.heading: Migrating old names
sections.body: Run ty migrate fix --write after reviewing your changes. Controller becomes RequestRoute. Client, WebCall and the Exchange names are retired. Use HTTPClient and the Request method annotations. RequestMapping and RestController become RequestRoute. CookieValue becomes FromCookie, and RequestPart becomes FromBody. Resource is retired: write Needs on a field whose name says which object it receives (ADR 0038). Behaviors is a name that Tachyon generates for its own code, not an annotation, so @Behaviors stops the build. Each old name stops the build with TY1308, and the message names the new one. GetMapping becomes GetRoute; the other verb mappings change the same way. GetRoute with Stream becomes StreamRoute, and a get method name starts with stream. Move Yon controllers into server/controllers/. Remove yon.* route markers and OPTIONS.schema.json after migrating their behavior. YonRequest and YonResponse are removed: ty migrate fix --write removes an unused YonRequest parameter and lists the rest, with the native request and response of each language (ADR 0062).

error-codes.title: Error codes
error-codes.summary: Every error from `ty` has a stable code, such as `TY1310`. The code stays the same when the message text changes, so you can search for it. This page lists every code, and the codes that a running page can get.

sections.heading: How to read an error
sections.body:
The first line of an error has a level, a code in square brackets, and a message, such as `error[TY1310]: ...`. The level is error, warning or information. An error stops the command. A warning or an information does not.

A line that starts with `-->` names the file and the place in the file. A line that starts with `help:` tells you how to fix the problem. The option `--diagnostic-format json` prints the same errors as JSON, for tools and CI (continuous integration).

sections.heading: Every code
sections.body:
Codes that start with `TY1` come from `ty` before your app runs. Codes that start with `TY2` come from the server or from the runtime of a language. Some codes cover several problems; the message says which one. The last column names the guide that explains the code, as topic / section, or a feature page.

Finding the project and its routes (`TY1001` to `TY1010`):

| Code | What it means | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TY1001` | `ty` cannot open the project folder, or a command got a wrong `--target`: a name that is not `web`, `macos`, `windows`, `linux`, `android`, `ios` or `all`, more than one target where the command takes one, or `web` where the command needs a native target. The removed `--render-mode` option and `TAC_RENDER_MODE` variable also stop here. | Targets / Targets |
| `TY1002` | The build found no page, no controller and no component in `tac.elements`. Add a `client/pages/tac.html` view, a controller in `server/controllers/`, or an exported element. | Components in other apps / Export a component |
| `TY1003` | Two views claim the same URL, or two controller methods answer the same HTTP method and path. Keep one view for each URL and one method for each route. | Pages and URLs / Folders become URLs; Controllers / Route rules |
| `TY1004` | A project file or folder is a symbolic link, or a source path leads out of its folder. Replace the link with a real file or folder. | Project folders and roles / Where each file goes |
| `TY1005` | A page folder name is not a valid part of a URL. Use lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens inside the name. A source path that is not valid Unicode also stops here. | Pages and URLs / Folders become URLs |
| `TY1006` | A dynamic page folder, such as `_id`, has a name that is not lowercase letters, digits and underscores, or one URL uses the same dynamic name twice. | Pages and URLs / Folders become URLs |
| `TY1008` | The project has a `yon.html` file. Yon answers with data, and it never renders HTML; return HTML with `Content-Type: text/html` from a controller instead. It also stops a `tac.*` file beside a view with an extension that Tachyon does not read. | Models and JSON answers / How return values become responses |
| `TY1009` | A compiler for a service failed, and the message shows its output. For a Dart service it is `dart compile wasm` from the Dart SDK 3.13 or newer on `PATH`. For a TypeScript file it is the TypeScript compiler, version 6 or newer, as a project dependency or on `PATH`. | WebAssembly compilers per language / Which compiler each language uses |
| `TY1010` | A native app has more than 128 native services. | Rust, Go and C# in the browser / Services are compiled in |

Writing the build output (`TY1201` and `TY1202`):

| Code | What it means | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TY1201` | `ty` cannot write the build output: the output folder has no parent that it can write, a file cannot be published, `client/manifest.json` is not a regular file of at most 1 MiB, or `ty api freeze` cannot write `server/api-baseline.json`. Check the folder permissions, and that no other program holds the output. | Build and deploy / Build and deploy |
| `TY1202` | The output folder is a symbolic link, passes through one, is not a folder, or is in a place that is not safe. Use a normal folder outside `client/`, `server/` and `.git/`. | Build and deploy / Build and deploy |
